question: What is Pure Land Buddhism / Amidism?
answer:
Pure Land Buddhism, sometimes called Amidism in older Western writing, is a major stream of Mahayana Buddhism centered on trust in Amitabha Buddha and the hope of rebirth in his Pure Land.

Amitabha (Amida in Japanese, Amituofo in Chinese) is honored as a Buddha of infinite light and life. According to the Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life, he vowed that those who hear his name and entrust themselves to him will be born in Sukhavati, the Western Pure Land, a realm free from ordinary suffering where the path to enlightenment is said to be sure. The central practice is calling on his name: nianfo in Chinese, nembutsu in Japanese, often with the words "Namo Amituofo" or "Namu Amida Butsu." The tradition looks mainly to three Pure Land sutras.

It is not all of one piece. Chinese Pure Land devotion has often been joined with moral effort, meditation, and other practices. In Japan, Honen and especially Shinran stressed other-power (tariki): birth in the Pure Land rests on Amida's vow, not on the devotee's own merit. Shinran's Jodo Shinshu remains one of Japan's largest Buddhist movements. In either form, Amitabha is not the Creator. He is an enlightened Buddha, and the hope is escape from the cycle of rebirth, not reconciliation to the living God.

That longing for mercy beyond one's own effort, and for a place free from suffering, is deeply human, and it deserves respect. The Bible locates the answer elsewhere. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and sinners are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:23-24). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died as an atoning sacrifice and rose bodily. He alone is the mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5; John 14:6). Saving faith is not entrusting oneself to Amida for a better rebirth. It is trusting Christ for justification, received by grace and not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 4:5).

If you are weighing these paths, I invite you to read the Gospel of John, and to turn from sin and trust Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for sinners. Are you asking mainly for a description, or is something in this tradition drawing you personally?

question: What does the Bible say about despair?
answer:
The Bible treats despair as a real and crushing experience, not a mood to be denied, and it answers it with the nearness of God and a hope grounded in His character and in Christ’s resurrection.

Scripture does not hide the darkness. The psalmist speaks to his own soul, “Why are you downcast, O my soul? Why the unease within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise Him, my Savior and my God” (Psalm 42:11). Elijah, worn out and afraid, asked that he might die (1 Kings 19:4). Job cursed the day of his birth (Job 3:1). Psalm 88 ends without a tidy sunrise, with darkness still close. Even Paul wrote that he and his companions “despaired even of life” under a burden beyond their strength, “in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Despair can visit genuine believers. It is not, by itself, proof that God has cast you off.

It is also not given the last word. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18). In the ruins of Jerusalem, Jeremiah turned from what he felt to what he knew: “Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:22–23). That “loving devotion” is the Hebrew *hesed*, God’s steadfast covenant love, which does not fail when our feelings do. Paul could later say believers are “perplexed, but not in despair” (2 Corinthians 4:8), not because the pain had vanished, but because Christ had not been defeated. The bleakest cry in Scripture, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1), was taken up by Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:46), so that those who belong to Him would not be finally forsaken.

That is where Christian hope stands. We have all sinned and stand guilty before a holy God (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died as a substitute in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Justification is God’s gift, by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not something we earn by climbing out of the dark (Ephesians 2:8–9). The God of hope fills His people with joy and peace as they believe, so that they overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:13). If you do not yet know Him, the way through final despair is not trying harder. Turn from sin and trust Jesus, who died and rose for you.

If you are in this weight now, take one concrete step today. Read Psalm 42 or Lamentations 3 slowly, and speak honestly to God about what you feel, asking Him to fix your hope on Christ rather than on your circumstances. Then tell a pastor, an elder, or a mature believer what you are carrying, so you are not alone in it. The Word, prayer, and the fellowship of the church are means of grace the Spirit uses to steady weary saints.

If the darkness includes thoughts of harming yourself, seek immediate help from emergency services or someone who can be with you right now. I do not provide medical or psychiatric advice, and a local church, with qualified care where needed, is the right place for ongoing support.

If you want to say whether this comes from a passage you are reading or from a burden you are carrying, I will gladly stay with you in the Scriptures.

question: The Fruit of the Holy Spirit – What is patience?
answer:
Patience, one expression of the fruit of the Holy Spirit, is the God-given longsuffering that lets a Christian endure provocation and delay without bitterness or retaliation (Galatians 5:22-23).

The Greek word behind “patience” here is makrothumia, meaning a long temper rather than a short one. In a culture that often honored swift revenge, the apostles taught that this calm endurance is produced by the Holy Spirit as He carries forward the work of progressive sanctification, shaping believers into the likeness of Christ, who patiently bore our sins (1 Peter 2:23-24; Hebrews 12:3).

It is not stoic self-control achieved by willpower. It grows when we walk by the Spirit and refuse to gratify the flesh (Galatians 5:16). In daily life that may look like remaining quiet and prayerful when a coworker criticizes you unfairly, then answering with truth spoken in love rather than a sharp retort.

Choose one relationship this week where your temper runs short. Each morning read Colossians 3:12-13, ask the Lord for patience in that specific setting, and tell a mature believer your request so they can pray with you (James 5:16).

question: What does the Bible say about libel?
answer:
The Bible does not use the modern legal word “libel,” but it clearly forbids the sin at its heart: publishing or spreading a false report that damages a neighbor’s name.

That prohibition is the ninth commandment. “You shall not give false testimony against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16). The same moral law reaches written words as well as spoken ones, because the issue is false witness against a person, not the medium. Scripture says, “You shall not spread a false report” (Exodus 23:1), and “Do not go about spreading slander among your people” (Leviticus 19:16). A false witness is listed among the things the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16–19), and “a false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5).

In the New Testament this is not softened. Believers are told to put away falsehood and speak truth to one another (Ephesians 4:25), to let no corrupting talk come from the mouth (Ephesians 4:29), and to put off “slander” along with malice (Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8–9). James warns that the tongue can set a whole life on fire, and that we must not speak against one another (James 3:5–10; James 4:11). Jesus says we will give account for careless words (Matthew 12:36). Secret slander is no safer than a public accusation (Psalm 101:5).

This is a sin against God and against the neighbor. A person’s name is bound up with the dignity of being made in God’s image, and love of neighbor “does no harm” (Romans 13:10). Libel breaks truth, harms the innocent, and often sows discord. Even where a statement is not legally libel, Scripture still condemns gossip, rash accusation, and speech that tears down rather than builds up (Proverbs 11:13; Ephesians 4:29).

If you have written or passed on a false, damaging claim, the biblical path is repentance: confess it to God, tell the truth to the person you harmed, and retract it as publicly as you spread it, so far as you are able (Luke 19:8; Matthew 5:23–24). Christ was Himself the victim of false testimony, and He died and rose to forgive sinners, including sins of the tongue, for all who turn from sin and trust Him (Matthew 26:59–60; 1 John 1:9).

If you have been libeled, do not answer evil with evil. Entrust vindication to the Lord, refuse bitterness, and seek wise help from your pastors (Romans 12:17–21; 1 Peter 2:23). Where brothers and sisters are involved, Jesus’ path is to go to the person directly before widening the circle (Matthew 18:15–17). Civil authorities exist to restrain wrongdoing (Romans 13:1–4), yet believers should be slow to sue one another and should prefer reconciliation where that is possible (1 Corinthians 6:1–8). I am not able to give legal advice; a qualified attorney can speak to the law where you live.

A concrete step: before you publish, post, or forward any damaging claim, stop and test it. Is it true? Is it necessary? Have you checked it with those who know? If it concerns a fellow believer, have you gone to that person first? Ask the Lord to set a guard over your mouth and your keyboard (Psalm 141:3), and let an elder or a mature believer help you keep that watch.

question: How can I show appreciation to my pastor?
answer:
One meaningful way to show appreciation to your pastor is to honor him highly in love for his labor, both by praying for him and by expressing specific thanks that makes his shepherding a joy.

Scripture calls the church to acknowledge those who work hard among you and to regard them very highly in love because of their work (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). Elders who lead well, especially in preaching and teaching, are worthy of double honor, a term that includes sincere respect and practical care (1 Timothy 5:17). Because your pastor watches over souls and must give an account, helping his work be a joy rather than a burden is itself an act of love toward him and toward Christ (Hebrews 13:17).

Pray for him by name this week, asking God to strengthen his preaching of the gospel, guard his own soul, bless his family, and sustain him against discouragement. A concrete step is to write a short note that names one specific sermon, visit, or word of counsel through which God helped you trust Christ more deeply, then give it to him personally or by mail. You can also share good things with the one who teaches you, whether through the church’s ordinary support, a simple meal, or protecting his time for rest (Galatians 6:6). Faithful presence in worship and speaking well of him among the congregation further refresh a shepherd and honor the Lord who gives pastors to equip His people (Ephesians 4:11-12).

What particular blessing from your pastor’s ministry stands out to you right now?

question: Can man live without God? Why do many people who reject God seem to live happy and fulfilled lives?
answer:
Many people who reject God do enjoy real happiness, love, success, and a sense of purpose in this life, and it is understandable to ask whether God is truly necessary if life can feel complete without Him. The Bible teaches that no one lives independently of God. He gives life, breath, and everything else to all people, so that in Him we live and move and have our being, whether we acknowledge Him or not (Acts 17:25; Acts 17:28). Physical life continues by His power, yet true and eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent (John 17:3). Apart from Christ, a person may exist and even thrive for a season while remaining spiritually dead in sin and separated from the life of God (Ephesians 2:1; Ephesians 2:12).

The happiness you notice comes largely from God’s common grace. He causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous (Matthew 5:45). Every good and perfect gift is from above (James 1:17). These gifts can produce genuine joy and accomplishment now, yet they do not remove our need to be reconciled to a holy God or secure a good end.

This tension troubled the psalmist Asaph. He envied those who seemed to prosper without God until he considered their final destiny (Psalm 73:3; Psalm 73:16–17). Solomon tested pleasure, wealth, and achievement to the full and still called life apart from God vanity, concluding that the whole duty of man is to fear God and keep His commandments (Ecclesiastes 2:10–11; Ecclesiastes 12:13). Apparent fulfillment can be real for a time and still leave a person unprepared to stand before God.

All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). People can enjoy God’s world while suppressing the truth about Him (Romans 1:18–21). Their peace does not prove innocence. The wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23).

God is holy, and His wrath against sin is real, yet He is also merciful and loving. He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. Jesus lived a perfect life, died on the cross as a penal substitute bearing the penalty sinners deserve, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He is now exalted as Lord (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Romans 5:8). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by how fulfilled they feel or by their own works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Jesus came that we might have life and have it abundantly, and fullness of joy is found in God’s presence (John 10:10; Psalm 16:11).

If you have been living as though God is optional, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and true life. A practical next step is to read Psalm 73 and John 17:3 this week, asking whether the good things you see are pointing you to the Giver or taking His place. What has prompted this question for you?

question: Was Joseph’s governing in Egypt an example of socialism?
answer:
Joseph’s governing in Egypt was not an example of socialism.

Socialism, in its usual modern sense, is an economic order in which the state or the community owns or tightly controls the means of production and distribution, typically aiming at greater equality and the reduction of private property. Genesis shows something else. By God’s wisdom Joseph told Pharaoh to store one-fifth of the harvest through seven years of plenty (Genesis 41:34–36). In the famine he sold grain first for money, then for livestock, and finally the people sold their land and themselves to Pharaoh for food and seed (Genesis 47:13–26). They became Pharaoh’s servants and thereafter gave him one-fifth of the produce while keeping four-fifths; the priests’ land was exempt (Genesis 47:22, 24–26). The people themselves said Joseph had saved their lives (Genesis 47:25).

That was crisis administration under an ancient absolute monarch, not a socialist program. It centralized grain and, in the end, land under the crown and produced lasting service to Pharaoh, yet it lacked any socialist ideology, any claim of worker ownership, or any design to erase social ranks. Scripture presents the episode as God’s providence to preserve life and the covenant family (Genesis 45:5–8; Genesis 50:20), not as a divine blueprint for political economy. Israel’s later laws guarded family land and provided for the poor in a different way (Leviticus 25).

How Christians should order modern economies is a non-essential matter on which faithful believers may disagree in Christian liberty (Romans 14:1–4). What Scripture does require is diligent work, honest stewardship, and generous care for the needy (Ephesians 4:28; Proverbs 19:17). This week read Genesis 47 slowly beside Leviticus 25, and ask the Lord to make you a faithful steward in the calling He has given you.

question: What is the meaning of “length of days” in Proverbs 3:16?
answer:
“Length of days” means long life, a prolonged span of years. In Proverbs 3:16, wisdom is pictured with long life in her right hand, so the phrase says that the way of wisdom is the path God ordinarily blesses with longevity.

The Hebrew behind the older wording is *orek yamim*, “length of days.” The Berean Standard Bible renders the line, “Long life is in her right hand; in her left hand are riches and honor” (Proverbs 3:16). In the ancient world the right hand was the place of favor and strength, so long life is set forward as a chief gift of wisdom, alongside riches and honor. The same hope runs through the chapter: keeping the father’s teaching adds years and peace (Proverbs 3:1–2), and “her ways are pleasant, and all her paths are peace” (Proverbs 3:17). Elsewhere, the fear of the LORD is what prolongs life (Proverbs 9:11; Proverbs 10:27). That language echoes the covenant, where loving and clinging to the LORD is called your life and the length of your days (Deuteronomy 30:20).

Two cautions keep the verse from being twisted into a formula. Proverbs gives proverbial wisdom, the general pattern of God’s moral order, not a guarantee that every wise person reaches old age and every fool dies young. Scripture itself knows the righteous who suffer and the wicked who prosper for a season (Psalm 73:3–17; Ecclesiastes 7:15). And the deepest life wisdom offers is not merely more birthdays. Christ is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and eternal life, knowing the Father and the Son, is the greater gift He gives (John 17:3). Earthly length of days is a real kindness. Life in the Son is life in its fullness (John 10:10).

This week, read Proverbs 3:13–18 slowly and ask the Lord to make you love wisdom more than shortcuts. Then take one concrete step of obedience you have been delaying, and treat that step as part of walking in the fear of the LORD.

question: What does it mean that our citizenship is in heaven?
answer:
Our citizenship in heaven means that those who belong to Jesus Christ have their true home, identity, and highest allegiance in God's kingdom, not in the nations and loyalties of this present age.

Paul teaches this to the church in Philippi: our citizenship is in heaven, and from there we eagerly await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body (Philippians 3:20-21). Philippi was a Roman colony, so its people knew what it meant to live far from the capital while still belonging to it. Their civic identity, rights, and loyalty were defined by Rome. Paul takes that familiar picture, using the Greek word *politeuma* for a people's governing allegiance, and redirects it. Believers live in earthly cities, yet heaven is their governing city because the risen Christ reigns there.

This is not a call to abandon work, family, or neighbor. It is a call to refuse earthly things as our final treasure. Paul sets citizens of heaven against those whose minds are fixed on earthly things and whose end is destruction (Philippians 3:19). The Christian hope is personal and bodily. Christ will return, and the same power by which He subdues all things will make His people like Him. That hope rests on His historical death, burial, and resurrection, and it is received by grace through faith, not earned as a wage.

Scripture says the same elsewhere. In Christ we are no longer strangers and aliens, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household (Ephesians 2:19). We live as sojourners and exiles, turning from sinful desires that war against the soul (1 Peter 2:11). The faithful before us confessed that they were seeking a better country, a heavenly one, which God has prepared (Hebrews 11:13-16). And because we have been raised with Christ, we set our minds on things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3:1-2).

So heavenly citizenship is both a present reality and a future hope, what Christians call the already and not yet of the kingdom. If you trust Christ, you already belong to Him, and you still wait for the day He makes all things new. That frees you to love your earthly country without worshiping it, to suffer without despair, and to obey Christ when the surrounding culture pulls the other way.

This week, name one loyalty that has been competing with Christ, whether success, politics, comfort, or the fear of people. Each morning, read Philippians 3:17-21, then pray in your own words that the Lord would make your choices fit a citizen of heaven. If you tell me what stirred this question, I can help you press this hope into that particular struggle.

question: Did Jesus mean that we should never refer to our earthly father as “father” (Matthew 23:9)?
answer:
No, Jesus did not mean that we must never call our earthly fathers “father.” In Matthew 23:9 He was rebuking religious leaders who craved honorific titles that exalted them and obscured the unique fatherhood of God.

In Matthew 23 Jesus confronts the scribes and Pharisees for loving places of honor, public greetings, and being called “Rabbi” (Matthew 23:5–7). His words about “father” and “instructor” target that spirit of self-promotion, not ordinary family speech or rightful respect. The same Gospel shows Jesus upholding the command to honor father and mother and condemning traditions that emptied it of force (Matthew 15:4–6). Elsewhere Scripture freely uses the language of earthly fatherhood and requires us to honor it: “Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12); “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. ‘Honor your father and mother’” (Ephesians 6:1–2). Paul even speaks of his gospel ministry in fatherly terms without contradicting Christ: “For though you may have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

The theological point is the absolute fatherhood of God. He alone is the source of all life and authority, so no human title may rival Him (Matthew 23:9; Ephesians 3:14–15). Calling your dad “father” obeys God’s command; it does not compete with the Father in heaven. A concrete step is to speak to your earthly father (or about him) with the respect Scripture requires, and in the same breath thank God that your deepest security rests in the heavenly Father who never fails.

question: What is wrong with the allegorical interpretation method?
answer:
The allegorical method goes wrong when it treats Scripture as a code of hidden meanings that can float free from what the author, carried by the Holy Spirit, actually said in grammar, history, and context. God spoke through real writers to real people, so the meaning of a text is the sense those words bear, not a private spiritual message we invent afterward (2 Peter 1:20-21).

Three problems follow from that.

First, the method is uncontrolled. Once the plain sense is set aside, almost any “deeper” reading can be claimed, and contradictory readings cannot be tested by the text itself. Scripture was given so that the sense could be heard and understood, not locked behind a special class of decoders (Nehemiah 8:8; Psalm 119:130). That clarity, often called the perspicuity of Scripture, assumes we can get at the author’s meaning.

Second, it can empty historical claims. Much of the Bible is narrative about what God did. If the exodus, the cross, or the resurrection is reduced to a symbol of an idea, the Gospel collapses, because the Gospel is news about events (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Jesus treated the Scriptures as speaking of real persons and acts, and he opened those same Scriptures as pointing to himself (Luke 24:27, 44). We find Christ where the text leads. We do not bypass the text to reach him.

Third, it confuses genre with license. Poetry, parable, prophecy, and apocalypse really do use figures, and the figurative sense is the meaning in those places. Typology is different again: God ordered real persons and events so that they foreshadowed greater realities, above all Christ. Paul’s use of “allegory” for Hagar and Sarah is an inspired reading of a historical story, not permission for us to allegorize at will (Galatians 4:21-31). We are not apostles, and we do not add meanings the Spirit did not put in the words.

Early and medieval teachers often reached for spiritual senses out of a real love for Christ in all of Scripture. The desire was understandable. The method still fails when reverence no longer lets the text govern the meaning, or when the literal sense is treated as an embarrassment to be escaped.

The faithful alternative is the grammatical-historical reading of Scripture: words in their grammar, literary context, historical setting, and place in the whole canon, then applied to life. That is how the Bible’s authority stays the authority, rather than the interpreter’s imagination.

A simple next step is this: before you ask what a passage means for you, write one sentence stating what the author was saying to the first audience, and check that sentence against the surrounding chapters. If a hard text still will not yield, bring it to your local church, where the Word is preached in context rather than in private symbols. If you have a passage where an allegorical reading and a historical reading seem to clash, we can walk through it together.

question: Is hell real? Is hell eternal?
answer:
Yes, hell is real, and Scripture teaches that its punishment is eternal.

Jesus warned of eternal punishment set in direct parallel with eternal life (Matthew 25:46), and He described a place of unquenchable fire where the worm does not die (Mark 9:43-48). John records that the lake of fire brings torment day and night forever and ever for the devil and for all whose names are not written in the book of life (Revelation 20:10; Revelation 20:15; Revelation 14:11). This is the just judgment of the holy God, whose wrath against sin is real.

You may wonder how a loving God could appoint eternal judgment, or whether such a sentence is fair. The Bible holds God’s perfect love and His perfect justice together without contradiction. Sin is rebellion against the infinitely holy God, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Yet God, rich in mercy, did not leave sinners without a Savior. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died on the cross as a penal substitute bearing the punishment sinners deserve, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Everyone who repents and trusts Him is justified, forgiven, and given eternal life instead of condemnation (John 3:16; John 5:24).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A practical next step is to read John 3 and Romans 5 this week, asking God to show you the truth of Christ’s saving work.

What questions does this raise for you about Jesus or about coming to know God?

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6)?
answer:
Isaiah 9:6 calls the promised Messiah the Prince of Peace, meaning he is the royal ruler who establishes God’s shalom: not a thin calm, but wholeness, reconciliation, and a kingdom of justice that will not end.

In Hebrew the title is sar shalom. Sar means prince or ruler, and shalom means peace in the full sense of completeness, harmony, and well-being. Isaiah spoke this word into a land sitting in darkness and threat (Isaiah 8:22–9:2). A child would be born and a son given, the government would rest on his shoulder, and of the increase of his government and of peace there would be no end (Isaiah 9:6–7). The child born is truly man, and the son given is the eternal Son, truly God. The Prince of Peace is not a gentle example only. He is the divine King.

That promise is fulfilled in Jesus Christ. Scripture is plain that we have sinned and stand at odds with a holy God (Romans 3:23; Romans 5:10). Peace with God is not achieved by calming our feelings or by moral effort. It is secured by penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty our sins deserved, shed his blood to reconcile us, and was raised bodily on the third day (Colossians 1:19–20; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Paul therefore says that, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). He also says Christ himself is our peace, tearing down the hostility that divided people from God and from one another (Ephesians 2:14–17).

This peace reaches further than a private feeling, and faithful Christians receive every layer of it without turning the timetable of the end into a test of fellowship.
- Peace with God now, by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Romans 5:1).
- Peace within, the rest Jesus gives his own, which guards the heart when we bring our anxieties to him (John 14:27; Philippians 4:6–7).
- Peace among his people, so those reconciled learn to keep the unity of the Spirit and to make peace (Matthew 5:9; Ephesians 4:3).
- Peace over the nations and the creation at his return, when his righteous reign is fully seen (Isaiah 9:7; Revelation 21:1–4).

Jesus also said he did not come to bring peace, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). That does not cancel Isaiah 9:6. He will not buy a false peace by compromising with sin or by leaving rebels comfortable in their rebellion. True peace comes only by surrender to his holy reign.

If you are weary, anxious, or aware of a breach with God, take this step today. Read Isaiah 9:6–7 with Romans 5:1 and Ephesians 2:14–17, and pray in your own words, asking him to show you where you are still trying to manufacture peace apart from Christ. If there is a broken relationship, take one humble step toward peace as someone who already belongs to the Prince of Peace.

You need a Savior because you have sinned against a holy God. Jesus died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Which part of this peace feels most distant to you right now: peace with God, peace in your own heart, or peace with someone else?

question: Should Muslims read the gospel of Barnabas as the true story of Jesus?
answer:
No. Muslims should not read the Gospel of Barnabas as the true story of Jesus. It is a late medieval writing, not an eyewitness account, and it contradicts the earliest records of his life, death, and resurrection.

It is understandable why some are drawn to it. If you have been taught that the New Testament was altered and that Jesus was only a prophet who was not crucified, a document that seems to say those things can feel like a welcome discovery. Christians believe, however, that the four Gospels were written in the first century by people close to the events, while the Gospel of Barnabas is known only from manuscripts centuries later and contains historical mistakes that place it long after Jesus and the apostles. It even denies that Jesus is the Messiah, which sets it against both the New Testament and claims made in the Quran. Early Christians never treated it as Scripture. The church received Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John because they faithfully report what the apostles preached.

Those Gospels present Jesus as truly God and truly man. "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us" (John 1:1, 14). He lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That death and resurrection are not optional details. They are how God reconciles guilty people to himself. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works or by following a later text that rewrites his story (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 14:6).

If you want the true story of Jesus, read the Gospel of John slowly, asking God to show you who Jesus really is. Turn from sin and trust in him who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What have you already heard about Jesus, and which part of his story feels hardest to accept?

question: What are the duties of an elder in the church?
answer:
An elder’s duties are to shepherd the flock, oversee the church, teach sound doctrine, guard the truth, and live as an example, all as an undershepherd of Jesus Christ, the Chief Shepherd.

In the New Testament these tasks belong to one office. The same men are called elders (presbyteros), overseers (episkopos), and shepherds or pastors (poimen). Paul told the elders of Ephesus that the Holy Spirit had made them overseers to care for the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood (Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28). Peter charged elders to shepherd the flock and exercise oversight, not by domineering, but by being examples (1 Peter 5:1-3).

They teach and protect sound doctrine. An elder must be able to teach, hold firmly to the faithful word, instruct in sound doctrine, and refute those who contradict it (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:9). Those who labor especially in preaching and teaching are worthy of double honor (1 Timothy 5:17). This is doctrinal guardianship, not private opinion.

They lead with pastoral oversight. Elders who rule well guide the church under Christ’s authority, and believers are called to submit to such leaders because they keep watch over souls and must give an account (1 Timothy 5:17; Hebrews 13:17). That rule is spiritual care, not harsh control.

They care for the whole flock, including the weak. Elders pray over the sick and anoint them in the Lord’s name (James 5:14). They watch both themselves and the church, because fierce wolves can arise and twist the truth (Acts 20:28-31).

They model a holy life. The qualifications show that the duty begins in character: above reproach, faithful in marriage, sober-minded, hospitable, not greedy, and managing his household well (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9). He leads by example, looking for the unfading crown when the Chief Shepherd appears (1 Peter 5:3-4).

How elder authority relates to the congregation is a secondary matter, not an essential of the faith, and faithful Christians differ here. Some hold an episcopal order, in which a bishop oversees more than one congregation, arguing that this preserves unity and orderly care as churches multiply. I hold, as one faithful option within historic Christianity, that a local church is best served by a plurality of elders who shepherd, teach, and oversee, while the congregation still affirms its leaders and shares in weighty decisions such as discipline, because the New Testament shows local elders caring for local flocks without a separate office set above them (Acts 14:23; Philippians 1:1).

This week, pray by name for your church’s elders, asking God to keep them faithful in the Word and gentle with His people, and read 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:5-9 so you can encourage them wisely and, if you aspire to the work, examine your own life before them in humility (1 Timothy 3:1).

question: Christian liberty — what does the Bible say?
answer:
Christian liberty is the freedom Christ gives His people: freedom from condemnation, freedom from sin’s ruling power, and freedom of conscience where Scripture neither commands nor forbids, always used in love and for God’s glory.

That freedom is purchased, not earned. In Galatia, some were pressing Gentile believers to add circumcision and Mosaic law-keeping as the basis of full acceptance with God. Paul answers that this is a return to slavery: it is for freedom that Christ has set us free, and believers must not submit again to that yoke (Galatians 5:1; Galatians 5:2–6). The word he uses, *eleutheria*, means the status of someone no longer owned by a master. In justification, God declares the sinner righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:28). There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, because the Spirit has set them free from the law of sin and death (Romans 8:1–2). If the Son sets you free, you are free indeed (John 8:36).

This is not permission to sin. Liberty is not a wide road to self-will. It is the open door out of the prison of guilt, so that a freed person may walk with his Redeemer. Paul says believers were called to freedom, yet must not use that freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but serve one another in love (Galatians 5:13). Peter says the same: live as free people, and do not use freedom as a cover for evil, but live as servants of God (1 Peter 2:16). In sanctification, we are freed from sin’s dominion so that we might obey from the heart (Romans 6:17–18). James even calls God’s Word “the law of liberty,” the Word that frees us to do what it says, not a ladder by which we climb into God’s favor (James 1:25; James 2:12).

So Christian liberty has clear boundaries. Christ has fulfilled the ceremonial requirements of the old covenant, and no one may bind you with food laws, festivals, or human rules as if those secured your standing with God (Colossians 2:16–17; Colossians 2:20–23). God’s moral will remains. Love for God and neighbor is still the path of a freed people (Galatians 5:14; Romans 13:8–10). What Scripture commands, obey. What Scripture forbids, refuse. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Romans 14:4; James 4:12).

Where Scripture is silent, conscience is free, and love governs the use of that freedom. These are often called *adiaphora*, things indifferent. Paul tells the church to welcome the one whose faith is weak, and not to quarrel over opinions (Romans 14:1). The one who eats must not despise the one who abstains, and the one who abstains must not judge the one who eats, for God has accepted him (Romans 14:3). At the same time, freedom must not become a stumbling block to the weak (1 Corinthians 8:9). All things may be lawful in such matters, but not all things are helpful or build others up (1 Corinthians 10:23). Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

How far to press these principles in later questions, such as food and drink, days, entertainment, customs, or schooling, is a non-essential. Faithful Christians may disagree because Scripture gives governing principles rather than a catalog of every later practice. Some stress the believer’s freedom and refuse to bind consciences with rules God has not given. Others stress voluntarily limiting freedom so that love, holiness, and a clear witness come first. Both concerns are biblical when they stay under the Word. Neither may be made a test of genuine faith. Romans 14 calls us to welcome one another and to keep such disputes from splitting the church (Romans 14:13; Romans 14:19; Romans 15:7).

A practical step: the next time a gray area arises, read Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8–10, and ask three questions. Is this commanded, forbidden, or left free? Would this choice honor Christ? Would it help or harm a brother or sister? Then bring it to your local elders rather than settling it by preference alone, and pray that the Spirit would keep your conscience tender to Scripture and generous toward others.

If a particular matter is weighing on your conscience, tell me what it is, and we can walk through it in light of these passages.

question: What does it mean to expose the works of darkness (Ephesians 5:11)?
answer:
Exposing the works of darkness means refusing fellowship with sinful deeds and instead bringing them into the light of God's truth so they are seen, rebuked, and turned from. In Ephesians 5:11 Paul commands believers, who were once darkness but are now light in the Lord, to have no fellowship with the fruitless deeds of darkness but rather to expose them (Ephesians 5:8; Ephesians 5:11).

The word translated "expose" carries the sense of convicting or reproving, the same idea used when the Holy Spirit convicts the world concerning sin (John 16:8) and when light makes hidden things visible (Ephesians 5:13). Darkness thrives on secrecy, and Paul notes that it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret (Ephesians 5:12). Exposure, then, is not gossip, crude storytelling, or public shaming for its own sake. It is truthful confrontation that unmasks sin so repentance and restoration can follow. This belongs to progressive sanctification, in which the Spirit uses the Word and the church to grow God's people in holiness.

This exposing happens in two ordinary ways. A life of goodness, righteousness, and truth stands in contrast to sin and thereby shows darkness for what it is (Ephesians 5:9; Ephesians 5:13-14; Philippians 2:15). Within the church, loving reproof begins privately and seeks the person's good, as Jesus teaches and as Paul urges when he says to restore a brother gently (Matthew 18:15-17; Galatians 6:1). Rightly practiced church discipline is one expression of this light-bearing love, not cruelty.

If you see a fellow believer drifting into a settled pattern of sin, pray for wisdom and humility, then speak to that person alone with Scripture and a desire for their restoration, remembering that you too were once in darkness and have been rescued by grace (Ephesians 2:1-5; Ephesians 5:8).

question: Why does Jesus say that “an evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign” (Matthew 12:39)?
answer:
Jesus calls that generation “evil and adulterous” because their demand for a sign came from hardened unbelief, not from a heart ready to receive Him.

The scribes and Pharisees had already watched Jesus heal and cast out demons, and they answered those works by charging that He did them by Beelzebul (Matthew 12:22-24). When they then asked for a sign, they were not starved for evidence. They were refusing the evidence in front of them (Matthew 12:38-39). In a parallel scene they are said to test Him by asking for a sign from heaven (Matthew 16:1). An evil heart can have light and still love darkness (John 3:19).

The word “adulterous” comes from the prophets. They charged Israel with spiritual adultery, breaking covenant with the Lord as a wife breaks faith with her husband (Jeremiah 3:8-9; Hosea 2:2). Jesus lays that same charge on a generation that had the Messiah among them and still would not be faithful to God. Their sign-seeking looked religious, but it was a way of delaying repentance.

Jesus does not treat every desire for confirmation as sin. God has given signs to accredit His word, and the Gospel accounts were written so that readers might believe that Jesus is the Christ (John 20:30-31). The sin is demanding another sign while rejecting the One already sent. So He promises no sign except the sign of the prophet Jonah (Matthew 12:39). As Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, the Son of Man would be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:40). His death, burial, and bodily resurrection are the sign that settles who He is.

That is why the comparisons cut so deep. The men of Nineveh repented at Jonah’s preaching, and the Queen of the South traveled far to hear Solomon’s wisdom, yet this generation had One greater than Jonah and greater than Solomon and would not turn (Matthew 12:41-42). More light did not produce faith. It exposed a heart set against God.

If this saying has stirred a question in you about what it takes to trust Christ, do not wait for a private wonder to replace the sign He already gave. This week, read one Gospel account of His cross and empty tomb, and pray honestly about whatever is holding you back. We have all sinned against a holy God, and none of us can save ourselves. Jesus died for sinners and rose bodily on the third day. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life.

What drew you to this word of Jesus?

question: What is the ontological Trinity?
answer:
The ontological Trinity is the truth that God, in His own eternal being, is one divine essence in three distinct persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, equal in power and glory.

This names who God is in Himself, not merely how He acts toward the world. Theologians often set it beside the economic Trinity, which describes the persons’ ordered work in creation and redemption. Scripture reveals one God (Deuteronomy 6:4) who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, sharing the one divine name (Matthew 28:19). The Son is eternally from the Father, truly God and not a creature (John 1:1; John 1:14; John 1:18), and the Spirit proceeds from the Father and is sent by the Son (John 15:26; John 16:7; John 16:13–15). Historic Christianity summarizes this as one essence and three persons: the same in substance, distinguished by their personal relations, not by any inequality of being or glory.

Because the Father has loved the Son from before the foundation of the world (John 17:24), God’s love is not something He acquired by making us. When you pray, you draw near to a God who is already complete in communion, so His welcome rests on fullness, not on need.

question: What is the star of David and is it biblical?
answer:
The Star of David is a six-pointed star formed by two overlapping triangles. It is a familiar emblem of Jewish identity and of the modern State of Israel. It is not biblical. Scripture never mentions this symbol, never presents it as King David’s required sign, and never commands God’s people to use it.

The Hebrew name Magen David means “Shield of David.” The figure became common in Jewish communities in the Middle Ages and spread widely in later centuries. A six-pointed star also appears in other cultures, so its meaning depends on its use, not on any instruction in the Bible.

Scripture points to something better. God gave Israel covenant signs He Himself appointed, and He promised a ruler to come. Balaam foretold a star that would come out of Jacob (Numbers 24:17). That hope is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David, who identifies Himself as the bright Morning Star (Revelation 22:16). Our confidence rests in His death and resurrection, not in a geometric figure.

Whether a Christian may wear or display the Star of David is a matter of Christian liberty, not a mark of orthodoxy. Some believers welcome it as a cultural reminder of God’s faithfulness to the Jewish people (Romans 11:1–2; Romans 11:28–29). Others set it aside because it is absent from Scripture and because the hexagram has also been used in mystical traditions outside the Bible. In matters like this, we are not to condemn one another (Romans 14:1–4; Romans 14:10). What we must never do is give any symbol the trust and worship that belong to God alone (Exodus 20:3–5).

If you are deciding about a necklace, a flag, or a church logo, pray about it, read those passages for yourself, and ask your pastors for counsel. Let any symbol serve love for Christ and for your neighbor, and let your true identity be that you belong to Him (Galatians 3:26–28).

question: Is loving God an emotion, a feeling, or a decision?
answer:
Loving God is a whole-person devotion that includes emotion, feeling, and decision together, not any one of them alone. It is the response of a heart renewed by the Holy Spirit, loving the God who first loved us.

Scripture commands, “And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Jesus called this the greatest commandment and added “with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37-38). In the biblical world the heart is the inner center where thoughts, desires, emotions, and choices meet as one. So love for God is never a passing mood, nor a bare decision stripped of affection. It is what has long been called holy affection: a settled delight in God that gladly chooses His ways.

We do not produce this love ourselves. “We love because He first loved us” (1 John 4:19). That love was displayed when Christ died for sinners and rose bodily, reconciling us to a holy God. Through faith in Him the Spirit pours God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5), so that we learn to delight in the Lord (Psalm 37:4) and to keep His commandments (John 14:15; 1 John 5:3). Obedience is the deciding side of love, and joy is its feeling side. Both deepen together in sanctification as we walk with Christ.

If your feelings toward God seem faint, do not assume the love is absent. Feelings rise and fall, yet genuine love returns to His Word and takes the next obedient step. This week, read Psalm 103 slowly once each day, thank God for one mercy you see there, and act on one clear command, such as offering a word of encouragement or confessing a sin without delay. Speak to the Lord in your own words about the coldness you feel, and ask a pastor or mature believer to pray with you. He who began this good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6).

question: How does God’s sovereignty work with free will?
answer:
Faithful Christians agree that God is fully sovereign and that people make meaningful choices for which they are accountable, yet they describe how these truths work together in more than one way. 
The strongest charitable argument for libertarian free will, held by many in the Arminian tradition, is that genuine responsibility and love require the real ability to have chosen otherwise, so God sovereignly knows and permits those choices without determining them. 
I hold compatibilism as one faithful option within historic Christianity: God’s sovereign decree includes every choice, while people act freely when they follow their own desires without coercion, remaining fully responsible and never making God the author of sin. 
This best reflects Scripture’s way of ascribing the same events both to God’s sovereign purpose and to human agency (Acts 2:23; Acts 4:27-28; Philippians 2:12-13). 
In your own walk, this invites both deep trust in the Father’s sovereign care and serious ownership of your decisions, so that you repent where you have sinned and obey where He calls, confident that He who began a good work will carry it on (Philippians 1:6). 
A practical next step is to pray through Proverbs 16:9 and Romans 8:28, asking the Lord to steady your heart in His rule and to align your choices with His revealed will, then share what you learn with a trusted pastor or mature believer.

question: What was the purpose of the biblical sign gifts?
answer:
The purpose of the biblical sign gifts was to authenticate the apostles and confirm that their gospel message was the very word of God.

A charitable argument from continuationists is that these gifts remain for building up the church and showing the Spirit’s power in this age, since the New Testament never announces that they must end before Christ returns.

I affirm cessationism as one faithful option within historic Christianity, because Scripture presents signs, wonders, and miracles as the marks of a true apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12) and as God’s confirmation of the great salvation first announced by the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4), so that we now rest on the finished foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20). This frees you to trust the Bible as sufficient and to grow through the ordinary means of grace: read a portion of Scripture each day, pray in light of what you read, and stay rooted in a local church where the Word is preached.

question: What is Shintoism?
answer:
Shinto, often called Shintoism in English, is the indigenous religious tradition of Japan, centered on reverence for the kami, spiritual beings associated with nature, ancestors, sacred places, and the life of the community.

It is less a fixed creed than a way of ritual life. People honor the kami at shrines, seek purification from impurity, and take part in seasonal festivals. It has no single founder and no scripture that functions as the Bible does, though texts such as the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki preserve important myths. In ordinary Japanese life it has long been practiced alongside Buddhism, so many people take part in both shrine and temple rites without treating them as rival systems.

Christians believe there is one true God who made heaven and earth, not one kami among many (Genesis 1:1; Isaiah 45:5). Scripture also teaches that every person needs forgiveness, and that Jesus Christ alone reconciles sinners to God through His death and bodily resurrection (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). Respect for Japanese neighbors and their customs should be genuine, yet the Gospel does not treat every religious path as equally true. If you are weighing a particular Shinto belief or practice against the Christian faith, I am glad to look at it with you carefully and without scorn.

question: Who is the man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12?
answer:
The man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12 is the figure of ultimate opposition to God who must be revealed before the day of the Lord, exalting himself in the temple of God and working Satan-empowered deception, only to be overthrown by the appearing of the Lord Jesus (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4; 2 Thessalonians 2:8-9).

Naming this figure with a specific person or institution is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians differ, because the prophetic language leaves room for more than one careful reading and does not decide anyone’s standing in Christ. We therefore extend liberty rather than judgment in such interpretations (Romans 14:1; Romans 14:4).

Many believers understand him as a future individual opponent of Christ who will be revealed in the last days. Others, including many of the Reformers, have seen the man of lawlessness in the papal claims to supreme authority within the church. A further reading stresses that the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, so rebellion takes various forms across history and intensifies before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2:7).

Beyond these differences, the passage is plain: a restrainer now holds this evil back, those who refuse to love the truth are left to deception, and the Lord Jesus will bring the lawless one to nothing (2 Thessalonians 2:6-12). Do not let questions about this figure unsettle you, as they once unsettled the Thessalonians (2 Thessalonians 2:1-2). This week, read 2 Thessalonians 1-2 slowly and prayerfully, asking God to fix your hope on the sure victory of Christ and to keep you loving the truth. Then talk through what you see with a pastor or mature believer in your local church.

question: What are some commonalities in Eastern religions?
answer:
Many Eastern religions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Taoism, commonly share a cyclical view of existence involving rebirth, the idea that karma shapes future states, and the pursuit of liberation or enlightenment through meditation, ethical discipline, and personal insight rather than a historical act of divine rescue. They also frequently understand ultimate reality as impersonal or all-encompassing, with hope located in inner harmony and human effort to transcend suffering or illusion.

These traditions differ in important details and reflect sincere longings for meaning and peace. Scripture, however, reveals a personal, holy, triune God who created all things, holds people accountable for sin, and justifies sinners by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works or self-realization (Genesis 1:1; Romans 3:23-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died for sins and rose bodily, and He alone is the mediator who brings people to the Father (John 14:6; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 1 Timothy 2:5). This good news addresses the human need for forgiveness and reconciliation that no path of striving can secure.

If you are comparing these claims because you are seeking what is true about God and eternity, consider reading the Gospel of John and weighing its historical testimony about Jesus. I would be glad to discuss any specific question that arises.

question: What is the bottomless pit (Revelation 9:1-12)?
answer:
The bottomless pit in Revelation 9:1-12 is the abyss, the deep place where God confines rebellious spiritual powers, opened for a limited judgment when the fifth trumpet sounds.

John sees a star that had fallen from heaven to earth, and it is given the key to the pit of the abyss. Smoke rises and darkens the sun and the air, and out of that smoke come locust-like beings with power like scorpions (Revelation 9:1-10). They are not ordinary insects. They are told not to harm grass, plants, or trees, and they are not permitted to kill. For five months they torment only those who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. Their king is the angel of the abyss, Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek, names that mean Destroyer (Revelation 9:11).

The Greek word behind "bottomless pit" is abyssos, "the deep." In Scripture it is a realm under God's lock, not a rival kingdom. Demons begged Jesus not to command them into the abyss, which shows both that the place is real and that Christ has authority over it (Luke 8:31). Later an angel holds that same key and binds Satan there for a time (Revelation 20:1-3). The release in Revelation 9 happens only because the key is given. Divine sovereignty, not demonic freedom, sets the boundary.

How far to press the imagery is a non-essential question. Faithful Christians may disagree, because Revelation is apocalyptic and less explicit about the exact form these agents take. Some read the vision in a more future-oriented way, as a coming release of demonic forces in a period of intense tribulation before Christ returns. Others read the locusts as symbolic of destructive spiritual powers that God permits, for a limited time, to torment those outside His protecting seal (Revelation 7:2-3; Revelation 9:4). Both can honor the text's main point. The judgment is real, measured, and does not erase God's care for His own.

If this vision unsettles you, let it lead you to Christ rather than to speculation. He is the One the demons feared, the One who died for sinners and rose bodily, and the One who keeps all who are His. Turn from sin and trust Him. A simple next step is to read Revelation 9 beside Luke 8:26-33 and Revelation 7:1-8, then pray honestly about any fear of judgment, asking God for a sober heart and a steady hope in Jesus.

Would you like to look next at how the abyss in Revelation 20 relates to this vision?

question: What is biblical theology?
answer:
Biblical theology is the study of God’s progressive revelation through redemptive history, tracing how Scripture’s one story moves from promise to fulfillment in Jesus Christ.

Unlike systematic theology, which organizes doctrine by topic, biblical theology follows the Bible’s own unfolding, attentive to covenant, type, and fulfillment. The risen Christ Himself interpreted Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms as speaking of Him (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44–47).

A simple next step is to read one passage this week and ask where it sits in that story, then how the cross and resurrection shape your trust and obedience today. All Scripture is God-breathed and useful for instruction, conviction, correction, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

question: Can people in heaven look down and see those of us who are still on the earth?
answer:
The Bible does not clearly teach that people in heaven look down and watch the details of our lives on earth. This is a non-essential question where faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture gives only limited detail about what believers perceive in the intermediate state.

Some Christians believe the redeemed have real awareness of earthly events. They note the joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:7; Luke 15:10), the great cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1), and the martyrs who speak of unfinished justice on earth (Revelation 6:9-10). In this reading, love for God’s people and interest in His saving work continue beyond death.

Others hold that these texts show heaven’s knowledge of God’s redemptive purposes without requiring ongoing observation of our daily lives. They stress that believers who die are at home with the Lord (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), that seeking information from the dead is forbidden (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and that our sure comfort is the watchful care of God and the intercession of Christ (Hebrews 4:13; Hebrews 7:25). Christian liberty leaves room for humble difference on what Scripture does not settle (Romans 14:1-5).

I believe it is wiser not to picture departed loved ones as spectators of our every moment. The New Testament fixes our hope on being with Christ now and on the resurrection still to come, when we will see Him and one another in glory. Until then, the eyes that matter most are our Father’s, who sees in secret and cares for His children (Matthew 6:4; 1 Peter 5:7).

If you are missing someone, remember that death is not the end for those who belong to Jesus. We have all sinned and stand in need of a Savior. Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily the third day, so that everyone who repents and trusts Him receives forgiveness and eternal life (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; John 3:16). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

This week, read Hebrews 12:1-3 slowly and ask God to fix your eyes on Jesus rather than on what we cannot fully know. If grief is heavy, share it with a pastor or mature believer who can pray with you (James 5:16). What is stirring this question for you right now?

question: Who are the Free Will Baptists, and what do they believe?
answer:
Free Will Baptists are a historic Baptist family that confesses the gospel of Jesus Christ and teaches that sinners have a real freedom to accept or refuse God’s saving grace. Their roots are in the English General Baptists, who taught that Christ died for all people, rather than in the Particular Baptists, who taught that He died especially for the elect. In America they took shape in the South in the 1700s and in New England under Benjamin Randall, and today most are linked through the National Association of Free Will Baptists, organized in 1935.

They stand with historic Christianity on the essentials. They confess one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They hold the Bible to be the inspired Word of God and the final authority for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16–17). They confess that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, born of the virgin Mary, that He died for sinners, and that He rose bodily from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). They teach that sinners are justified by grace through faith in Christ, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Their name marks their distinctive doctrine. They are Arminian. They teach a general atonement, that Christ died for the sins of the whole world, and they often appeal to texts such as John 3:16 and 1 John 2:2. They generally teach conditional election, that God chooses those whom He foreknows will believe. They teach that the Spirit enables a response to the gospel, but that this grace can be resisted. They also teach conditional security: a person who has believed may fall from grace through persistent unbelief and willful sin, and so must continue in faith. In church life they practice believer’s baptism by immersion, observe the Lord’s Supper, and, in their Treatise, also count washing the saints’ feet as an ordinance. Local churches govern themselves and associate freely with other churches.

On whether a true believer can finally fall away, they answer yes, because Scripture warns against drifting and falling (Hebrews 3:12–14; Hebrews 6:4–6; 2 Peter 2:20–22). I hold the perseverance of the saints, that those truly united to Christ are kept by God’s power and will not finally be lost, because salvation is God’s work from first to last and Christ loses none whom the Father has given Him (John 6:37–40; John 10:27–29; Philippians 1:6). That is a serious difference, but it is a difference among Christians who confess the same Lord, not a denial of the Trinity, the deity of Christ, or salvation by grace through faith.

If you are visiting a Free Will Baptist church, read their Treatise of the Faith and Practices and ask the pastor how the church teaches assurance, repentance, and abiding in Christ. Listen for whether Christ crucified and risen is preached as the only Savior, and whether people are called to repent and trust Him alone.

question: What does it mean that you are the head and not the tail in Deuteronomy 28:13?
answer:
Deuteronomy 28:13 means that, if Israel carefully obeyed the LORD’s commandments, He would set them in a place of leadership and honor among the nations rather than leaving them trailing in defeat and dependence. The image is concrete: the head leads and is first, while the tail follows and is last. The surrounding verses make this plain. Obedience would bring abundance so that Israel lent to many nations and did not borrow, always rising and never sinking (Deuteronomy 28:12–14). Disobedience would reverse the picture, so that the foreigner became the head and Israel the tail (Deuteronomy 28:43–44). These were real covenant blessings and curses tied to life in the land under the Mosaic covenant, not vague spiritual slogans.

In the ancient Near East, such language of elevation or humiliation described a people’s actual standing before other nations, and Moses used it to press the seriousness of covenant faithfulness. The promise was conditional. It rested on hearing and doing what the LORD commanded (Deuteronomy 28:1–2, 13).

Christians are not national Israel under that covenant. Christ has fulfilled the law (Matthew 5:17), and every promise of God finds its yes in Him (2 Corinthians 1:20). Our primary blessing is spiritual: we are blessed with every spiritual blessing in Christ (Ephesians 1:3), and He Himself is the head of the church (Colossians 1:18). We are justified by grace through faith, not by our performance, and we are being sanctified as we walk in grateful obedience. The call to careful obedience remains, yet it flows from grace already given, not from an attempt to secure earthly dominance.

This week, read Deuteronomy 28 in one sitting, noting both the blessings and the warnings, then ask the Lord to show you one concrete area of daily obedience that honors Him.

question: What is theistic agnosticism / agnostic theism?
answer:
Agnostic theism, also called theistic agnosticism, is the view that one believes God exists while also holding that this cannot be known with certainty, or that knowledge of God is unattainable.

It treats belief and knowledge as separable, so a person may trust that God is real on the basis of faith, experience, or practical reasons without claiming proof. Scripture, however, teaches that God has made Himself known. Paul writes that what may be known about God is plain to people, because God has shown it to them, and that His invisible attributes, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived since the creation of the world, leaving people without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1), and in these last days God has spoken by His Son, the radiance of His glory (Hebrews 1:1-3).

Christians therefore confess the knowability of God: we may know Him truly, though never exhaustively (Deuteronomy 29:29; 1 Corinthians 13:12). Jesus Himself defines eternal life as knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent (John 17:3), and John writes so that believers may know that they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). This knowledge rests on God’s revelation in creation and, above all, in the person and work of Christ, received by grace through faith.

If you find yourself drawn toward God yet unsure whether He can be known, set aside a few quiet minutes each day this week to read the Gospel of John slowly, asking the Lord to show you who Jesus is. That simple, concrete step of seeking Him in His Word is one way to move from uncertainty toward the personal knowledge He offers.

question: The Fruit of the Holy Spirit – What is kindness?
answer:
Kindness, as a fruit of the Holy Spirit, is the Spirit-wrought quality of gentle benevolence that actively seeks the good of others.

In Galatians 5:22-23, Paul lists kindness among the fruit the Holy Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ. The underlying Greek word, chrēstotēs, points to a gracious usefulness and moral kindness, not mere surface politeness or a naturally easy temperament. This is a mark of progressive sanctification, the Spirit’s ongoing work of conforming believers to the character of Christ rather than a virtue we manufacture by effort alone.

It takes its pattern from God Himself. The kindness of God is meant to lead sinners to repentance (Romans 2:4), and that kindness appeared in the saving mercy of Christ, who came not because of works we had done (Titus 3:4-5). Having received such kindness, believers are called to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, forgiving one another as God in Christ has forgiven them (Colossians 3:12; Ephesians 4:32).

This week, choose one relationship where irritation comes easily and plan one quiet, concrete act of help, such as a patient conversation, a practical favor, or a word of encouragement, while you ask the Lord directly to bear this fruit in you as you stay in His Word.

question: How should Christians view the idea of reparations for slavery?
answer:
Christians should condemn chattel slavery as a grave sin against God's image-bearers and uphold biblical justice, while recognizing that faithful believers may disagree on whether modern government reparations are a wise or required remedy.

This is a non-essential matter of prudential judgment and Christian liberty rather than a doctrine that defines orthodoxy. Scripture clearly hates oppression, commands restitution for identifiable wrongs, and rejects both partiality and holding the innocent guilty for others' sins, yet it does not spell out a detailed public policy for injustices committed by people long dead. Romans 14:1-4 therefore calls for charity where applications differ.

One Christian view supports reparations in some form. Advocates argue that unpaid labor and later legal discrimination produced lasting harms that public justice should repair. They appeal to Old Testament restitution patterns (Exodus 22:1-4) and the Jubilee theme of restoring what was lost (Leviticus 25), treating repair as love of neighbor and the righteousness God requires (Micah 6:8).

Another major Christian view urges caution or opposition to race-based government reparations. These believers fully agree that American slavery violated God's prohibition of man-stealing (Exodus 21:16; 1 Timothy 1:10) and that churches should lament historic compromises. They also insist Scripture forbids charging children with their fathers' guilt (Ezekiel 18:20; Deuteronomy 24:16) and warns against partiality (James 2:1, 9). In this view, coercive transfers that punish later generations or unrelated immigrants create fresh injustice, while true healing comes through the Gospel, personal responsibility, voluntary generosity, and the church's mercy rather than political programs that risk division.

Both perspectives can affirm that living offenders should make restitution where possible (Luke 19:8), that slavery must never be excused, and that Christ has already broken down the dividing wall between peoples (Ephesians 2:14-16; Galatians 3:28). Weigh history, evidence, and likely fruits with an open Bible, and extend patience to brothers and sisters who reach different policy conclusions.

Keep the cross central: only Christ's atoning death and bodily resurrection pay the debt of sin and reconcile enemies to God and to one another. If this question weighs on your conscience, bring it to the Lord in prayer while meditating on Micah 6:8 and Ephesians 2, and talk it through with your pastors so that truth and love remain joined.

question: Who are we to pray to, the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit?
answer:
Christians pray to the one God who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Each person of the Trinity may rightly be addressed in prayer, since each is fully God, though Scripture especially directs us to pray to the Father through the Son and by the help of the Holy Spirit.

Jesus taught His disciples to begin, “Our Father in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). Through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father (Ephesians 2:18), and we ask in Jesus’ name so the Father is glorified (John 14:13). The Spirit helps us when we do not know how to pray (Romans 8:26). At the same time, believers call on the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:2), and Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59). Because the Son is truly God, that prayer is due worship. The Holy Spirit, sharing the same divine nature, may also be addressed when we ask Him to work according to Scripture.

In daily practice it is wise to speak chiefly to the Father, coming only through Christ’s finished work and relying on the Spirit to shape our desires. Set aside a few quiet minutes each morning to thank your heavenly Father for one specific mercy and to bring one specific request, then ask a mature believer in your local church to join you in prayer once this week.

question: Why does God hate sin?
answer:
God hates sin because He is perfectly holy, and sin is the direct opposite of His pure, righteous character. Scripture presents God as holy, holy, holy, set apart from all evil, so that His eyes are too pure to look on wrongdoing and He cannot tolerate it (Isaiah 6:3; Habakkuk 1:13; 1 Peter 1:15-16). Sin is lawlessness, a willful rejection of God’s good rule that falls short of His glory, corrupts what He made, and separates people from Him (1 John 3:4; Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). It earns death as its wage, and God’s just wrath against it is the necessary expression of His love for what is good and His refusal to call evil acceptable (Romans 1:18; Romans 6:23).

This same holy God, in mercy, did not abandon sinners. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as the substitute who bore the penalty sin deserves, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, securing forgiveness for all who trust Him (Romans 3:25-26; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9).

If this truth weighs on you, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. This week, read Psalm 51 and Romans 5 slowly, and speak to God in your own words about both the seriousness of sin and the sufficiency of Christ. What led you to ask this?

question: What will we look like in Heaven?
answer:
We will look like ourselves, yet gloriously changed. Believers will not spend eternity as ghosts. At the resurrection we will have real, physical, glorified bodies, made like the risen body of the Lord Jesus, free from sin, weakness, and decay.

When a Christian dies, the soul is at once with Christ, which is better by far (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). That is not the end of the story. Our final hope is the resurrection of the body and life in the new heaven and new earth, where death, mourning, crying, and pain are gone (Revelation 21:1-4). Paul says the body is sown perishable, in dishonor and weakness, and raised imperishable, in glory and power, a spiritual body, meaning a true body fully alive by the Holy Spirit, not a non-physical one (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). As we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven (1 Corinthians 15:49). Christ “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (Philippians 3:21), and “we shall be like Him, for we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3:2).

Jesus’ risen body shows what that means. He could be touched, He bore the marks of the cross, and He ate with His disciples, yet He was no longer subject to death (Luke 24:36-43; John 20:19-27). So there is real continuity. You will still be you, and God’s people will know one another. There is also real transformation. Sin, sickness, aging, and the curse will not cling to that body. We are not told every detail of height, hair, or exact age, and faithful Christians should not invent them. We also are not told that male and female disappear. Jesus taught that in the resurrection people neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30). That ends marriage in that age. It does not erase the persons God made.

This hope is for those who belong to Christ. God is holy, and we have all sinned and fallen short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and this resurrection life.

If this hope is yours, let it steady you in a frail body. This week, read 1 Corinthians 15 slowly and thank God that death does not have the last word. What draws you to this question?

question: What is sola scriptura?
answer:
Sola Scriptura means “Scripture alone.” It is the doctrine that the Bible is the sole infallible authority for Christian faith and practice.

Because all Scripture is God-breathed, it is useful for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness, so that the believer may be complete and equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Creeds, pastors, and church traditions can serve that Word faithfully, but none of them may stand beside it or overrule it as an equal authority. The Bereans showed this posture when they examined the Scriptures daily to test what they heard (Acts 17:11).

This guards the sufficiency of Scripture: God has given in the Bible all that is necessary for salvation and godly living, so you are not left waiting for a secret tradition or a new revelation. When a question about faith or obedience arises this week, open a clear passage that speaks to it and let that text, rather than custom or mere feeling, settle your conscience before the Lord.

question: What did Jesus mean when He said He would give us “whatever you ask in my name”?
answer:
Jesus did not mean that every wish is guaranteed if we add the words “in Jesus’ name.” He meant that His people may ask the Father with Christ’s authority, in line with His character and purposes, so that the Father is glorified in the Son (John 14:13-14).

In Scripture, a name stands for the person. To ask in Jesus’ name is to come as one united to Him, on the ground of who He is and what He has done, not to use His name as a formula. He ties the promise to abiding in Him, with His words abiding in us, and to asking the Father as those He has chosen and sent (John 15:7; John 15:16; John 16:23-24). That is prayer through Christ our Mediator, not a technique detached from Him.
