Two boundaries keep the promise clear. The aim is the Father’s glory in the Son, not our plans alone (John 14:13). And asking in His name means asking according to His will. John writes, “If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14-15). James warns that wrong motives can block what we seek, “because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures” (James 4:3). The Lord’s Prayer itself trains us to say, in effect, “Your will be done” (Matthew 6:9-10).

So Jesus can speak largely, and the Father can still withhold a particular request, without breaking His word. He hears those who come through Christ, who always lives to intercede for them, and He answers in a way that fits His holy, good, and sovereign will (Hebrews 4:14-16; Hebrews 7:25). Sometimes the answer is yes. Sometimes it is a better gift than we knew to ask. Sometimes, as with Paul, it is grace to endure what we begged to have removed (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). An unanswered prayer can ache. It does not mean the Father has stopped listening.

Take one request you are carrying, read John 14:13-14 and 1 John 5:14-15, and then pray it to the Father in Jesus’ name, asking Him to shape it toward His glory and His will. If the wait is heavy, bring it also to a mature believer or to your church elders, so you do not carry it alone (James 5:16). If a particular prayer is weighing on you, you are welcome to share it.

question: What does the Bible say about witchcraft? Should a Christian fear witchcraft?
answer:
The Bible condemns witchcraft as rebellion against God and a forbidden pursuit of spiritual power and hidden knowledge apart from Him. A Christian should not fear witchcraft, because Jesus Christ has already triumphed over every spiritual enemy and keeps His people secure.

God forbade His people from practicing divination, sorcery, witchcraft, or consulting the dead, calling these things an abomination (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:6). He even compared rebellion itself to the sin of divination (1 Samuel 15:23). In the ancient world these practices were common attempts to manipulate spiritual forces instead of trusting the living God, and Scripture treats them as real spiritual danger, not harmless custom.

The New Testament gives the same verdict. Sorcery (Greek pharmakeia, referring to magical spells and potions) is listed among the works of the flesh, and those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:19-21). Believers in Ephesus who turned to Christ burned their books of magic as fruit of repentance (Acts 19:18-19). Those who continue in sorcery without repentance are named among those shut out of the eternal city (Revelation 21:8; Revelation 22:15).

Christians are not called to live in fear of curses, spells, or occult power. Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them by the cross (Colossians 2:15). The Spirit who lives in every believer is greater than the spirit who is in the world (1 John 4:4). Neither angels nor rulers nor powers can separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:38-39). Our safety rests on His penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection, not on anxious vigilance or counter-rituals.

Do not treat what God calls sin as a curiosity or a game. If fear, fascination, or past involvement has drawn you toward these practices, turn from them fully. Remove related objects and habits, confess the sin to the Lord, and walk in the light with your local church. This week, read Colossians 2:13-15 and Ephesians 6:10-18 slowly, and bring your specific concerns to God in your own words, asking Him for deeper trust in Christ’s victory and for strength to obey. If the weight feels heavy, speak with your pastor or elders so they can pray with you and shepherd you.

All of us have sinned and need a Savior. Jesus Christ died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead. Turn from witchcraft and every sin, and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

What prompted this question for you?

question: Why am I here?
answer:
You are here because the living God made you on purpose, to know Him, to reflect His glory, and to enjoy fellowship with Him.

Scripture does not treat your life as an accident. God created human beings in His image, to represent Him and to live in relationship with Him (Genesis 1:26–27). He formed His people for His glory (Isaiah 43:7). That is why a full schedule, real achievements, and even good relationships can still leave a restlessness underneath. You were made for God, and the heart is not at home apart from Him.

Sin broke that fellowship. We have all turned from God, and the wages of sin is death, separation from the One who made us (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). God did not abandon us there. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Romans 5:8). His penal substitutionary death is sufficient to reconcile sinners to God. People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by earning a place with God (Ephesians 2:8–9). In Christ, the question “Why am I here?” finds its answer: to be reconciled to God, and then to glorify Him in ordinary faithfulness, work, love, and worship (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A concrete next step is to read John 1 and John 3 this week, and to pray directly to God about this question, asking Him to show you who Jesus is and why He made you. If you can, talk it through with a pastor at a church that teaches the Bible.

What is stirring this question for you right now?

question: Did Adam and Eve have belly buttons / navels?
answer:
The Bible does not tell us whether Adam and Eve had belly buttons, and this is a non-essential detail where faithful Christians may disagree without harming fellowship.

Scripture is silent on the point, which is why it remains open. God has not revealed every physical feature of the first humans, and we are to treasure what He has made known rather than speculate beyond it (Deuteronomy 29:29). Differing thoughts here do not affect the doctrine of creation or our unity in Christ.

One view held by many believers is that Adam and Eve had no navels. The navel is simply the scar left where the umbilical cord once joined a child to his or her mother. Adam was formed by God from the dust of the ground, and Eve was fashioned from Adam's rib, so neither experienced birth or an umbilical cord (Genesis 2:7; Genesis 2:21-22). Their bodies were the product of special creation, made mature and whole from the first moment.

Another view suggests that the Lord may have created them with navels anyway, giving the first man and woman every ordinary mark of the human form He designed, so their appearance would match the pattern for all who followed. Still others wisely say the whole question lies outside what God has spoken, and pressing for an answer adds nothing to faith or obedience.

Romans 14 reminds us to welcome one another and refuse to quarrel over disputable matters. Whether Adam and Eve bore that small mark or not, the greater wonder is that God made them in His image, breathed life into them, and set them in a good world (Genesis 1:26-27; Genesis 2:7).

A simple next step is to set aside ten minutes this week to read Genesis 2 slowly, thanking God for His careful, personal work in creating humanity, and asking Him to deepen your trust in everything He has clearly revealed.

question: What is an appropriate level of physical intimacy before marriage?
answer:
God reserves sexual intimacy for the covenant of marriage, so the appropriate level of physical intimacy before marriage is warm, honorable affection that does not arouse or pursue sexual desire. Scripture calls believers to abstain from sexual immorality and to control their bodies in holiness and honor, not in passionate lust (1 Thessalonians 4:3-5; Hebrews 13:4).

Sexual union is a one-flesh gift God gave within marriage, not a stage of dating (Genesis 2:24; 1 Corinthians 7:2-5). Jesus teaches that lustful intent itself is sin in the heart (Matthew 5:27-28). Paul tells believers to flee sexual immorality, because the body belongs to the Lord and is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:18-20). Song of Solomon also warns against awakening love before its proper time (Song of Solomon 2:7). The question is not “How far can we go without technically sinning?” but “Will this help us love God and one another in purity?”

Intercourse, oral sex, genital contact, and prolonged sexual making-out are not appropriate before marriage. Those acts are sexual, and they are meant to move a couple toward the union God placed inside marriage. Lighter gestures such as holding hands or a brief kiss are places where Christians have applied wisdom differently, because Scripture does not catalog every touch. Even those should be examined. If an action inflames desire that cannot be righteously fulfilled, stirs lust, or pressures a brother or sister, it is unwise and should be refused (Romans 13:13-14; 1 Corinthians 10:23-24). Love protects the other person’s holiness. It does not use their body for pleasure you are not free to complete.

Set the boundaries before you are alone and tempted. Avoid private settings that make restraint unlikely, talk honestly with the person you are dating, and invite a pastor or a mature married couple to ask you hard questions. If you have already crossed a line, do not rename the sin or hide in shame. Sexual sin is real, and it wounds conscience, trust, and fellowship. Christ still receives sinners. He died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Those who repent and trust Him are justified by grace through faith, cleansed, and called into progressive sanctification by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:9-11; 1 John 1:9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

This week, read 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8 slowly and write down concrete boundaries you will keep. Then share them with a trusted believer who will pray with you and hold you accountable.

Are you asking for help setting boundaries in a current relationship, or are you carrying guilt from something that has already happened?

question: What are the unfruitful works of darkness (Ephesians 5:11)?
answer:
The unfruitful works of darkness are the sinful deeds that belong to life apart from God, barren of any true good and rooted in spiritual blindness. In Ephesians 5:11 Paul tells believers to have no fellowship with them, but rather to expose them.

The traditional wording “unfruitful works of darkness” is the same phrase the Berean Standard Bible renders “fruitless deeds of darkness.” Paul has just named what he means: sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, which he calls idolatry, together with obscenity, foolish talk, and coarse joking (Ephesians 5:3–5). These are not small social slips. They flow from a heart turned from the Lord, and they produce shame rather than the fruit of the light, which is all goodness, righteousness, and truth (Ephesians 5:8–10). The word behind “unfruitful” means barren. Such deeds cannot grow into life with God.

The same contrast appears elsewhere. The works of the flesh stand against the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:19–23). Jesus said people love darkness rather than the light because their deeds are evil (John 3:19–20). Those deeds are “of darkness” because they belong to the dominion from which the Father rescues His people and brings them into the kingdom of His beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). Once you were darkness; now you are light in the Lord, so walk as children of light (Ephesians 5:8). That walk is sanctification: a new identity in Christ, worked out by refusing the old deeds.

To have no fellowship with them means refusing partnership, participation, and secret complicity, not merely protecting a reputation. To expose them is not a license to gossip or to linger over shameful details, for Paul says it is shameful even to mention what the disobedient do in secret (Ephesians 5:12). Exposure happens as the light of Christ, through a holy life, truthful speech, and loving correction in the church, makes sin visible so it can be forsaken (Ephesians 5:13–14; 1 John 1:5–7).

If a hidden habit, relationship, or conversation is drawing you into these deeds, bring it into the light this week by confessing it to the Lord and to a mature believer or elder, and ask them to walk with you in repentance. Children of light do not negotiate with darkness.

If a particular situation is on your mind, I am glad to look at it with you in light of this passage.

question: How can an unmarried person relieve sexual tension in a non-sinful way?
answer:
Sexual desire is a good gift from God, yet He has reserved its physical expression for the marriage covenant between one man and one woman. An unmarried person has no righteous way to relieve sexual tension through sexual activity, stimulation, or release. The biblical call is self-control by the Holy Spirit’s power, not gratification.

The tension you feel is real and can be heavy. Scripture meets it with both honesty and hope. Paul writes that it is good to remain unmarried if one can exercise self-control, yet “if they cannot control themselves, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with passion” (1 Corinthians 7:8-9). Jesus teaches that lustful desire itself is sin, equating it with adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:27-28). Therefore masturbation, pornography, or fantasy-driven release do not offer a clean outlet; they train the heart in the very immorality we are commanded to flee (1 Corinthians 6:18). The marriage bed alone is honorable and undefiled (Hebrews 13:4).

This struggle belongs to progressive sanctification. Every person falls short of God’s holiness (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as our substitute bearing the penalty for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, defeating sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by our purity or effort. If you repent and trust in Jesus Christ who died and rose for you, you receive full forgiveness and the indwelling Spirit who produces self-control as fruit (Galatians 5:22-23; Romans 6:4). Even longtime believers need this same grace daily when desire flares.

Walk it out through the means of grace. Pray each day, confessing specific temptations and asking the Father for strength to resist and a way of escape; He promises to provide one (1 Corinthians 10:13; Hebrews 4:16). Make no provision for the flesh by removing triggers such as unfiltered devices or stirring media (Romans 13:14). Pursue regular fellowship and accountability with a mature believer of the same sex in your local church who will pray with you and ask direct questions. Channel energy into exercise, service, and undivided devotion to the Lord, which singleness uniquely allows (1 Corinthians 7:32-35). If marriage is a godly desire, seek your elders’ counsel on pursuing it wisely and purely rather than remaining in prolonged burning.

A concrete step this week is to tell one trusted church friend or elder about the struggle and agree on one clear boundary they will help you keep. God is patient and faithful; He sympathizes with our weakness and supplies mercy (Hebrews 4:15-16). What particular habit or moment of temptation feels hardest for you right now?

question: What does it mean to be devout?
answer:
To be devout is to live with sincere reverence and wholehearted devotion to God: a heart that fears Him, and a life ordered toward His glory, not a show of religious activity.

Scripture paints this plainly. Simeon is called "righteous and devout," waiting for the consolation of Israel with the Holy Spirit upon him (Luke 2:25). Cornelius and his household were "devout and God-fearing," marked by generosity and regular prayer (Acts 10:2). Words rendered "devout" in the New Testament, including eulabēs (reverent, careful before God) and eusebēs (pious, godly), point to holy reverence rather than empty ritual. The apostles name this life godliness, a training that holds promise for this life and the next (1 Timothy 4:7–8), and grace itself teaches believers "to live sensible, upright, and godly lives" (Titus 2:12).

Devotion is not how we earn acceptance with God. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and a devout life is the fruit of that grace, the Spirit's work of progressive sanctification in those who belong to Jesus (Ephesians 2:8–10; Philippians 1:6).

This week, set aside fifteen quiet minutes to read Luke 2:25–32 slowly, and ask the Lord to show you one place where your practice has grown routine without reverence. Then do the next clear act of obedience His Word puts in front of you, whether prayer, confession, generosity, or simply slowing down to fear Him again.

If you want, tell me whether you are asking about your own devotion, or about what the Bible means when it calls someone devout.

question: Are we supposed to use musical instruments in church?
answer:
The use of musical instruments in church is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians may disagree, because the New Testament gives no explicit command that either requires or forbids them for the gathered church.

One major view welcomes instruments as a fitting aid to praise, drawing on the Psalms’ calls to worship God with harp, lyre, and trumpet (Psalm 150:3-5) and seeing them as gifts that can support joyful, united singing centered on Christ. Another major view, often shaped by the regulative principle of worship, holds that churches should sing without instruments, since the apostolic pattern speaks of psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs and of making melody in the heart to the Lord (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16) without mentioning instruments, which belonged to the old-covenant temple service fulfilled in Christ.

These are disputable matters of conscience and practice, not tests of orthodoxy. Romans 14:1-5 and Romans 14:19 call us to welcome one another, to be fully convinced in our own minds, and to pursue what makes for peace and mutual upbuilding rather than quarrels. Whatever your congregation does, the aim remains worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23-24), with songs that teach and admonish so the word of Christ dwells richly among you. Speak with your elders about how your church applies Scripture here, and come ready to offer your voice and heart to the Lord who alone is worthy of praise.

question: What does the Bible say about miscarriage?
answer:
Miscarriage is a real and heavy grief, and the Bible treats both the little life lost and the parents’ sorrow as matters that matter to God.

Scripture teaches that a child in the womb is personally formed and known by the Lord, not a mere potential or an accident. David says the Lord knit him together in his mother’s womb, saw his unformed substance, and wrote all his days in His book before one of them came to be (Psalm 139:13-16). The Lord told Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). Life at its earliest stage already bears the Creator’s care and bears His image.

God’s law also guarded the pregnant woman and her child. Exodus 21:22-25 requires justice when they are harmed, up to life for life where there is serious injury. The unborn stood under the protection of God’s righteous law.

The Bible likewise places even the hidden work of the womb under the Lord’s sovereign hand. Freedom from miscarriage is named among old-covenant blessings (Exodus 23:26), and a miscarrying womb appears in a word of judgment on a rebellious people (Hosea 9:14). Those texts do not mean that every miscarriage today is a personal punishment. We live in a world groaning under the curse that entered through sin (Romans 5:12; Romans 8:20-22). When others assumed a tragedy must be someone’s specific fault, Jesus refused that simple equation (John 9:1-3). If guilt has settled on you, hear this clearly: miscarriage is not proof that God is paying you back for some failure.

He draws near to the brokenhearted. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit” (Psalm 34:18). Jesus says, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4). He is the God of all comfort, who comforts us in every affliction (2 Corinthians 1:3-4). You may lament before Him. The psalms give language for tears, questions, and even protest, and He remains a refuge.

On the child who dies before birth, Scripture does not answer every question we wish it would, yet it gives real grounds for hope. After his infant son died, David said, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23). Jesus welcomed little children and said the kingdom of God belongs to such as these (Mark 10:14). Faithful Christians have long rested in God’s mercy toward these little ones, trusting that the Savior who died and rose is able to apply His grace even where personal faith cannot yet be expressed. We hold that hope humbly, anchored in God’s just and merciful character rather than in speculation. Faithful believers may differ on how fully Scripture settles every case, and charity should mark that difference.

Death remains an enemy and the wages of sin, yet it does not have the last word. Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 6:23). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works or by how well we bear suffering (Ephesians 2:8-9). One day He will wipe away every tear, and death will be no more (Revelation 21:4). If you have never trusted Him, or if this loss has left you unsure, repent of sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Psalm 139 and Psalm 34 slowly, and speak to the Lord in your own words about your sorrow, your questions, and your need of His comfort. Ask a pastor, elder, or mature believer to grieve and pray with you, for the prayer of a righteous person has great power (James 5:16). You were not meant to carry this alone.

What part of this loss, or of God’s Word, weighs on you most right now?

question: Is religion the cause of most wars?
answer:
No, religion is not the cause of most wars. The large majority of conflicts in history have been driven by political power, territorial ambition, economic gain, and ethnic or ideological rivalry.

It is understandable why the question arises. The Crusades, the European wars of religion, and modern extremist violence are real and tragic, and people who have claimed the name of Christ have sometimes pursued bloodshed in ways that flatly contradict His commands. Those sins should be named honestly and repented of, not excused.

Yet the historical record does not support the claim that religion causes most wars. One major survey, the Encyclopedia of Wars, examined 1,763 conflicts and classified only about 7 percent as primarily religious. The twentieth century, the bloodiest on record, saw enormous death tolls under explicitly atheistic regimes motivated by communist ideology, not by faith in God. Secular nationalism and the naked quest for dominance have fueled far more violence than creed.

The Bible teaches that the root of conflict lies in the sinful human heart, not in the mere presence of religion. James 4:1-2 locates quarrels and fights in the passions at war within us: we crave what we do not have, so we fight and quarrel. This is the doctrine of human depravity. Apart from God’s grace, people are bent toward selfishness and violence whether they are religious or secular.

Christians believe that Jesus Christ is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). He taught His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44). Through His death on the cross and bodily resurrection He reconciles sinners to God and breaks down hostility between people (Ephesians 2:14-16; Colossians 1:20). Where the church has forgotten this and grasped for worldly power, it has sinned. Where it has been faithful, it has often restrained violence and pursued mercy.

Lasting peace will not come from erasing belief in God but from the reign of the risen Christ, who will one day make wars cease (Psalm 46:9; Isaiah 2:4). In the meantime He calls people to repent of their own hostility and trust in Him alone. When you see conflict, whether between nations or in ordinary relationships, the biblical step is to examine your own heart first and to pursue peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18).

What particular wars or events have most shaped your view on this?

question: What does it mean to “in all your ways acknowledge Him” in Proverbs 3:6?
answer:
To “acknowledge Him” in Proverbs 3:6 means to know the LORD personally and practically in every path of life: to recognize His rule, seek His will, and submit your plans to Him rather than merely mentioning His name.

The Hebrew verb behind “acknowledge” is *yada*, a word for knowing that includes recognition and relational awareness, not a casual nod. In Proverbs, that knowing is the daily outworking of the fear of the LORD. Solomon has just commanded, “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5). Verse 6 shows what that trust looks like on the road. In all your ways, your work, relationships, money, and ordinary choices, you keep God in view and yield to Him. The promise follows in the same verse: “He will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:6). By His providence He directs and establishes your course according to His wisdom. That is not a guarantee that every preference will be granted.

This is humble dependence, not a technique for controlling outcomes. You acknowledge Him when you ask what pleases Him before you choose, when you test your plans by Scripture, and when you refuse to treat your own insight as final. “Do not be wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil” (Proverbs 3:7). James presses the same posture: do not boast about tomorrow as if your plans were certain, but say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). The New Testament gathers it into one sentence: “whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him” (Colossians 3:17).

Before your next significant decision this week, pause with Proverbs 3:5–6, write the choice down, search one or two passages that speak to it, and if you belong to a local church, ask a mature believer to help you weigh it. Then act in faith, trusting the Lord to straighten what you cannot see.

question: Does God still give visions to people today? Should believers expect visions to be a part of their Christian experience?
answer:
Believers should not expect visions as a normal part of Christian experience, because the revelatory gifts that included such visions belonged to the foundational era of the apostles and prophets and have ceased. Continuationists make a sincere case that the Spirit still grants visions and related gifts to build up the church until Christ returns, always to be tested by Scripture and never allowed to stand above it. I hold the cessationist view as one faithful option within historic Christianity, since God has spoken His final word in the Son and confirmed that word through the apostolic witness, so that the completed Scriptures are sufficient for all faith and practice (Hebrews 1:1-2; Hebrews 2:3-4; Ephesians 2:20; Jude 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

The New Testament ties signs, wonders, and visions to the unique work of establishing the church and delivering the faith once for all, not to an ongoing office of new revelation (2 Corinthians 12:12). Today the same Spirit illumines the Word He inspired, giving wisdom and guidance through what is already written rather than through fresh visions (John 16:13; James 1:5; Psalm 119:105). God remains sovereign and may order circumstances or even use a dream in His providence, yet we are not to seek or wait for extraordinary experiences when He has given ordinary means of grace.

Set your hope on those means: open Scripture daily, pray for understanding, and stay under the preaching and counsel of a local church. If a strong impression or dream comes, bring it at once to the Bible and to mature believers, for the Spirit never contradicts the Word He has given (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21; Acts 17:11). This week, read slowly through John 14-16 and ask the Lord to lead you by the truth already revealed there.

question: Is physical abuse an acceptable reason for divorce?
answer:
Physical abuse is a grave sin and is never acceptable in a marriage, and Scripture does not list it as an independent ground for divorce, though severe unrepentant abuse may in some cases be judged as willful desertion after other remedies have failed. A major historic Christian view holds that only sexual immorality and the departure of an unbelieving spouse permit divorce, so abuse calls for separation, protection, and church discipline, but not dissolution of the bond. I hold, as one faithful reading within historic Christianity, that when physical abuse is ongoing and unrepentant, and neither the church nor the civil magistrate can restore a safe marriage, it can constitute willful desertion that dissolves the bond, because the abuser has abandoned covenant love and peaceable companionship.

If you or someone near you is in immediate danger, leave now and contact emergency services. God does not require you to remain where you are being harmed. Marriage is a lifelong covenant (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:6), and the Lord hates the tearing of that covenant (Malachi 2:16). Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:32; Matthew 19:9). Paul teaches that if an unbelieving spouse departs, the believer is not bound in such cases, for God has called us to peace (1 Corinthians 7:15). Physical cruelty violates the call to love as Christ loved the church and to live with one’s spouse in an understanding and honoring way (Ephesians 5:25–29; 1 Peter 3:7). It is wickedness, not a marital right.

The first response is protection, not a private rush to end the marriage. Report the abuse to civil authorities, whom God has appointed to restrain evil (Romans 13:1–4). Bring it to your pastors or elders so that sin can be named and the unrepentant confronted (Matthew 18:15–17). Separate if needed so that you and any children are safe. If the abuser professes faith yet refuses to repent, the church may eventually treat that person as an unbeliever. Only when desertion of this kind cannot be remedied should divorce be considered, and even then under the guidance of wise church leaders, not by personal decision alone. Separation for safety is right even when divorce is not yet clear (1 Corinthians 7:10–11).

I cannot give legal, medical, or psychiatric advice. Please take one concrete step today: get to safety, and contact emergency help or a faithful pastor who will protect the vulnerable. God is a refuge for the oppressed (Psalm 9:9; Psalm 46:1), and Christ, our merciful high priest, invites the wounded to draw near for help in time of need (Hebrews 4:14–16). Pray in your own words for protection, wisdom, and justice, and ask a mature believer to pray with you. If you want to share more of what you are facing, I will listen and keep pointing you to Scripture.

question: Why is “You shall not steal” in the Ten Commandments?
answer:
“You shall not steal” is in the Ten Commandments because it belongs to God’s moral law: the holy God who owns all things forbids taking what He has entrusted to your neighbor. It is the eighth command, given at Sinai as part of the covenant summary of how redeemed people are to reflect His justice (Exodus 20:15; Deuteronomy 5:19).

The Ten Commandments are not a random list of social tips. They are God’s own words, written to bind love of God and love of neighbor together (Exodus 31:18; Matthew 22:37–40). Stealing breaks that second love. It treats a neighbor, made in God’s image, as someone whose livelihood, inheritance, or trust may be seized for your gain. Scripture sets this beside other commands that guard human life in community, and Paul later gathers “You shall not steal” under the one word, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Romans 13:9; Leviticus 19:18).

The command also reaches further than a hand in someone else’s purse. In Israel it stood with bans on fraud, oppression, and dishonest measures, because theft can wear respectable clothes (Leviticus 19:11, 13, 35–36). The New Testament does not retire it. The one who stole must stop, work honestly, and learn to give (Ephesians 4:28). Coveting shows that theft often begins in the heart before it reaches the hand (Exodus 20:17; Matthew 15:19).

This week, name one place where you are tempted to take what is not yours, whether money, time, credit, or a small advantage, and replace it with honest work and one concrete act of generosity. The command is good, and it also exposes us, since none of us has loved our neighbor perfectly (Romans 3:23). Its kindness is that it leads us to Christ, who fulfilled the law and bore the curse for lawbreakers, so that sinners may be forgiven and made new (Matthew 5:17; Galatians 3:13, 24).

question: What does it mean that “His mercy endures forever” (Jeremiah 33:11 and Psalm 136)?
answer:
“His mercy endures forever” means that the LORD’s covenant love does not fail, expire, or wear out. The Hebrew word behind the older translation “mercy” is chesed, which the Berean Standard Bible renders “loving devotion.” It is God’s loyal, promise-keeping kindness, stronger than a passing feeling of pity.

In Psalm 136, Israel repeats that line after every work of God, from creation to the exodus and the gift of the land. The same enduring chesed that spread out the heavens also redeemed His people and led them through the wilderness (Psalm 136:1–26). The refrain turns history into thanksgiving. God’s goodness is not an idea floating above life. It is seen in what He has done, and it will not run out.

Jeremiah 33:11 sets the same words in a harder place. Jerusalem is under judgment, yet God promises that joy, wedding songs, and thank offerings will return. Worshipers will again say, “Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (Jeremiah 33:11). Exile does not cancel His covenant mercy. He remains faithful when His people have not been.

This rests on who God is. He declared His name as abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6–7), and Jeremiah later confessed that His loving devotion never fails (Lamentations 3:22–23). Because God does not change, His chesed does not change. In the New Testament that mercy comes to its fullness in Jesus Christ. God, being rich in mercy, made sinners alive with Christ (Ephesians 2:4–5), and the blood of the eternal covenant secures a hope that will not collapse (Hebrews 13:20–21).

This week, read Psalm 136 slowly. After each “His loving devotion endures forever,” name one concrete kindness of God in your own life before you go on. Let that refrain steady both your thanks and your hope when your circumstances feel temporary. Where do you most need to remember that His loving devotion has not run out?

question: Is the Church of God in Christ (COGIC) a good biblical church?
answer:
The Church of God in Christ (COGIC) affirms the essential doctrines of the Christian faith, so its congregations can function as biblical churches when they preach the Gospel clearly, even while differing from a Reformed understanding of the Spirit’s gifts and of sanctification.

COGIC confesses the Trinity, the true deity and true humanity of Jesus Christ, His virgin birth, His sacrificial death for sinners, and His bodily resurrection. These truths stand at the heart of the Gospel. Scripture teaches that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works or by any later spiritual experience (Romans 3:21-26; Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Where a local COGIC church holds and proclaims this Gospel, it stands on solid biblical ground.

The main differences lie in secondary matters. COGIC, shaped by the Holiness and Pentecostal traditions, commonly teaches a definite second work of sanctification and a subsequent baptism in the Holy Spirit evidenced by speaking in tongues. Continuationists argue from Acts and from 1 Corinthians 12-14 that the Spirit still gives these gifts for the church’s life and mission today. I hold the cessationist view: the foundational sign gifts accredited the apostles and the completed revelation of Scripture, so the church now grows through the ordinary means of grace and progressive sanctification by the Spirit (2 Timothy 3:16-17; Hebrews 2:3-4; Philippians 1:6; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Believers still battle remaining sin and are called to ongoing repentance and growth rather than to a single crisis that eradicates the sin nature (Romans 7:14-25; 1 John 1:8-10).

A church proves biblical, whatever its name, by the faithful preaching of Christ, the right practice of believer’s baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and loving discipline that guards the flock (Acts 2:42; Matthew 28:19-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26; Matthew 18:15-17). Local congregations vary, so test what you hear by the written Word (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

If you are weighing a particular COGIC congregation, set aside time this week to read their stated beliefs beside Galatians 2:16 and Ephesians 2:1-10, then ask the pastor how a person can be sure of salvation. Pray for wisdom to treasure Christ’s finished work above every experience, and stay close to a body where Scripture rules.

question: What is the voice of one calling in the wilderness (Isaiah 40:3; John 1:23)?
answer:
The voice of one calling in the wilderness is John the Baptist. He took that title for himself, saying he was the voice Isaiah had foretold (John 1:23; Isaiah 40:3).

Isaiah pictured a herald announcing comfort: the LORD Himself was coming to His people, and the road must be cleared for His arrival (Isaiah 40:1–5). In the Hebrew, the cry can be heard as a call to prepare the LORD’s way in the wilderness. John, and the Gospels after him, also place the caller in the wilderness, which fits where he preached, at Bethany beyond the Jordan (John 1:23; John 1:28; Matthew 3:1–3).

John was not the Christ. He was the forerunner. He preached a baptism of repentance and pointed past himself to Jesus, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:20; John 1:26–29; Mark 1:4). That claim is weighty. Isaiah says the way being prepared is the way of the LORD, Israel’s God. The New Testament applies that coming to Jesus, which belongs to the confession that He is truly God and truly man.

The wilderness voice does not tell sinners to smooth their own record before God. It calls them to repent, to let the crooked be made straight, and to receive the Savior who died and rose for them. If that call reaches you, repent and trust Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read John 1:19–34 slowly, ask God to show you one place where your heart still resists His straight path, and bring that honestly to Him in prayer.

question: What is neonomianism?
answer:
Neonomianism is the error that treats the gospel as a new and milder law, under which God justifies sinners for faith and sincere obedience rather than by the imputed righteousness of Christ received through faith alone.

The name means “new law.” It is associated especially with Richard Baxter in the seventeenth century, and a related dispute surfaced later in Scotland’s Marrow Controversy. Baxter meant to guard against lawlessness. He taught that Christ had satisfied the old covenant of works and purchased easier gospel terms, so that evangelical faith and repentance, sincerely performed, become the righteousness God accepts. Historic Protestant teaching judged that cure worse than the disease, because it shifts the ground of acceptance from Christ’s obedience to ours.

Scripture keeps justification and sanctification distinct. Justification is God’s verdict that a sinner is righteous because of Christ’s life and death, not because of the sinner’s evangelical performance (Romans 3:21–28; Romans 4:4–5; Philippians 3:9). Faith is the empty hand that receives Christ, not a work that itself makes us righteous (Galatians 2:16). Real obedience follows, but it is the fruit of those already accepted, not the legal condition of their acceptance (Romans 8:1–4).

The difference is peace. If God’s verdict waits on how sincere your repentance and obedience have been, you can never be sure you have done enough. If it rests on Christ crucified and risen, credited to you by grace through faith, you obey as a child already loved, not as a defendant still earning a verdict.

question: What does it mean that neither height nor depth separates us from the love of God (Romans 8:39)?
answer:
Neither height nor depth can separate us from the love of God means that no place in all creation, however high or however deep, can cut off those who are in Christ from God’s saving love.

Paul says this at the climax of Romans 8. He has already said there is “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1), and that “if God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). He then names every threat he can think of: “neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). The Greek words behind “height” and “depth” simply mean the upper and lower extremes. In Paul’s world, people also feared spiritual powers thought to rule from the heavens or menace from the abyss. He leaves none of that standing. Height and depth are still part of creation, and no creature can undo what God has done in his Son.

The love in view is not a feeling that rises and falls with our mood. It is God’s love located in Christ Jesus our Lord, the love that justifies sinners and keeps them in union with Christ. That is why this verse is one of the strongest grounds for the perseverance of the saints: those truly in Christ are held by God’s power, not by the strength of their own grip (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:35–39).

So if you are in a high place and feel untouchable, or in a deep place of guilt, grief, or fear and feel forgotten, this promise still stands. This week, read Romans 8:31–39 slowly, and when the fear returns, tell God the truth in your own words: Christ died and rose, and his love holds those who trust him. This promise belongs to those who are in Christ by faith, not to a vague religious feeling.

What height or depth made this verse matter to you?

question: What is the doctrine of preterition?
answer:
The doctrine of preterition is the teaching, found especially in Reformed theology, that God in eternity passes over the non-elect, sovereignly deciding not to grant them the grace of salvation and leaving them in their sins.  
Those who oppose this doctrine maintain that such a passing over would contradict God’s revealed will that none should perish but that all should come to repentance, so condemnation arises only from the sinner’s own rejection of Christ rather than from any prior divine preterition (2 Peter 3:9).  
I affirm the doctrine of preterition as a biblical aspect of the decree of reprobation within unconditional election, because the apostle Paul teaches that God has mercy on whom He desires and hardens whom He desires, grounding the difference not in human willing or running but in God’s merciful purpose (Romans 9:15–18).  
If you belong to Christ, let this stir humble thanks that your salvation rests on His electing love alone, and let it move you to pray for the lost and proclaim the gospel to everyone you can, trusting the Lord to draw His own.

question: Are there supposed to be any rituals in Christianity?
answer:
Yes. Jesus Christ commanded His church to observe two ordinances, baptism and the Lord's Supper, yet these do not save or earn God's favor. People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by ceremonies (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:21-28).

Under the Old Covenant, God appointed many ceremonies that foreshadowed the Messiah. Christ fulfilled those shadows by His perfect life, penal substitutionary death, and bodily resurrection, so the church no longer keeps the ceremonial law (Hebrews 10:1-14; Colossians 2:16-17). Baptism is a washing with water that pictures union with Christ in His death and resurrection (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3-4). The Lord's Supper uses bread and the cup to remember and proclaim His body and blood given for the forgiveness of sins until He returns (1 Corinthians 11:23-26). He is spiritually present to strengthen those who receive the Supper by faith, but the meal itself is never the ground of acceptance with God.

Some Christians baptize the infant children of believers, seeing a continuity of covenant signs given to households. Scripture, as I understand it, shows the baptism of those who personally repent and believe, by immersion, as the outward sign of inward grace already received. These differences are secondary and must not hide the gospel. What God rejects is any outward form that replaces a heart trusting Christ (Mark 7:6-13). True worship is in spirit and truth (John 4:23-24).

The early church also devoted itself to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers (Acts 2:42). Word, prayer, and the ordinances are means of grace by which the Spirit carries forward sanctification. A concrete next step is to read Matthew 28:18-20 and 1 Corinthians 11:23-29 this week, then ask the elders of a local Bible-teaching church how they practice these commands and whether your hope rests wholly on Jesus who died and rose for sinners.

question: What is the Presbyterian Church in America (PCA), and what do they believe?
answer:
The Presbyterian Church in America (PCA) is a confessional Reformed denomination in the United States, formed in 1973 by churches that left the Presbyterian Church in the United States in order to hold the Bible as the inspired, inerrant Word of God and to keep the historic Reformed faith.

Its officers subscribe to the Westminster Confession of Faith and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. On the essentials, the PCA confesses what the church has long held: the Trinity, Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man (the hypostatic union), the authority of Scripture, justification by grace alone through faith alone, and the necessity of Christ’s penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection (John 1:1-14; 2 Timothy 3:16-17; Romans 3:21-26; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). A person is not made right with God by church membership or moral effort, but by trusting Christ.

What marks the PCA more particularly is covenant theology, Presbyterian government, and infant baptism. A local church is led by a session of elders, accountable to a regional presbytery and then to the General Assembly. They appeal to a biblical pattern of elder oversight and wider counsel (Acts 15:6-29; 1 Timothy 5:17), and they hold that the ordained offices of elder and deacon are for qualified men (1 Timothy 3:1-13). In the Lord’s Supper they affirm Christ’s spiritual presence: the bread and cup remain bread and cup, yet believers truly feed on Christ by faith (1 Corinthians 10:16). Baptism, ordinarily by sprinkling or pouring, is taught as a sign and seal of the covenant of grace for professing believers and for their children (Acts 2:38-39).

That last point is a real difference among Christians who love the same Gospel. The strongest case for infant baptism is that God still deals with households in covenant, so the sign once given in circumcision now comes to believers’ children in baptism (Genesis 17:7; Colossians 2:11-12). I hold believer’s baptism, because the New Testament joins the sign to personal repentance and faith, and the new-covenant people are those who know the Lord (Acts 2:38; Jeremiah 31:31-34). Church government is likewise secondary: Presbyterian order stresses wider accountability, while elder-led congregational churches stress the responsibility of each local body. Faithful Christians may differ here without breaking fellowship in the Gospel.

If you are looking at a PCA church, spend several Sundays under the Word, read the Westminster Shorter Catechism, and ask the elders how they shepherd people in baptism, discipline, and mission. Test everything by Scripture, and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

Are you comparing the PCA with a Baptist or another Reformed church on a particular point?

question: Where is God now? Where is God when it hurts?
answer:
If you are hurting, it can feel as though God has gone quiet, or gone away. That ache is real, and Scripture does not scold you for asking where He is.

God is near. He is not a remote idea watching from a safe distance. The Bible teaches that there is nowhere we can flee from His presence, and that the LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 139:7-10; Psalm 34:18). He is present now as the living God who upholds all things, and He draws especially close to those who are crushed.

Many people ask how a loving and powerful God can allow such pain. That question has weight. Silence can feel like absence, and suffering can feel like proof that no one good is in charge. The Bible takes hurt seriously and does not call evil good. Jesus stood at the tomb of a friend and wept (John 11:35). He is not unable to sympathize with our weakness (Hebrews 4:15-16).

The clearest answer is the incarnation and the cross. The eternal Son took on our flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). He became a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3). We have all sinned and need a Savior, not only relief from pain. On the cross Christ bore the penalty our sin deserved, so that guilty people could be reconciled to a holy God. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily. His resurrection means death and pain do not get the last word. One day He will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more mourning, crying, or pain (Revelation 21:4).

Where is He now? He is risen and reigning, and He has promised His people, "I am with you always" (Matthew 28:20). Nothing in all creation can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God (Romans 8:38-39). Even the darkest valley is a place where the Shepherd is present, not a place He has abandoned (Psalm 23:4). He cares for you, and He invites you to cast your anxiety on Him (1 Peter 5:7).

If the hurt is heavy this week, do not carry it alone. Read Psalm 23 and Psalm 34 once each day, and tell God plainly what aches, even if your words are few. Ask a pastor or a trusted believer to walk with you.

If you have been keeping Him at a distance, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What hurt is weighing on you? If you want to say more, I am here to listen.

question: What is the just war theory?
answer:
Just war theory, often called the just war tradition, is a historic Christian moral framework for judging when war may be permitted and how it must be fought if it is waged.

It treats war as a grave and sorrowful last measure for restraining evil, not as something good in itself. Shaped especially by Augustine and later by Thomas Aquinas, it distinguishes two questions. Jus ad bellum, justice in entering war, asks for a just cause such as defense of the innocent, lawful authority, right intention, last resort, and a reasonable hope that the good secured will outweigh the harm. Jus in bello, justice in the conduct of war, requires proportionality and discrimination, so that force stays limited and people not engaged in the fighting are not deliberately targeted.

This tradition tries to hold together biblical truths that can seem to pull apart. Scripture teaches that governing authorities are God’s servants and bear the sword to punish evil (Romans 13:1–4; 1 Peter 2:13–14). It also calls disciples to be peacemakers and to love their enemies (Matthew 5:9; Matthew 5:44). The church’s mission is the gospel, not conquest, yet love of neighbor may sometimes require protecting the weak from violent harm.

Faithful Christians have not all agreed, and this question does not decide who belongs to Christ. Some, especially in pacifist traditions, believe Jesus’ teaching and example rule out all killing, so they refuse military force and entrust justice to God. Others, including many in the Reformed tradition, believe a Christian may support or serve in war when just war criteria are truly met. Scripture gives moral principles rather than a modern military code, so conscience and humility matter (Romans 14:1–5). I hold, as one reading within historic Christianity and not as a test of orthodoxy, that the civil magistrate may wage just war and that a Christian may participate with a clear conscience when those conditions are satisfied.

If a decision about service or a present conflict is before you, set aside time to pray, read Romans 13 and Matthew 5 slowly, and seek counsel from your pastors or elders before you act. Nations may fight, but lasting peace belongs to the Lord Jesus, the Prince of Peace, who will judge rightly and make all things new (Isaiah 9:6; Revelation 21:4). If a particular conflict or calling is on your mind, you are welcome to say more.

question: What does it mean that women should have a gentle and quiet spirit (1 Peter 3:4)?
answer:
A gentle and quiet spirit is the unfading beauty of a meek, peaceful heart that trusts God, which Peter says is precious in His sight (1 Peter 3:4). It is not a command for a woman to erase her personality, never speak, or live in fear.

Peter is writing to wives, including some whose husbands do not believe the word, in a Greco-Roman world where a wife's faith could bring real tension at home (1 Peter 3:1-2). He contrasts beauty that depends on braided hair, gold, or fine clothes with "the inner disposition of the heart" (1 Peter 3:3-4). The Greek word behind "gentle" belongs to the same family Jesus uses of Himself: "I am gentle and humble in heart" (Matthew 11:29). It means strength yielded to God, not weakness or passivity. "Quiet" means tranquil and undisturbed, the opposite of anxious strife and restless display. That is why Peter can say these women hope in God and "do not give way to fear" (1 Peter 3:5-6). A quiet spirit is calm trust, not a gag.

This virtue is Christlike, and gentleness is a fruit of the Spirit for every believer, men and women alike (Galatians 5:22-23). In this passage Peter applies it to a wife's witness: her settled hope in God can commend the gospel when arguments cannot. Scripture still honors women of courage, wisdom, and faithful speech. What God treasures here is an inner adorning, a heart being sanctified rather than a life driven by fear or the need to control.

If this verse has felt heavy, bring that weight to the Lord in your own words. This week, read 1 Peter 3:1-6 beside Matthew 11:28-30, and ask Him to show you one place where fear is louder than trust. Has this verse been a comfort to you, or has it felt like a burden?

question: What does it mean to be free from sin?
answer:
To be free from sin means that, by union with Jesus Christ, you are released from sin’s condemning penalty and from its ruling power, though not yet from every trace of its presence.

Sin is not a minor flaw. It is rebellion against a holy God, and its wage is death (Romans 6:23). In John 8, Jesus speaks to people who insisted they had never been enslaved, and He uses the ordinary picture of a household slave who has no permanent standing. “Everyone who sins is a slave to sin,” and only the Son can set such a person free (John 8:34; John 8:36). We cannot liberate ourselves.

God met that bondage in the gospel. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross in penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He is Lord. Through faith in Him, God justifies the ungodly: He counts Christ’s righteousness to us and cancels our condemnation. “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). That is freedom from sin’s penalty, received by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by cleaning yourself up first.

Freedom also means a change of masters. Our old self was crucified with Christ so that we would no longer be slaves to sin (Romans 6:6–7). “Sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace,” and “you have been set free from sin and have become slaves to righteousness” (Romans 6:14; Romans 6:18). This is sanctification. The Holy Spirit progressively puts sin to death in us and grows real obedience. It is not permission to keep sinning. Christ set us free so we would not submit again to a yoke of slavery, and we must not use that freedom as an opportunity for the flesh (Galatians 5:1; Galatians 5:13).

It does not yet mean you never sin. “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” while confession meets a faithful God who forgives and cleanses (1 John 1:8–9). Full freedom from sin’s presence waits until Christ appears and we are made like Him (1 John 3:2). Some Christians in the Wesleyan tradition argue that God can so cleanse the heart in this life that willful sin no longer reigns, because the Spirit who justifies also promises to purify. I hold progressive sanctification as one faithful reading within historic Christianity: real freedom from sin’s dominion now, with a real remaining struggle until glorification, because Scripture both declares us free and still calls us to put sin to death (Romans 6:18; Colossians 3:5; 1 John 1:8). Those truly in Christ are kept by God’s power and will not finally fall away.

If you belong to Christ, take one concrete step this week. Name a specific sin that still grips you, confess it to the Lord in your own words, perhaps with Psalm 51 or Romans 6 open before you, and ask a mature believer in your church to walk with you toward the opposite obedience.

If you are not yet trusting Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What feels heaviest to you right now: the guilt of past sin, a habit you cannot break, or uncertainty about whether Christ has really set you free?

question: Is God man-made? Did man create the idea of God?
answer:
Many people ask this because God can look like a comfort invented to face death, or like a story cultures used to explain what they could not control. Those concerns notice something real: people do invent gods. They do not, however, describe the God of Scripture. God is not man-made, and man did not create Him.

The Bible teaches the opposite order. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). We are made in His image, which is why a sense of God, of right and wrong, and of meaning shows up so widely (Genesis 1:27). Christians believe this awareness is a response to a God who is already there, not the cause of His existence. Theologians call this God's aseity: He exists from Himself. He is not kept in being by our belief, our temples, or our arguments. We are the ones who depend on Him.

Scripture itself separates man-made gods from the living God. When Paul spoke in Athens, he said that the God who made the world does not live in temples built by human hands, and that we should not think of the Divine Being as an image formed by man's skill and imagination (Acts 17:24; Acts 17:29). Idols are fashioned by us. The true God gives everyone life and breath, and He is not far from each one of us (Acts 17:25; Acts 17:27).

Paul also says that what may be known about God is plain, because God has shown it. His eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen in what has been made, so people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). The deeper issue is not a lack of traces, but that we suppress the truth in unrighteousness and exchange the glory of the immortal God for lesser things (Romans 1:18; Romans 1:21-25). Scripture calls that sin. It leaves us guilty before a holy God, since all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). We need a Savior, not a better theory.

God has spoken most clearly in His Son. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. He lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute, bearing the penalty sinners deserve, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (John 1:1-3; John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That resurrection is God's public proof that Jesus is Lord and that He will judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31). Forgiveness is not earned by constructing a more impressive idea of God. It is given by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

If you have lived as though God were optional, imaginary, or useful only when convenient, turn from that and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A concrete next step is to read Acts 17:22-31 and Romans 1:18-25 slowly this week, and to tell God your doubts directly, asking Him to make Himself known. If you can, bring the same questions to a pastor or a mature believer who will sit with you patiently.

What has made the thought that God might be man-made seem most convincing to you?

question: What is the significance of the statement “God is within her; she will not fall” in Psalm 46:5?
answer:
Psalm 46:5 means that the city of God stands secure because God Himself dwells in her midst, so she will not be overthrown. Her safety is not self-made. It is the gift of God's presence.

"She" is the city of God in the previous verse, "the holy place where the Most High dwells" (Psalm 46:4). The psalm sets that city against a shaking world. Waters roar, mountains tremble, and nations rage, yet God's people are told not to fear, because God is their refuge and strength (Psalm 46:1-3, 6). Whether the line is rendered "she will not fall" or "she will not be moved," the sense is the same: she will not totter, slip, or be toppled. The ground of that promise is not her walls or armies, but the God who is within her.

In its first setting, this is the language of Zion. God had chosen Jerusalem as the place where He caused His name to dwell and where He met His covenant people (Psalm 46:4-5; 1 Kings 8:13). That is why the song returns to the same confession: the LORD of Hosts is with us, and the God of Jacob is our fortress (Psalm 46:7, 11). The theological term for this nearness is divine immanence, God's real covenant presence among His people, joined to His sovereign power.

The New Testament gathers up that hope in Jesus Christ, Immanuel, which means "God with us" (Matthew 1:23). Through His perfect life, His death on the cross for sinners, and His bodily resurrection, He reconciles His people to God. By the Spirit He now dwells in the church, so that believers are being built together into a dwelling place for God (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:19-22). The church's safety, like Zion's, rests on Christ, not on her size, reputation, or calm circumstances. The promise reaches its fullness when God dwells with His people forever and death is no more (Revelation 21:3-4).

If the ground under your own feet feels unsteady, let this verse turn you from self-reliance to the God who keeps His people. Read Psalm 46 once each day this week, and in prayer name one fear, asking the Lord to be your refuge as He has promised to be the refuge of His city.

Would you like help seeing how this psalm speaks into a particular fear or season you are walking through?

question: What does the Bible say about worship?
answer:
The Bible teaches that worship is the wholehearted honor, reverence, and service that belong to God alone, offered both when His people gather and in the whole of daily life. It is not first a musical style or a feeling. It is the creature’s right response to the holy God who made us and redeems us.

Scripture gives this honor to the Lord and to no other. When tempted, Jesus answered from Deuteronomy, “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:10; Deuteronomy 6:13). The first commandment forbids bowing to any rival (Exodus 20:3–5). In the ancient world, worship was often a set of rituals meant to secure a god’s favor. Israel’s worship was different. It was a covenant response to the God who had already redeemed them: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2).

Jesus made the heart of worship plain to the woman at the well. She asked whether true worship belonged on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem. He said the Father seeks worshipers who worship “in spirit and in truth,” for “God is Spirit” (John 4:23–24). True worship is not tied to a sacred hill. It is sincere, spiritual, and shaped by God’s Word, not by human tradition. God rejects honor that stays on the lips while the heart is far from Him (Matthew 15:8–9).

Worship is also larger than a service. In view of God’s mercy, Paul urges believers to present their bodies as living sacrifices, “which is your spiritual service of worship” (Romans 12:1). The prophets warned worshipers who loved the ceremonies but neglected justice, mercy, and a humble walk with God (Isaiah 1:11–17; Micah 6:6–8). Whatever we love, trust, and serve most is what we worship, which is why Scripture can call greed idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

When the church gathers, worship is corporate and centered on Christ. The early believers devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42). They sang psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude, letting the word of Christ dwell richly among them (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19), and they did not neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:24–25). They drew near through Jesus, the great High Priest, whose death and resurrection opened a new and living way, and they offered a sacrifice of praise (Hebrews 10:19–22; Hebrews 13:15). Heaven itself worships the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:9–13). Acceptable worship is filled with gratitude, and also with reverence and awe, “for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29).

Faithful Christians differ on musical style and the exact order of a service. Scripture is more explicit about the object, the heart, and the chief means of worship than about every outward form, so those differences call for humility and charity, not for division (Romans 14:1–4). What must not be compromised is this: we worship the one true God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, through Jesus Christ, by the Spirit, according to Scripture (Philippians 3:3).

This week, read Psalm 95 slowly before the Lord, then gather with a Bible-teaching church ready to hear His Word and to give Him thanks, not merely to judge the music.

question: What is more important, the death of Christ or His resurrection?
answer:
Neither the death of Christ nor His resurrection is more important than the other. Both stand together as the Gospel of first importance, and Scripture never asks us to choose between them.

Paul delivered as of first importance that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, and that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). His death is the penal substitution by which the sinless Son bore the wrath our sins deserved and reconciled us to the holy God (Romans 5:8-10; 2 Corinthians 5:21). His bodily resurrection is the Father’s declaration that the sacrifice was accepted, that death is defeated, and that believers are justified (Romans 4:25). If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17).

Without the cross there is no atonement for sin. Without the empty tomb there is no living Lord and no sure hope that the atonement has prevailed. They are one saving work. When guilt or the fear of death presses on you, look to the crucified and risen Jesus: your debt is paid and the grave is conquered. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life.

How does holding both truths together shape the way you face guilt or hope today?

question: What is the emerging / emergent church movement?
answer:
The emerging church, often called the emergent church, was a late twentieth and early twenty-first century movement that tried to reshape Christian belief and practice for a postmodern culture. It prized conversation, community, mystery, and mission, but important parts of it also questioned or redefined doctrines historic Christianity has treated as essential.

It grew especially in the 1990s and 2000s in North America and the United Kingdom, through voices such as Brian McLaren, Rob Bell, and Doug Pagitt, and through networks such as Emergent Village. Many of its leaders were reacting to cold modern certainty, consumer-style church life, and a church that seemed distant from its neighbors. They often reached for older worship forms, neighborhood presence, and concern for justice.

The movement was not all one thing. Some churches called emerging mainly changed methods, music, or mission strategy while still confessing the gospel. Others, more often called emergent, treated doctrine itself as an open conversation. In that second stream, the authority of Scripture, the necessity of Christ’s atoning death, the reality of final judgment, and Jesus as the only way to the Father were frequently softened or set aside. The “emergent” label has largely faded, but some of those instincts remain in churches that prize experience and inclusion over the clarity of God’s Word.

Scripture does not leave those matters optional. It is God-breathed and sufficient for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The gospel is that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by a vague spirituality or moral effort (Romans 3:21-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). Paul warns that a different message is no gospel at all (Galatians 1:6-9).

Two terms mark the line. Sola Scriptura means Scripture, not the shifting mood of a community, is the final authority. Penal substitution means Christ bore the penalty our sins deserved so guilty people could be reconciled to a holy God. Where the emerging conversation treated those truths as optional or harmful, it moved outside historic orthodox Christianity, however real its desire to love neighbors.

Not every criticism of church culture was wrong. The church is sent into the world without becoming like the world, and Paul became all things to all people so that some might be saved (John 17:14-18; 1 Corinthians 9:19-23). Faithful Christians may differ on worship style, ministry methods, and how best to serve a city. Those are matters of Christian liberty, not the gospel itself (Romans 14:1-4). What cannot be surrendered is “the faith that was once for all entrusted to the saints” (Jude 1:3).

If you are weighing this, read Galatians slowly this week, noting what Paul says must never be compromised, and then talk it through with a pastor who will open the Bible with you rather than only trade impressions. Hold fast to Christ, and speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:14-15).

question: What does the Bible say about underage drinking?
answer:
The Bible does not set a legal drinking age. That line is drawn by civil law, and it differs by country and even by household. What Scripture does address plainly is drunkenness, self-control, wisdom for the young, and obedience to parents and governing authorities.

Drunkenness is sin. Paul commands believers not to get drunk on wine, but to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18). Proverbs says wine is a mocker and strong drink a brawler, and that whoever is led astray by them is not wise (Proverbs 20:1). The same book describes the misery, confusion, and wounds of those who linger over wine (Proverbs 23:29-35). Drunkenness stands among the works of the flesh, and those who practice such things without repentance show that they are outside the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:19-21; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10).

Scripture does not treat alcohol itself as unclean. Jesus made wine at the wedding in Cana (John 2:1-11). The psalmist speaks of wine that gladdens the heart as part of God's provision (Psalm 104:14-15). Paul tells Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). The issue is the heart, the amount, the setting, and the effect, not a total ban on fermented drink.

For someone under the legal age, two further commands decide the matter in practice. Children are to obey their parents in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1-3). Every person is to be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:13-17). Where the law forbids alcohol before a certain age, drinking anyway is not Christian liberty. It is disobedience. Liberty is never a license to sin or to shrug off God-ordained authority (Galatians 5:13; 1 Corinthians 6:12). Laws are not identical everywhere. Some places allow a parent to give a child a small amount at home. Even then, a son or daughter still owes obedience to that parent, and love should keep anyone from causing another person to stumble (Romans 14:13-21).

Youth adds a call to wisdom. Paul tells Timothy to flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace (2 Timothy 2:22). Alcohol clouds judgment, and the young are summoned to grow in wisdom rather than chase what dulls it (Proverbs 1:1-7).

Faithful Christians differ on whether adults should drink in moderation or abstain altogether. Some refuse alcohol for the sake of witness, wisdom, or a brother or sister with a tender conscience. Others receive moderate, legal use with thanksgiving, never to excess. Both can honor Christ if drunkenness is rejected. Neither view excuses illegal drinking.

If this question is close to home, take one clear step this week. Read Proverbs 23:29-35 and Romans 13:1-5, then speak honestly with a parent or a trusted elder about the pressure you feel. Pray to the Lord for self-control, and ask Him to make obedience a joy rather than a grind. If you have already drunk illegally or to excess, do not hide it. Such were some of God's people, and they were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11). Turn from it, trust Christ, who died and rose for sinners, and ask a mature believer to walk with you. That is the path of sanctification, the Spirit's patient work of making you more like Christ.

question: Will there be a great apostasy / falling away during the end times?
answer:
Scripture teaches that a rebellion will occur before the day of the Lord. Paul states that this day will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed (2 Thessalonians 2:3), and Jesus warned that many will fall away while the love of most grows cold (Matthew 24:10-12).

The exact scale and timing of this falling away, often called the great apostasy, belong to eschatology, a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may disagree. Prophetic texts use vivid imagery and do not supply one detailed timeline that every interpreter arranges identically, so differences here need not divide those who share the gospel.

One historic view, common among premillennial Christians, expects a future widespread departure from the faith in the period immediately before Christ returns, bound up with the revealing of the man of lawlessness. Another historic view, held by many amillennial and postmillennial believers, understands the last days as the entire age since Christ first came (Hebrews 1:2), so that abandoning the faith remains a recurring danger (1 Timothy 4:1; 2 Timothy 3:1) even while the rebellion of 2 Thessalonians 2 still precedes the end. Paul notes that the mystery of lawlessness is already at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7). In the midst of these warnings the Lord Jesus promises that His sheep will never perish and that no one can snatch them from His hand (John 10:28-29), and those who depart show they did not truly belong to Him (1 John 2:19).

Because this is not essential to the faith, believers should extend liberty and charity rather than quarrel over opinions (Romans 14:1). The shared duty is to love the truth and remain watchful. A concrete step is to read 2 Thessalonians 2 and Matthew 24 together this week, asking God for a steadfast heart that holds fast to Christ until He comes.

question: Should all pronouns referring to God be capitalized?
answer:
Capitalizing pronouns that refer to God is a matter of editorial style and Christian liberty, not a command of Scripture or a mark of orthodoxy. Faithful believers have long differed here because the Bible never requires a particular English capitalization practice, and the ancient Hebrew and Greek texts did not set divine pronouns apart by special capitals.

One common practice is to capitalize pronouns such as He, Him, and His when they clearly refer to God, as a visible sign of reverence that can help a reader notice the divine reference. Another widespread practice, followed by many careful English translations, is to keep those pronouns in ordinary lowercase, holding that honor is shown by truthful and reverent words rather than by typography.

Romans 14:1-5 teaches us to welcome one another and not to quarrel over opinions where God has left us free. You may capitalize divine pronouns if that habit stirs you to worship, or you may leave them uncapitalized with a clear conscience. Either way, do not bind another believer’s conscience or pass judgment where Scripture is silent (Romans 14:10-13). Let your words remain clear, truthful, and full of grace (Colossians 4:6).

question: What is Kabbalah?
answer:
Kabbalah is a mystical, esoteric stream within Judaism that seeks hidden knowledge of God through symbolic readings of Scripture, meditation, and a "received" tradition, rather than through the plain teaching God has given.

The Hebrew word behind Kabbalah means something received or handed down. Its classic texts include the Sefer Yetzirah, the Bahir, and especially the Zohar, which took literary form in medieval Spain, with major later development in the sixteenth-century teaching of Isaac Luria. Central ideas include the Ein Sof, God as infinite and beyond ordinary comprehension, and the ten sefirot, emanations or attributes through which the divine is said to relate to the world. Some streams also teach reincarnation and elaborate letter and name mysticism. This is not the same as ordinary Jewish prayer and Torah study. Many Jewish teachers have treated it as restricted or even hazardous, and a recent popular "Kabbalah" has also circulated far outside its original setting, often detached from Jewish life altogether.
