Christians should not practice Kabbalah or treat it as a way to God. Scripture says the secret things belong to the Lord, while what He has revealed belongs to His people (Deuteronomy 29:29). God has spoken finally in His Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Paul warns against being taken captive by philosophy and empty deceit, and against visions and angel speculation that go beyond Christ (Colossians 2:8; Colossians 2:18). The Bible also forbids divination and occult inquiry (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Isaiah 8:19–20). A system that promises secret access through emanations, codes, or divine names conflicts with the sufficiency of Scripture and with the Creator-creature distinction: God is not a set of forces to be mapped or managed. He is the holy Lord who reveals Himself and saves sinners.

People are often drawn to Kabbalah because ordinary religion can feel thin and they long for depth. That longing is understandable, but it is answered in Christ, not in a hidden tradition. We are sinners, separated from a holy God, and we are reconciled not by technique but by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, who died for sins, was buried, and rose bodily (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Ephesians 2:8–9; John 14:6). Renaissance "Christian Kabbalah" tried to baptize these ideas. That does not make them biblical.

If this has stirred your curiosity or your practice, set those methods aside, read the Gospel of John slowly, and talk with a pastor who will open the Bible with you. If you want to know God, repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you. What led you to ask about Kabbalah?

question: Should a Christian be a prepper or in any way involved with doomsday prepping?
answer:
Whether a Christian should be a prepper is a matter of Christian liberty, not an essential of the faith. Faithful believers may differ because Scripture gives principles of wisdom and trust in God’s providence rather than a detailed rule for modern survival scenarios, and judgments about risk and the end times vary.

One approach sees measured preparation as wise stewardship. Joseph stored grain ahead of famine under God’s guidance (Genesis 41:33-36), the ant gathers food in season (Proverbs 6:6-8), and the prudent person sees danger and takes refuge (Proverbs 22:3). Providing for one’s household is commended (1 Timothy 5:8). In this view, keeping basic supplies for storms, shortages, or local crises can honor God when it stays generous and does not become an idol.

Another approach warns that doomsday prepping easily turns into fear-driven self-reliance that competes with trust in the Father’s care. Jesus tells His disciples not to worry about food, drink, or clothing, because your heavenly Father knows your needs and you are to seek first His kingdom (Matthew 6:25-34). Our refuge is the Lord, not a bunker (Psalm 46:1), and life does not consist in the abundance of possessions (Luke 12:15). Withdrawal from the church and from neighbors can work against love and against gathering as the body of Christ.

In the freedom described in Romans 14:1-4, neither the careful planner nor the one who lives more simply should despise the other, so long as each acts from faith and not from greed or panic. A humble path many find faithful is ordinary preparedness without obsession: keep a reasonable reserve for foreseeable hardships, stay ready to share with those in need, remain rooted in a local church, and rest your hope in Christ’s return rather than in human survival plans. No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), so spiritual readiness matters more than stockpiles.

This week, read Matthew 6:25-34 slowly and ask the Lord to search your motives. If fear is driving you more than wisdom, bring that to your pastor or a trusted believer and let them help you walk in peace. God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control (2 Timothy 1:7).

question: What is the church?
answer:
The church is the people of God, the assembly of those called by the gospel and united to Jesus Christ. It is not first a building, a brand, or a human organization, but the body of Christ, the company of men and women He has purchased with His blood.

The New Testament word is *ekklesia*, an assembly called together. Jesus said, "I will build My church" (Matthew 16:18). Paul calls that church Christ's body, of which He is the Head (Colossians 1:18; 1 Corinthians 12:27), and the bride for whom He gave Himself (Ephesians 5:25-27). Peter uses the language of Israel's calling and applies it to those who trust Christ: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation (1 Peter 2:9-10). In Him, Jew and Gentile are built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Ephesians 2:19-22).

Christians have long spoken of the church in two related ways. The universal church is the whole company of the elect, everyone truly joined to Christ by faith, across every age and place. Theologians sometimes call this the invisible church, because only the Lord perfectly sees the heart. The local church is a visible congregation of professing believers who gather to hear Scripture, pray, love one another, and practice baptism and the Lord's Supper (Acts 2:41-42; Hebrews 10:24-25). Some historic traditions stress the church mainly as a worldwide institution continued through bishops. The stronger biblical emphasis is that Christ Himself gathers His people by the Word and the Spirit, and that this people becomes visible wherever believers assemble under His lordship.

A true church is marked by the faithful preaching of the gospel, the right practice of the ordinances, and loving discipline that guards holiness (Matthew 18:15-20; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). In a Reformed Baptist understanding, those congregations are made up of baptized believers and are shepherded by elders, while remaining a local body accountable to Christ. Other faithful Christians order leadership differently, and that difference should not break our love, even where we cannot share the same practice.

If you belong to Christ, do not try to follow Him alone. This week, commit to a local church where the Bible is opened, Christ is honored, and you can both receive care and serve others. The Christian life is learned in the company of the saints (Hebrews 10:24-25).

question: Does a cashless society have anything to do with the end times?
answer:
A cashless society is not itself the mark of the beast, nor does Scripture treat it as proof that the end has arrived. Revelation 13:16-17 describes a mark on the right hand or the forehead, without which no one can buy or sell, and that mark is bound to the beast’s name and to worship of him (Revelation 13:15-17; Revelation 14:9-11). The passage never mentions coins, paper money, cards, or digital payment. It describes coerced allegiance.

How to read this is a matter of eschatology, a non-essential on which faithful Christians may disagree. Revelation is apocalyptic literature, full of symbols, and the Bible does not give a timetable of modern technology, so unity does not require one reading (Romans 14:1-4). Some Christians, often in futurist readings, expect a coming ruler to impose a literal economic mark, and they see cashless or biometric systems as a possible preparation for that pressure. Others, in preterist, historicist, and idealist readings, take the mark as a symbol of loyalty to anti-Christian power, whether under the Roman imperial cult or whenever people must choose between Christ and the world’s demands. On that view, exclusion from buying and selling pictures the social cost of refusing idolatry, not a specific payment method. The hand and forehead also echo Israel’s call to bind God’s words there (Deuteronomy 6:6-8), so the contrast is ownership: the beast’s mark, or the Lamb’s name (Revelation 14:1).

A payment system becomes spiritually dangerous when it is joined to a demand that people deny Christ or give another lord the worship that belongs to God alone. Ordinary caution about privacy and unjust control is wisdom. Treating every financial change as a prophetic countdown is not. No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and it is not ours to decode every headline (Acts 1:7). Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11; Revelation 22:12). The urgent question is not which currency we use, but whether we have turned from sin and trusted him. He died for sinners and rose bodily, and salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in him alone, not by works or by surviving the right economic system. If you have not yet done so, repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

This week, read Revelation 13 and 14 in one sitting, then talk with your pastor about what the passage stresses, endurance and worship of the Lamb, rather than chasing online theories. If worry about the future prompted this, bring that concern to the Lord in prayer and ask him for a steadfast heart.

What led you to ask this?

question: I am a former Catholic. Should I continue to go to Catholic Church so I can reach people for Christ?
answer:
Your longing to reach people for Christ is a good and godly desire, but you should not keep attending a Catholic church as your regular place of worship in order to evangelize. Worship the Lord where His gospel is preached clearly, and love Catholic people from that settled place.

Many Catholics sincerely revere Jesus, treasure parts of Scripture, and show real moral seriousness. We can thank God for every true glimpse of Christ among them. At the same time, official Roman Catholic teaching denies a core truth of the faith: that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, apart from works. Scripture says, "For we maintain that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law" (Romans 3:28; see also Ephesians 2:8-9). The Council of Trent formally rejected that gospel. Paul did not treat a different way of being made right with God as a small disagreement. He warned that a contrary gospel is no gospel at all (Galatians 1:6-9). Staying week after week inside that system can dull your own confidence in Christ’s finished work and send a mixed message to the people you hope to help.

The Mass itself presses the issue. It presents the Eucharist as a sacrifice offered for sins. Hebrews teaches that Christ offered one sacrifice for sins for all time and then sat down, because redemption was accomplished (Hebrews 10:12-14). Prayers directed to Mary and the saints, together with teachings on merit and purgatory, also obscure the Bible’s claim that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). God seeks worshipers who worship Him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). Your regular church home should be a congregation where that gospel is loved, preached, and lived.

Leaving the Mass does not mean abandoning Catholic friends, family, or neighbors. Jesus drew near to people who did not yet believe Him, and Paul reasoned with others in their own settings without joining false worship (Luke 15:1-2; Acts 17:16-17). Keep those relationships. Ask honest questions. Tell your own story of how Christ saved you by His death and resurrection, not by your merits or the sacraments. Invite someone to read a Gospel with you. Pray for them by name. Occasional presence at a family wedding or funeral, without receiving the Eucharist, can sometimes be an act of love. That is different from making Catholic worship your pattern so you can "reach people." A confused witness rarely clarifies Christ.

This week, do two simple things. Commit to a local church where the Bible is taught faithfully and the gospel of justification is clear, and ask a pastor how you can grow and serve there (Hebrews 10:24-25). Then choose one Catholic person you care about and invite them to read the Gospel of John with you. Bring both steps to the Lord in prayer, asking for wisdom, courage, and genuine love (James 1:5; James 5:16).

What relationships are heaviest on your heart right now, and what first convinced you to leave the Catholic Church?

question: What does the Bible say about world missions?
answer:
The Bible presents world missions as God’s purpose to make disciples of all nations through the proclamation of the gospel of Jesus Christ, so that people from every people group would worship Him.

God’s plan was never limited to one family or nation. He promised Abraham that in him “all the families of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). The prophets looked ahead to the Servant of the Lord as “a light for the nations,” that God’s salvation would reach the ends of the earth (Isaiah 49:6). The psalms likewise summon all peoples to praise the Lord (Psalm 67:1–4; Psalm 96:1–3).

That promise comes to its center in Christ. After His death and resurrection, Jesus gave the Great Commission: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:18–20). He told His followers they would be His witnesses “in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The church at Antioch obeyed by setting apart and sending Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:1–3), and the book of Acts traces that witness outward.

The message of mission is the gospel, not moral improvement or cultural export. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). At the heart of that good news is penal substitution: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Paul states the missionary logic plainly: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” Yet how can they call on Him unless they believe, and how can they believe unless they hear, and how can they hear without a preacher who is sent (Romans 10:13–15)? Jesus is the only mediator between God and man (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5).

The aim is disciples, not mere decisions, and the end is worship. Scripture looks forward to a multitude from every tribe, language, people, and nation praising the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:9; Revelation 7:9). Until Christ returns, the church is sent as ambassadors of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18–20).

A concrete next step is to ask your local church elders how you can pray, give, welcome, send, or go, and this week to pray by name for one people group that has little access to the gospel while looking for one person near you with whom you can speak of Christ.

If you have never turned from your sin and trusted Jesus, the mission begins with you. Repent and trust in Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What part of the Bible’s call to the nations are you most wanting to understand or obey right now?

question: How should we live our lives in light of our identity in Christ?
answer:
We live from our identity in Christ, not in order to earn it. United to him by faith, we are justified, adopted, and made new, so we walk in holiness, love, and hope by the Spirit rather than striving to become acceptable to God.

God is holy, and every one of us has sinned and falls short of his glory (Romans 3:23). We cannot build a righteous identity by effort or reputation. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). By grace alone, through faith alone, sinners are united to him. That union is the root of Christian identity. If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted him, begin there: repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

For those who are in Christ, the order matters. Justification is God's once-for-all declaration that you are righteous in Christ, not a prize you keep by performance (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8-9). Because that verdict is already yours, you are free to obey. You have died with Christ and been raised with him, so you reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God (Romans 6:4, 11). You are a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). Your failures, status, and wounds do not get the last word over what God has said about you in his Son.

That identity then takes shape in daily life through progressive sanctification, the Spirit's patient work of making us more like Christ:

- Set your mind where your life is hidden. Seek the things above, where Christ is seated, and let that hope govern your choices (Colossians 3:1-4).
- Put off the old and put on the new. Put to death sexual immorality, greed, anger, and lying, and put on compassion, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, and love (Colossians 3:5-14; Ephesians 4:22-24). Name the sin clearly, confess it to the Lord, and take the next obedient step.
- Offer ordinary life as worship. Present your body, work, speech, money, and relationships to God, and refuse to be squeezed into this world's pattern (Romans 12:1-2).
- Abide in Christ with his people. Stay in the Word, pray, gather with a local church, and receive the Lord's Supper in faith. We do not grow in isolation (John 15:4-5; Hebrews 10:24-25).
- Love your neighbor and bear witness with humility. A people belonging to God live so that others see his mercy, not our self-made goodness (1 Peter 2:9-12; Matthew 5:16).

This week, read Colossians 3:1-17 each morning. Ask the Lord to show you one sin to put off and one grace to put on that day, then bring that specifically to him in prayer and share it with a mature believer or your church elders so you are not walking alone. He who began this good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6).

Where do you most want this identity to shape your life right now, whether in a relationship, a habit, your work, or a place of weariness?

question: How do I know the Bible is not just mythology?
answer:
Many people ask this because the Bible includes miracles, a flood, and a resurrection, and because other ancient cultures told stories later set aside as legend. Those comparisons are understandable, and the distance of time can make any ancient writing feel remote. Christians believe the Bible is not mythology because it presents itself as a record of God’s acts in real history, and that claim is open to examination rather than hidden in a timeless tale.

The Bible teaches that its message rests on eyewitness testimony, not invented fables. Peter wrote that the apostles did not follow cleverly devised myths but were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty (2 Peter 1:16). Luke states that he carefully investigated everything from the beginning so readers could know the certainty of what they had been taught (Luke 1:1–4). These writers tie their accounts to named people, places, and public events in a way pure myth does not. The New Testament books were composed within living memory of the events, and the manuscript evidence for them is early and extensive compared with other ancient literature. Most decisively, the bodily resurrection of Jesus, witnessed by those who saw Him alive after the crucifixion, confirms that He is who He claimed to be and that the Scriptures He affirmed are true (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). If Christ rose, the Bible’s central claims are history, not legend. Scripture itself is God-breathed, the inspired Word of God, profitable for teaching and for training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

This is not a side issue. The Bible teaches that God is holy and that all have sinned and fall short of His glory, so that the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross in penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What specific account or claim in Scripture feels most like mythology to you? A steady next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly over the coming weeks, asking God to show you whether these things are true, and to speak with a pastor at a church that teaches the Bible as God’s Word.

question: What does it mean that the Bible is infallible? What is biblical infallibility?
answer:
Biblical infallibility means that the Bible, as the Word of God, will not fail, deceive, or lead you astray. It is a sure and trustworthy rule for faith and life because it comes from the God who cannot lie.

The word infallible means “not able to fail” or “not able to mislead.” Christians use it for Scripture because God Himself is truthful. “God, who cannot lie, promised before time began” (Titus 1:2), and Jesus prayed, “Your word is truth” (John 17:17). He also said that “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). The Bible is not a human guess that sometimes happens to be right. “Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21), and “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). The Greek word behind “God-breathed,” theopneustos, means that Scripture is breathed out by God. That is what we call inspiration, and more fully, verbal plenary inspiration: God so guided the human authors that the words they wrote are His Word, while they still wrote as real people in real places.

Infallibility belongs with inerrancy, and the two should not be pulled apart. Inerrancy means the Bible is without error in everything it affirms, in the original writings. Infallibility stresses that this Word will not fail you or mislead you. Some people today use “infallible” in a thinner way, as if the Bible were trustworthy only for spiritual ideas while still mistaken in history or fact. That is not what the churches have meant, and it does not fit the Bible’s own claim. “The testimony of the LORD is trustworthy” (Psalm 19:7), and “Every word of God is flawless” (Proverbs 30:5). A word that affirms what is false has already failed. Infallibility and inerrancy may be distinguished, but they cannot be separated.

This doctrine does not ignore how the Bible speaks. Poetry, parable, proverb, and apocalypse are true in the way those forms of writing actually teach. Infallibility means the text does not err in what the Spirit-led author affirms, not that every image is a laboratory report. It also applies first to the original manuscripts. Faithful copies and careful translations carry that same Word. A small number of copyist differences exist, but they do not overturn the message or any doctrine of the faith. And infallibility belongs to the text, not to every reader. Our interpretations can fail. Scripture does not.

Because the Bible is infallible, it stands over our preferences, our fears, and the shifting judgments of the age. It is able to make us “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15), and it equips the believer for every good work (2 Timothy 3:16-17). A practical step: this week, take one passage that presses on your conscience or your doubts, read the surrounding verses slowly, and ask what God is truly affirming there. Then speak to Him about it in your own words, and if you can, bring that passage to a pastor or a mature believer in your church so you are not left alone with a private guess.

If a particular verse feels difficult, tell me which one, and we can walk through it together.

question: What does the Bible mean when it says something is unclean?
answer:
In the Bible, calling something “unclean” means it is defiled or impure, and therefore unfit to draw near to the holy God, whether as ritual impurity under the old covenant or as moral corruption by sin.

Under the Law of Moses, uncleanness was often ceremonial. The Lord distinguished clean and unclean animals and gave rules for skin diseases, bodily discharges, and contact with a dead body (Leviticus 11:1–47; Leviticus 13:1–15:33; Numbers 19:11–22). A person in these states was not always guilty of personal sin, yet the impurity kept them from the tabernacle until washing or the appointed sacrifice restored them. These laws taught Israel that the Lord is holy and that His people must be set apart from what defiles (Leviticus 11:44–45). The Hebrew word behind “unclean,” tame’, means defiled or impure, and the whole system showed that sin and death create a barrier only God can remove.

Scripture also speaks of moral uncleanness. Idolatry, sexual immorality, and a defiled heart make a person unclean before God (Leviticus 18:24–30; Isaiah 6:5). Jesus taught that what comes out of the heart, not what enters the mouth, is what truly pollutes (Mark 7:20–23).

Jesus Christ fulfilled the ceremonial law. He declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and by His death and resurrection He provides the cleansing that sacrifices only pictured. God told Peter not to call unclean what He had made clean (Acts 10:15). The blood of Christ purifies the conscience so that we may serve the living God (Hebrews 9:13–14), and if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). Believers are called to holiness, not by returning to food laws, but by putting off the moral uncleanness of the old life (2 Corinthians 7:1).

This week, read Mark 7:14–23 and Leviticus 11:44–45 slowly. Ask the Lord to show you any moral defilement, then confess it to Him directly, resting in the cleansing promised through Christ. Share what you learn with a mature believer in your local church.

question: What is the meaning of life?
answer:
The meaning of life is to know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent, and to glorify Him in everything. Jesus said that eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent (John 17:3).

God made us in His image to reflect His glory and enjoy fellowship with Him (Genesis 1:27; Isaiah 43:7). Yet we have all sinned and fallen short of His holy standard, and the wages of that sin is death, a separation from the life we were created for (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). In love God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man. He lived without sin, died on the cross as a penal substitutionary sacrifice bearing the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). He is now exalted as Lord.

We are justified, declared righteous before God, by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:24). That restored relationship gives every part of life its purpose: whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God, loving Him and loving your neighbor (1 Corinthians 10:31; Matthew 22:37-39). Ordinary work, relationships, and even hardship take on eternal weight when lived in fellowship with Him, and we look forward to unbroken joy in His presence.

If you sense your need for forgiveness and a purpose that death cannot end, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for new life. A practical next step is to read the Gospel of John, a chapter a day, bringing your questions to God in prayer and talking them over with a pastor at a Bible-teaching church.

What has shaped your own search for meaning so far?

question: How can there be subordination in the Trinity?
answer:
There is no subordination of essence or deity within the Trinity. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, co-equal and co-eternal, each fully sharing the one undivided divine nature.

What Scripture and the church’s historic confession do affirm is an eternal order of personal relations, together with ordered roles in the work of redemption. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; these relations of origin mark real personal distinctions without making the Son or the Spirit less than fully God (John 1:1–3; John 5:26; John 15:26). Because will belongs to the one divine nature, the three persons are not three competing authorities. They act in perfect harmony.

In the economy of salvation that order becomes visible as mission and willing obedience. The incarnate Son came not to do his own will but the will of the One who sent him (John 6:38), humbling himself to the point of death on a cross while remaining equal with God (Philippians 2:6–8). That mediatorial submission belongs to his office as the sent Redeemer; it does not imply that the eternal Son is a lesser divine being. The Father sends, the Son accomplishes, and the Spirit applies, yet the work is the work of the one God.

Some faithful Christians describe this pattern as eternal functional subordination, seeing the economic roles as grounded in eternal relations of authority. Others, wishing to guard both the single divine will and the Son’s full equality, speak only of relations of origin and of roles freely taken up in the covenant of redemption, without an eternal subordination of authority inside the Godhead. Both concerns arise from love for the same biblical witness: the Son is true God from true God, and he became obedient for sinners.

Holding the classic confession of eternal generation and procession, I understand the order as one of relation and redemptive mission, not a hierarchy that diminishes the Son’s deity or divides the divine will. The practical fruit is worship and rest. This week, read John 17 slowly and notice how the Son speaks of the glory he shared with the Father before the world existed, even as he prays in perfect accord with the Father’s will. Let that shape your own approach to God: come to the Father through the Son, by the Spirit, trusting the salvation that the one Triune God has planned, accomplished, and applies.

If a particular passage or objection is weighing on you, tell me which one and we can open it together.

question: Why are there so many religions? Do all religions lead to God?
answer:
The sheer number of religions can feel confusing, and it is understandable to wonder whether sincere people in every tradition are already accepted by a loving God, especially when many faiths share some moral concerns.

The Bible teaches that this variety comes from humanity’s fallen condition. God has made Himself known through creation and conscience, yet people suppress that truth and exchange the worship of the Creator for images and ideas of their own making (Romans 1:18-25). Religions often express the human attempt to reach God on our own terms rather than receiving the revelation He has given in Scripture and in Christ.

Not all religions lead to God. Christians believe, and the Bible teaches, that Jesus Christ is the only mediator between God and people. Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5). Other faiths may contain fragments of moral insight, yet they do not provide the way of reconciliation with the holy God.

God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). Jesus, truly God and truly man, lived a sinless life, died on the cross bearing the penalty of sin in our place (penal substitution), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by religious effort (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What experiences or questions about other religions have most shaped how you see this?

question: Do Mormons believe in the Trinity?
answer:
No, Mormons do not believe in the Trinity. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints teaches that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are three separate and distinct beings united in purpose, not one God sharing the same divine essence.

The Bible teaches the doctrine of the Trinity: one God eternally existing in three persons, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, each fully God, yet not three gods. "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus includes all three when He commands baptism "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), and John writes that the Word, who became flesh, "was God" (John 1:1; John 1:14). The persons are distinct, as when the Father speaks, the Spirit descends, and the Son is baptized (Matthew 3:16-17), yet they are one in being. This is a core doctrine of the Christian faith. Rejecting it, as official Mormon teaching does, places that view outside orthodox Christianity, even though many Latter-day Saints are sincere in their devotion.

This matters because knowing the true God is bound up with salvation. All have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Forgiveness comes by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 14:6).

I invite you to repent of sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. If it would help, we can look together at a few passages on the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. What draws you to this question?

question: Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?
answer:
The moral law is summarily comprehended in the Ten Commandments.

God delivered these commands at Sinai as the concise summary of the moral duties we owe to Him and to one another (Exodus 20:1-17; Deuteronomy 5:6-21). The Lord Jesus upheld their authority and gathered their whole intent into love for God with all the heart and love for neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37-40; Matthew 5:17-19).

This holy law exposes sin and cannot justify anyone; it serves as a tutor that drives us to justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24; Galatians 2:16). Those already justified still receive it as a guide for sanctification, delighting to walk in its ways by the Spirit’s power (Romans 8:3-4; Psalm 119:97).

Read Exodus 20 slowly this week, ask the Lord to search you by it, and rest again in the perfect obedience of Jesus, who fulfilled every command for all who trust Him.

question: What does it mean to be contrite? What is contrition?
answer:
To be contrite is to have a heart crushed and humbled by the knowledge of your sin before a holy God. Contrition is that inward brokenness: grief that sin is an offense against God, not merely that it has brought painful consequences.

Scripture uses this language for the person God receives. After his sin, David prayed, "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" (Psalm 51:17). "The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit" (Psalm 34:18). The Holy One who dwells on high also draws near "to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 66:2). The words behind "contrite" picture something bruised or ground down. That matches the tax collector who would not lift his eyes, but cried, "God, have mercy on me, a sinner" (Luke 18:13). In that world people tore their garments to show grief. God asked for torn hearts instead (Joel 2:13).

Contrition belongs to repentance, but it is not the same as mere regret. Paul distinguishes godly sorrow, which "brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret," from worldly sorrow, which "brings death" (2 Corinthians 7:10). Worldly sorrow grieves lost comfort, reputation, or freedom. Godly sorrow grieves that God has been dishonored, and it turns from sin toward Him.

Contrition does not earn forgiveness. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by how deeply you feel your guilt (Romans 3:23–26; Ephesians 2:8–9). A crushed heart is the Spirit's work that drives you to the Savior, not a payment you offer God. Christ bore the penalty our sins deserved in His death on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). God does not despise the contrite because the sacrifice He accepts is Christ's, received by faith.

If you are examining your own heart, do not wait until you feel "sorry enough." Name specific sins before the Lord in prayer, ask Him for grief over the offense against Him and not only over the fallout, and then rest on Christ's finished work rather than on the intensity of your feelings. Where you have wronged someone, take a concrete step of confession and making things right as far as it depends on you (Matthew 5:23–24).

If you have never trusted Christ, contrition itself will not save you. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

If a particular burden of guilt is weighing on you, what would it look like to bring that specific sin to Christ rather than only regretting its consequences?

question: What does it mean that “at your right hand are pleasures forevermore” (Psalm 16:11)?
answer:
"At your right hand are pleasures forevermore" means that the highest and most lasting joy is found in God's favor and presence, and that this joy never ends. In the Berean Standard Bible the verse reads, "You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, with eternal pleasures at Your right hand" (Psalm 16:11).

In Scripture the right hand is the place of honor, power, and intimate welcome. God invites the Messiah to sit at His right hand until His enemies are subdued (Psalm 110:1), and the risen Christ has been exalted there (Acts 2:33). These pleasures are not passing amusements. They are the delightful fullness of covenant fellowship with God, held secure by His faithfulness rather than by changing circumstances.

Peter shows the fullest meaning of these words at Pentecost. David foresaw the resurrection of Christ, whom God did not abandon to decay, so the path of life runs through Jesus' death, burial, and bodily rising (Acts 2:25-31). Christian faith calls this hope eternal communion with God: a real joy begun now by faith, and completed in His presence forever.

If lesser pleasures have grown thin, set aside ten quiet minutes today and read Psalm 16 slowly, asking the Lord to satisfy you with Himself through His Word and prayer. That everlasting delight is not a wage we earn. It is the gift of grace. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, and you will find pleasures at His right hand that never end.

What part of this hope feels most alive, or most distant, to you right now?

question: What is divine providence?
answer:
Divine providence is God’s active, sovereign care by which He preserves, governs, and directs all things in creation according to the wise counsel of His will.

Scripture teaches that the Son “upholds all things by His powerful word” (Hebrews 1:3) and that “in Him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). God “works out everything by the counsel of His will” (Ephesians 1:11), so that even a sparrow does not fall apart from the Father’s will, and the hairs of your head are numbered (Matthew 10:29–31). For those who love God and are called according to His purpose, He works all things together for good (Romans 8:28). Joseph could therefore say that what others intended for evil, God intended for good (Genesis 50:20). This is not cold fate. It is the holy, good, and personal government of the living God, who rules without canceling human responsibility.

When worry rises over something you cannot control, bring that specific concern to the Lord in prayer today and read Matthew 6:25–34, asking Him to help you rest in His fatherly providence rather than in anxious self-rule.

question: In what ways is the Christian life like the Olympics?
answer:
The Christian life is like the Olympics in its demand for disciplined training, enduring focus, and a prize worth more than any medal. Scripture uses the games of the ancient world to picture discipleship, while making one vital distinction: we do not run to earn God’s favor.

**Training, not casual effort.** Olympic athletes submit to strict discipline for a wreath that fades. Paul says believers train for an imperishable crown, bringing the body and its desires under control rather than running aimlessly (1 Corinthians 9:24-27). Godliness itself is a form of training, and it holds promise for this life and the life to come (1 Timothy 4:7-8). In practice, that looks like a set time in Scripture and prayer, the way an athlete keeps a training schedule even when motivation is low.

**A race marked out, run with endurance.** We are not inventing our own course. We lay aside weights and the sin that entangles, and we run with endurance the race set before us, fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith (Hebrews 12:1-2). The “cloud of witnesses” in Hebrews 11 is less a cheering section than a company of finishers whose lives say the course can be completed by trusting God. Focus matters: Paul forgot what lay behind and pressed toward the goal (Philippians 3:13-14).

**Rules, not shortcuts.** An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules (2 Timothy 2:5). Faithfulness is not spiritual gamesmanship. We do not redefine obedience, nurse secret compromise, or treat grace as permission to leave the course.

**A finish line and a crown, not a single gold medal.** Near the end Paul could say he had fought the good fight, finished the race, and kept the faith, with the crown of righteousness laid up for him and for all who love Christ’s appearing (2 Timothy 4:7-8). Unlike the Olympics, believers are not rivals for one prize. The church is a body, not a bracket. Your brother or sister’s faithfulness is reason for joy, not envy.

Here the likeness stops, and the gospel must govern the picture. An Olympian earns a medal by performance. A sinner is justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by spiritual athleticism. Christ’s sin-bearing death and bodily resurrection are the victory already won. The Christian race is progressive sanctification, the Spirit-empowered perseverance of those already accepted in Christ, not a way to put God in our debt. We labor, yet the strength is His (Philippians 2:12-13).

This week, name one weight to lay aside and one simple training rhythm to keep, then tell a mature believer in your church so you are not running alone. Pray honestly about where your endurance feels thin, asking God for strength to fix your eyes on Christ.

Where does the race feel heaviest for you right now?

question: What should be the Christian perspective on nudity in art?
answer:
The Christian perspective on nudity in art starts from Scripture: the body is God’s good creation, yet after the fall nakedness is tied to shame, and lust is sin. Believers therefore honor the body’s dignity and refuse any use of it that stirs sexual desire outside of marriage.

God made us in His image, and before sin the man and woman were naked and unashamed (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:25). After they rebelled, they hid, and the Lord Himself clothed them (Genesis 3:7; Genesis 3:21). Clothing is a mercy in a fallen world, not a denial that the body is good. Modesty is love for God and neighbor where desire is disordered (1 Timothy 2:9-10). Because every person bears the image of God, the body must never be reduced to an object for consumption.

Jesus located the issue in the heart. Looking at a person in order to lust is adultery already committed within (Matthew 5:28). What matters is whether eyes and imagination are being trained toward purity or toward sin (Matthew 15:18-19; Philippians 4:8). Pornography, made to arouse, violates that command and should be rejected outright. So does any artwork, however serious its reputation, that you seek for sexual stimulation.

Scripture does not give a catalogue of every painting or sculpture, so faithful Christians have sometimes differed about particular works. That difference is a matter of wisdom in application, not a debate over the moral law. Some, weighing the weakness of the flesh and the duty not to cause a brother or sister to stumble, avoid nude figures altogether (Romans 14:13; Romans 14:21). Others note that the Bible itself speaks frankly of the body, and that some depictions, such as a medical illustration or a non-erotic scene of suffering, need not be lustful. Christian liberty never licenses making provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14; 1 Corinthians 6:12). Lust remains sin either way (Hebrews 13:4).

A wise pastoral application, not a new law laid on every conscience, is caution. In a culture flooded with sexual images, it is usually better to be slow to gaze. If a work draws desire where it does not belong, turn away. Job made a covenant with his eyes not to look lustfully (Job 31:1). Practically, that may mean leaving a gallery room, choosing a different film, or not displaying an image where it would tempt you or others in your home. If you are unsure, abstain for a season and ask a pastor or a mature believer to help you think it through. Guarding the eyes is part of progressive sanctification, the Spirit’s patient work of teaching redeemed people to love what God loves.

If you have already looked with lust, do not hide in shame or excuse it. Christ died for sinners and rose bodily to forgive and make His people new. Confess the sin, receive His cleansing, and walk by the Spirit rather than by the flesh (1 John 1:9; Galatians 5:16). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for a clean heart and a new way of seeing.

Is there a particular work, or a habit of looking, that you want to think through together?

question: Should we allow false teachers into our home?
answer:
No. Scripture tells believers not to receive false teachers into their homes in a way that welcomes or supports their message.

John is plain: if someone comes and does not bring the true teaching about Christ, do not receive him into your house or welcome him, because the one who welcomes him shares in his wicked work (2 John 1:10-11). The teaching he has in view is the apostolic confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh as the Son of the Father (2 John 1:7-9). In that setting, household hospitality was how traveling teachers were housed, fed, and sent on. To open the door that way was to partner with their mission. John forbids that partnership when the teacher denies the incarnate Christ and the gospel.

This is not a ban on every kind conversation, nor a command to be harsh with a confused neighbor. You may speak at the door in order to point someone to the real Jesus. You must not treat a false teacher as a faithful brother, give him a platform in your living room, or commend his work with lodging, money, or a greeting that says his message is safe. Paul gives the same boundary in another form: watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching you learned, and turn away from them (Romans 16:17). Jesus warned that false prophets come in sheep’s clothing, and that you know them by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-16).

So test what is taught against Scripture (1 John 4:1-3; Acts 17:11). If someone denies the Trinity, the true deity and humanity of Christ, His atoning death and bodily resurrection, or justification by grace alone through faith alone, do not make your home a base for that message. Love the people in your house enough to guard them, especially children and those young in the faith. Refuse with gentleness, and pray that God would grant repentance to those who oppose the truth (2 Timothy 2:24-26). A relative who is still learning, or a guest who asks hard questions, is not the same case as a teacher who arrives to spread a different Christ. Even then, do not let error disciple your household.

This week, read 2 John slowly with your family, and ask your elders how your church keeps the door open to the lost without opening it to false teaching.

question: How is God’s Word a lamp to my feet (Psalm 119:105)?
answer:
God's Word is a lamp to your feet because it gives you enough light for the next obedient step, so you can walk with God instead of stumbling in the dark (Psalm 119:105).

In the ancient Near East, a night traveler carried a small clay oil lamp. It did not light the whole road. It lit the ground just ahead of his feet. The psalmist takes up that ordinary picture. Scripture is not usually a floodlight on your entire future. It is a faithful lamp for the path you must walk today.

That lamp does real work. It warns you before you stumble into sin (Psalm 119:105; Proverbs 6:23). It gives understanding when you open it and receive it: "The unfolding of Your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple" (Psalm 119:130). And it equips you for a holy life, since "All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work" (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

This is what Christians call illumination. The Holy Spirit does not hand you a second Bible. He opens your eyes to the Word God has already spoken, so that truth becomes a path under your feet (Psalm 119:18). Over time, that steady light is one of God's means of grace for your sanctification. You learn His ways, you repent where the light exposes you, and you take the next step in faith.

The written Word also leads you to Christ, the true Light. Jesus said, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life" (John 8:12). Scripture keeps your feet on His way when feelings, opinions, and the culture pull you off it (Psalm 119:9).

Do not wait for a map of the next ten years. Tomorrow morning, read a short portion of Scripture, perhaps a few verses of Psalm 119, and ask the Lord to show you one command to obey or one promise to trust that day. Then take that step, and share what you are learning with a mature believer in your local church, so you are not walking by a private light.

What next step feels dark to you right now?

question: Why were the people guilty for a priest’s sin?
answer:
The people were held guilty for the anointed priest’s sin because he represented the whole nation before God. Leviticus 4:3 states that if the anointed priest sins, he brings guilt on the people, and he must offer a young bull without blemish as a sin offering.

In Israel’s covenant worship the high priest stood in the people’s place. He drew near to the Lord on their behalf and guarded the holiness of the sanctuary that belonged to them all. When he sinned, that mediatorial bond was defiled and the guilt of his failure rested on the community he represented until atonement was made. The offering required was the same costly bull demanded when the entire congregation sinned (Leviticus 4:13-14), showing that his office carried national weight. This is the biblical pattern of covenant representation: the one who mediates bears consequences that touch those he represents.

That pattern reaches its goal in Jesus Christ. The earlier priests had to sacrifice first for their own sins, but our great High Priest is holy, innocent, undefiled, and set apart from sinners (Hebrews 7:26). He offered Himself once for all, not to cover His own guilt, but to remove the guilt of His people (Hebrews 7:27). Rest in His perfect representation rather than in any human leader, and make it your practice to pray for the pastors and elders who shepherd your church, asking the Lord to keep them faithful for the good of the whole flock.

question: What is spiritual mapping?
answer:
Spiritual mapping is a modern practice in which some Christians research a place’s history, sins, and cultural patterns in order to identify supposed demonic strongholds or territorial spirits, then aim prayer at those spirits so evangelism can advance.

Scripture does teach real spiritual conflict. Ephesians 6:12 says our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers, authorities, the powers of this world’s darkness, and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. Yet the New Testament never tells the church to chart territorial demons or to seek special intelligence about them. Believers are called to stand in the armor of God, pray in the Spirit, resist the devil, and make disciples by proclaiming Christ (Ephesians 6:13–18; James 4:7; Matthew 28:18–20).

The decisive victory already belongs to Jesus. Colossians 2:15 declares that He disarmed the powers and authorities, triumphing over them by the cross. Our confidence rests in His penal substitution and bodily resurrection, not in techniques that claim hidden knowledge of the spirit realm.

Sincere believers have used spiritual mapping because they long to see people saved, and that longing is right. The method itself, however, goes beyond what is written and can draw attention away from the ordinary means of grace: the Word, prayer, and the life of the local church. A wiser path is to intercede from Scripture for your neighbors and leaders, share the gospel personally, and join your congregation’s prayer for Christ’s kingdom (1 Timothy 2:1–4). This week, read Ephesians 6 slowly and turn each piece of the armor into a short prayer for the place where you live, then ask your pastor how you can serve the church’s witness.

question: What is God’s design for marriage?
answer:
God’s design for marriage is a lifelong, exclusive covenant between one man and one woman, joining them as one flesh for companionship, the gift of children, and a living display of Christ’s love for His church.

From the beginning God made humanity male and female in His image and brought the woman to the man so that a husband would leave his father and mother, hold fast to his wife, and the two would become one flesh (Genesis 1:27-28; Genesis 2:18-24). Jesus affirmed this creation pattern as God’s unchanging intent, teaching that what God has joined together no one should separate (Matthew 19:4-6). The apostle Paul unfolds the same design as a profound mystery: husbands are to love their wives with sacrificial, cleansing love just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, and wives are to respect and submit to their own husbands as the church submits to Christ (Ephesians 5:22-33). This is a covenant before God, not a private contract, marked by faithful exclusivity and by sexual intimacy kept only within that one-flesh bond (Malachi 2:14; Hebrews 13:4; 1 Corinthians 7:2-5).

The complementary callings of husband and wife are part of this wise design, not a mere cultural preference. Both spouses depend on the grace of the Holy Spirit to die to self and to serve one another under the lordship of Christ. If you are married, sit down this week with your spouse, read Ephesians 5:22-33 aloud, and ask the Lord to reshape your daily love after the pattern of Christ’s self-giving. If you are single, honor the same design now by pursuing purity and, should you marry, by seeking a spouse who treasures Christ and this covenant. Beautiful as marriage is, it points beyond itself to the greater union in which sinners are reconciled to God through the death and resurrection of Jesus and are kept by His faithful love.

question: What is the value of group Bible study?
answer:
Group Bible study is a God-given means of growing in the truth, in love, and in holiness together, not a private hobby added onto the Christian life. Scripture calls believers to hear and speak the Word with one another, and to stir one another up to love and good works (Hebrews 10:24-25).

The value shows up in several concrete ways.

Understanding deepens. The same Spirit who inspired Scripture illumines the church, and believers bring different gifts, questions, and life experience. Paul urges the church to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly as they teach and admonish one another in all wisdom (Colossians 3:16). A brother or sister may see in the text what you have missed, and you may do the same for them. Group study does not replace personal reading. It guards you from reading the Bible only through your own habits and blind spots.

Sanctification becomes practical. Sanctification is the Holy Spirit's ongoing work of making God's people more like Christ. In a group, a passage does not stay abstract. Someone asks how a command meets a hard week. Someone confesses a struggle. Someone prays. "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Humble, biblical correction is a mercy, not an attack, when it is done gently and with a view to restoration (Galatians 6:1). Daily encouragement also helps keep hearts from being hardened by sin's deceitfulness (Hebrews 3:12-13).

Fellowship becomes shared life in Christ, not mere friendship. The early church devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship (Acts 2:42). The word often translated fellowship, koinonia, means a real participation together in Christ and in His gifts. Group study trains that shared life. It also serves the body's growth, as believers speak the truth in love and each part does its work (Ephesians 4:15-16).

A few boundaries keep the gift from being spoiled. The group should sit under Scripture, not over it. The aim is faithfulness to the text in its context, with Christ at the center, not a circle of clever opinions. Not every voice carries equal weight, so humble leadership and a willingness to be taught matter (James 3:1). The healthiest study is tied to a local church, where the Word is preached, the ordinances are observed, and shepherds can care for souls (Hebrews 13:17).

If you want a simple next step this week, ask your pastor whether you may join an existing study, or invite one or two believers to read one chapter of a Gospel with you. Before you open the Bible, pray for light, humility, and love. Then ask three questions of the text: What does this say about God? What does it say about us? How should we respond in faith and obedience?

question: How can I overcome a feeling of spiritual emptiness?
answer:
That feeling of spiritual emptiness can leave the soul parched and restless, as if the very center of life has gone dry. Scripture names this thirst plainly. The psalmist cried that his soul panted for God as a deer pants for water (Psalm 42:1-2), and Jesus still invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, promising living water that springs up to eternal life (John 4:14; John 7:37-38).

Emptiness like this often shows that the heart, made for God, has been trying to draw life from somewhere else. Apart from Christ we can do nothing (John 15:5). Fullness comes through union with Christ: by faith we are joined to Him, and in Him we are made complete (Colossians 2:10). If you already belong to Him, this dryness frequently calls you back to the means of grace the Spirit uses in our sanctification, daily Scripture, honest prayer, and the fellowship of a local church where Christ is preached. Unconfessed sin can also dull the soul; bring it openly to God, for if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us (1 John 1:9).

God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of His glory, leaving us empty and separated from Him (Romans 3:23). Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as the penal substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by our striving (Ephesians 2:8-9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, and He will satisfy the thirst nothing else can touch.

A concrete next step is to read John 4:1-26 slowly tomorrow, then speak to God in your own words about the emptiness you feel, asking Him to draw you near and fill you with Himself. Share this struggle with a pastor or mature believer who can walk with you. What has seemed to deepen this sense of emptiness most in recent days?

question: How can I, a Muslim, become assured of paradise?
answer:
Your longing to be assured of paradise is a weighty and sincere desire. Many Muslims hope that faith and good deeds will be accepted through Allah’s mercy, yet still lack certainty because the outcome rests on a judgment no one can fully predict in advance. You may also have been taught that Jesus was a prophet who was not crucified, so what follows may sound unfamiliar at first.

The Bible teaches that no one enters paradise by the balance of their works. God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). In love God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. Jesus lived without sin, died on the cross as a penal substitute bearing the judgment sinners deserve, was buried, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

Anyone who repents and trusts in Him is justified, declared righteous by grace alone through faith alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 5:1). Because His saving work is finished, those who believe can know they have eternal life: “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and the sure hope of paradise.

What questions do you have about who Jesus is, or about how a person is made right with God?

question: What is the spiritual gift of miracles?
answer: The spiritual gift of miracles is the Holy Spirit’s special empowerment of certain believers to perform supernatural works that display God’s power, listed among the gifts in 1 Corinthians 12:10 and 1 Corinthians 12:28–29. Continuationists argue charitably that the New Testament never declares these gifts ended and that texts such as 1 Corinthians 1:7 and 1 Corinthians 13:8–12 point to their continuance until Christ returns, so the Spirit may still distribute miraculous works for the church’s good today. I hold the cessationist position that this gift functioned chiefly as a sign authenticating the apostles and the foundational revelation now completed in Scripture (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4; Ephesians 2:20), and therefore ceased with the apostolic age, even while God remains free to act miraculously by His own sovereign will; cessationism is one faithful option within historic Christianity. In practice, rest in the sufficiency of the written Word (2 Timothy 3:16–17) and ask the Spirit to strengthen you through the ordinary means of grace in your local church rather than seeking ongoing sign-gifts as the normal pattern of ministry.

question: What does it mean that God is merciful?
answer:
God is merciful means that He is full of compassionate pity toward sinners and sufferers, and that He freely withholds the judgment we deserve. His mercy is not a soft mood that overlooks sin. It is the holy compassion of the covenant Lord, who sees our misery and acts to save.

When the Lord passed before Moses, He proclaimed Himself compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness (Exodus 34:6-7). The word behind that loving devotion, chesed, names God's steadfast covenant love, the loyalty that does not abandon His people. Another word, rachamim, pictures a father's deep pity for his children (Psalm 103:8-13). The New Testament says the same thing when it calls God rich in mercy (Ephesians 2:4).

Mercy and grace belong together, yet they are not identical. Grace is God giving favor we have not earned. Mercy is God sparing us the condemnation we have earned. Both meet in the Gospel. We have sinned and stand under God's just wrath (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross in penal substitutionary atonement, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). God presented Him as a propitiation, so that He might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25-26). We are saved not by righteous deeds we have done, but according to His mercy (Titus 3:5).

If guilt is weighing on you, do not hide it or try to outwork it. Confess that sin to God today, and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Then extend to others the mercy you have received, for Jesus said, "Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful" (Luke 6:36).

question: Who is the head of the church, biblically speaking?
answer:
Jesus Christ is the head of the church. He is not merely its founder or model, but its living Lord, the one who rules, nourishes, and holds it together.

Ephesians 1:22-23 says God put all things under Christ’s feet and gave Him as head over all things to the church, which is His body. Colossians 1:18 calls Him the head of the body, the church, so that in everything He might have the preeminence. Ephesians 5:23 likewise says Christ is the head of the church, His body, and its Savior. This headship is His mediatorial reign: He governs His people by His word and Spirit, and the church lives only as it remains joined to Him (Colossians 2:19; Matthew 16:18).

Human leaders are under-shepherds, not a substitute head. Elders shepherd the flock under the Chief Shepherd and must give an account to Him (1 Peter 5:1-4; Hebrews 13:17). Practically, that means a congregation tests its teaching, worship, and decisions by Scripture, and members follow Christ together in a local church rather than treating any person or office as the church’s final authority.

question: Who is the ancient serpent of Revelation 12:9?
answer:
The ancient serpent of Revelation 12:9 is Satan, also called the devil. The verse itself identifies the great dragon as that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world (Revelation 12:9).

Scripture links this figure to the serpent who deceived Eve in the garden (Genesis 3:1-5, 13-15) and confirms the same identity later when it speaks of “the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan” (Revelation 20:2). In the world of the New Testament, John is making explicit what the biblical story has shown from the beginning: a real, personal adversary who opposes God and seeks to deceive humanity. His schemes are not ultimate, however. Those who belong to Christ overcome him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony (Revelation 12:11).

When deceptive thoughts or temptations press in, answer them with the truth of God’s Word and stay near the means of grace, just as Jesus met the tempter with Scripture in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1-11).

question: Book of 1 John - Bible Survey
answer:
First John is a pastoral letter, received from the earliest days of the church as the work of the apostle John, written so believers may be sure they have eternal life and may walk in real fellowship with God.

The letter itself does not sign John's name, yet its voice, vocabulary, and themes match the Gospel of John, and the early church consistently attributed it to him. It was most likely written near the end of the first century to churches in Asia Minor. Some people had left those churches and were denying that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh. John writes as a shepherd who has seen, heard, and touched the Word of life, not as a speculator (1 John 1:1-3; 1 John 2:19; 1 John 4:2-3).

**Purpose.** John states his aim plainly: "I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life" (1 John 5:13, BSB). He also writes so that joy may be full, sin may be confessed and forsaken, false teaching may be refused, and love may be practiced (1 John 1:4; 1 John 2:1; 1 John 2:26).

**Central claims.** God is light, and God is love (1 John 1:5; 1 John 4:8). Fellowship with Him is not a mood. It is walking in the light, confessing sin, and trusting the Son. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. He has come in the flesh, and to deny that is the spirit of the antichrist, not a permitted Christian option (1 John 4:2-3; 1 John 2:22). His death is a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns aside God's just wrath against sin, and He remains the believer's Advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1-2; 1 John 4:10). The church has long named this saving work penal substitution. Eternal life is received by believing in the name of the Son of God, not by moral effort (1 John 5:11-13).

**Tests of real life.** John gives three marks of the new birth, not as a way to earn salvation, but as evidence that regeneration has taken place. Those born of God confess Jesus as the Christ come in the flesh, obey His commands rather than treating sin as a way of life, and love the brothers (1 John 2:3-6; 1 John 3:9-10; 1 John 3:14-18; 1 John 4:2-3). Those who departed showed they had never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). Assurance rests on Christ's finished work, and it is confirmed by this fruit.

**A simple outline.**
- The Word of life and fellowship with the Father and the Son (1 John 1:1-4).
- Walking in the light, confessing sin, and resting in the Advocate (1 John 1:5-2:2).
- Obedience, love, and remaining in the truth (1 John 2:3-27).
- Children of God, and the difference between righteousness and ongoing lawlessness (1 John 2:28-3:24).
- Testing the spirits, and the love God showed at the cross (1 John 4:1-21).
- Faith that overcomes, prayer, and the knowledge of eternal life (1 John 5:1-21).

This week, read First John in one sitting, then reread 1 John 1:5-2:2 slowly. Where the letter exposes lovelessness, hidden sin, or a thin confession of Christ, bring that honestly to God in prayer, and ask a mature believer in your church to walk through it with you.

question: What happens at the final judgment?
answer:
At the final judgment, Jesus Christ will return personally and bodily, raise all the dead, and judge every person who has ever lived. Those who belong to Him by faith will enter eternal life in the renewed creation, while those who have rejected Him will face just condemnation for their sins.

Faithful Christians differ on some details of timing and sequence in the last days, and those differences need not divide us. Scripture is clear, however, about the judgment itself. God has fixed a day on which He will judge the world in righteousness by the Man He has appointed, and He has given assurance of this by raising Jesus from the dead (Acts 17:31). Christ will come in glory, sit on His throne, and separate all people, welcoming those who are His into eternal life and assigning eternal punishment to the others (Matthew 25:31-46). The dead will stand before the throne, books will be opened, and people will be judged according to their deeds. Anyone whose name is not found written in the book of life will be cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:11-15). All who are in the tombs will hear His voice and come out, some to the resurrection of life and some to the resurrection of judgment (John 5:28-29).

This judgment according to deeds does not mean anyone is saved by works. People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by their own record (Ephesians 2:8-9). There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Believers will give an account at the judgment seat of Christ, where the fruit of faith is assessed, but their acceptance with God rests entirely on Christ’s finished work (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Because God is holy, He must judge sin, and every person has sinned and falls short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute bearing the penalty sinners deserve, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). His penal substitutionary atonement reconciles sinners to God, and the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and the hope of eternal life.

A practical step is to read Matthew 25:31-46 and Romans 8:1 this week, then bring what you find honestly to the Lord in prayer. What comes to mind for you when you think about standing before Jesus on that day?

question: In what ways is becoming a Christian becoming an entirely new man / woman?
answer:
Becoming a Christian is God making you an entirely new person, not a repaired version of the old one. Scripture calls this the new birth and a new creation: the Holy Spirit gives life where there was spiritual death, and you are united to Christ so that your standing, heart, and destiny are changed at the root.

We were made for God, yet we have turned from Him. Sin is rebellion that leaves us guilty, enslaved, and separated from the holy God (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:1–3). We cannot renovate ourselves into His family. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute bearing the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). God justifies the ungodly by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Romans 3:24–26; Ephesians 2:8–9).

That faith is the response of a heart God has made new. Those who receive Christ have been born of God (John 1:12–13; John 3:3–8). Regeneration is God’s act of giving a new heart and putting His Spirit within a person, so that repentance and trust become possible and real (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Titus 3:5).

That newness shows itself in several ways.

You receive a new standing before God. In union with Christ you are forgiven, justified, and adopted. God no longer counts your sins against you, and He receives you as His child (Romans 5:1; Romans 8:1; Romans 8:15–16). Christ secured this. You do not earn it.

You receive a new identity. If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away, and the new has come (2 Corinthians 5:17). The old self is put off, and the new self is put on, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness (Ephesians 4:22–24; Colossians 3:9–10). Your truest name is no longer defined by guilt and slavery, but by belonging to Christ, even while you still fight remaining sin.

You receive a new power and a new direction. You died with Christ to sin’s reign and were raised to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4–11). The Spirit indwells you, opposes the flesh, and bears fruit such as love, patience, and self-control (Romans 8:9–11; Galatians 5:16–25). Obedience becomes the path of the freed, not a ladder for the condemned (Titus 2:11–14).

You receive a new family and a new hope. You are joined to Christ’s people, and you share a living hope of bodily resurrection and life forever with God (1 Corinthians 12:13; 1 Peter 1:3–5).

This newness is real now and still growing. Justification is complete the moment you trust Christ. Sanctification is the lifelong work of the Spirit, conforming you to Jesus through the Word, prayer, and the church (Philippians 1:6; 2 Corinthians 3:18). The new man is not sinless yet, but he is no longer at home in sin. When you fall, you confess and rise, because God who began this work will finish it.

If this new life is what you long for, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. If you already belong to Him, name one habit of the old life this week, bring it honestly to God in prayer, and ask a mature believer in your church to walk with you as you put on the new.

What part of this new life feels most unclear, or most needed, for you right now?

question: What are the Pauline epistles?
answer:
The Pauline epistles are the thirteen New Testament letters written by the apostle Paul. They are Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, and Philemon.

Paul wrote them to churches and to fellow workers, unfolding the gospel, correcting error, and directing Christian life and ministry. In them he teaches justification by faith, the church as Christ’s body, and the hope of the Lord’s return (Romans 3:21–26; Ephesians 2:8–10; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Peter already treated Paul’s letters as Scripture, even while noting that some were twisting them (2 Peter 3:15–16).

Hebrews does not name its author, so it is not one of the Pauline epistles, though some early Christians linked it with Paul.

A fruitful next step is to read Romans slowly, noticing how sinners are counted righteous through faith in Christ and how that grace then shapes ordinary obedience.

question: How can I be sure I am praying according to the will of God?
answer:
You can be confident you are praying according to God’s will when your requests are shaped by Scripture and offered with a surrendered heart that truly means, “Your will be done.”

The longing to pray in line with God’s heart is itself a gracious work of the Spirit in you. God’s revealed will is not a riddle we must solve. He has made it known in the Bible, which equips us for every good work, including prayer (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The apostle John gives this assurance: “And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). When you ask for what God has clearly commanded or promised, such as wisdom, holiness, daily provision, forgiveness, and the advance of His kingdom, you are praying within His will (James 1:5; 1 Thessalonians 4:3; Matthew 6:9-13).

You do not pray alone. “The Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words,” and “the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God” (Romans 8:26-27). Ask Him to conform your desires to the Father’s heart. Our Lord Jesus showed the same posture in Gethsemane: “Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done” (Luke 22:42). Praying according to God’s will includes holding even cherished requests with open hands, trusting that His sovereign purposes are wiser and kinder than our own (Romans 8:28).

This confidence rests on Christ, not on the perfection of our words. Because He died for our sins, rose again, and now lives as our great High Priest, we may approach the throne of grace with boldness (Hebrews 4:14-16).

This week, read the Lord’s Prayer in Matthew 6:9-13 slowly and let each petition reshape one specific request you are carrying. Then bring that request to a mature believer in your church so you can seek the Lord together (James 5:16). As you do, take your questions about His will straight to Him in prayer, asking for the wisdom He promises to give.
