question: What does the Bible say about busyness / being too busy?
answer:
The Bible treats honest work as a good gift, yet it warns that anxious, crowded busyness can become a kind of unbelief, crowding out rest, prayer, and love.

God put the man in the garden to work and keep it, so labor itself is not the problem (Genesis 2:15). Scripture also rebukes laziness, so the answer is not idleness (Proverbs 6:6-11). The danger is disordered striving. God commands rest so his people will stop and remember that he, not their output, sustains them (Exodus 20:8-11). It is vain to rise early and stay up late in anxious toil, as if everything depended on us, for the Lord gives sleep to his beloved (Psalm 127:1-2). Believers are also called to wise stewardship of time, walking carefully and redeeming the time, because the days are short and serious (Ephesians 5:15-16). Hurry without wisdom misses the way (Proverbs 19:2), and plans that leave God out become a quiet boast (James 4:13-15).

Jesus worked with real urgency and compassion, yet he withdrew to pray, and he called his disciples aside to rest when the crowds pressed in (Luke 5:16; Mark 6:31). In Martha’s house he did not condemn service. He named the danger of being worried and upset about many things while missing the one necessary thing, sitting at his feet and hearing his word (Luke 10:38-42). A full calendar can feel like faithfulness while the soul grows thin. Activity, even good activity, becomes costly when it displaces communion with Christ and patient love for the people nearest you.

There is a deeper rest than a better schedule can give. Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him and find rest for their souls (Matthew 11:28-30). That rest is gospel rest. You are not justified by productivity, a spotless reputation, or the feeling that everyone needs you. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, who died for sinners and rose again (Ephesians 2:8-9). When your identity rests there, you can work heartily as for the Lord without making work your savior (Colossians 3:23-24). If constant motion has become your way of earning peace, turn from that striving and trust Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you.

This week, guard one daily window, even fifteen minutes, for Scripture and prayer before the tasks begin. Then name one commitment you can lay down or postpone so rest and love have room, and bring that specific choice to the Lord in your own words, asking him to teach you to be still and know that he is God (Psalm 46:10). If the pressure feels crushing, talk with your pastor or a mature believer who can help you sort true duty from drivenness.

What part of your schedule feels hardest to slow down right now?

question: What are the seven baptisms mentioned in the Bible, and what do they mean?
answer:
Scripture does not present a formal numbered list called “the seven baptisms,” yet it uses baptism language in seven distinct ways that careful readers have long observed. Each must be understood in its own context rather than treated as the same act.

The baptism into Moses appears in 1 Corinthians 10:1-2, where Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” This was not a ritual but a shared deliverance that identified the people with Moses as God’s mediator in the exodus.

The baptism of John was a water baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, preached to prepare Israel for the coming Messiah (Mark 1:4; Luke 3:3). It called for turning from sin and pointed forward to Christ; it was never meant to continue unchanged after His arrival.

The baptism of Jesus occurred when He was immersed by John in the Jordan (Matthew 3:13-17). Sinless, He submitted to fulfill all righteousness, identifying with the sinners He came to save. The Father’s voice and the Spirit’s descent displayed the Trinity at the opening of His public ministry.

The baptism with the Holy Spirit is the promise John gave and Jesus fulfilled (Acts 1:5; 1 Corinthians 12:13). By this work the Spirit places every believer into the body of Christ at the moment of saving faith, effecting our union with Christ. It is not a later experience to be sought after conversion.

The baptism with fire is announced in the same saying (Matthew 3:11). The immediate context of the winnowing fork and the burning of chaff with unquenchable fire (Matthew 3:12) shows this to be Christ’s judgment on the impenitent. Some connect the fire instead to the tongues at Pentecost, yet the judgment imagery is the plainer reading of the passage.

The baptism of suffering is the overwhelming ordeal Jesus said He must undergo (Luke 12:50; Mark 10:38-39). He spoke of the cross, where He would bear the wrath of God in the place of sinners, accomplishing penal substitution so that all who trust Him might be forgiven.

Christian water baptism is the ordinance Christ commanded when He sent His people to make disciples and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). It signifies a believer’s union with Christ in His death, burial, and resurrection (Romans 6:3-4; Colossians 2:12). A strong historic argument for also baptizing the infants of believers appeals to covenant continuity, viewing baptism as the new-covenant counterpart to circumcision. Believer’s baptism by immersion is one faithful option within historic Christianity, following the New Testament pattern in which baptism comes after personal faith and vividly pictures burial and rising with Christ; those who hold infant baptism while embracing the gospel remain brothers and sisters in Christ.

Ephesians 4:5 speaks of “one baptism,” referring to the spiritual reality that unites all true believers, not to a denial of these varied uses. Only the water baptism of disciples remains an ongoing ordinance of the church. The others are historical, figurative, unique to Christ, or the Spirit’s sovereign work in salvation. If you have trusted Christ, speak with your pastor about obeying Him in baptism as a public testimony, and read these passages in context this week, asking the Lord for clearer sight of His grace.

question: What do you think about the Bible codes? Is there any validity to them?
answer:
Bible codes do not have real validity as messages from God, as a method of interpretation, or as proof you should trust. The claim is that hidden predictions sit in the Hebrew text as equidistant letter sequences, words formed by skipping a fixed number of letters. That idea became popular in the 1990s, and it does not hold up.

It is understandable why people were drawn to it. A long text will throw up striking letter patterns, and a desire to see Scripture confirmed by something that feels mathematical is not a foolish desire. The trouble is that the method can manufacture those patterns almost anywhere.

Skip any fixed number of letters through a long book and short words appear by chance. Hebrew, written mostly with consonants, makes those accidental strings even easier to “read” as names or events. Researchers who tested the famous rabbi-name experiment found that the results depended on flexible choices of names and spellings, and that similar “codes” could be produced in other Hebrew texts, including a translation of War and Peace. Popular code books also announced specific future events that never happened. A method that finds assassinations in novels and failed predictions in the Torah is not prophecy. It is pattern-hunting after the fact.

There is a deeper problem than the statistics. God has tied his authority to what Scripture actually says, in sentences, in context, not to a crossword hidden under the letters. “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). That usefulness is the plain word, sufficient for faith and life. “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Jesus did not unlock Moses and the Prophets by counting letter skips. He opened them as testimony about himself (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). The “mystery” the apostles preach is the gospel once concealed and now made public in Christ, not a private code (Ephesians 3:4–6).

Treating skip sequences as divine forecasts also slides toward divination, which Scripture forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Even the remarkable care of Jewish scribes does not rescue the theory. Real textual details, including spelling differences and the Ketiv and Qere readings, would scramble any letter-perfect skip code. Literary beauty in the Bible is real. Acrostics, careful wordplay, and prophecy fulfilled in history are part of the text’s glory. Those are features of what the authors wrote, not permission to mine the consonants for tomorrow’s headlines.

You do not need a hidden code to know that this book is from God. The clearer wonder is penal substitution and the resurrection: the Holy One bearing sin for the ungodly, buried, and raised bodily, so that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. If a video or book has left you anxious that you are missing a secret message, set the skip charts down this week and read Luke 24 slowly, asking only what the passage says about Jesus. Then talk it through with a pastor who will keep you in the text God has actually given. If you want, tell me which code claim you have heard, and we can look at that specific one.

question: How can I see the hand of God moving in my life?
answer:
The longing to see God’s hand at work is itself a mercy, drawing you toward the God who is never absent. You recognize His hand most clearly by looking first to Jesus Christ in Scripture, then tracing His providence, His sovereign, purposeful care over every detail, through the promises He has already spoken.

In Scripture, “the hand of the Lord” names God’s mighty power to save, guide, and sustain His people (Exodus 15:6; Psalm 139:10). That same power is displayed supremely in the gospel: Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, so that everyone who repents and trusts Him is brought from death to life and kept by God’s power (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; John 10:28-29). If you belong to Christ, His hand is already upon you, finishing the good work He began (Philippians 1:6; Romans 8:28).

You learn to notice that hand in ordinary life by staying close to His Word until His character is familiar, by remembering concrete past mercies so your heart expects His faithfulness (Psalm 77:11-12), and by watching for the Spirit’s fruit and growing holiness, the quiet evidence of sanctification (Galatians 5:22-23; 2 Corinthians 3:18). Wise believers in a local church help you test what you see, so you are not left to feelings or coincidences alone (Proverbs 11:14; Hebrews 10:24-25).

For the next seven days, read one psalm each morning. Write down one truth about God’s character, then speak to Him in your own words about how that truth meets what you are facing. At week’s end, share one observation with a pastor or mature Christian friend.

God has spoken finally in His Son and continues to work all things according to the counsel of His will (Hebrews 1:1-2; Ephesians 1:11). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, and you will know the God whose hand upholds you. What part of your story feels most hidden from His care right now?

question: Are we to love the sinner but hate the sin?
answer:
Yes, we are to love sinners and hate sin. Scripture holds both together as the way God has treated us and the way He commands His people to live.

God proves His love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8; John 3:16). That death was penal substitution, Christ bearing the wrath sin deserves so that the guilty may be justified by grace through faith alone. At the same time God is holy and hates evil. He does not delight in wickedness, and no evil can dwell with Him (Psalm 5:4; Habakkuk 1:13).

We are therefore told both to love our neighbors and our enemies (Matthew 5:44; Matthew 22:39) and to hate evil, detesting what is evil while clinging to what is good (Psalm 97:10; Romans 12:9). Every person bears the image of God and must be treated with dignity and compassion (Genesis 1:27). Sin is rebellion against that same God, so it must be opposed and never approved (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23).

Jesus drew near to tax collectors and sinners with real kindness, yet He called them to repentance, saying He came to call sinners, not the righteous, to turn from their sin (Luke 5:30-32). Love that will not name sin leaves people in what destroys them. Love that names sin without patience and gentleness fails to reflect the Savior who is full of grace and truth (Ephesians 4:15).

This begins with our own hearts. We hate sin first by confessing and turning from our own, so we do not point out specks while ignoring logs (Matthew 7:3-5; 1 John 1:9).

Choose one person whose sin grieves you, pray for them by name this week, and ask the Lord for one concrete kindness you can show without calling evil good. If a door opens, point them gently to the Christ who died and rose so sinners can be forgiven and made new.

What situation led you to ask this? I am glad to think it through with you from Scripture.

question: Is the Buddhist concept of Zen compatible with the Christian faith?
answer:
No, the Buddhist concept of Zen is not compatible with the Christian faith. Zen pursues enlightenment through meditation and direct insight into emptiness and no-self, apart from the personal Triune God and the saving work of Jesus Christ, while Scripture teaches that eternal life is found only in Him.

It is understandable that people are drawn to Zen’s promise of stillness and release from anxious thoughts in a restless world; that longing for peace is real. Yet the Bible warns us not to be taken captive by philosophy and empty deception that are not according to Christ (Colossians 2:8). Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6). Salvation exists in no one else (Acts 4:12).

All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). His death was a penal substitutionary atonement, and we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by meditative insight or self-realization (Ephesians 2:8–9). He gives a peace the world cannot give (John 14:27).

Turn from every other path and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. This week, read John 1 and John 14 slowly, asking God to show you who Jesus is, and bring your questions to a pastor or elder in a Bible-teaching church.

What draws you to compare Zen with the Christian faith?

question: What is the Wailing Wall / Western Wall?
answer:
The Western Wall, often called the Wailing Wall, is the ancient western retaining wall of the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. It is the holiest place where Jewish people can freely pray, near the site of the biblical Temple.

This wall is not the sanctuary building itself. It belongs to the massive platform Herod the Great built in the decades before Jesus’ birth to support the Second Temple and its courts. Jesus walked those courts, taught in them, and cleansed them (John 2:13–16; Matthew 21:12–13). In AD 70 the Romans destroyed the Temple, just as He had said: not one stone of those buildings would be left on another (Matthew 24:1–2). The Western Wall remained.

The name “Wailing Wall” reflects long Jewish grief over the Temple’s loss. Worshipers still gather at these stones to pray and to lament.

Christians receive this history as real. Under the old covenant the Temple was God’s appointed meeting place with Israel, where sacrifice was offered and His glory dwelt (1 Kings 8:10–11). The New Testament teaches that Jesus Christ fulfilled what the Temple foreshadowed. He spoke of His own body as the temple (John 2:19–21), and by His atoning death and bodily resurrection He opened a new and living way into the Father’s presence (Hebrews 10:19–22). Those who trust Him are themselves a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16).

We can respect the sincerity of those who pray at the Wall and the weight of that history. Yet nearness to God is no longer tied to a place in Jerusalem. It is given through Jesus Christ, the one mediator between God and man (1 Timothy 2:5; John 4:21–24).

If you are thinking about this place, read John 2:13–22 and Hebrews 10:19–22, and thank God that the way to Him stands open in Christ.

question: What is Taizé worship, and is it biblical?
answer:
Taizé worship is the contemplative prayer style of the Taizé Community in France, built around short repetitive chants (often drawn from Scripture), periods of silence, and Bible readings in a simple, ecumenical setting.

Faithful Christians may disagree about how fully biblical this form is, because Scripture supplies principles and elements for worship more than one fixed musical or liturgical pattern, so there is room for Christian liberty in secondary matters of style (Romans 14:5-6).

Some value it as a help to meditation. Repetition can let the word of Christ dwell richly in the heart, as the Psalms themselves use refrains, and silence answers the call to be still and know that the Lord is God (Psalm 46:10; Colossians 3:16). When the chants stay close to Scripture and keep Christ central, this approach can serve quiet devotion.

Others urge caution, especially those who hold the regulative principle of worship (that corporate praise should include what Scripture positively warrants). Extended chanting can drift toward the empty repetition Jesus warned against (Matthew 6:7). More importantly, critics observe that the community’s pursuit of ecumenical reconciliation has at times appeared to soften a clear witness to justification by faith alone and the final authority of Scripture, truths at the heart of the gospel (Galatians 2:16; 2 Timothy 3:16-17). Unity matters, yet it must be unity in the truth (Ephesians 4:15; John 17:17).

I receive the simple, Word-centered songs and the gift of quiet prayer as potentially fruitful when they keep Christ’s cross and resurrection in view. At the same time, I would not take the broader Taizé approach as a model for the church’s worship, because the gospel’s distinctives should not be blurred. That is one faithful way of weighing the practice; other believers who love the same Lord may differ on the style itself.

Bring any worship form, including this one, under Scripture together with your local church, and ask whether it teaches the apostles’ doctrine, builds up the saints, and keeps the finished work of Christ central (Acts 2:42; 1 Corinthians 14:26). If you want to grow in prayer, begin a steady rhythm of reading a Gospel alongside the Psalms, and talk with your pastor about practices that serve that aim in your own congregation.

question: Does the Old Testament truly predict a second advent of the Messiah?
answer:
Yes, the Old Testament truly predicts a second advent of the Messiah. It reveals both his suffering to atone for sin and his later coming in glory to judge and reign, two advents held together in the biblical witness.

Some argue that the prophets never describe two comings, so the second advent must be a Christian idea read back into the text after Jesus did not immediately set up an earthly kingdom. Others note that much traditional Jewish reading expects one future messianic age rather than a Messiah who comes, departs, and returns. Those concerns deserve a fair hearing, because the Old Testament often holds the Messiah’s humiliation and exaltation in one prophetic view. Yet the Scriptures themselves distinguish the sufferings of Christ from the glories that would follow (1 Peter 1:11). Jesus made the distinction clear when he read Isaiah 61, announced the year of the Lord’s favor, and left the day of vengeance still ahead (Luke 4:16-21; Isaiah 61:1-2).

Particular prophecies point to a coming that has not yet occurred. Zechariah 14:4 declares that on that day the LORD’s feet will stand on the Mount of Olives and the mountain will be split from east to west. This did not take place at the first coming. Jesus ascended from the Mount of Olives, and the angels said he will return in the same way (Acts 1:9-12). Daniel 7:13-14 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom. The Lord Jesus applied that vision to his future coming on the clouds with power and great glory (Matthew 24:30; Matthew 26:64). Zechariah 12:10 foretells that they will look on the one they have pierced, and Revelation 1:7 joins that looking to the day every eye sees him coming.

These promises give firm hope. The Messiah who was pierced will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead. We all have sinned and need a Savior. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, so that his advent brings joy rather than dread.

This week, read Daniel 7 and Zechariah 14 slowly, and ask the Lord in your own words to make his promised return a steady hope in your heart. What part of these prophecies most strengthens or challenges you right now?

question: Contemporary Christian music - is it honoring to God? Should it be used in church services?
answer:
Contemporary Christian music is not honoring or dishonoring to God merely because it is contemporary. A song honors God when its words are true, the heart offering it is sincere, and the church is built up. Worship style is a non-essential. Faithful Christians may disagree because Scripture commands singing and worship in spirit and truth, yet it does not bind the church to one century’s melodies, instruments, or production style. This is a matter of Christian liberty, not a test of orthodoxy.

Two concerns deserve a charitable hearing. Some believers prefer psalms and older hymns out of love for reverence and doctrinal weight. They worry that much popular Christian music borrows the habits of entertainment, centers the singer’s feelings, and says little about God’s holiness or Christ’s saving work. Others note that the church has long set biblical truth to the musical speech of its own people, that Scripture calls for a new song (Psalm 96:1), and that instruments now called traditional were once new. They treat style as indifferent when the lyric is faithful and the aim is God’s glory.

The same tests govern every song, old or new. True worshipers must worship the Father in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). The word of Christ is to dwell richly among us as we teach and admonish one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing to the Lord from the heart (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19). Whatever we do is to be done for God’s glory and for the building up of the body, properly and in order (1 Corinthians 10:31; 1 Corinthians 14:26; 1 Corinthians 14:40). A cherished hymn sung in pride does not please Him. A newer song, if it tells the truth and is offered in humility, may.

Contemporary songs may therefore be used in church services, and they need not be. Judge the particular lyric and the manner, not the marketing label. Elders are responsible to guard what a congregation sings. Prefer what the whole church can sing together over a performance that leaves the saints as an audience. Where a style wounds a tender conscience or threatens peace, love limits liberty (Romans 14:13-19; 1 Corinthians 8:9-13). Unity in the gospel matters more than winning a style debate.

Choose songs, whether written this year or centuries ago, that are God-centered, honest about sin, and full of Christ’s person and atoning work. Our singing is a response to justification by grace through faith, not a work that earns God’s favor. This week, take one song your church sings and read its words slowly beside Colossians 3:16, asking what it teaches about God and whether the congregation can offer it with understanding. If this is stirring conflict, speak with your elders before you speak against your brothers. Are you weighing a specific song, or the whole direction of your church’s worship?

question: What does it mean to test the spirits?
answer:
To test the spirits means to examine teachings, prophecies, and claimed spiritual influences to see whether they truly come from God, rather than accepting every spiritual claim. The apostle John commands this because many false prophets have gone out into the world (1 John 4:1).

In John’s setting, some teachers denied that Jesus Christ had truly come in the flesh. His test is plain: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God (1 John 4:2–3). That confession affirms the incarnation, which the church has long summarized as the hypostatic union: Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. A message may sound spiritual, but if it denies Christ’s person, twists His saving work, or leads people away from the gospel, it fails the test (Galatians 1:6–9).

This is spiritual discernment, not suspicion for its own sake. The Bereans received the word eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether the teaching was true (Acts 17:11). Paul likewise says to test all things and hold fast to what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Scripture, not a feeling, a sign, or a forceful personality, is the measure.

When a sermon, a “word from the Lord,” or a strong inner impression comes, write down the claim and set it beside Scripture, especially who Christ is and what He has done. If you are unsure, bring it to your elders rather than acting on it alone. Discernment grows as you stay in the Word and walk with a local church that loves the truth.

If a particular teaching is on your mind, I would be glad to help you weigh it by Scripture.

question: Why should I get married?
answer:
Marriage is worth pursuing when God gives both the desire and a wise, godly opportunity, because He designed it as a covenant gift, not as a cure for loneliness or a mark of spiritual success.

From the beginning, God made marriage a one-flesh covenant between one man and one woman, for companionship, mutual help, faithful intimacy, and the nurture of children (Genesis 2:18-24; Genesis 1:27-28). In Christ, that covenant also becomes a living picture of the gospel: a husband is called to love as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her, and a wife is called to a respectful, willing partnership, so that ordinary life displays sacrificial love (Ephesians 5:22-33). Marriage is also God's holy setting for sexual desire, protecting both spouses from using one another and giving them a place to give themselves freely (1 Corinthians 7:2-5; Hebrews 13:4). Malachi even calls marriage a covenant before God, not a private arrangement we may reshape when it costs us something (Malachi 2:14-16).

Scripture does not say every Christian must marry. Singleness is also a gift, and it can free a person for undivided devotion to the Lord (1 Corinthians 7:7-8; 1 Corinthians 7:32-35). So do not marry to escape sadness, please family, or prove you are mature. Marry, if you marry, to glorify God with a brother or sister in Christ who will help you follow Jesus for life.

This week, read 1 Corinthians 7 slowly and pray specifically for wisdom, contentment, purity, and, if it is God's will, a spouse who loves Christ. Then talk with a pastor or mature believer who knows you, and ask them to help you test your motives. Are you weighing marriage in general, or a particular person?

question: Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath?
answer:
Sunday is the Christian Sabbath in one major historic view, but not in another, and this is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians may disagree. The difference turns on interpretive emphasis: how the fourth commandment’s call to rest relates to the new covenant, since the New Testament shows the church gathering on the first day without an explicit, detailed command that settles every question of obligation.

One view holds that the Sabbath principle belongs to God’s moral law, rooted in creation and the Ten Commandments, and that the day of observance moved to the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, because of Christ’s resurrection and apostolic practice. On this understanding the day is set apart for worship and rest from ordinary work (Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11; Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10).

Another view holds that the Old Testament Sabbath was a ceremonial shadow whose substance is Christ Himself, so no particular day binds the conscience as a Sabbath. Believers still gather joyfully on the first day, yet they have freedom regarding days and must not judge one another (Colossians 2:16-17; Romans 14:5-6; Hebrews 4:9-10).

In the Reformed understanding of covenant continuity I hold the first view: the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, a gracious provision for resting in Christ’s finished work and worshiping together. This is one faithful approach within historic Christianity, not a requirement for recognizing fellow believers. Romans 14:1-6 calls us to welcome one another without quarreling over disputable matters.

Read Romans 14 and Hebrews 4 this week, then talk with your pastor or a mature believer about how your church practices the Lord’s Day, so your convictions are shaped by Scripture and expressed in love.

question: What does it mean that those who humble themselves will be exalted (Matthew 23:12)?
answer:
Matthew 23:12 means that God Himself brings down those who grasp at honor, and He lifts up those who take the low place before Him and others. Jesus said this in the temple courts, warning His disciples not to copy the scribes and Pharisees, who loved public greetings, the best seats, and religious titles (Matthew 23:5-12).

In that honor-seeking setting, Jesus reversed the usual measure of greatness: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted" (Matthew 23:11-12). This is not a technique for getting ahead in this life. It is a promise about God's holy judgment and His gracious rule. Pride reaches for a throne God has not given. Humility bows, serves, and waits. "God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble" (James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5-6). Biblical humility is not self-hatred or pretending you have no gifts. It is a sober estimate of yourself before God, a refusal to grasp at glory, and a willingness to use what He has given for others (Romans 12:3).

The Lord Jesus is both the pattern and the power for this. He did not exploit His equality with God. He took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient to death on a cross, and therefore God highly exalted Him (Philippians 2:6-11). The same truth meets us in the temple when a proud Pharisee and a repentant tax collector pray. The one who begged for mercy went home justified, declared right with God, "for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted" (Luke 18:14). That exaltation is God's work, in His time: sometimes in this life, and fully when Christ is revealed in glory (1 Peter 5:6; James 4:10).

This week, ask the Lord to show you one place where you crave recognition, then take one quiet step of service that no one is likely to praise (Psalm 139:23-24). Where do you most feel the pull to be noticed rather than to serve?

question: How should poetry in the Bible be interpreted?
answer:
Biblical poetry should be interpreted as God-breathed truth expressed through artistic form. It is fully authoritative, yet it must be read as poetry, not flattened into prose or treated as mere feeling without content.

Large parts of Scripture are poetry, including the Psalms, Job, Proverbs, Song of Solomon, and much of the Prophets. Hebrew poetry works through parallelism, metaphor, imagery, and sometimes hyperbole. The second line often restates, contrasts, or advances the first. Psalm 19:1 is a clear example: "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands." Creation does not speak with an ordinary human voice, yet the verse truly teaches that the created world displays God's glory.

A sound reading follows the sense the Spirit-inspired author intended in that literary form. Figures should be taken as figures, while the realities they affirm remain real. When Psalm 91:4 says, "He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge," the point is not that God is a bird. The point is His actual, tender protection of those who trust Him. Where poetic lines recall God's acts in history, those acts are real events, sung rather than merely chronicled.

Scripture interprets Scripture. Jesus taught that what is written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). All Scripture, poetry included, is God-breathed and useful for instruction, conviction, correction, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). So ask what each image reveals about God's character, human need, and the hope secured in Christ, then let that truth govern both worship and obedience.

This week, take one psalm, such as Psalm 23 or Psalm 51. Name its main images, write one sentence on the truth each image teaches, and bring a real concern of your life to the Lord in the psalm's own language. If a particular passage is on your mind, tell me which one and we can walk through it together.

question: What is the significance of the statement in Romans 1:22 that “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”?
answer:
Romans 1:22 means that people who reject the knowledge of God and boast in their own insight do not become truly wise. They fall into spiritual folly. In the Berean Standard Bible the verse reads, "Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools."

Paul is explaining why God's wrath is revealed against human ungodliness (Romans 1:18). God has made Himself plain through general revelation in creation, so people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). Yet "although they knew God, they neither glorified Him as God nor gave thanks to Him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal man and birds and animals and reptiles" (Romans 1:21-23). Writing into a Greco-Roman world that prized philosophers, Paul shows the irony: claimed wisdom, cut off from the Creator, does not enlighten. It darkens, and it ends in idolatry, exchanging "the truth of God for a lie" (Romans 1:25).

This is what Christians call the noetic effects of sin. Sin does not only corrupt behavior. It darkens the mind, so that autonomous human wisdom becomes futile. Scripture sets the contrast clearly: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding" (Proverbs 9:10). Later Paul says God has made foolish the wisdom of the world, and that Christ "has become for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:20; 1 Corinthians 1:30). The label for this whole descent is idolatry: worship redirected from the immortal God to created things.

When a clever argument tempts you to set Scripture aside, test it by one question this week: does it lead you to honor the Creator, or to remake Him after the pattern of created things? Bring that question to the Lord in prayer, and let a mature believer in your church help you weigh it by the Word.

question: What does it mean that sin is lawlessness?
answer:
Sin is lawlessness means that sin is the breaking of God’s law, a rebellious disregard for His commands and authority. Scripture states this directly: sin is lawlessness (1 John 3:4).

The Greek word behind this statement is anomia, which describes living without law or in active violation of it. John uses the term to show that practicing sin is not a harmless slip but a settled opposition to the God who gave the law, in contrast to the righteousness that marks those born of God (1 John 3:4-10). The law itself is holy, righteous, and good; it simply exposes the lawlessness already in us (Romans 7:12; Romans 3:20).

This matters because lawlessness is personal offense against a holy God, and every one of us has lived that way and falls short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The remedy is not trying harder to keep the law. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, fulfilled the law perfectly, died on the cross as the substitute who bore the penalty our lawlessness deserved, and rose bodily on the third day. Through faith in Him alone we are justified, declared righteous by grace, and given the Spirit’s power to walk in new obedience rather than rebellion (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 8:3-4).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A practical next step is to read the Ten Commandments slowly in Exodus 20:1-17 this week, name one specific way you have lived lawlessly, confess that honestly to God, and rest in Christ’s righteousness rather than your own record.

How does this definition of sin meet you right now?

question: Has anyone ever seen God?
answer:
No one has ever seen God in His full, unveiled essence, for He is spirit and dwells in unapproachable light, and no one can see Him and live (John 1:18; John 4:24; Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16).

Yet God has revealed Himself through theophanies, real but partial visible appearances in the Old Testament, and supremely through His Son. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, declared that whoever has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9), because He is the image of the invisible God and the exact imprint of His nature (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). In the hypostatic union, the eternal Word became flesh so that we might behold God’s glory in a way we can bear (John 1:14).

One day those cleansed by Christ will see God face to face (Matthew 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 3:2). Until then we walk by faith. Set aside time this week to read John 14, asking God to show you the Father’s heart through the words of Jesus.

Our sin separates us from this holy God (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2), so we need the Savior He has given. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4), and all who repent and trust in Him alone are forgiven and brought near by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Peter 3:18). If you have not yet done so, turn from sin and believe in Jesus Christ for the forgiveness and life He alone gives.

How does this truth about seeing God through Christ speak to you today?

question: Are books such as 90 minutes in Heaven and 23 minutes in Hell biblically based?
answer:
No. Books such as 90 Minutes in Heaven and 23 Minutes in Hell are not biblically based. They are personal stories of claimed visions or near-death experiences, not teaching drawn from Scripture, and they must not be treated as revelation.

God has already spoken sufficiently about death, judgment, heaven, and hell. Scripture is inspired and enough for faith and practice, so we do not need private tours of the afterlife to know the truth (2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:19-21). Paul was caught up into paradise and heard things he was not permitted to tell (2 Corinthians 12:2-4). In Jesus' account of the rich man and Lazarus, Abraham will not send a messenger back from the dead, because those who refuse Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded by someone rising from the grave (Luke 16:27-31). It is appointed for people to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27).

Heaven and hell themselves are biblical. To be away from the body, for the believer, is to be at home with the Lord, and the final hope is resurrection and the new creation where God dwells with His people (2 Corinthians 5:6-8; Philippians 1:23; Revelation 21:1-4). Hell is God's just, conscious judgment on unrepentant sin (Matthew 25:41-46; Revelation 20:11-15). Those truths stand. Clocks, conversations, sensory tours, and return trips are not given to us as binding doctrine. Where these books repeat Scripture, they add nothing necessary. Where they go beyond it, they should not shape your hope or your fear. Test everything, and do not treat a moving story as equal to the Word (1 Thessalonians 5:21; 1 John 4:1).

Read Luke 16:19-31 and Revelation 21-22 this week, and ask your pastor to walk through them with you. Assurance does not come from someone else's minutes in glory or torment. All have sinned and fall short of God's glory (Romans 3:23). Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, whose penal substitutionary death and resurrection secure forgiveness and eternal life.

Would you like to look at what Jesus Himself said about how a person can be sure of belonging to Him?

question: Why does God not seem to care about the millions of starving children in the world?
answer:
The hunger of children is a grief that should break our hearts, and your question is one Scripture does not brush aside. It can feel impossible that a God who is both good and powerful would allow millions of little ones to starve. Many people conclude from that pain that God must not care, or that He cannot be both loving and in control.

The Bible teaches that God does care. He is “a father to the fatherless” and the defender of the oppressed, and He “gives food to the hungry” (Psalm 68:5; Psalm 146:7-9). Jesus welcomed children, fed hungry crowds, and said that caring for “the least of these” is caring for Him (Mark 10:13-16; Matthew 14:13-21; Matthew 25:35-40). Whoever oppresses the poor shows contempt for their Maker (Proverbs 14:31). Indifference to starving children is not God’s heart. It is sin.

Suffering continues because we live in a world broken by the Fall. God made a good creation, but human rebellion brought curse, death, and disorder into it (Genesis 3:17-19; Romans 8:20-22). Children suffer, not because God delights in their pain and not because each child is being punished for a private crime, but because we live downstream of sin’s ruin. Much hunger is also the direct fruit of human wickedness: war, theft, corruption, and the refusal of those with food and power to share. God judges that injustice. He is sovereign over suffering without being the author of sin. He permits what He hates, and He will not leave it unanswered.

He has also given His people a clear command. Pure religion includes caring for the vulnerable, and the early church shared so that none among them lacked (James 1:27; Acts 2:44-45). When those who name Christ hoard while others starve, that exposes our failure, not His. His ordinary way of feeding the hungry is often through people who obey Him.

That still does not erase the ache or explain every case. Scripture gives room for lament. The psalmists cry, “How long, O Lord?” and Job never receives a full diagram of his pain. The secret things belong to the Lord (Deuteronomy 29:29). What is revealed is His character: holy, just, patient, and merciful. History is moving toward a day when He will judge evil and wipe away every tear, and those who belong to Him “will never again hunger” (Revelation 7:16-17; Revelation 21:3-4).

The clearest proof that God cares is Jesus Christ. The eternal Son took on our humanity, lived among the poor, and went to the cross. There He bore the penalty our sins deserve, died, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (John 1:14; Isaiah 53:4-6; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That is penal substitution: the innocent One suffering in the place of the guilty, so rebels could be forgiven. If God gave His Son, He has not withheld His care (Romans 8:32).

If this question is also about whether you can trust Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Bring this honestly to God in your own words, perhaps with Psalm 10 or Psalm 13, and ask Him to make you someone who relieves hunger rather than only questions it. This week, consider giving or serving through your local church, or through a careful Christian relief work that feeds children in Jesus’ name.

What part of this sits heaviest on you right now?

question: What is postmodern therapy, and is it biblical?
answer:
Postmodern therapy is a set of counseling approaches, especially narrative therapy and related collaborative or social-constructionist methods, that treat problems, identity, and even truth as stories people and cultures construct through language rather than as objective realities given by God.

It is not biblical in its foundations. Scripture presents truth as real, public, and anchored in God Himself, not as one preferred narrative among many. Jesus says, “I am the way and the truth and the life” (John 14:6), and He prays, “Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth” (John 17:17). The Bible is the inspired, inerrant Word of God and the final authority for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Postmodern therapy, by contrast, typically denies or sidelines any binding metanarrative and locates authority in the client’s preferred story. That conflicts with the Christian confession that we are creatures, not the authors of reality.

People are often drawn to these methods because they want to be heard, to escape cold labels, and to believe change is possible. Those desires are understandable. Scripture also honors the dignity of every person made in God’s image and calls believers to bear one another’s burdens with real compassion (Galatians 6:2; James 1:19). Listening well and refusing to reduce someone to a diagnosis can be good. But compassion is not the same as agreeing that sin, guilt, and disorder are merely social constructions. The Bible names sin as real rebellion against a holy God (Romans 3:23; 1 John 1:8-10), locates our truest story inside creation, fall, redemption, and new creation, and offers forgiveness and a new heart through Christ’s death and bodily resurrection, received by grace alone through faith alone, not by re-authoring our own narrative (2 Corinthians 5:17-21; Ephesians 2:8-9).

Colossians 2:8 warns believers not to be taken captive by philosophy and empty ideas that are not according to Christ. Techniques such as careful listening or noticing how words shape a person’s outlook can sometimes be used under Scripture’s authority. The postmodern claim that there is no objective truth to submit to cannot. Where suffering has medical dimensions, seek appropriate medical care. Where the issues concern the soul, meaning, guilt, identity, or obedience, bring them under the Word in the care of a local church and, when needed, a biblical counselor who treats Scripture as sufficient for those matters.

A concrete step this week: take one struggle you are facing, read how Scripture names both the problem and Christ’s provision (for example in Psalm 32, Romans 8, or 1 Peter 5:6-7), and talk it through with a mature believer or pastor rather than treating your preferred story as the final authority. If you are weighing a specific therapist or method for yourself or someone you love, what is the main concern you are trying to address?

question: I am a Christian who is addicted to smoking. How can I quit?
answer:
Friend, I am glad you want to be free from this addiction to smoking. That desire is itself a mercy, and the Lord is able to help you walk it out.

Scripture does not name tobacco, yet it speaks directly to being mastered by a habit. Paul refuses to be brought under the power of anything, even what is otherwise permissible (1 Corinthians 6:12). Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and you were bought with a price, so you are called to glorify God with your body (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Self-control is fruit the Spirit produces in those who belong to Christ (Galatians 5:22-23). Quitting is not bare willpower. It is progressive sanctification: God gradually forming you as you depend on Christ and use the means He gives, including ordinary help.

Begin with these steps this week.

Bring the struggle to the Lord every day. Confess where smoking has mastered you, thank Him that sin shall not be your master because you are under grace (Romans 6:14), and ask specifically for self-control in the moment of craving. Speak honestly. You do not need polished words.

Do not fight alone. Tell a pastor, elder, or trusted believer, and ask them to pray for you and check in regularly. James urges believers to confess to one another and pray for one another so that they may be healed (James 5:16). Isolation feeds addiction. The local church is one of God's ordinary means of grace.

Use wisdom for the body. I am not a physician and cannot give medical advice, so please speak with a doctor about safe ways to quit, including whether a cessation plan is wise for you. Seeking medical counsel is not a lack of faith. God often helps through ordinary means.

Name your triggers before they hit. When the craving comes, have a replacement ready: step away and pray one honest sentence, drink water, text your accountability partner, or recite a verse you have memorized, such as the promise that God provides a way of escape in temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13).

If you fall, do not hide in shame. Confess it quickly, receive God's forgiveness in Christ, and begin again the same day. He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6). Your standing with God rests on Christ's finished work, not on a perfect quit date.

A concrete next step: before this week ends, message one mature believer and ask for ongoing accountability, and make an appointment with your doctor about quitting.

What part of quitting feels most difficult for you right now?

question: What is mortification of sin / the flesh?
answer:
Mortification of sin, or of the flesh, is the Spirit-enabled work of putting sinful desires and deeds to death in the life of a believer, as part of progressive sanctification. Some historic holiness and Wesleyan Christians have argued, with real zeal for holiness, that God intends a deeper crisis of entire sanctification in which the inward bent toward sin is so cleansed that willful sin need not continue. I hold the Reformed view that sin’s reign is broken at conversion, yet remaining sin must still be killed daily until we see Christ, because Scripture both tells us to count ourselves dead to sin and still commands us to put sin to death (Romans 6:11; Romans 8:13).

Paul states it without softness: “if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13). He also writes, “Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature” (Colossians 3:5). The words behind “put to death” mean to kill, not to rename or merely manage. In Paul’s letters, “the flesh” is not the physical body as such, but the fallen sinful inclination that still wars against the Spirit in those who belong to Christ (Galatians 5:16–17; Galatians 5:24).

This is not how a sinner is justified. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, on the ground of His penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection (Romans 3:21–26; Romans 4:25). Mortification is what follows union with Christ. The old self was crucified with Him, so sin no longer reigns, and yet the flesh remains and must be opposed until glory (Romans 6:6–14; Philippians 3:12). Flesh cannot kill flesh. The same Spirit who raised Jesus dwells in His people and supplies the power (Romans 8:11–13). John Owen’s old counsel still holds: be killing sin, or it will be killing you.

In practice, mortification looks like this. Name the sin in biblical terms and refuse to negotiate with it. Set your mind on Christ, crucified and risen, and count yourself dead to that sin and alive to God (Romans 6:11; Colossians 3:1–5). Cut off its usual feeding points with seriousness, not with harm to your body (Matthew 5:29–30). Replace the empty space with the Word, prayer, and the fellowship of a local church, putting on the new life Christ gives (Colossians 3:12–17). Confess honestly, knowing that “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

This week, write down one recurring sin, bring it before the Lord in your own words with Psalm 51 and Romans 8:13 open before you, and tell a mature believer in your church so you are not fighting alone. If you do not yet trust Christ, the first need is not a program of self-improvement, but to repent and rest in Jesus, who died and rose for sinners. What sin are you finding hardest to put to death right now?

question: Is God’s love reckless?
answer:
No, God’s love is not reckless. It is perfect, holy, and wise, fulfilling His eternal purposes without carelessness or any risk of failure.

Reckless describes rash action that ignores consequences. The living God loves with infinite wisdom and sovereign power. He set His love on His people before the foundation of the world and sent His Son at the appointed time to redeem them (Ephesians 1:4-5; Galatians 4:4-5). Nothing in that love is impulsive or out of control.

At the cross this love appears in the penal substitutionary atonement. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us, bearing the penalty our sins deserved so that God remains just and becomes the justifier of everyone who trusts in Jesus (Romans 5:8; Romans 3:25-26). The Father gave His only Son, and the Son laid down His life of His own accord (John 3:16; John 10:17-18). The cost was fully known and willingly paid. That is lavish, pursuing grace, not recklessness.

Some songs use “reckless” to express how undeserved and overwhelming this pursuit feels, much like the father who runs to embrace his returning son (Luke 15:20). The joy of that grace should humble and delight every believer. Yet the father acts with full knowledge and abundant resources. Scripture’s own witness is stronger: His love endures forever (Psalm 136:1).

Because this love is reliable, you can trust it when life feels unsteady. If you belong to Christ, nothing can separate you from it (Romans 8:38-39; John 10:28). Read Romans 5:6-11 today, linger on how God’s love is proven at the cross, and thank Him directly in your own words for a love that is strong, wise, and sure.

question: Does the Bible teach that there is a gift of celibacy?
answer:
Yes, the Bible teaches that there is a gift of celibacy. God gives some believers a gracious enablement to live unmarried and content, so they may serve Christ with undivided concern.

Paul states it plainly: “I wish that all men were as I am. But each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that” (1 Corinthians 7:7, BSB). In context he means the unmarried state. He calls it good for those who have received it, while directing those who lack self-control to marry rather than burn with passion (1 Corinthians 7:8–9).

Jesus taught the same truth. When His disciples wondered whether it was better not to marry, He replied, “Not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it has been given. For there are eunuchs who were born that way; others were made that way by men; and still others live like eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. The one who can accept this should accept it” (Matthew 19:11–12, BSB). The ability to remain single for the kingdom is therefore given by God; it is not a universal command.

Scripture does not treat this gift as superior to marriage. The one who marries has not sinned (1 Corinthians 7:28), and marriage is to be honored by all (Hebrews 13:4). The practical difference is that the single believer can give full attention to pleasing the Lord without the rightful responsibilities that marriage brings (1 Corinthians 7:32–35).

If you are seeking to discern whether you have this gift, ask the Lord for honesty about your own desires, read these passages slowly, and talk with your pastors. They can help you see whether God is giving you contentment for lifelong singleness or leading you toward marriage in the Lord.

question: What did it mean that Satan wanted to be like the Most High in Isaiah 14:14?
answer:
In Isaiah 14:14, the boast “I will make myself like the Most High” means a rebellious claim to God’s unique sovereignty, glory, and right to be worshiped, not a desire to reflect His character in humble obedience.

The immediate setting is a taunt against the king of Babylon (Isaiah 14:4). Yet the five “I will” declarations rise beyond any human ruler: ascending to heaven, lifting a throne above the stars of God, sitting enthroned over the assembly, rising above the clouds, and making himself like the Most High (Isaiah 14:13-14). Historic Christian reading has long heard in this language the pride of Satan, the spiritual power behind proud earthly kings, whose fall Jesus Himself described (Luke 10:18; compare Revelation 12:7-9). To be “like” the Most High here is to grasp at equality of rank and prerogative with God, the very thing no creature may seize.

God alone is the Most High. His supreme rule is His alone, and pride that reaches for it is judged (Isaiah 14:15; Proverbs 16:18; James 4:6). The Lord Jesus, truly God, did not treat equality with God as something to exploit for self-exaltation. He humbled Himself to the cross and was therefore exalted by the Father (Philippians 2:6-11).

If you feel that same pull to set your will above God’s, bring it to Him in honest prayer and read Philippians 2 slowly this week, asking Him to form in you the mind of Christ.

question: What does the Bible say about the hornet?
answer:
The Bible speaks of the hornet in three places, and in each one the LORD Himself sends it to drive the nations of Canaan out before Israel.

In Exodus 23:28 He promises to send the hornet ahead of His people to drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites. Deuteronomy 7:20 says He would send the hornet among them until even those who hid from Israel had perished. Looking back, Joshua says the LORD sent the hornet before them, and the two Amorite kings were driven out not by Israel’s sword or bow (Joshua 24:12).

The Hebrew word in these verses, *tsirah*, is what English Bibles translate “hornet.” The stress of the passages is God’s providence. The land was His gift, not Israel’s conquest. He can use what looks small to keep His covenant word.

Christians have discussed whether God used literal hornets or whether the word also pictures the terror He cast on those nations, the “terror” named just before in Exodus 23:27. That detail is not an essential of the faith, and either reading leaves the same confession standing: the victory was the LORD’s.

When something before you looks stronger than you are, do not rest your hope on your own strength. Name that specific fear to the Lord in your own words, and take the next obedient step His Word already makes plain.

question: What were the key events in the life of Jesus Christ?
answer:
The key events in the life of Jesus Christ are His incarnation and virgin birth, His sinless public ministry, His atoning death and burial, His bodily resurrection, and His ascension to the Father.

Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem, truly God and truly man in one person, what Christians call the hypostatic union (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-35; Luke 2:1-20). He grew in wisdom and stature, and at about thirty years of age He was baptized by John in the Jordan. There the Father spoke and the Spirit descended, so that the Trinity was revealed as the Son began His work (Matthew 3:13-17; Luke 3:21-23).

He was tempted in the wilderness and did not sin. He then called disciples, proclaimed the kingdom of God, healed the sick, cast out demons, and taught with authority (Matthew 4:1-11; Mark 1:14-34). On the Mount of Transfiguration His glory was briefly unveiled before Peter, James, and John (Matthew 17:1-8).

In Jerusalem He entered as King, instituted the Lord's Supper, and was betrayed, tried, and crucified under Pontius Pilate. On the cross He bore the penalty sinners deserved, a penal substitution that reconciles people to God, and then He was buried (Matthew 26:26-29; Matthew 27:32-61; John 19:16-42; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). On the third day He rose bodily from the dead and appeared to many witnesses (Matthew 28:1-10; Luke 24:1-49; 1 Corinthians 15:5-8). After forty days He ascended to the Father's right hand, and He will return to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:3-11; Acts 17:31).

Scripture presents these as real events in history, and they are the heart of the Gospel. We have sinned and stand separated from a holy God, so we need a Savior. Jesus lived the life we could not live, died the death we deserved, and rose so that sinners may be justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works (Romans 3:23-26; Ephesians 2:8-9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A practical next step is to read the Gospel of John this week, one chapter a day, asking God to show you who Jesus is and what His death and resurrection mean for you.

Which of these events would you like to look at more closely?

question: Do Christians need a day of rest?
answer:
Christians need rest for body and soul. Whether God requires one specific day of rest each week, however, is a non-essential matter on which faithful believers may disagree, because the Scriptures speak both of a lasting rhythm of rest and of freedom from judgment over days.

Reformed believers commonly teach that the Sabbath principle endures as a creation ordinance and part of God's moral law, calling Christians to keep the Lord's Day by resting from ordinary work so they may worship, hear the Word, and show mercy (Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11; Isaiah 58:13-14). Other Christians, with equal desire to obey, read the apostles as teaching that those sabbaths were shadows now fulfilled in Christ, so each person should follow a fully convinced conscience without condemning another who differs (Colossians 2:16-17; Romans 14:5-6; Hebrews 4:9-11).

Neither view is a test of whether someone truly belongs to Christ. I am persuaded that a weekly day set apart for holy rest is a gracious gift that helps us delight in the Lord rather than in our own busyness, and I receive this conviction as one faithful path within the church, not the only orthodox one.

In all things let Christian liberty be guided by love: welcome one another, and do not pass judgment on disputable matters, for we all stand or fall before our own Master (Romans 14:1-4). Take this practical step: ask a trusted elder how your local church approaches the Lord's Day, then deliberately clear several hours soon to stop your usual labor, meditate on Mark 2:27-28, and enjoy the kindness of Jesus, who made the Sabbath for man and who Himself is our true rest.

question: How can I be a good Christian?
answer:
The longing to be a good Christian is a mercy, yet the Christian life does not begin with your goodness. It begins with God's grace. You become a Christian by trusting Jesus Christ, and you grow as a Christian by walking with Him in repentance, faith, and obedience.

God is holy, and we are not. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Our sin separates us from Him, and no religious effort can remove that guilt. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin and died on the cross in our place. That is penal substitution: He bore the penalty our sins deserved. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, showing that sin and death are defeated (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). He is the risen Lord. People are justified, declared righteous before God, by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:24-26).

If you want to be a Christian, do not try to earn God's favor. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

The life that follows is sanctification, the Holy Spirit's ongoing work of making us more like Christ. Apart from Him we can do nothing, and the one who remains in Him bears fruit (John 15:5). That fruit looks like loving God with all your heart and loving your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37-39), hearing and doing His Word (James 1:22), praying honestly, confessing sin quickly (1 John 1:9), and gathering with a local church where Christ is preached and believers stir one another up to love and good works (Hebrews 10:24-25). In time, follow the Lord in baptism and share the Lord's Supper with His people. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control grow over time, not overnight (Galatians 5:22-23). God, who begins this good work, will carry it on (Philippians 1:6).

This week, read the Gospel of John, even one chapter a day. Before you read, ask God to show you who Jesus is and to give you a repentant, believing heart. After you read, thank Him for Christ, confess specific sins, and ask for strength to obey one clear thing you have seen. If you can, tell a pastor at a Bible-teaching church that you want to follow Jesus.

What is behind your question right now: are you seeking to know Christ for the first time, or are you already trusting Him and wanting help to walk more faithfully?

question: What does the Bible say about lawsuits / suing?
answer:
The Bible permits the lawful pursuit of justice, yet it strongly warns Christians against suing one another, especially in secular courts, and calls them to seek peace rather than personal vindication.

In 1 Corinthians 6:1-8, Paul rebukes believers who take their disputes before unbelievers instead of settling them within the church. He says that the very fact of such lawsuits means they are already defeated, and he asks, "Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?" The concern is not only the money or the grievance. It is the damage to the church's witness and the failure to treat a brother or sister as someone to be reconciled with in Christ.

Scripture does not treat civil courts as evil in themselves. God ordains governing authorities to punish wrongdoing and uphold justice (Romans 13:1-4). Under Moses, judges were appointed so disputes could be heard fairly (Exodus 18:13-26; Deuteronomy 16:18-20). Paul himself appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen and to Caesar when justice was at stake (Acts 16:37-39; Acts 25:10-12). Seeking legal protection against real harm, restraining crime, or fulfilling a civic duty is not the same thing as a vengeful suit against a fellow believer over a personal grievance.

Jesus also calls His people to settle matters quickly and to refuse a spirit of retaliation (Matthew 5:25-26; Matthew 5:38-42; Romans 12:17-21). The aim is not careless passivity in the face of serious injustice. It is a heart that entrusts final judgment to God and prefers reconciliation, truth, and the good of others over winning at any cost. Faithful Christians differ on some hard cases, such as defending against a suit or protecting the vulnerable through the courts, because wisdom is required where the text does not give a single procedure for every situation.

If the dispute is with another Christian, go first to that person, and then to your church elders, before any thought of court (Matthew 18:15-17). If the matter involves crime, abuse, fraud that harms others, or a clear legal duty, do not hide it. Seek godly counsel and the proper authorities. Pray for freedom from bitterness, and ask your elders to help you discern whether this calls for patient endurance or a rightful appeal for justice.

Is this about a disagreement with another believer, or a situation involving serious harm?

question: What is kingdom now teaching?
answer:
Kingdom Now teaching is a contemporary movement, often linked with dominion theology and the New Apostolic Reformation, which claims that the church must establish God’s visible kingdom on earth through spiritual warfare, cultural takeover, and political influence before Jesus Christ returns.

Its advocates commonly urge believers to “take the seven mountains” of society and look to present-day apostles and prophets to lead that advance, so that the nations are brought under Christian dominion in this age. The Bible teaches something fuller and more sober. Jesus announced that the kingdom of God had drawn near in His own ministry (Mark 1:15), so the kingdom is already inaugurated. Its consummation, however, waits for His personal, bodily return, when He delivers the kingdom to the Father and the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; Revelation 11:15). Kingdom Now teaching tends to collapse that “already and not yet” tension, shifting hope from Christ’s coming to human strategy and present power.

Jesus told Pilate, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). The church’s commission is to make disciples by preaching the gospel, baptizing, and teaching obedience to all that Christ commanded (Matthew 28:18–20). Scripture alone remains the final authority for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16–17), so claims of new governing revelation must be tested by the apostolic word and refused where they add to it or contradict it (Acts 17:11; Revelation 22:18–19).

Faithful Christians have long differed on how the kingdom advances before the end. Historic premillennial, amillennial, and postmillennial readings all confess Christ’s return, the resurrection, and final judgment, and those differences are tertiary matters that should not break fellowship (Romans 14:1–4). Kingdom Now teaching often steps beyond those historic options by redefining church authority and by treating present dominion as the church’s chief hope.

Labor, then, in the ordinary means of grace, the Word, prayer, and a faithful local church, while you wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who will make all things new (Titus 2:13; Revelation 21:1–5). If a particular claim from this teaching is pressing on you, set it beside the Gospels and the letters and ask your pastors to search the Scriptures with you.

question: What is The Infinite Way?
answer:
The Infinite Way is a mystical spiritual teaching developed by Joel S. Goldsmith in the mid-twentieth century. It centers on God as infinite Spirit and on finding peace and healing by realizing an inner oneness with that presence.

Goldsmith, shaped by Christian Science and the wider New Thought stream, taught meditation and a universal “Christ consciousness.” In this approach, matter and evil are largely treated as appearances to be transcended, and “the Christ” functions more as a principle available within everyone than as the unique incarnate Son. Scripture is often read through that inner experience rather than as the final authority over it.

That is not the gospel the Bible proclaims. Scripture teaches that God is personal and holy, that sin is real rebellion, and that sinners are reconciled to Him by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by awakening to a divine self already within (Romans 3:23–26; Ephesians 2:8–9). Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. His sacrificial death is a real penal substitution, necessary and sufficient to reconcile sinners to God, and His bodily resurrection confirms His victory over sin and death (John 1:1–14; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). He alone is the mediator (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5). The apostles warn against teachings that empty the cross of its power or replace the historic Jesus with another “Christ” (Colossians 2:8–10; 1 John 4:1–3).

If you are drawn to The Infinite Way because you want peace with God, that longing is understandable, but peace comes through Christ’s finished work, not a technique of realization. A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly, asking whether Jesus presents Himself as a symbol to outgrow or as the Lord who must be trusted. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for sinners, for forgiveness and new life. If you want, tell me what first brought this teaching to your attention.

question: Does God have favorites?
answer:
God does not have favorites in the sense of unjust partiality. He is the great and mighty God, "showing no partiality and accepting no bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Peter came to see that "God does not show favoritism" (Acts 10:34), and Paul says the same: "For God does not show favoritism" (Romans 2:11). Wealth, status, ethnicity, and religious performance do not buy His smile (James 2:1–9; Galatians 2:6).

He does show real kindness to all people. He sends sun and rain on the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). At the same time, Scripture speaks of a particular saving love, and Christians have long differed on how to understand it.

Many faithful Christians hold that God loves every person with the same saving intent and chooses those He foresees will believe, so He has no favorites in salvation, only those who freely receive Christ. I hold, as one historic Christian position and not the only orthodox one, that this love is unconditional election. God chose a people in Christ before the foundation of the world, "according to the good pleasure of His will," not because they were better than others (Ephesians 1:4–6). Israel was not chosen for being numerous, but because the Lord loved them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Paul says the same of Jacob and Esau, "before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad," so that God's purpose in election might stand (Romans 9:11–13). In that covenant setting, "hated" means set aside, not petty spite.

That is not sinful favoritism. Human favoritism is unjust, swayed by appearance or advantage. God's choice is holy. No sinner deserves mercy. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and He remains just when He justifies those who trust Christ (Romans 3:23–26; Romans 9:14–18). Mercy to some and justice toward others both display His glory. Election should produce humility, not pride.

If you belong to Christ, you are not loved because you outperformed anyone. You are loved because the Father gave you to the Son, and Christ died and rose for you (Romans 8:32–39). If you fear you have been overlooked, do not hunt for a secret sign. Look to Jesus. He is truly God and truly man. He died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily on the third day. Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:9–13). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Ephesians 1:3–14 and Romans 10 slowly, and pray honestly to the Father about whether you are resting in Christ's finished work or still trying to earn His affection. If the question is heavy, sit with a pastor who will open the Scriptures with you.

What is behind your question? Are you wondering whether God could really love you, or whether His choice of some people is fair?

question: How can I live a holy life?
answer:
A holy life is a life set apart for God and growing in likeness to Jesus Christ. Scripture calls this sanctification, and it is both a gift God gives and a calling He places on every believer.

God Himself is holy, and He summons His people to share His character. "But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: 'Be holy, because I am holy'" (1 Peter 1:15–16). Holiness is not a cold performance, and it is not a private project of self-improvement. It flows from union with Christ. In one sense, every believer is already sanctified, set apart as God's own (1 Corinthians 1:2). In another sense, we are being sanctified day by day as the Spirit conforms us to Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18). Those who trust Him are justified, declared righteous by grace alone through faith alone, and then the Holy Spirit progressively makes them holy in heart and conduct (1 Corinthians 6:11; Philippians 2:12–13).

You cannot produce this life in your own strength. Jesus said, "Apart from Me you can do nothing" (John 15:5). The same grace that saves also instructs us "to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives" (Titus 2:12). Christ's death broke sin's ruling power, and His resurrection gives new life, so we are to count ourselves dead to sin and alive to God (Romans 6:11).

In practice, holiness grows through the means of grace God has given. Walk by the Spirit rather than by the flesh, and ask Him to bear His fruit in you: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:16, 22–23). Stay in the Word, for the psalmist asked, "How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to Your word" (Psalm 119:9). Pray with honesty. Name specific sins before God, because "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9), and then ask for strength to put off the old self and put on the new (Ephesians 4:22–24). Do not try to do this alone. Gather with the church, sit under the preaching of Scripture, and let a mature believer know where you are tempted (Hebrews 10:24–25; James 5:16).

Pursue holiness as a settled direction, not as a flawless record. "Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord" (Hebrews 12:14). When you fall, do not hide. Return quickly to Christ. He is a sympathetic High Priest, and He will never drive away the one who comes to Him (Hebrews 4:15–16; John 6:37). If you are truly in Christ, the God who began this work will carry it on to completion (Philippians 1:6).

This week, choose one concrete area, perhaps your speech, purity, anger, or generosity. Read 1 Peter 1:13–21 each morning, pray specifically about that area, and ask one trusted believer in your church to pray with you.

If you have never trusted Christ, holiness begins there. We are sinners, separated from a holy God. Jesus, truly God and truly man, died for our sins and rose bodily on the third day. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life.

What part of holy living feels most difficult for you right now?

question: What is the sinner's prayer?
answer:
The sinner’s prayer is a short, set prayer that many evangelicals invite people to repeat, asking Jesus to forgive their sins and “come into their heart.” It became common in modern crusade and tract evangelism, though the Bible never gives a required formula of words that must be spoken in order to be saved.

God does hear the genuine cry of a sinner. The tax collector prayed, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner,” and went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). Paul also writes that “if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved,” and that “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:9–13). Calling on the Lord is the fruit of faith, not a magic phrase that creates faith or earns justification. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by any work, including the work of reciting a prayer (Ephesians 2:8–9).
