The Bible teaches that Christians should pay the taxes they owe to civil authorities, while giving God their ultimate allegiance.

When opponents tried to trap Jesus over the Roman tax, He said, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matthew 22:21; Mark 12:17; Luke 20:25). The coin bore Caesar’s image and belonged to Caesar’s realm. People bear God’s image, so their worship and obedience belong to God (Genesis 1:27). Paying the tax was not a denial of God’s kingship.

Paul states the duty plainly: governing authorities are established by God, and believers are to pay taxes, revenue, respect, and honor to those to whom they are due (Romans 13:1–7). Peter likewise calls Christians to submit to human institutions for the Lord’s sake (1 Peter 2:13–17). Jesus even paid the temple tax, though as the Son He was free from it, so as not to cause unnecessary offense (Matthew 17:24–27).

This is civil submission under God’s providence and honest stewardship, not a blanket endorsement of every government policy. Rome was often unjust, yet Jesus and the apostles still required payment. Only when human commands require sin must believers obey God rather than people (Acts 5:29). Ordinary tax obligations do not fall into that category. Concealing income or refusing what is lawfully due is not faithfulness. It is a failure to render what is owed.

A practical step this season is to review what you owe, set it aside, and file honestly, without concealment or bitter resentment. As you do, pray for those in authority, that you may live a peaceful and godly life (1 Timothy 2:1–2), and keep giving God your heart, since you bear His image.

question: Should Christian women wear pants?
answer:
Whether Christian women should wear pants is a non-essential matter of Christian liberty, where faithful believers may disagree because Scripture gives principles rather than a clothing list for every culture.

Some Christians believe women should not wear pants. They appeal to Deuteronomy 22:5, which forbids a woman to wear a man’s garment, and they treat trousers as masculine clothing that blurs the distinction God made between male and female. In that view, dresses or skirts better express modesty and femininity.

Other Christians believe modest women’s pants are permissible. They understand Deuteronomy 22:5 as condemning intentional cross-dressing, not later garments designed for women whose cultural meaning is not masculine. They emphasize 1 Timothy 2:9–10, where women are called to respectable, modest dress and good works, and Romans 14:1–4, where believers must not pass judgment on one another in disputable matters.

What Scripture does require is a heart set on honoring Christ, clothing that is modest rather than sensual, and love that will not stumble a brother or sister (1 Peter 3:3–4; Romans 14:13). The garment is secondary to whether you are dressing to display Christ or to draw attention to yourself.

If your conscience is troubled, do not wear pants, for whatever is not from faith is sin (Romans 14:23). If you are free in conscience, wear them humbly, without despising those who abstain, and with care for your local church. A wise next step is to pray for pure motives and to talk with your pastor or a mature Christian woman in your congregation.

question: Why wasn't Jesus named Immanuel?
answer:
Jesus was named Jesus, not Immanuel, because God commanded that personal name, while Immanuel is a title that reveals who he is.

You may notice that Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23 say the child will be called Immanuel, yet the angel tells Joseph to name him Jesus. Matthew sets both side by side in the same account, so he does not treat them as a contradiction. The angel says, "She will give birth to a Son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). The name Jesus means "The LORD saves," which matches that explanation exactly. Matthew then quotes the prophet and adds that Immanuel means "God with us" (Matthew 1:23; Isaiah 7:14). In this kind of prophetic language, to call someone by a name often means to recognize what is true of him, not merely to assign a legal name at birth.

The same pattern appears in Isaiah 9:6, where the promised child "will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace." Those words truly describe him, even though they were not his everyday name. Jesus likewise bears many titles in Scripture, while the name given by the angel remains Jesus.

What Immanuel announces is the incarnation. The eternal Son of God took on human nature and dwelt among us, so that in him God is truly with his people (John 1:14). He is truly God and truly man. His name Jesus declares his saving work, and the title Immanuel declares that the Savior is God himself drawn near. That is why believers can take comfort in his promise, "I am with you always, even to the end of the age" (Matthew 28:20). Read Matthew 1 slowly, and bring your questions to him in prayer, asking him to show you that he is both the Savior and God with you.

question: How is choosing a good name better than choosing riches (Proverbs 22:1)?
answer:
A good name is better than riches because integrity and a reputation for wisdom honor God and outlast wealth that can vanish in a moment. Proverbs 22:1 says, "A good name is more desirable than great riches; to be esteemed is better than silver or gold."

In ancient Israel a person's name stood for their character and standing in the covenant community. Honor gained by truthful words and just dealings mattered more than silver, because the people lived under the fear of the Lord, where righteousness held life together (Proverbs 1:7). Riches tempt the heart and often disappear (Proverbs 23:5; Proverbs 11:4), while a name built by faithfulness brings lasting esteem and quiet influence for good (Proverbs 10:7). God weighs the heart, not the size of a fortune (1 Samuel 16:7), so choosing a good name is choosing what He Himself values.

This wisdom points to sanctification, the Spirit's patient work of forming honest, Christlike character that money cannot buy. This week, in one concrete decision at work or at home, choose honesty even if it costs you financially, then bring that choice to the Lord in prayer and ask Him to guard your name for His glory.

question: What is the lust of the eyes?
answer:
The lust of the eyes is the sinful craving stirred by what we see, a covetous desire to possess or enjoy what looks desirable apart from the will of God. Scripture names it in 1 John 2:16, along with the desires of the flesh and the pride of life, as part of the world that is not from the Father.

John has just commanded, "Do not love the world or anything in the world" (1 John 2:15). The world here is not the good creation, but human life organized in rebellion against God. The word behind "lust" or "desires" is the Greek epithymia, a strong craving. Joined to the eyes, it means the heart reaching through sight for what it wants: another person's beauty, someone else's goods, a lifestyle, an image, or an experience God has not given. Sight itself is not the sin. The sin is the consenting desire that turns what is seen into an idol.

That pattern is as old as the fall. Eve saw that the forbidden tree was pleasing to the eyes, and she took it (Genesis 3:6). The tenth commandment already forbids this inward reach, coveting a neighbor's house, spouse, or possessions (Exodus 20:17). The Lord Jesus pressed the matter to the look itself: "anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart" (Matthew 5:28). Sexual lust is one severe form of this sin, but 1 John 2:16 is broader than that. It includes any covetous gazing after visible splendor. Paul names the root plainly: greed, which is idolatry (Colossians 3:5). What the eyes linger on, the heart begins to worship.

This struggle is common in a world of screens, storefronts, and comparison, and naming it as sin is meant to lead you to a Savior, not to leave you in shame. Jesus Christ lived with a pure heart, died on the cross for covetous desires, and rose bodily so sinners might be forgiven and made new. Turn from this lust and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and a new way of seeing.

Bring Psalm 119:37 before the Lord in your own words, asking Him to turn your eyes from worthless things, and then fix your eyes on Jesus (Hebrews 12:2). If a particular habit of looking has taken hold, confess it to God and to a mature believer in your church (James 5:16). Where have your eyes been training your heart lately?

question: What does the Bible say about Voodoo? How should a Christian view Voodoo?
answer:
The Bible does not mention Voodoo by name, yet it clearly and repeatedly forbids the occult practices, spirit invocation, magic, and idolatry that stand at the heart of it. Christians must reject Voodoo entirely as incompatible with worship of the one true God and with trust in Jesus Christ alone.

Scripture calls such practices detestable. Deuteronomy 18:10-12 warns against divination, sorcery, witchcraft, casting spells, and consulting the dead, declaring that anyone who does these things is detestable to the Lord. Leviticus 19:31 and Leviticus 20:6 likewise forbid turning to mediums and spiritists. These descriptions match central features of Voodoo (or Vodou), including the invocation of loa or other spirits, ritual possession, magical workings, and communication with the dead or ancestral powers. The New Testament continues the same line. Galatians 5:19-21 lists sorcery among the works of the flesh, and those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. First Corinthians 10:20-21 teaches that sacrifices offered in idolatrous systems are offered to demons, so a believer cannot share the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. When people in Ephesus turned to Christ, they publicly burned their magic books as an act of repentance (Acts 19:19).

Voodoo, in its various cultural forms, often blends African spirit traditions with elements of Roman Catholicism. That blending is syncretism, not biblical Christianity. It obscures the Gospel and treats created spirits or rituals as sources of power, protection, or guidance. The Bible insists on the exclusive claims of Christ: He alone is the way to the Father (John 14:6), and there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as a penal substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, triumphing over sin, death, and the spiritual powers (Colossians 2:15). Any system that directs worship, trust, or ritual power elsewhere stands in opposition to that finished work.

People drawn to Voodoo are often seeking real help amid suffering, fear, illness, or cultural pressure, and that human longing deserves compassion. Yet compassion does not mean approval. These practices are sin because they replace reliance on the living God with reliance on other spirits and rites. God remains holy, gracious, and ready to forgive. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by rituals, initiations, or spirit contact (Ephesians 2:8-9). Anyone who repents and trusts Jesus receives forgiveness, new life, and freedom from spiritual bondage.

If you or someone you love is involved, the concrete next step is to renounce every connection to these practices, remove related objects, and seek counsel from elders in a church that teaches the Bible faithfully. Pray directly to God the Father in the name of Jesus, asking for wisdom and deliverance, and let Scripture such as Deuteronomy 18 and Ephesians 6:10-18 shape your prayers and your confidence in Christ’s victory.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Is there a particular situation or question about sharing this with someone that you would like to talk through?

question: What is the meaning of Lent?
answer:
Lent is a traditional season of about forty days before Easter, kept by many Christians for repentance, prayer, fasting, and self-examination as they prepare to remember the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

The name comes from an old English word for spring. The forty days recall the forty days Jesus fasted in the wilderness before His public ministry (Matthew 4:1-2). In Western churches the season often begins on Ash Wednesday. It is a historic church rhythm, not a command written in Scripture.

Observing Lent is not essential to the Christian faith. Faithful believers disagree about it because the Bible does not require this particular season, so Christian liberty applies (Romans 14:5-6).

Some churches, including Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, and many Lutheran congregations, keep Lent together. They treat shared fasting, prayer, and generosity as a help for humbling themselves before God and fixing their hearts on the cross, in line with the call to return to the Lord (Joel 2:12-13) and with Jesus' teaching that fasting is for the Father, not for show (Matthew 6:16-18).

Others, including many Reformed and Baptist churches, do not bind consciences to Lent. They affirm repentance and fasting as good, yet they refuse to make a man-made calendar a test of faithfulness. They stress that justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and that turning from sin belongs to the whole Christian life, not only to forty days before Easter.

I do not treat Lent as required. That is one faithful option within historic Christianity, not the only one. If you observe it unto the Lord, with your hope resting on Christ's penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection rather than on your own restraint, you may do so with a clear conscience. If you do not observe it, you are not disobeying a command of God. Either way, do not turn the season into a performance. God looks on the heart.

This week, read Matthew 4:1-11 and one chapter of the passion narrative, such as Matthew 26 or Matthew 27, and ask the Lord to show you one specific area where you need to repent and trust Him more fully. If you belong to a local church, ask your pastor how your congregation approaches this season so you can walk in unity with them.

question: What doth every sin deserve?
answer:
Every sin deserves God's wrath and curse, both in this life and in the life to come.  
Sin transgresses God's holy law and therefore brings real guilt before His justice. The Bible teaches that the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23), that everyone who does not continue in all things written in the Book of the Law stands under a curse (Galatians 3:10), and that the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness (Romans 1:18). Even a single stumble renders a person guilty of the whole law (James 2:10), so no sin is small in His sight.  

This retributive justice leaves every person helpless to remove the penalty. Yet Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, bore that curse as our substitute through His death on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. His penal substitutionary atonement satisfies God's wrath, so that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him (Galatians 3:13; Romans 5:8-9; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).  

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life instead of the wrath every sin deserves. Read Galatians 3:10-14 today, ask God to show you both the weight of sin and the sufficiency of Christ, and then speak with a pastor or mature believer about what you see. How does knowing what sin deserves deepen your thanks for the cross?

question: What does the Bible say about diligence?
answer:
The Bible presents diligence as steady, wholehearted effort in the work God gives, offered to Him in gratitude, not as a payment to earn His favor.

Scripture sets diligence against sloth. Idle hands lead to poverty, but diligent hands bring wealth (Proverbs 10:4). The sluggard craves and gets nothing, while the soul of the diligent is satisfied (Proverbs 13:4). Careful plans lead to plenty, but haste leads to poverty (Proverbs 21:5). Even the ant is held up as a quiet picture of timely, persistent labor (Proverbs 6:6-8). The Hebrew word often translated "diligent," charutz, means someone determined and industrious, not merely busy.

The New Testament places that same steadiness under the lordship of Christ. Believers are not to lag in zeal, but to be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord (Romans 12:11). Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as for the Lord and not for human masters, because it is the Lord Christ you are serving (Colossians 3:23-24). Peter calls Christians to make every effort to grow in godly character and to make their calling and election sure (2 Peter 1:5-10). The Greek word behind that effort, spoude, means earnest eagerness, a holy purposefulness rather than panic. Hebrews urges the same diligence to the end, so that hope is made sure and sluggishness does not take root (Hebrews 6:11-12).

This belongs to progressive sanctification, not to justification. God declares sinners righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, on the ground of Christ's penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection, not on the ground of our effort (Romans 3:23-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). Those united to Christ are then created for good works God prepared beforehand (Ephesians 2:10). Diligence confirms grace; it does not purchase it. Those truly in Christ are kept by God's power and will persevere (John 10:28-29; 1 Peter 1:5).

This week, choose one ordinary sphere, your work, your home, your studies, or a neglected habit of Scripture and prayer. Before you begin, remember Colossians 3:23 and ask the Lord for steady faithfulness in that one place. Resist both laziness and anxious hurry. When you grow weary, take heart that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58; Galatians 6:9).

If one duty feels especially heavy, tell me what it is, and we can look at it in light of these passages.

question: What is agnosticism?
answer:
Agnosticism is the claim that a person does not know, or cannot know, whether God exists. The word comes from Greek roots meaning "without knowledge." It names a suspension of judgment, not a proof that God is absent.

It is not the same as atheism. An atheist says there is no God. An agnostic says the question is unsettled, or even beyond human reach. Some mean only "I do not know yet." Others mean "No one can know."

Scripture does not leave God as an unreachable mystery. It teaches that God has made Himself known. His eternal power and divine nature are clearly seen in what He has made, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). In Athens, Paul found an altar "to an unknown god," then proclaimed the God who is not far from any of us and who will judge the world by the risen Christ (Acts 17:23-31). Theologians call this witness in creation and conscience general revelation. God has also spoken in Scripture and, supremely, in His Son, which is special revelation (Hebrews 1:1-2).

That matters because eternal life is knowing the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom He has sent (John 17:3). Our real barrier is not divine silence. It is sin: we fall short of God's glory and cannot save ourselves (Romans 3:23). Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is the one mediator between God and people (1 Timothy 2:5).

Honest questions are welcome. A settled claim that God cannot be known is not. If you are unsure, read the Gospel of John this week and note what Jesus says about the Father and about Himself. Pray in your own words, telling God your doubts and asking Him to make Himself known. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What has led you to ask about agnosticism?

question: What does it mean to “be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:4)?
answer:
Psalm 4:4 means that anger, even strong agitation, need not become sin if it is restrained, examined before God, and kept from harmful words or actions. In the psalm David urges those troubling him to tremble or be stirred and yet not sin, then to search their hearts in the quiet of their beds and be silent before the Lord (Psalm 4:4). The Greek translation of that line, “Be angry and do not sin,” is taken up by the apostle Paul so that believers may feel righteous indignation against evil without letting anger fester or give the devil a foothold (Ephesians 4:26-27).

The Hebrew verb behind the phrase can mean to tremble, be disturbed, or be angry, so the original call is both a summons to reverent fear of God that stops sin and a warning against uncontrolled rage. Scripture distinguishes this from the anger of man, which does not produce the righteousness of God (James 1:20). Jesus Himself knew holy grief and anger at hard hearts without sinning (Mark 3:5), showing that emotion aligned with God’s holiness is possible. Sinful anger, by contrast, is selfish, nursing, or vengeful, and it must be put away as part of progressive sanctification (Ephesians 4:31-32).

When anger rises, follow the psalm’s own counsel: step aside, search your heart for pride or bitterness rather than only the other person’s fault, and stay silent in prayer before you speak or act. Ask the Lord to show you what is truly driving the heat and to help you release it before the day ends. That quiet searching is one concrete way the Spirit trains us to reflect Christ’s patience instead of our own impatience.

question: How will the covenant with death be annulled (Isaiah 28:18)?
answer:
The covenant with death is annulled by the Lord Himself. He sweeps away the refuge of lies and sets a sure foundation in its place.

In Isaiah 28 the scoffing rulers in Jerusalem boasted that they had made a covenant with death and an agreement with Sheol, so that the overwhelming scourge would not touch them, “because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place” (Isaiah 28:15). In the flow of Isaiah 28–31, that boast is a false security, commonly tied to a political alliance, especially with Egypt, and to trust in deceit rather than in the Lord (Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 31:1–3). God answers that their pact will not stand: “Your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand. When the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be trampled by it” (Isaiah 28:18). Hail sweeps away the refuge of lies, and water overflows the hiding place (Isaiah 28:17). No human treaty can bind the Judge of all the earth.

The same oracle shows the means. The Lord GOD lays “a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation,” and “the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16). Justice is the measuring line and righteousness the level (Isaiah 28:17). The false covenant collapses because it rests on lies. The true foundation holds because God Himself sets it.

The New Testament identifies that cornerstone with Jesus Christ (Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:6). Death’s claim is not finally broken by diplomacy or self-protection, but by His penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection. He shared in our humanity “so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death” (Hebrews 2:14–15). In Him, “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54).

So the covenant is annulled in two related ways. Historically, God judged the false refuge of Jerusalem’s leaders. Finally and fully, Christ the cornerstone conquers death for all who trust Him. If you have been leaning on a hidden agreement with fear, compromise, or self-made safety, set that refuge beside Isaiah 28:16 in prayer today, and rest your weight on Christ alone, who died and rose so that death cannot keep its bargain with those who believe.

Would you like to walk through Isaiah 28:14–22 line by line?

question: What is the Hindu caste system?
answer:
The Hindu caste system is a traditional social order, long associated with Hindu society in India, that sorts people into hereditary groups affecting marriage, work, status, and social contact.

It is usually described with two related ideas. Varna names four broad classes: Brahmins (priests and teachers), Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), Vaishyas (farmers, traders, and artisans), and Shudras (laborers and servants). Jati names the many smaller birth communities within and beyond those classes. People later called Dalits were treated as outside the varna order and, under the practice of untouchability, faced severe exclusion from temples, wells, meals, and ordinary social life. Passages such as the Rig Veda’s hymn of the cosmic person, and later law books such as the Manusmriti, have been used to explain these ranks, though practice has varied by region and century, and many Hindus today reject caste discrimination as unjust.

India’s constitution abolishes untouchability and forbids caste discrimination, yet caste still shapes marriage, politics, and opportunity for many people.

Christians believe every person bears the imago Dei, the image of God, so human worth is not assigned by birth, surname, or ritual purity (Genesis 1:26–27; Acts 17:26). Scripture condemns partiality, and it teaches that in Christ the old walls of status come down (James 2:1–9; Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11). In practice, that means a believer must not rank a neighbor’s dignity by family line or occupation, and must welcome those whom society despises. Where churches have copied caste prejudice, that is sin to repent of, not a Christian ideal. The same Savior died and rose for people of every people and rank, and all who trust him are received into one family by grace, not by birth.

question: What does the Bible say about rest and relaxation?
answer:
The Bible treats rest and relaxation as good gifts from God, both as needed care for the body and as a deeper rest found by trusting Christ rather than our own striving.

God rested on the seventh day after creation, not from weariness, but to crown His finished work and set a pattern for human life (Genesis 2:2-3). Israel was later commanded to stop ordinary labor and remember the Lord who redeemed them (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15). Hebrews then says a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God, entered by faith as we cease from works-righteousness and rest in what Christ has finished (Hebrews 4:9-11). That is the heart of justification by faith: we are accepted by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by anxious labor.

Jesus also honored ordinary human tiredness. He said, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:28-29). He called His disciples away to rest (Mark 6:31), and He Himself withdrew to quiet places to pray (Luke 5:16). Sleep is called a gift (Psalm 127:2), and God "richly provides us with all things to enjoy" when received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 6:17; see also Ecclesiastes 3:12-13; 1 Timothy 4:4). Rest is not the same as laziness, which Scripture rebukes (Proverbs 6:6-11; 2 Thessalonians 3:10), nor is relaxation an excuse for sinful escape.

Faithful Christians differ on how the weekly Sabbath applies now. Some hold that Christ fulfilled the old Sabbath and that the form of weekly rest is a matter of wisdom and Christian liberty (Romans 14:5-6; Colossians 2:16-17). Others, including the historic Reformed Baptist conviction, hold that the Lord's Day remains a day for worship and rest from ordinary work. Either way, our deepest rest is not a schedule. It is Christ Himself, who died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day.

This week, set aside one real block of time to stop productive work, read Matthew 11:28-30 slowly, and pray in your own words about what you are carrying, asking for trust, sleep, and a thankful enjoyment of some simple good gift. If exhaustion has become heavy, tell a mature believer or your pastor so you are not bearing it alone.

If you are weary in soul as well as body, turn from self-reliant striving and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and true rest. What kind of weariness are you feeling most right now?

question: What is deism? What do deists believe?
answer:
Deism is the belief that God created the world and then does not intervene in it by miracle, special revelation, or personal care. The deist God is a Maker, but not the speaking, saving, covenant-keeping Lord of Scripture.

Deists generally hold these points together. God exists and can be known by reason and the order of nature, often called general revelation. The Bible is treated as a human religious book, not the inspired and inerrant Word of God. Miracles, prophecy, and prayer as real petition are set aside, on the idea that a perfect Creator would not interrupt the laws He established. Jesus is often respected as a moral teacher, while His true deity, virgin birth, substitutionary death, and bodily resurrection are denied. Right and wrong are grounded in natural reason, and some deists still expect a future judgment based on moral living. The view took clearer shape in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries among certain European writers, though not everyone called a deist affirmed every detail in the same way.

The Bible teaches a different God. He is the transcendent Creator, and He also upholds all things and draws near to His people (Hebrews 1:3; Psalm 139:7-10). He has spoken, and in these last days He has spoken by His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). Creation displays His eternal power and divine nature, yet that light does not reconcile sinners to a holy God (Romans 1:19-20). The Christian confession is that the eternal Son took on our nature, died for sins, and rose bodily, so that sinners are justified by grace through faith in Him, not by moral effort (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9).

If you are weighing these claims, read John 1:1-18 beside Romans 1:18-25, and notice the difference between a distant designer and the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us.

question: Is the distinction between clergy and laity biblical?
answer: The New Testament does not establish a clergy-laity caste that divides Christians into two spiritual classes, though it does set apart elders and deacons for particular offices. Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christians argue, with real historical weight, that Christ instituted a distinct clerical priesthood through the apostles so that ordained ministers alone consecrate the sacraments and exercise a mediating authority laypeople do not share. I hold, as one faithful option within historic Christianity, that every believer belongs to a royal priesthood with direct access to God through Christ, while qualified men are recognized as elders to teach and shepherd without becoming a higher spiritual order. This follows from the whole church being priests (1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6) together with the clear duties and limits given to overseers, who serve as fellow elders among the flock rather than lords over it (1 Timothy 3:1-7; 1 Peter 5:1-3). In practice, honor your pastors’ leadership and teaching, and at the same time take up your own share in speaking the truth and building up the body (Ephesians 4:11-16; Hebrews 13:17).

question: What does it mean to have a wilderness experience?
answer:
A wilderness experience is a season in which God leads His people through testing, scarcity, or felt distance so that their faith is refined and their trust rests on Him alone.

In Scripture, the wilderness was both a place of discipline and a school of grace. After the Exodus, the Lord led Israel forty years in the wilderness to humble them and test what was in their hearts, teaching them that man does not live by bread alone but by every word that comes from the mouth of the Lord (Deuteronomy 8:2–3). He gave manna and water, yet the people often grumbled, exposing unbelief even in the midst of His care (Exodus 16:1–4; Numbers 14:1–4). The wilderness was not God abandoning them. It was God stripping away false supports so they would learn to depend on Him.

The New Testament shows the fulfillment of that pattern in Christ. Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, tempted by the devil for forty days, and answered every temptation with the Word of God without sinning (Matthew 4:1–11; Hebrews 4:15). He is the faithful Son who succeeded where Israel failed. His obedience, and later His atoning death and bodily resurrection, secure life for all who are united to Him by faith. Believers are not left to wander alone. Our High Priest has already walked through weakness and testing.

For Christians today, a wilderness experience may look like prolonged waiting, grief, spiritual dryness, or circumstances that remove familiar comforts. These seasons are often part of progressive sanctification, the Holy Spirit’s work of conforming us to Christ. Trials test and prove genuine faith, producing endurance and a deeper hope that does not put us to shame (James 1:2–4; 1 Peter 1:6–7; Romans 5:3–5). God remains present even when His presence feels hidden (Psalm 23:4).

If you are in such a season, take one concrete step this week: each morning read a short portion of Scripture, perhaps Psalm 23 or Matthew 4, and speak honestly to the Lord about what you fear and what you need. Draw near with confidence, for He invites the weary to find mercy and grace to help in time of need (Hebrews 4:14–16). If this describes where you are, you are welcome to say more, and I will gladly point you to further passages for the road you are walking.

question: What does Malachi 2:16 mean when God says, ‘I hate divorce’?
answer:
In Malachi 2:16, when the LORD says, “I hate divorce,” He is condemning the treacherous breaking of the marriage covenant, not expressing contempt for people who have suffered a broken marriage.

The setting is Judah after the exile. Men were abandoning “the wife of your youth,” the companion bound to them “by covenant,” and joining themselves to foreign women devoted to other gods (Malachi 2:11-14). The LORD Himself had been “a witness” between husband and wife (Malachi 2:14). Sending her away was not a private rearrangement. It was faithlessness, treachery against both wife and God, and, as He says, a covering of one’s garment with violence (Malachi 2:16). In that world, spreading a garment over a woman could picture the protection of marriage, so the man who should have sheltered his wife had stained that covering with injustice.

The Hebrew of Malachi 2:16 is difficult, and some translations read it as condemning the man who hates his wife and divorces her. Either way, the chapter is clear. God opposes this divorce because He is holy and just, because marriage is a covenant He witnesses, and because He seeks a faithful people and godly offspring (Malachi 2:15). “I hate” is moral opposition, the same kind of holy hatred God shows toward idolatry and oppression. He hates the violence of covenant-breaking. He does not hate the spouse who has been abandoned, and He does not treat a wounded person as beyond mercy.

In the whole of Scripture, this upholds what God established at creation: a man and a woman become one flesh, and what God has joined is not to be torn apart lightly (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6). Jesus taught that Moses permitted a certificate of divorce because of hardness of heart, not because divorce was God’s design from the beginning (Matthew 19:7-8). He also named sexual immorality as a real breach (Matthew 19:9), and Paul addressed an unbelieving spouse who abandons the marriage (1 Corinthians 7:15). Those texts do not soften Malachi. They show that divorce remains a grave matter, never a light option, and never an excuse for treachery, even while Scripture itself names certain grievous sins that can destroy a marriage. Faithful Christians have sometimes differed on the narrow questions that follow, but not on this: God loves covenant faithfulness, and He hates the violence of breaking faith.

If this verse has been laid on you like a curse, hear the difference. God’s anger in Malachi falls on the one who deals treacherously. If you were left, betrayed, or endangered, you are not the villain of this text. A spouse in danger should seek safety and tell faithful pastors and the proper authorities. If you have been the one who broke faith, this is a call to repent, not a notice that grace has ended. Christ is the faithful bridegroom who keeps covenant with His people, and forgiveness is found in His death and resurrection, not in pretending the sin was small.

This week, read Malachi 2:10-16 slowly and ask the Lord to show you where your spirit needs guarding, whether in loyalty to a spouse, in repentance, or in healing from someone else’s treachery. If you are weighing divorce, do not walk that road alone. Bring it to elders who will open Scripture with you before any decision hardens.

Are you asking in order to understand God’s design for marriage, or because this verse has left you unsure of His heart toward you?

question: How transparent should church finances be?
answer:
Church finances should be transparent enough for the congregation to see that money is handled with integrity, as a matter of faithful stewardship rather than secrecy or suspicion.  

The exact degree and method are a non-essential matter of local church prudence. Scripture gives clear principles but no single policy manual, so faithful Christians and historic traditions have differed in application without dividing over the gospel itself. One common approach, especially in congregational churches, opens regular reports and budget summaries to the membership so the body can give, pray, and oversee with understanding. Another approach, often in churches with stronger centralized elder or board oversight, keeps detailed ledgers with trusted leaders and offers the congregation honest summaries, lest endless line-item scrutiny breed distrust or distract from mission. Both can be practiced by people who love Christ.  

A wise and fitting path is substantial openness with the church’s own members, joined to proper limits. Paul arranged the collection for the saints so that no one could blame them in its administration, taking pains to do what is honorable not only before the Lord but also before people (2 Corinthians 8:20-21). Stewards must be found faithful (1 Corinthians 4:2), and overseers and deacons must be free from greed (1 Timothy 3:3, 8; Titus 1:7; 1 Peter 5:2). In practice that looks like shared counting of offerings, more than one person authorizing expenditures, regular financial summaries to the members, and a willingness to answer sincere questions. Individual giving records should stay private, in keeping with Jesus’ call to give without display (Matthew 6:3-4), and sensitive personnel or security details need discretion. Transparency serves love and credibility; it is not a tool for gossip or control.  

If you help lead, set or review a simple rhythm of clear reporting to the church and invite accountability from godly deacons or a small finance team under the elders. If you are a member, ask your pastors or deacons, gently and without accusation, how funds are overseen and reported, then pray for wisdom as they steward what belongs to the Lord.

question: Is intinction the correct way to do communion?
answer:
Intinction is not the exclusively correct way to observe the Lord's Supper. Faithful Christians may disagree on this non-essential matter of practice, because Scripture clearly institutes the ordinance yet does not supply an exhaustive rule that either requires or forbids dipping the bread into the cup.

Some churches practice intinction, receiving both elements together as a reverent and practical expression of partaking in Christ. Others distribute the bread and the cup separately so that the congregation distinctly eats and drinks as the Lord commanded. Romans 14:1-6 and Romans 14:13-23 teach Christian liberty in such matters and call us not to judge one another when each seeks to honor Christ.

As one faithful approach within historic Christianity, the Reformed Baptist practice of separate reception follows most closely the pattern Jesus gave: He took bread, broke it, and said, "Take and eat," then took the cup and said, "Drink from it, all of you" (Matthew 26:26-28; see also 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). This keeps clear the remembrance of His body given and His blood shed, while the heart of the ordinance remains worthy participation by faith, discerning the body, and receiving Christ's spiritual presence as a means of grace (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). Participate gratefully according to the order of your local church, and if questions linger, ask your elders to walk through these passages with you so you may come to the Table with a clear conscience and in unity.

question: What is the church suffering?
answer:
The church suffers because she is united to Christ and still lives in a fallen world that often opposes Him. Until Jesus returns, His people share in tribulation, persecution, weakness, and the ordinary pains of life under the curse, even while they already share in His victory.

Jesus told His disciples that in the world they would have tribulation, and then told them to take courage because He has overcome the world (John 16:33). Paul and Barnabas strengthened the churches by teaching that we must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God (Acts 14:22). Scripture also says that all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Timothy 3:12), and that believers are co-heirs with Christ if indeed they suffer with Him, so that they may also be glorified with Him (Romans 8:17). Peter tells suffering Christians not to treat the fiery trial as something strange, but to rejoice that they share in the sufferings of Christ (1 Peter 4:12-13).

This suffering does not mean Christ's saving work is unfinished. His death was a penal substitution, necessary and sufficient to reconcile sinners to God. What remains is the church's witness-suffering in union with Him. Paul speaks of filling up in his flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ's afflictions for the sake of His body, the church (Colossians 1:24). Those afflictions do not add to the cross. They display it. Christians have long called the church on earth the church militant: still in the fight, kept by God's power, not yet at rest in glory. That suffering is real today, whether it comes as open persecution, quiet pressure, grief, or the slow work of being made holy.

Sometimes the phrase "the church suffering" is used in Roman Catholic teaching for souls said to be purified in purgatory after death. That is not what the Bible teaches. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). By a single offering Christ has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). Man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment (Hebrews 9:27), not to finish paying for sin. In the biblical sense, the suffering church is the church still on earth under the cross, waiting for the resurrection.

If you are in a hard season, you are not outside the Shepherd's care. This week, read 1 Peter slowly, bring your specific burden to the Lord in your own words, and let a pastor or mature believer in your local church carry it with you.

Are you asking about the trials believers face now, or about that older phrase for the state of the dead?

question: What does it mean that a person will not inherit the kingdom of God (1 Corinthians 6:9-11)?
answer:
Not inheriting the kingdom of God means being shut out from the eternal life and reign God gives to those who belong to Christ, and remaining under His righteous judgment instead.

In 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 Paul warns the church in Corinth, a city where sexual immorality and greed were ordinary, not to be deceived. He writes, “Do you not know that the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God. And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:9-11). The list describes a settled way of life, not the occasional stumble of a repentant believer. Those who practice such sins without repentance show that they are still outside Christ’s kingdom. The same warning appears when Paul says those who practice the works of the flesh will not inherit the kingdom of God (Galatians 5:19-21), and when John says no one who makes a practice of sinning has been born of God (1 John 3:9).

The hope of the passage is in the word “were.” Justification is God’s declaration that a sinner is righteous in His sight, not by personal reform, but because Christ’s perfect life and penal substitutionary death are credited through faith. Those who trust Christ are washed and set apart by the Spirit, so these sins no longer define them. True faith produces repentance and a new direction, even while sanctification remains incomplete in this life and believers still battle remaining sin.

All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read 1 Corinthians 6:9-11 and Romans 3:21-26 slowly, asking God to show you both the seriousness of sin and the sufficiency of Christ. If you are part of a local church, speak with a pastor about what repentance and faith look like where you are. What part of this passage is weighing on you most?

question: Is it wise for Christian teens to be dating?
answer:
Young people naturally long for closeness, and that desire is part of how God made us, yet whether Christian teens should date is a matter of wisdom and Christian liberty rather than a direct biblical command. Scripture does not describe modern dating practices, so faithful Christians differ, largely because of varying judgments about maturity, cultural temptation, and the best way to pursue holiness.

Some believers encourage carefully bounded, parent-involved dating for mature older teens, seeing it as practice in Christlike communication and love under accountability, with marriage in view. Others counsel that it is generally wiser for teens to postpone exclusive romantic relationships, investing instead in friendships, group settings, and personal growth so that love is not awakened before hearts are ready.

In every case the call to purity remains non-negotiable as part of progressive sanctification. Believers are to flee sexual immorality because the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:18-20), to guard the heart with all diligence (Proverbs 4:23), and not to arouse love before its proper season (Song of Solomon 2:7; Song of Solomon 3:5; Song of Solomon 8:4). Christian liberty allows different family convictions on timing (Romans 14:1-6), yet it never permits even a hint of sexual immorality or a romantic bond with an unbeliever (Ephesians 5:3; 2 Corinthians 6:14).

A concrete next step is to sit down this week with your parents or church elders, read these passages together, and honestly examine motives, boundaries, and whether this season is better spent growing in Christ than entering an exclusive relationship. Rest in the love of Jesus, who satisfies the heart more deeply than any earthly romance.

question: Why does God allow us to go through trials and tribulations?
answer:
It is understandable to ask this when a trial presses hard, and Scripture never treats suffering as a small thing. God allows trials because, in His wise providence, He uses them to sanctify His people, to show that His grace is sufficient, and to fix our hope on Christ rather than on an easy life.

He refines genuine faith. James says to consider it pure joy when you encounter trials, because the testing of faith develops perseverance, and perseverance matures you so that you are complete (James 1:2–4). Peter says grief in various trials proves faith more precious than gold refined by fire, unto praise when Jesus Christ is revealed (1 Peter 1:6–7). That is sanctification, the Holy Spirit’s patient work of making you like Jesus. God never tempts anyone to sin, though a trial can expose the sin already in the heart (James 1:13–14).

He forms a hope that does not disappoint. Suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces character, and character produces hope, because God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:3–5). He also disciplines those He loves, for our good, so that we may share His holiness. The training is painful now, and later it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace (Hebrews 12:6; Hebrews 12:10–11). If you belong to Christ, this is not condemning wrath. In penal substitution, Jesus bore that wrath in our place on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily (Romans 5:8–9; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

He comforts us so we can comfort others with the comfort we have received from Him (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). And we still live in a fallen world that groans under the curse, waiting for the renewal Christ will bring (Romans 8:20–23). Not every hardship comes with a private explanation. Job suffered terribly, his friends guessed wrongly, and the Lord gave him Himself rather than a full diagram of the reasons. Joseph could later say that what others intended for evil, God intended for good (Genesis 50:20). For those who love God and are called according to His purpose, He works all things together for good, to conform them to the image of His Son (Romans 8:28–29). He keeps His own by His power through faith (1 Peter 1:5).

Jesus said, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). Nothing, including tribulation, can separate those who are in Him from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 8:35–39). If these trials have exposed your need, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. He does not promise a storm-free path. He promises Himself, and a glory that far outweighs this present trouble (2 Corinthians 4:17).

This week, read Psalm 23 or Romans 8 slowly each day, and tell the Lord honestly what hurts. Ask Him for wisdom and steadfastness (James 1:5), and share the burden with a pastor or a mature believer so you do not carry it alone (Galatians 6:2).

What trial is heaviest on you right now?

question: What does Deuteronomy 10:12 tell us God requires of us?
answer:
Deuteronomy 10:12 tells us that God requires us to fear the LORD, to walk in all His ways, to love Him, and to serve Him with all our heart and with all our soul.

This is the heart of what the LORD seeks: reverential awe that produces obedient living, genuine love, and undivided service rather than empty outward acts (Deuteronomy 10:12). Jesus later names loving God with all the heart, soul, and mind as the greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38).

Because no one meets this standard perfectly, the requirement exposes our need and points us to Christ. He alone fulfilled it through His sinless life and substitutionary atoning death, so that by grace through faith we are justified and then grow in sanctification as the Spirit enables us to walk in God's ways (Romans 3:23-24; Galatians 5:16).

This week, read Deuteronomy 10:12-13 slowly, ask the Lord to show you one specific way to love and serve Him more wholeheartedly in your relationships or work, and then take that step in dependence on Him.

question: Is it okay to get tattoos if they are of a Christian nature?
answer:
Whether a tattoo of a Christian nature is fitting is a non-essential matter of Christian liberty, where faithful believers may disagree because the New Testament gives no direct command and the Old Testament text must be read in its covenant context.

Some Christians hold that Leviticus 19:28 forbids tattoos, since the Lord commanded Israel not to make cuts on the body for the dead or to tattoo themselves. They understand this as guarding against pagan practices and against marking the body in ways that dishonor its dignity, and therefore they counsel against tattoos even when the design intends to honor Christ.

Other Christians understand Leviticus 19:28 as addressing specific idolatrous mourning rites of the nations around Israel, a ceremonial boundary of the old covenant rather than a universal moral rule binding believers in Christ. On this view a tattoo that points to the Lord may be received in liberty if it is done from faith, for God’s glory, and without causing a brother or sister to stumble (Romans 14:13-23; 1 Corinthians 10:31-33).

In such questions Scripture calls each person to be fully convinced in his own mind and to refuse whatever does not proceed from faith, for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:5; Romans 14:23). Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, bought at a price, so glorify God in your body (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). Not every permissible choice is beneficial (1 Corinthians 10:23).

Set aside unhurried time to pray, asking the Lord to show whether this desire truly magnifies Christ or mainly serves other motives. Then talk it through with your pastor or elders, weighing your conscience, your public witness, and love for anyone who might be stumbled. If doubt remains, it is wiser to wait or refrain.

question: What day is the Sabbath, Saturday or Sunday?
answer:
The question of whether the Sabbath is Saturday or Sunday is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may disagree, because the Old Testament identifies the seventh day while the New Testament records gathering on the first day and calls for liberty rather than division over days.  

One major view holds that the Sabbath remains Saturday, the seventh day, as the creation ordinance and the fourth commandment present it, a sign to be kept holy. Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11  

Another major view, long held in Reformed churches, holds that the moral principle of one day in seven for worship and rest now falls on Sunday, the Lord’s Day, in light of Christ’s resurrection and the apostolic pattern of meeting. Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10  

Christian liberty governs this difference. Romans 14:5-6 teaches that one person esteems one day above another while another esteems every day alike, and each should be fully convinced in his own mind without judging a brother. Colossians 2:16-17 likewise warns against passing judgment over a Sabbath, since these things are a shadow and the substance belongs to Christ.  

This week, gather with a local church for the Word, prayer, and fellowship on the day your conscience, informed by Scripture, sets apart, and rest in Jesus Himself, who is Lord of the Sabbath and gives true rest to the weary. Mark 2:27-28; Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9-10

question: Why did God punish Pharaoh for Abram’s lie (Genesis 12:17)?
answer:
God afflicted Pharaoh’s house because Sarai had been taken as Abram’s wife, not because Pharaoh told the lie. Genesis 12:17 states that the LORD sent great plagues on Pharaoh and his household because of Sarai, Abram’s wife. The affliction protected her, upheld their marriage, and guarded the covenant promise God had just spoken to Abram.

The tension you feel is understandable: Abram’s fear produced the deception, yet Pharaoh bore the plagues. Scripture presents the Lord as holy and just, and here His action exposed the wrong, brought the truth to light, and secured Sarai’s release. Psalm 105:14-15 later summarizes God’s care for the patriarchs: He allowed no one to oppress them and rebuked kings for their sake. The parallel in Genesis 20 makes the purpose even clearer, as God kept Abimelech from touching Sarah so that the king would not sin against Him.

Abram did sin when he asked Sarai to say she was only his sister, choosing self-protection over trust (Genesis 12:11-13). Still, God did not abandon His word. He had promised to make of Abram a great nation and to bless all the families of the earth through him (Genesis 12:2-3), and by His providence He preserved that line, the very family through whom the promised offspring, Christ, would come (Galatians 3:16). The episode therefore displays both God’s justice, which will not treat the taking of a wife lightly, and His covenant faithfulness, which overcomes human failure.

When fear tempts you to manage outcomes by half-truths, turn to the Lord who sees and keeps His people. Set aside time this week to read Genesis 12 slowly and pray honestly about any place where fear is pulling you from simple obedience.

question: Christmas Story — Day 4 — Do Christians worship Mary?
answer:
No. Christians do not worship Mary. She is honored in the Christmas story as the virgin mother of Jesus, but worship, prayer, and saving trust belong to God alone.

Mary is truly blessed. By the Holy Spirit she conceived, and the eternal Son took on human nature in her womb (Luke 1:26–35; Matthew 1:18–23). She answered in faith, “I am the Lord’s servant. May it happen to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). That is humble obedience, not a claim to be worshiped. She herself sang, “My spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (Luke 1:47). A woman who needs a Savior is not divine, and she is not the one who saves.

Jesus kept the focus where it belongs. When someone cried out a blessing on Mary, He replied, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it” (Luke 11:28). Mary’s own word at Cana was, “Do whatever He tells you” (John 2:5). The apostles taught that “there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). Scripture never tells us to pray to Mary, to trust her intercession, or to give her honor that belongs to Christ alone. When people in the Bible were tempted to bow before exalted servants, they were told, “Worship God” (Revelation 19:10; Revelation 22:9).

Some church traditions speak of “veneration” rather than worship, and they ask Mary to pray for them. That intention should be understood kindly. Even so, those practices grew up long after the apostles, and they go beyond what Scripture teaches. The Bible, not later custom, is the authority for faith and practice. Respect for Mary must never become devotion directed to her.

Christmas does not stop at the mother. It announces the incarnation: Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, came to save sinners. He lived without sin, died on the cross as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Mary rejoiced in that Savior. We are called to do the same. If you have looked to Mary, or to anyone else, as a mediator, turn from that and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A simple next step: read Luke 1:26–56 and Luke 2:1–20, and each time Mary appears, notice how the passage keeps pointing you to her Son.

Would you like to walk through those chapters and see how the Christmas story itself honors Mary without ever worshiping her?

question: What is Kemetic spirituality / Kemetism?
answer:
Kemetic spirituality, often called Kemetism, is a modern revival of the polytheistic religion of ancient Egypt. The name comes from Kemet, the ancient Egyptian name for Egypt, meaning "the black land," a reference to the dark, fertile soil left by the Nile.

Practitioners honor the netjeru, the gods and goddesses of the Egyptian pantheon, such as Ra, Isis, Osiris, Horus, and Thoth. Common themes include Ma'at, the ideal of truth, justice, and cosmic order; household shrines and offerings; festivals drawn from an Egyptian calendar; and, for many, hope of an afterlife shaped by ancient funerary texts. Some communities, notably Kemetic Orthodoxy, are organized and treat the many gods as faces of one divine source. Others are independent reconstructionists working from temple inscriptions, the Pyramid Texts, and the Book of the Dead, or more eclectic pagans who blend Egyptian deities with wider modern spirituality. Ancient Egyptian religion itself stretched across many centuries, was centered in temples and kingship, and was not handed down as one continuous church. Modern Kemetism rebuilds practice from incomplete sources and reinterprets them for today.

The draw is understandable. The art, the rituals, and the promise of order can feel weighty, and many people are honestly seeking something sacred. Studying Egyptian history, language, and beauty is not itself wrong. Worship is the line Scripture will not move. The Bible teaches that the LORD alone is God: "You shall have no other gods before Me" (Exodus 20:3). When He delivered Israel, He said, "I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD" (Exodus 12:12). He also declares, "I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God besides Me" (Isaiah 45:5). Offering worship, prayer, or trust to those gods is idolatry, not another faithful name for the true God.

Christians believe every person has sinned and is separated from this holy God, and that no rite, ancestor, or pantheon can close that gap. There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily on the third day (1 Timothy 2:5; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Forgiveness is by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by keeping Ma'at or honoring other gods. If you are weighing this path, set it beside Scripture and look at Christ Himself. Turn from every other trust and rest in Jesus, who died and rose for you.

If you want, tell me what draws you toward Kemetic spirituality, and we can look at it together in the light of Scripture. A wise next step is to read Exodus 20 and the Gospel of John, and to bring your questions honestly to God in prayer, or to a pastor who will sit with you patiently.

question: Should Christians be concerned about the idea of Sharia Law?
answer:
Yes, Christians should be thoughtfully concerned about Sharia Law as a governing vision, because its classical sources and applications often restrict the freedom of conscience that allows people to hear and embrace the Gospel without coercion.

Sharia (“the path”) is the body of Islamic divine law drawn from the Quran and the traditions of Muhammad. In its traditional schools it includes rules on apostasy, blasphemy, and the unequal legal standing of non-Muslims. Where these have been enforced, Christians and converts have faced real pressure, imprisonment, or worse. That outcome clashes with the Bible’s teaching that saving faith is the Spirit’s work in the heart, not a result the state can compel. Jesus said His kingdom is not of this world and that His servants do not advance it by earthly force (John 18:36). Paul likewise urged prayer for rulers so believers might live peaceful, quiet lives in godliness (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Every person bears God’s image (Genesis 1:27) and therefore deserves justice and the chance to hear that Jesus alone is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

This concern is not a call to fear or despise Muslim neighbors. Scripture commands us to love them (Matthew 22:39) and to give a reason for our hope with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Many Muslims do not seek to impose the full classical code on pluralistic societies, and Christians rightly reject stereotyping. At the same time, love does not require us to ignore what the sources themselves teach or the persecution that continues in various places today. Historic Christian conviction, especially the Baptist insistence on liberty of conscience, holds that the Gospel spreads by persuasion, not by the sword, and that civil law should protect that freedom for all rather than enforce one religion’s penalties for unbelief.

Let the concern move you to prayer and witness rather than anxiety. Ask God to give wisdom to those in authority, to strengthen believers under pressure, and to open hearts. This week, pray by name for one Muslim person you know and look for a simple way to show practical kindness, trusting the Lord for any opportunity to explain the forgiveness and new life found only in Christ’s death and resurrection. No legal system, Islamic or otherwise, can reconcile sinners to God. That comes by grace alone through faith alone in Jesus alone.

How has this question arisen for you, and is there a particular aspect you would like to think through from Scripture?

question: What is the meaning of the foxes in Song of Solomon 2:15?
answer:
In Song of Solomon 2:15, the little foxes are small pests that spoil a vineyard just as it comes into bloom, and in the poem they picture threats that can ruin a tender, growing love if they are not dealt with early.

The line belongs to a springtime scene of covenant love. The beloved has called her lover to come away while “the blossoming vines spread their fragrance” (Song of Solomon 2:13), and then comes the plea, “Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that ruin the vineyards, for our vineyards are in bloom” (Song of Solomon 2:15). In that ancient setting, foxes and jackals damaged vineyards by eating blossoms and young fruit and by digging among the vines. The word “little” matters. The danger is not only a large, obvious enemy, but the small destroyer that is easy to ignore while the vines are most vulnerable.

In the Song, the vineyard often stands for the woman and for the couple’s shared love (Song of Solomon 1:6; Song of Solomon 8:11–12). So the lovers are asking that their blossoming affection be guarded. Petty resentment, neglect, jealousy, harsh words, outside interference, or secret compromise can strip a relationship before its fruit has time to mature. Even love that is “as strong as death” still needs wise protection while it is young (Song of Solomon 8:6). Some readers have taken the foxes more narrowly as cunning rivals; the image itself simply names whatever spoils what is just beginning to flourish.

Because Scripture later says that marriage points beyond itself to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32), Christians have also applied the line, carefully and secondarily, to communion with Christ. On that reading, little foxes can name small sins and distractions that chill affection for Him when joy in Him ought to be in bloom. That is an application of the poem, not a replacement for its first meaning.

If you are married, sit with your spouse this week and name one little fox already nibbling at tenderness, then agree on one simple guardrail. If you are walking with Christ, ask Him to show you one small compromise that is spoiling your joy in Him, and bring it honestly to Him rather than managing it alone.

question: What is the false cause fallacy?
answer:
The false cause fallacy is the error of treating one thing as the cause of another when the evidence only shows that they happened together or one after the other, not that one produced the other.

It often appears in two familiar forms. Post hoc ergo propter hoc assumes that because B followed A, A must have caused B. Cum hoc ergo propter hoc assumes that because two things rise or fall together, one must cause the other. A simple example is concluding that ice cream causes drownings because both increase in summer, when hot weather better explains both. Sequence and correlation can be clues, but they are not proof of causation. Other factors, coincidence, or a shared cause may be at work.

Christians are called to careful judgment rather than hasty conclusions. “The simple believe every word, but the prudent consider their steps” (Proverbs 14:15). “Test all things. Hold fast to what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). That applies to everyday claims and to how we read Scripture and providence: we should not invent causes God has not revealed, nor ignore real causes He has made plain.

question: Is it a sin to share copyrighted material on the internet?
answer:
Unauthorized sharing of copyrighted material that breaks the law is a sin. It disobeys God’s command to submit to governing authorities and ordinarily amounts to taking what belongs to another.

Scripture says, “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20:15), and calls believers to submit to the authorities God has established (Romans 13:1–2). Those who have stolen are told to steal no longer, but to work honestly so they may have something to share (Ephesians 4:28). Copyright law protects a creator’s right to control and benefit from the fruit of their labor. Uploading or distributing songs, books, films, software, or similar works without permission therefore wrongs the neighbor and rejects the civil rule God has placed over that matter.

Not every act of sharing is unlawful or sinful. You may share what you have permission to share, what the law in your country expressly allows, or what the owner has released freely. Works whose copyright has expired are in the public domain and may be shared without wrong.

I do not provide legal advice. Rules differ by country and by the kind of use, so a qualified professional is the right person to consult if you need to know whether a particular case is permitted.

If you have shared material unlawfully, stop, confess it to God, and make restitution where you reasonably can. Every person has sinned and needs a Savior. Jesus Christ died on the cross for our sins and rose bodily from the dead. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What is on your heart as you think about this?

question: What does the Bible say about Christian fathers?
answer:
The Bible calls Christian fathers to reflect the compassion and holiness of God the Father by providing for their children, teaching them the ways of the Lord, and disciplining them with patience rather than harshness.

Fathers are not to provoke their children to anger or discouragement, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21). That nurture is household discipleship: keeping God's words on the heart and talking of them with children in the ordinary rhythms of home, travel, rest, and rising (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). The aim is generational hope in God, so that children hear the praises of the Lord and do not forget His works (Psalm 78:5-7). Provision belongs to this calling as well. Anyone who does not provide for his own household has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever (1 Timothy 5:8). Managing children with dignity is also a mark of fitness for wider spiritual care (1 Timothy 3:4-5).

Earthly fatherhood is meant to image the heavenly Father. As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him (Psalm 103:13). The Lord disciplines those He loves, and faithful discipline, though painful for a time, yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Hebrews 12:7-11). Jesus reasons from this pattern: if imperfect fathers know how to give good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask Him (Matthew 7:9-11). Christian fathers do this work as sons first. They have received the Spirit of adoption and cry out to God as Father, so their leadership rests on grace, not on flawless performance (Romans 8:15).

Where anger, neglect, or failure has marked your fathering, name it as sin, turn from it, and rest in Christ's sufficient atonement and the Spirit's help for progressive sanctification. This week, read Ephesians 6:1-4 with your family at one meal or bedtime, then pray for each child by name, asking God for wisdom, patience, and a heart that points them to Jesus. If the weight feels heavy, seek the counsel of your local church elders.

question: What was the process of deciding on the Old Testament canon?
answer:
The Old Testament canon was recognized by God’s people as inspired Scripture, not invented by a later church council. From Moses through the prophets, Israel received writings that carried the authority of the Lord, and by the time of Jesus the Hebrew collection of the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings was already the Scripture He and the apostles treated as final.

Jesus affirmed that body of writings in word and practice. He said that everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). His mention of righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah runs from the first book of the Hebrew Bible to the last in its traditional order (Matthew 23:35). The apostles likewise preached Christ from these same Scriptures, which had been entrusted to Israel as the oracles of God (Acts 17:2-3; Romans 3:2).

The process was recognition, not a vote that created authority. Books were received because they came with prophetic authority, agreed with earlier revelation, and were preserved and used as God’s word in Israel’s worship and life. After Malachi, the prophetic voice was understood to have ceased until the Messiah. The church does not make a book canonical; it recognizes the canon, the measuring standard God has already given.

The early church inherited this Old Testament. Greek-speaking Christians often read the Septuagint, which also contained other Jewish writings later called the Apocrypha or deuterocanonical books. Those writings can be useful as history, yet they were not part of the Hebrew canon Jesus received, and neither He nor the New Testament writers cite them as Scripture in the same way. Many early teachers kept them distinct from the canonical books. In the sixteenth century the Roman Catholic Church formally included them. Reformed churches, following the Hebrew Scriptures and the example of Christ, hold to the thirty-nine books.

A common argument for the wider list is that long church use, and the presence of those books in many early Christian copies, shows they belong in the canon. The stronger standard is the Scriptures entrusted to Israel and affirmed by Jesus, not a later ecclesiastical definition. That conviction protects the sufficiency of God-breathed Scripture for faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

You can open the Old Testament with confidence that you are reading the Scriptures Christ read and fulfilled. This week, read Luke 24 and then one of the passages He opens, asking God to show you how the Law and the Prophets speak of Him.

question: Is cyber-sex / phone sex a sin?
answer:
Yes, cyber-sex and phone sex are sins when they involve sexual arousal or erotic interaction with anyone other than your husband or wife.

God designed sexual expression exclusively for the one-flesh covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4). What is commonly called cyber-sex or phone sex is deliberate sexual stimulation pursued apart from that covenant, and Scripture names this sexual immorality. Jesus teaches that lustful intent itself is adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:27-28). Paul commands believers to flee sexual immorality because it is sin against the body, which belongs to the Lord (1 Corinthians 6:18-20), and he states that God’s will is our sanctification, so that we abstain from sexual immorality and control our bodies in holiness rather than lustful passion (1 Thessalonians 4:3-5). There must not be even a hint of such impurity among God’s people (Ephesians 5:3).

The pull of this temptation is strong in a digital age, and repeated failure can leave a person feeling trapped and ashamed. Yet every one of us has sinned and falls short of God’s glory, and we cannot make ourselves clean (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as a penal substitutionary sacrifice for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Forgiveness and new life are given by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our efforts to reform (Ephesians 2:8-9).

Turn from this sin in repentance and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for full forgiveness and the Holy Spirit’s power to walk in holiness. A concrete next step is to confess this specifically to a pastor or mature believer in your local church this week, ask them to walk with you in accountability, and remove the apps, numbers, or access points that lead you into it while replacing that time with daily reading of 1 Corinthians 6 and Psalm 51. Bring the struggle honestly to God in your own words, asking Him for a deeper love for Christ that displaces these desires and for strength to flee when temptation comes.

What led you to ask this question today?

question: Do unbelievers immediately go to hell when they die?
answer:
Many Christians answer yes: unbelievers enter conscious punishment right after death. This concerns the intermediate state, a non-essential matter where faithful believers may differ because Scripture says more about final judgment and resurrection than about every detail of the time between death and that day.

One longstanding reading holds that the unrighteous are in anguish at once. Jesus described a rich man who died, was buried, and immediately found himself in torment in Hades, able to see and cry out (Luke 16:22-24). That fits the statement that people are appointed to die once and after that to face judgment (Hebrews 9:27), and it parallels the hope that believers depart and are at once with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). A second view, often called soul sleep, teaches that the dead remain unconscious until the resurrection. Those who hold it usually appeal to Old Testament pictures of silence in Sheol. These differences do not decide who is a Christian. Romans 14 urges charity where God has not spelled out an explicit rule that settles every question. Historic Christianity still agrees that death does not erase a person before God and that those outside Christ meet His righteous judgment.

God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). In love He sent His Son. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as a penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8-9). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). If you have not yet repented and trusted Christ alone, turn from sin and rest in Jesus, who died and rose for you. He is the only mediator between God and people (1 Timothy 2:5).

Read Luke 16:19-31 slowly this week, then speak honestly to God about your own standing before Him and ask for mercy and light from His Word. If you belong to a church, talk with a pastor as well. What passage or concern lies behind your question? I am glad to look at it with you.

question: How should Christians react to persecution against the LGBTQ community?
answer:
