Christians should oppose violence and cruelty against every person, and they should also refuse to approve what God calls sin.

Every human being bears the image of God, so hatred, mockery, and physical harm against people who identify as LGBTQ are wrong and must be resisted (Genesis 1:27; James 3:9-10). Jesus commands love even for those who reject His ways (Matthew 5:43-45; Luke 6:27-28). A believer who enjoys someone's suffering has already stepped off the path of Christ. People can feel real pain when others will not celebrate their desires. Christians should not add contempt to that pain.

Love is not the same as approval. Scripture teaches that God made us male and female, and that sexual union belongs only within marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6). Homosexual practice is sexual immorality, named among the sins that keep people from the kingdom of God unless they are forgiven in Christ (Romans 1:26-27; 1 Corinthians 6:9-11). Temptation is not the same as practiced sin, yet both the act and an identity that celebrates it contradict God's design. Warning someone of that danger is not persecution. It is truthful love (Galatians 6:1; Ephesians 4:15).

Be careful with the word persecution. In Scripture, persecution is suffering for righteousness, often for confessing Christ (Matthew 5:10-12; 2 Timothy 3:12). Disagreement with LGBTQ ideology, or refusal to celebrate pride, is not persecution. In many places it is Christians who face pressure for holding the Bible's teaching. Where anyone is truly beaten, imprisoned, or killed, Christians should seek justice, protect the weak, and refuse revenge (Romans 12:17-21; Micah 6:8). They must not call evil good in order to appear kind (Isaiah 5:20).

The right reaction is therefore steady. Grieve real harm done to image-bearers. Do not join in scorn. Do not trade the Gospel for cultural approval. Speak with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15), and point people to Jesus. Some in the Corinthian church had practiced these very sins, and yet they were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 6:9-11). That is hope.

All of us stand guilty before a holy God, not only those whose sins are currently praised or despised (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, bore the penalty our sins deserve on the cross and rose bodily on the third day (Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Forgiveness is not earned by self-improvement. It is received by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, pray that God would restrain violence against any person, and that He would give you courage to love a neighbor in sexual sin by telling the truth about Christ. Then ask a pastor in a Bible-teaching church to help you think through any specific situation you are facing.

Would you like help thinking through how to speak with a particular person about this?

question: How did Satan and other angels sin if heaven is sinless?
answer:
Satan and the angels who followed him sinned by freely choosing proud rebellion against God while their created holiness could still be lost, after which He cast them out so that heaven remains undefiled.

God created every spiritual being through Christ, and what He made was good (Colossians 1:16). These angels served before Him with real moral agency, yet some did not remain in the domain and authority He assigned them. Jude 1:6 speaks of angels who abandoned their proper dwelling and are now kept in eternal chains for judgment. 2 Peter 2:4 records that God did not spare the angels when they sinned but cast them into hell, holding them for judgment. The Lord Jesus affirmed the event when He spoke of seeing Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). Their ruin sprang from pride, the same conceit that leads into the condemnation of the devil (1 Timothy 3:6).

Isaiah 14:12-15 and Ezekiel 28:12-17 address arrogant human kings in their immediate setting, yet the church has long recognized in their language an echo of a higher rebellion. The New Testament states the fact plainly: there was war in heaven, and Satan was thrown down with his angels (Revelation 12:7-9).

Heaven is sinless because the rebels have been removed and the angels who stood firm are the elect angels, preserved by God (1 Timothy 5:21). They are no longer in a mutable state where falling remains possible. In the end, the new heaven and new earth will be the home of righteousness alone, where nothing impure enters and the curse is gone (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:27; Revelation 22:3).

God is not the author of this sin. He is light, and in Him is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). He tempts no one (James 1:13). The iniquity began when creaturely wills turned from their Creator. In sovereign wisdom He permitted the fall and governs it so that Satan’s real malice cannot overturn the display of divine justice or the triumph of grace in Christ.

Let this both warn and steady you. Pride cast angels down, and it still endangers human hearts. Set aside time this week to read Philippians 2:1-11, tracing how the Son refused to grasp at glory and humbled Himself to the cross. Then speak directly to the Lord about any pride you see in yourself, asking Him to keep you lowly and secure in His grace.

question: What is the greatest sin?
answer:
The greatest sin is unbelief in Jesus Christ, the settled rejection of Him as Lord and Savior. Jesus taught that the Holy Spirit convicts the world concerning sin precisely because people do not believe in Him, and He warned that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, a hardened refusal that treats God’s saving work as evil and will not repent, will not be forgiven (John 16:8-9; Matthew 12:31-32; Mark 3:28-29).

Every other sin, however dark, can be cleansed by Christ’s blood, yet unbelief leaves a person condemned already because it refuses the only Mediator God has given (John 3:18; Hebrews 10:26-29). This is the root expression of pride: the heart that will not love the Lord with all its being and instead clings to self-rule.

There is real hope. Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as the penal substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, so that all who trust Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone, not by works (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9). If you fear you have crossed a line beyond forgiveness, that very sorrow shows the Spirit has not left you, for a truly seared conscience does not grieve. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What keeps you from resting in Him today?

question: What does the Bible say about sedition?
answer:
The Bible treats sedition, the stirring up of rebellion against lawful civil authority, as a serious wrong, because God establishes governing authorities and calls His people to honor and submit to them.

Paul teaches that there is no authority except from God, and that resisting authority means opposing what God has instituted, which brings judgment (Romans 13:1-2). Peter commands believers to submit to every human institution for the Lord's sake, whether king or governor, and to honor the emperor (1 Peter 2:13-17). The church is to be reminded to be submissive to rulers and authorities, obedient, and ready for every good work (Titus 3:1). Proverbs 24:21 warns God's people to fear the Lord and the king, and not to join with the rebellious. Christians are also told to pray for those in authority so that we may live peaceful and quiet lives in all godliness (1 Timothy 2:1-2).

That submission has a clear boundary. When human rulers forbid what God commands or command what God forbids, "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29). Daniel's friends refused idolatry and accepted the furnace rather than raising a revolt (Daniel 3). The apostles kept preaching Christ when ordered to stop, and they suffered for it, but they did not stir a mob against Rome (Acts 4:19-20; Acts 5:40-42). Jesus distinguished Caesar's claim from God's and paid what was due (Matthew 22:21; Matthew 17:24-27). Our deepest allegiance is to Christ, and we are citizens of heaven even while we live as respectful sojourners on earth (Philippians 3:20).

Scripture also records rebellions that God judged. Korah's uprising against Moses was rebellion against the Lord (Numbers 16:1-35; Jude 1:11). Absalom's seizure of the kingdom from David brought bloodshed and his own ruin (2 Samuel 15:1-18:18). Charges of sedition were leveled at Jesus and at Paul, and both the Gospels and Acts present those charges as false (Luke 23:1-5; Acts 24:5-13; Acts 25:8).

How far Christians may go in resisting a government that has become thoroughly tyrannical is not an essential of the faith, because Scripture gives less explicit detail there than it does on the general duty to submit. Some, reading Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2, hold that private citizens must suffer injustice rather than take up arms. Others, pointing to the role of lesser authorities in Scripture and in later Protestant reflection, have argued that lower magistrates may resist a ruler who has abandoned the task of punishing evil and praising good. In either case, the Bible never blesses private rage, rumor, or disorder for its own sake. Charity should mark how we speak about brothers and sisters who weigh these texts differently (Romans 14:1-4).

This week, set aside time to pray by name for the leaders over you, asking God for just and peaceable rule (1 Timothy 2:1-2). If a law presses your conscience, speak with your pastors before you act, and let your conduct be marked by truthfulness and good works rather than by contempt.

Beneath political rebellion lies a deeper one. All have sinned and rebelled against God's holy rule, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, did not lead a sedition against Caesar. In penal substitution He bore the penalty of our rebellion on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, so that rebels might be justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him (Romans 5:8-10; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). If you have never turned from your rebellion against God, repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

Would you like to look more closely at one of these passages, or at how to pray for leaders where you live?

question: What is the International Christian Church (ICC), and what do they believe?
answer:
The International Christian Church (ICC) is a church-planting movement started in 2006 by Kip McKean after he left the International Churches of Christ (ICOC). It calls people to “sold-out” discipleship and is associated especially with the City of Angels International Christian Church in Los Angeles. It is related to the older ICOC, but it is a separate, stricter group.

In public teaching, the ICC affirms that the Bible is God’s Word and that Jesus is the Son of God who died, was buried, and rose. It also teaches that a person is not forgiven until baptized by immersion “for the forgiveness of sins,” generally in their own fellowship, and that earlier baptisms in other churches do not count. Members are expected to live under intense one-on-one “discipling,” often with a discipler directing time, money, dating, and major decisions, and to evangelize through structured “first principles” studies aimed at baptism into their church.

Test that message by Scripture. God justifies sinners by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, not by a rite or a religious system (Romans 3:21–26; Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8–9; Galatians 2:16). Jesus’ penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection are sufficient to reconcile us to God (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; 1 Peter 3:18). Baptism is a real command and a sign of union with Christ (Matthew 28:19; Romans 6:3–4; Acts 2:38). Faithful Christians have long differed over how closely baptism is tied to receiving grace, so that debate itself is not the whole issue. A message that says faith in Christ is not enough until you are baptized by us, and then kept by our discipleship standard, adds works and a human institution to Christ’s finished work. Paul calls that a different gospel (Galatians 1:6–9).

Scripture also knows one church, made up of all who truly trust Christ, not one modern network (Ephesians 4:4–6; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Rebaptizing believers because they were not immersed in your group is the party spirit Paul rebuked (1 Corinthians 1:10–13). Biblical discipleship is mutual and under Scripture and qualified elders (Matthew 28:18–20; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Peter 5:1–3). It is not a pyramid in which one disciple rules another’s conscience (Colossians 2:20–23). Many former members of this movement and its parent movement have described pressure, isolation, and spiritual harm. Take that history seriously, and still love the people involved.

If you are considering the ICC, or someone you love is in it, compare every claim with the Bible, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). Ask plainly, “According to you, what must I do to be forgiven?” If the answer is anything other than repentant trust in Jesus crucified and risen, do not join. Talk with a pastor who serves under a plurality of elders and welcomes correction from Scripture. If a group urges you to cut off family, hide doubts, or obey a discipler over God’s Word, that is not the freedom Christ gives (Galatians 5:1; Mark 7:9–13).

God is holy, and we cannot save ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily. He saves those who trust Him, not those who join the right organization (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Are you looking into visiting an ICC church, or trying to understand someone close to you who is involved?

question: Do some Christmas traditions have pagan origins?
answer:
Many people hear that the December date, Christmas trees, or other customs were borrowed from pagan midwinter rites, and the desire to worship God without mixture is a right concern. Some peripheral customs in parts of Europe had earlier cultural associations that Christians later reinterpreted, yet the claim that Christmas itself is pagan in origin does not hold up under careful history, and the feast remembers a real event: the birth of Jesus Christ.

Scripture neither commands nor forbids a special day for His birth, so this is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may differ because the Bible gives less explicit detail here than on the gospel itself. Some believers, wary of excess or of any uncertain background, keep the season very quiet or pass over the date entirely. Others mark it with joy, receiving trees, lights, and gifts as creaturely things that can point to Christ the Light and the Father’s greatest gift. Each should act from faith and for the Lord, as Romans 14:5-6 teaches.

The date appears in early Christian reflection tied to the timing of the incarnation, not merely as a copy of Roman festivals, though scholars still discuss the details. Later northern customs involving greenery were often filled with new meaning once idolatry was renounced. What decides the matter now is whether a practice is offered to God or tangled with superstition. Do all to the glory of God, as 1 Corinthians 10:31 says.

The heart worth guarding is the incarnation: the eternal Son took on true humanity through the virgin birth, as Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 2:1-20 record. He lived without sin, died in our place, was buried, and rose bodily so that sinners could be reconciled to the holy God. If you have never trusted Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This season, set aside time to read Luke 1 and 2 slowly, thanking God for sending His Son, and let any custom that troubles your conscience be set aside in love. What aspect of the birth of Christ, or of the way it is remembered, has been weighing on you?

question: Where does the Old Testament predict the coming of Christ?
answer:
The Old Testament predicts the coming of Christ from its earliest chapters through the prophets, promising a Redeemer who would defeat evil, be born in a specific place, suffer for sinners, and reign as King. Genesis 3:15 gives the first promise that the seed of the woman would crush the serpent. Isaiah 7:14 announces a virgin conceiving and bearing Immanuel, Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the birthplace, and Isaiah 9:6-7 describes a child who is Mighty God with an everlasting government. Isaiah 53 portrays the servant pierced for our transgressions and bearing the iniquity of many, while Daniel 9:26 speaks of the Anointed One being cut off, and Psalm 22 anticipates the suffering of the cross.

These Messianic prophecies are fulfilled in Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, whose penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection confirm Scripture’s truth and God’s faithful plan of redemption. This week, read Isaiah 53 alongside one Gospel account of the crucifixion and note how the ancient words match the historical events.

Every person has sinned and falls short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23) and needs a Savior. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4), so that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Which of these prophecies would you like to explore further?

question: What is spiritual adultery?
answer:
Spiritual adultery is unfaithfulness to God. Scripture uses the language of a broken marriage to describe idolatry and any loyalty that rivals the Lord, who has bound Himself to His people in covenant love.

The Old Testament prophets make this charge explicit. Hosea’s marriage to an unfaithful wife was a sign of Israel’s adultery against the LORD (Hosea 1:2; Hosea 3:1). Jeremiah says Israel has been treacherous like a wife who leaves her husband (Jeremiah 3:20), and Ezekiel 16 portrays Jerusalem’s pursuit of other gods as shameless harlotry. This names a real violation of exclusive worship, the first commandment (Exodus 20:3; Exodus 34:14). The covenant background makes the image sharp: the LORD is the divine Husband, and turning to other gods is treachery against Him.

The New Testament speaks the same way to the church. James 4:4 calls those who befriend the world in opposition to God adulteresses, because such friendship is hostility toward Him. Believers are betrothed to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2), so a divided heart is spiritual unfaithfulness (Revelation 2:4).

God’s jealousy is the holy jealousy of a faithful husband, not a petty insecurity (Exodus 34:14; James 4:5). It harms us because rival loves cannot satisfy and pull us from the only source of life.

A practical step is to read James 4:1-10 and Hosea 14 slowly, then ask the Lord to reveal any rival affection in your own heart, whether approval, comfort, money, or self-rule. Confess it specifically and draw near to Him. He gives grace to the humble and promises to heal those who return (James 4:6-8; Hosea 14:4).

Christ is the faithful Bridegroom who loved an unfaithful people and gave Himself for them. His cross and resurrection answer our wandering hearts (Ephesians 5:25-27). If this description exposes something in you, repent and trust Him.

question: How can we rely on the power of God?
answer:
We rely on the power of God by faith in Jesus Christ, humbly depending on the Holy Spirit rather than our own strength or effort. God’s power is perfected in our weakness, and His grace is sufficient for every need (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus said that apart from Him we can do nothing, so true reliance means remaining in Him as branches abide in the vine (John 15:4-5).

This dependence flows from union with Christ. Those who trust Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone, and the same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in them to give life and strength for obedience (Romans 8:11; Ephesians 3:16). We do not generate this power; we receive it as we turn to God daily in prayer, feed on His Word, and walk with other believers in a local church through fellowship and the Lord’s Supper.

A practical step this week is to name one specific weakness or challenge you face. Each morning read Ephesians 6:10, ask the Lord to strengthen you with His mighty power for that situation, and then take the next small step of obedience in faith.

God’s saving and sustaining power comes only through Christ’s death on the cross for sinners and His bodily resurrection. If you have not yet trusted Him, turn from sin and rest in Jesus alone for forgiveness and new life. What situation are you hoping to rely on God’s power for right now?

question: What does it mean that Jesus fulfilled the law, but did not abolish it?
answer:
Jesus fulfilled the Law and the Prophets by bringing them to their appointed goal, not by tearing them down or setting them aside. In the Sermon on the Mount he says, "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. For I tell you truly, until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished" (Matthew 5:17-18). "Abolish" means to dismantle or destroy. "Fulfill" means to fill up, complete, and bring to fullness. He is not a lawbreaker who discards God's commands, and he is not a teacher who leaves the Law unfinished.

That fulfillment holds together several strands in his person and work. He rendered active obedience, loving God and neighbor perfectly in heart and life where we have failed (Matthew 5:21-48; Hebrews 4:15). He also bore the Law's curse in his death. This is penal substitution: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13). And he is the reality to which the ceremonies pointed. Sacrifices, priesthood, and holy days were shadows; the substance belongs to Christ (Hebrews 10:1; Colossians 2:16-17). The prophets spoke of him, and in his life, death, and resurrection what was written is accomplished (Luke 24:44).

So the Law is not abolished as a revelation of God's holy character, and it is not a ladder by which we earn a standing with God. "Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes" (Romans 10:4). "End" there means both goal and completion. The Law still exposes sin and leads us to Christ (Galatians 3:24; Romans 3:20-22). To be "not under law, but under grace" is to be free from the Law as a condemning covenant, not free to ignore God's will (Romans 6:14). There is now no condemnation for those in Christ, and the Spirit works so that "the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit" (Romans 8:1-4). Love is the fulfillment of the Law, not as a new way to merit favor, but as the fruit of a heart already accepted in him (Romans 13:8-10).

This week, read Matthew 5:17-20 beside Romans 8:1-4. Ask the Lord to keep you from treating his commands as optional, and from treating your obedience as the ground of your acceptance. Rest in Christ's finished fulfillment, then take one concrete command, such as truthfulness or purity of heart, and ask the Spirit to shape you by it.

If you have never trusted him, the Law you cannot keep, he kept, and the judgment you deserve, he bore, and he rose. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Is there a particular command that feels heavy to you, or would you like to see how this shapes a Christian reading of the Ten Commandments?

question: What are the Major Prophets and Minor Prophets?
answer:
The Major Prophets are the longer prophetic books of the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, and Daniel. The Minor Prophets are the twelve shorter books, often called the Book of the Twelve: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

“Major” and “minor” describe length, not rank or authority. A long book such as Isaiah and a short book such as Obadiah are alike the inspired, infallible Word of God, profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

These prophets served as covenant messengers. They exposed sin, summoned God’s people to repentance, and held out hope of restoration through the promised Messiah. Scripture teaches that God, having spoken in many times and ways through the prophets, has spoken finally in His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2), and that Christ fulfills what is written in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44).

Read them as living Scripture that still confronts pride and comforts the repentant. This week, read one Minor Prophet, such as Micah, and carry one of its promises about the Lord’s justice and mercy into your own prayer and obedience.

question: Why believe in Jesus?
answer:
Believe in Jesus because He is God the Son, truly God and truly man, and the only one who can bring sinners to the Father. The Bible teaches, "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6; Acts 4:12; 1 Timothy 2:5).

You may feel that this claim is too narrow, or that a sincere and decent life should be enough on its own. Those are understandable concerns. Christianity does not ask you to trust Jesus because you are worse than other people. It says every one of us stands before a holy God.

God is holy, and His glory is the standard, not our comparison with neighbors (Isaiah 6:3). "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God," and "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). Sin is not a small flaw. It is rebellion that separates us from God, and no amount of good effort can erase it.

Jesus Christ took on our human nature, was born of the Virgin Mary, and lived the perfect life we have not lived. On the cross He died in our place. That saving work is penal substitution: the righteous One suffered for the unrighteous, and "the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6; 1 Peter 3:18; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He was buried, and He rose bodily on the third day, defeating sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is risen and exalted as Lord.

We are justified, declared righteous before God, by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works we can boast about (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 10:9).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A practical next step is to read the Gospel of John this week and ask God directly to show you who Jesus is. If you can, talk with a pastor at a Bible-teaching church who will walk through these things with you.

What is the biggest question or obstacle you still have about Jesus?

question: What is a Bible Baptist Church, and what do Bible Baptists believe?
answer:
A Bible Baptist Church is typically an independent, autonomous Baptist congregation that stresses the Bible as the final authority for faith and practice, standing in the fundamentalist stream of Baptist life rather than in a larger denominational structure.

Bible Baptists generally affirm the essentials of the Christian faith. They confess one God eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and they hold that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. They teach that His death was a penal substitutionary atonement, the necessary and sufficient sacrifice that reconciles sinners to God, and that people are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:21–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Ephesians 2:8–9). They proclaim Christ’s bodily resurrection and His personal return to judge the living and the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Acts 1:9–11).

They practice believer’s baptism (credo baptism) by immersion as an ordinance and outward sign of faith already given, not as the cause of salvation (Matthew 28:19; Acts 8:36–38; Romans 6:3–4). The Lord’s Supper is kept as a memorial of Christ’s death. Each local church governs itself, usually under pastoral leadership, and remains free to associate with like-minded churches for missions and mutual help. Scripture is received as the inspired, inerrant Word of God (2 Timothy 3:16–17), and many of these churches use the King James Version in worship. Personal holiness, separation from sinful practices, and active evangelism are strongly urged (1 Peter 1:15–16; 2 Corinthians 6:14–17).

“Bible Baptist” names a family of churches rather than one binding confession, so convictions on non-essentials such as the precise details of Christ’s return, worship style, or matters of Christian liberty often differ from congregation to congregation. Faithful believers may disagree on these points while holding the gospel in common (Romans 14:1–5).

If you are considering a particular Bible Baptist church, read its statement of faith, visit its services, and ask the pastor how the church understands the cross, baptism, and the authority of Scripture. Measure what you hear by the Bible itself, and look for a body where Christ is clearly preached and believers are shepherded in both truth and love.

question: What is sexual ethics?
answer:
Sexual ethics is the moral teaching that governs sexual desire, behavior, and relationships. For Christians, that standard is not personal feeling or cultural consensus, but the holy will of God revealed in Scripture.

God created sex as a good gift, to be received with thanksgiving inside the covenant marriage of one man and one woman, where husband and wife become one flesh (Genesis 2:24; Hebrews 13:4). Outside that covenant, sexual activity is sin. Scripture calls this sexual immorality, from the Greek word porneia, and it includes fornication, adultery, homosexual practice, and lustful intent, which Jesus identifies as adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:27–28; Romans 1:26–27; 1 Corinthians 6:9–10). Believers are commanded to flee sexual immorality, because the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and we were bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:18–20; 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5).

This belongs to sanctification, the Spirit’s work of making God’s people holy in desire as well as in deed. A practical step is to bring sexual temptation into the light: confess it to the Lord, set clear boundaries with media and relationships, and ask a mature believer in your local church to walk with you in accountability.

The same passages that name the sin also announce gospel hope. Those who repent and trust Christ are washed, sanctified, and justified, not left defined by their past (1 Corinthians 6:11). Christ’s cross is sufficient for sexual shame, and His resurrection life is strong enough for a new obedience.

question: What is spiritual sickness? What does it mean to be spiritually sick?
answer:
Spiritual sickness is the Bible’s picture of the human soul corrupted by sin and cut off from the life of God, a condition Scripture describes as disease, blindness, and even death that we cannot cure ourselves.

The prophets used this language for a people ruined by rebellion. Isaiah says the whole head is sick and the whole heart faint because of sin (Isaiah 1:5-6). David, under conviction, speaks of wounds that fester and no soundness in his flesh (Psalm 38:3-5). Jesus took up the same image when He said it is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick, and that He came to call sinners, not those who imagine they are righteous (Matthew 9:12-13; Mark 2:17). To be spiritually sick, then, means you are dead in trespasses and sins, by nature a child of wrath, with a mind hostile to God and unable to please Him (Ephesians 2:1-3; Romans 8:7-8). Theologians call this spiritual death, the fruit of original sin. No religious effort or moral resolve heals it.

Christ alone is the Physician. He, truly God and truly man, bore our sins in His body on the tree so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness; by His wounds we are healed (1 Peter 2:24; Isaiah 53:4-6). He died for our sins, was buried, and was raised bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). God makes alive those who were dead when they trust Him, and this salvation is by grace alone through faith alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:4-9). Believers may still feel spiritually weak or dull when they neglect God’s Word, prayer, and fellowship, or when they harbor unconfessed sin, yet they are no longer dead; they are being progressively sanctified. The terminal sickness belongs to those still outside of Christ.

If this describes your heart, repent of your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and new life. This week, read Isaiah 53 and Ephesians 2 slowly, asking God to show you both the depth of your need and the sufficiency of the cross, and speak with a pastor or mature believer in a local church about what you see.

What has stirred this question in you?

question: What is fellowship with God?
answer:
Fellowship with God is a real sharing of life with the Father, through the Son, by the Holy Spirit. It is not a vague religious mood or God merely tolerating us from a distance. It is the Father welcoming His children into communion with Himself.

Scripture names this fellowship with a word that means shared life, partnership, and communion. John writes that the apostles proclaim Christ "so that you also may have fellowship with us. And our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ" (1 John 1:3). Paul blesses the church with "the fellowship of the Holy Spirit" (2 Corinthians 13:14), and he says, "God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful" (1 Corinthians 1:9). Eternal life itself is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent (John 17:3).

This fellowship rests on union with Christ. A holy God cannot treat sin lightly, and we have all sinned and stand separated from Him. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross in our place, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). That death is penal substitution: He bore the penalty our sins deserved. Those who trust Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone, declared righteous, and given peace with God (Romans 5:1). We do not earn nearness by moral effort. We receive it as a gift.

Christians have long distinguished that secure bond from the daily joy of communion. Sin does not make God cease to be Father to those He has adopted in Christ, yet it does grieve the Spirit and cloud the sweetness of fellowship. John is plain: "If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin" (1 John 1:6–7). Confession restores the enjoyment of that communion, for "He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9). The same fellowship that joins us to God also joins us to His people.

This week, read 1 John 1 slowly each day. Confess specific sins to the Lord in your own words, thank Him for the cleansing blood of Christ, and take one concrete step toward a local church where the gospel is loved and believers walk together in the light.

If you do not yet know this fellowship, the way in is Christ, not self-improvement. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Where do you most long to know God's nearness right now?

question: What role does Iran play in the end times?
answer:
Iran is not named in the New Testament’s teaching about the last days. The passage usually in view is Ezekiel 38:5, where Persia, the ancient empire in the region of modern Iran, appears in a hostile alliance, and faithful Christians disagree about whether that text predicts a future Iranian role.

This is a non-essential matter of eschatology, the doctrine of the last things. Believers may differ here without breaking fellowship, because these chapters use ancient nation names and apocalyptic imagery, and Scripture never gives an explicit map of modern states. What is essential, and not optional, is this: the Lord Jesus will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead, and he will renew all things (Acts 1:11; Revelation 21:1-5; Revelation 22:12). No one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36).

One major view, common among futurist and especially dispensational readers, takes Ezekiel 38-39 as a still-future war. Persia is listed with Gog against Israel, and because ancient Persia corresponds to the land of modern Iran, these readers expect Iran to join a coalition that the Lord himself will overthrow (Ezekiel 38:5; Ezekiel 38:18-23; Ezekiel 39:1-6). Their aim is to read that nation list concretely.

Another major view, common among amillennial readers and many in the historic Reformed tradition, treats Ezekiel 38-39 as apocalyptic prophecy. Persia, Cush, and Put are names from Ezekiel’s world, picturing a vast hostility that cannot stop the Lord from vindicating his holiness and keeping his people (Ezekiel 38:5; Ezekiel 39:21-29). On this reading, the point is God’s certain victory, not a forecast of Iranian policy. Daniel’s Persia, by contrast, is the historical empire already known in Scripture, not a code for a later government (Daniel 8:20; Daniel 10:13).

The Hebrew name Paras is simply the Bible’s word for Persia. That ancient identification is solid. The further step, tying today’s Iranian government to a specific future war, is an inference, and Christians who trust the same Scriptures reach different conclusions about it.

Because this is disputable, Christian liberty applies. Receive one another without contempt, and do not let charts or news cycles divide the church or breed fear or scorn toward any people, including the people of Iran (Romans 14:1-4).

Read Ezekiel 38 and Ezekiel 39 this week in one sitting, asking first what they say about God’s name and God’s people. Then pray for Iran’s people, including believers who follow Christ there under pressure, and pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Set your hope on the returning Christ, not on speculation.

The end presses a more urgent question than any nation’s rank in prophecy: whether we are ready to meet the Judge. God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of his glory (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in him alone. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What have you been taught about Iran and Ezekiel, and would it help to walk through that passage together?

question: What does Jesus mean when He says, “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly,” in the gospels?
answer:
When Jesus says “Verily, verily” or “Truly, truly,” He is giving a solemn assurance that what follows is absolutely certain and binding. The words translate the Greek *amēn amēn* (from the Hebrew *amen*), which means “it is firm” or “truly.”

In ordinary Jewish practice, people said “amen” at the end of a prayer or statement to affirm that it was true. Jesus does something unique. He places “amen” at the front of His own words, and in John’s Gospel He doubles it: “Truly, truly, I tell you” (John 3:3; John 5:24). Prophets said, “Thus says the LORD.” Jesus speaks on His own authority as the incarnate Son, sealing His teaching with His own name.

The doubled form heightens the weight of the saying. It often introduces a truth about the kingdom, new birth, judgment, or eternal life, as when He says, “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment” (John 5:24; see also John 3:5; John 6:47). It is not a filler. It is Christ’s own pledge that His word can be trusted completely.

So when you meet “Truly, truly” in the Gospels, receive those words as sure and act on them. This week, choose one such saying, read it slowly, and ask the Lord to help you trust and obey it.

question: What should we learn from the tribe of Asher?
answer:
The tribe of Asher teaches us to receive God’s rich provision with gratitude while refusing to let comfort excuse incomplete obedience. Jacob said Asher’s food would be rich and yield royal delicacies (Genesis 49:20). Moses called Asher most blessed of the sons, favored by his brothers, dipping his foot in oil, with bolts of iron and bronze and strength equal to his days (Deuteronomy 33:24–25). Their coastal territory was fertile, especially for olive oil, so the blessing was concrete. God supplies His people generously, including daily strength matched to the path He gives.

The same record warns against settling. Asher did not drive out the Canaanites of several cities and lived among them (Judges 1:31–32). When Israel was summoned to battle, Asher stayed at the coast and remained in his harbors (Judges 5:17). Ease became a hiding place, and partial obedience left them entangled with what God had told them to remove. Material blessing is not the same as spiritual maturity. Sanctification, the Spirit’s ongoing work of holiness in those united to Christ, still requires saying no to compromise even when life feels secure.

God was not finished with them. Anna, a prophetess of the tribe of Asher, never left the temple but worshiped with fasting and prayer, and she spoke of the child Jesus to all who were waiting for redemption (Luke 2:36–38). A tribe often remembered for harbors and oil also produced a woman who recognized the Messiah. Faithfulness can grow where earlier generations compromised.

Thank God this week for one ordinary provision, the “oil” of strength for the day in front of you. Then name one place where comfort may be keeping you in the harbor, bring that honestly to the Lord in prayer, and share it with a mature believer in your local church so you do not carry it alone.

question: Why does the Bible speak against braided hair?
answer:
The Bible does not forbid braided hair as something sinful in itself. In 1 Timothy 2:9-10 and 1 Peter 3:3-4, Paul and Peter use elaborate braided hairstyles, together with gold, pearls, and costly clothing, as examples of outward display that should not be a Christian woman’s focus.

In the first-century Greco-Roman setting, wealthy women often wore intricate braids woven with jewels and gold as public signs of status, expense, and attention-seeking beauty. The apostles are not issuing a timeless hairstyle rule. They are contrasting that kind of adornment with what truly suits women who profess godliness: respectable clothing, modesty, self-control, and good works, together with the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight (1 Timothy 2:9-10; 1 Peter 3:3-4). The concern is the heart, whether appearance is being used to impress others or to reflect contentment in Christ and a holy life.

The principle of modesty is biblical and applies to every believer’s conduct. Exact applications, including ordinary braids versus showy styles, are matters where faithful Christians may differ by culture and conscience, exercising Christian liberty with care for others (Romans 14:13-19). A simple, practical braid can be entirely fitting. What matters is whether our choices flow from a desire to honor the Lord rather than to draw praise to ourselves.

This week, read 1 Peter 3:1-6 slowly and ask the Lord to shape in you the gentle and quiet spirit He calls precious, then talk it over with a mature sister or your pastor if questions remain about how modesty looks in your setting.

question: What is the difference between a covenant and a contract?
answer:
A covenant is a sacred, oath-bound relationship that God sovereignly initiates and upholds, often sealed by sacrifice, while a contract is a mutual agreement whose force depends on the negotiated performance of both parties.

In Scripture this appears when God alone passes between the pieces to confirm His promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:17-18) and when He pledges, in the new covenant, to forgive iniquity and write His law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:31-34; Hebrews 8:8-12). The New Testament word diatheke carries the sense of a testamentary disposition of God’s will rather than a symmetrical bargain, underscoring the covenant of grace in which God binds Himself to save through Christ.

Because your standing with God is covenantal rather than contractual, you do not purchase His favor by flawless rule-keeping. Trust the promises already secured in Jesus and answer with grateful obedience. This week, linger over one “I will” statement in Jeremiah 31 and bring a concrete struggle to God in prayer, asking Him to keep His word in you.

question: If Jesus was God, why did He say "No one is good but God alone"?
answer:
Jesus was not denying that He is God, or that He Himself is good, when He said, "No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18). He was pressing a man to face what those words actually require.

It is understandable that this sentence is sometimes read as Jesus distancing Himself from God, or as a modest brush-off of empty praise. Lifted out of the conversation, it can sound that way. Read in context, it does the opposite.

A man ran up, knelt, and asked, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" (Mark 10:17). Jesus answered, "Why do you call Me good? No one is good except God alone" (Mark 10:18). He is not saying, "I am not good." He is asking whether the man knows what "good" means, and whom he is addressing. Absolute goodness is not a human achievement. It belongs to God. If the man calls Jesus good in that sense, he must reckon with Jesus as more than a respected teacher.

Jesus then names the commandments, and the man claims he has kept them from his youth (Mark 10:19-20). Jesus looks at him, loves him, and shows that his heart still belongs to his wealth (Mark 10:21-22). The problem is not that Jesus falls short of goodness. The problem is that the man thinks he can inherit life by being good enough.

The rest of Scripture agrees that Jesus does not fall short. He was tempted in every way, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21). He says, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30). Christians confess the hypostatic union: Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. So when only God is truly good, and the Son is without sin, His question does not weaken His deity. It uncovers it. The incarnate Lord is searching a heart that has not yet seen who stands before him.

That same search reaches us. The Bible says there is no one who does good, not even one (Romans 3:12). We cannot earn eternal life by moral effort. Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by our goodness.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What has kept you from receiving Him as Lord, and not only as a good teacher?

question: What does it mean that God will reveal the hidden things (Daniel 2:22 and 28)?
answer:
In Daniel 2:22 and 28, God revealing the hidden things means that He alone knows what is concealed from human sight and freely discloses mysteries according to His will, as He did when He made known King Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and its interpretation to Daniel.

The Babylonian magicians and enchanters could not tell the dream or its meaning, because no human wisdom uncovers what the Lord keeps secret (Daniel 2:10–11, 27). Daniel therefore blessed the God of heaven who “reveals deep and hidden things,” who “knows what lies in darkness,” and with whom “light dwells” (Daniel 2:22). The mystery concerned “what will happen in the latter days,” so the passage displays God’s omniscience and His sovereign rule over history (Daniel 2:28).

These verses do not promise that God will uncover every private curiosity. The secret things belong to the Lord, while the things revealed belong to His people so they may walk in obedience (Deuteronomy 29:29). When something remains unclear, bring it to Him in prayer, search the Scriptures He has already given, and seek counsel from mature believers in your local church, refusing any practice that hunts hidden knowledge apart from Him. He knows what lies in darkness and is faithful to supply the wisdom needed for faithful obedience.

question: What items should be included in a church constitution?
answer:
A church constitution should state, in plain and orderly language, what the church believes, who belongs, who leads, how decisions are made, and how the body corrects, restores, and amends its life together under Scripture.

These are the items wise churches usually include:

1. **Name, purpose, and final authority.** Give the church’s name and its aim to worship God, preach the gospel, make disciples, and love one another. Affirm that Scripture is the inspired and final authority for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16-17; Acts 2:42).

2. **Statement of faith.** Put the essentials in writing: the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, the incarnation and virgin birth, penal substitution, justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, the bodily resurrection, and Christ’s return to judge the living and the dead. Many churches also receive a fuller historic confession as a teaching standard, while keeping the constitution itself readable. Guard the gospel; do not leave core doctrine vague (Galatians 1:6-9; Jude 3).

3. **Membership.** Define a regenerate membership: a credible profession of faith, submission to the church’s doctrine and discipline, and a commitment to love and serve the body (Acts 2:41; Romans 12:4-5). Explain how members are received, what is expected of them, and how membership ends. A separate church covenant often sits beside the constitution and describes how members promise to walk together.

4. **Officers.** Name the biblical offices of elder, also called pastor or overseer, and deacon. Include the qualifications in 1 Timothy 3:1-13 and Titus 1:5-9, the duties of each office, and how officers are recognized, supported, and, if necessary, removed (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:1-4; Hebrews 13:17).

5. **Government, meetings, and voting.** State which matters belong to the elders and which belong to the congregation, such as receiving members, affirming officers, major financial or property decisions, and discipline. Include notice, quorum, and voting rules so the church acts decently and in order (1 Corinthians 14:40; Matthew 18:17). Faithful Christians differ on polity. Some presbyterian churches entrust shared oversight to elders beyond the local congregation, seeking connectional care and doctrinal stability. A Reformed Baptist constitution ordinarily affirms elder-led congregational government, because the New Testament joins qualified shepherds with a local assembly that acts under Scripture in membership, officer recognition, and discipline.

6. **Ordinances.** State the church’s practice of baptism and the Lord’s Supper, including who administers them and who receives them. Historic Christians differ on baptism. Those who baptize infants appeal to covenant continuity with the children of believers. Those who baptize believers only see baptism as the sign that follows a profession of faith, ordinarily by immersion (Acts 2:41; Romans 6:3-4). State your actual practice clearly. The Supper proclaims Christ’s death and is for those who examine themselves and belong to Him (1 Corinthians 11:23-29).

7. **Discipline and restoration.** Outline private correction, wider witness, and, where there is no repentance, removal from membership. The aim is always repentance and restoration, not humiliation (Matthew 18:15-17; Galatians 6:1; 2 Corinthians 2:6-8).

8. **Marriage and moral boundaries.** If you include them, state plainly that marriage is the covenant union of one man and one woman, and that sexual intimacy belongs only there (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4-6; 1 Corinthians 6:9-11). This is the Bible’s standard, not a matter of preference. Hold it with truth and with real hope of forgiveness in Christ for every sinner who repents.

9. **Finances, property, and records.** Say who stewards money, how budgets are approved, how property is held, and how records are kept. Have a qualified attorney in your jurisdiction review these civil sections. I cannot give legal advice, and nonprofit and property law differs from place to place.

10. **Associations, amendments, and dissolution.** Local churches may freely associate with like-minded churches for mission and counsel without surrendering their own responsibility under Christ. Require advance notice, a high threshold, and consistency with the statement of faith for amendments. Direct remaining property, if the church dissolves, to a like-minded gospel ministry rather than to private persons.

Do not load the constitution with tertiary preferences such as worship style, schooling, or diet. Romans 14 leaves room for Christian liberty in matters Scripture does not bind. Be clear on essentials and on the church’s actual practice, and charitable where faithful Christians may differ.

Ask your elders to read Matthew 18, Acts 6, Acts 20, 1 Timothy 3, and Titus 1 together, then draft a short constitution and give the congregation several weeks to pray over it before any vote.

question: What is topical preaching? Should a pastor preach topically?
answer:
Topical preaching is the practice of choosing a subject, such as prayer, suffering, or the church, and then gathering biblical passages that address it so the sermon is organized around that theme.

This is a non-essential matter of ministry wisdom where faithful Christians may differ, because Scripture commands us to preach the Word but does not prescribe one fixed sermon form, and Christian liberty applies to methods that truly serve that command (Romans 14:1-6). Some pastors rely mainly on topical preaching so they can answer the questions people are actually asking, teach doctrine in an orderly way, and speak to urgent needs in the congregation. Others make sequential exposition their regular pattern, holding that preaching through books of the Bible helps the church receive the whole counsel of God and learn to read each passage in its own setting, as when the Law was read and explained so the people understood it (Nehemiah 8:8; Acts 20:27).

A sound and charitable approach, and the one I would commend as a faithful option among historic Christians, is to let careful exposition of Scripture form the main diet of the church, while using topical sermons occasionally for real pastoral needs. In every topical message the preacher must still honor the context of each text rather than bending verses to fit a preferred outline, so that the charge to preach the word remains central (2 Timothy 4:2). If you are shaping a preaching plan, choose a book of the Bible for your next series and ask the Lord for grace to say what the text says, then consider only those topical messages that truly serve your people without replacing that steady opening of Scripture.

question: What are tribulation saints?
answer:
Tribulation saints are believers who, in certain end-times interpretations, trust in Christ during a future period of severe trial (often linked to Daniel’s seventieth week) and are distinguished from the church raptured beforehand.

This is a non-essential matter of eschatology. Faithful Christians may disagree because prophetic passages such as Daniel and Revelation use symbolic language and do not spell out one required timeline for Christ’s return or the exact nature of the tribulation.

One major view, common in dispensational premillennialism, teaches a pretribulation rapture of the church (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Afterward, many people, including a renewed witness among Israel, come to faith amid the judgments and are called tribulation saints. Passages such as Revelation 7:9–14 picture a great multitude coming out of the great tribulation, and some of these saints are martyred yet raised at Christ’s coming (Revelation 6:9–11; Revelation 20:4).

A contrasting historic view, held by many posttribulationists, historic premillennialists, and amillennialists, does not separate a distinct class of tribulation saints from the church. All who belong to Christ are simply the saints, God’s holy ones (Romans 1:7; Ephesians 1:1). Any final intensification of suffering is endured by the one people of God together (Matthew 24:21–22; Revelation 13:7), whether that tribulation is read as the church’s long experience or a climactic end-time trial.

In these differences of sequence and emphasis we are to show liberty and charity (Romans 14:1–4; Romans 14:19), while holding firmly to what Scripture makes plain: Jesus will return bodily, the dead will be raised, and He will judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11; John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15).

A wise next step is to read Revelation slowly in the light of the whole Bible, perhaps with your pastor or a small group, asking less “Which chart is mine?” and more “How does this call me to endurance, worship, and hope in Christ’s victory today?”

question: Who are the Black Hebrews / Black Israelites?
answer:
The Black Hebrews, usually called Black Hebrew Israelites, are various religious groups, mostly African American, who teach that Black people are the true descendants of the ancient Israelites and that the Jewish people of today are not.

These movements took shape mainly in the United States from the late nineteenth century onward, as some sought dignity and a biblical identity after slavery and in the face of racial injustice. They are not one church, and not every group holds every extreme claim. Many teach that the curses in Deuteronomy 28 were fulfilled in the slave trade, that Jesus was Black, and that covenant standing or salvation belongs especially or only to Black people. Some camps preach open hostility toward Jewish people and white people. That teaching is neither historic Christianity nor Judaism.

Scripture does not support a racial gospel. God made His covenant with the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and He has not rejected them (Romans 11:1–2). From the start, that promise was meant to bless all nations (Genesis 12:3). Jesus Himself was born a Jew, of the line of David (Romans 1:3), and the apostles were Israelites. In the New Testament, no one becomes a child of God by skin color or ancestry. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:28–29). Paul calls any message that adds ethnic or legal conditions to Christ “a different gospel” (Galatians 1:6–9).

Hatred of Jewish people, or of any people, breaks the command to love your neighbor (Matthew 22:39) and denies the peace Christ made by His blood (Ephesians 2:14–16). The so-called curse of Ham does not teach that Black people are cursed. Noah’s words fell on Canaan, not on every descendant of Ham (Genesis 9:25). People from every tribe and nation are welcomed to the Lamb (Revelation 7:9). Faithful Christians of African descent are full members of Christ’s body. Their identity is in Him, not in this movement.

Every person, of every color, has sinned and falls short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by race, law-keeping, or ancestry (Romans 3:28; Ephesians 2:8–9). A longing for dignity and belonging is understandable, but only Christ gives a name that cannot be taken away. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

If these claims have unsettled you, read Romans 9–11 and Galatians 3 slowly, and take your questions to a pastor who preaches Christ for all nations. Which of their teachings, or which passage, would you like to look at together?

question: What does the Bible say about church-hopping?
answer:
The Bible does not use the word "church-hopping," but it does call believers to steady, accountable fellowship in a local church, not a pattern of leaving whenever a congregation becomes inconvenient.

Those who believed were added to a recognizable people and devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:41–42). Scripture describes the church as a body in which each member belongs to the others, so encouragement, correction, and service happen among people who actually know one another (Romans 12:4–5; 1 Corinthians 12:12–27). Hebrews urges believers not to neglect meeting together, "as some have made a habit," but to encourage one another and to consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds (Hebrews 10:24–25). That is difficult to obey if a person is always arriving and always leaving.

The New Testament also assumes shepherds and a flock. Elders are charged to care for the church of God, which Christ purchased with His own blood (Acts 20:28; 1 Peter 5:1–3). Believers are told to submit to leaders who keep watch over their souls (Hebrews 13:17). Even church discipline presupposes a defined congregation that can hear a matter (Matthew 18:15–17). Together these passages commend durable belonging, in which sanctification is pursued through the means of grace: the Word, prayer, the Lord's Supper, and mutual care.

Leaving a church is not automatically unfaithful. A move to another city, a persistent denial of the gospel, or a refusal by leaders to address serious sin or abuse can be a righteous reason to depart, and the departure should be as peaceable and honest as the situation allows (Galatians 1:6–9; Romans 12:18). What Scripture does not commend is a consumer habit: rotating churches over music, personality, minor offenses, or a desire to avoid correction. Worship style and similar preferences are non-essential matters where faithful Christians may disagree, and Romans 14 calls us to bear with one another rather than to keep searching for a perfect fit (Romans 14:1–4; Ephesians 4:1–3). Every true church is a company of sinners being sanctified, so some disappointment is normal.

Christians do differ on how formal commitment must be. Some argue that the New Testament stresses union with Christ and living fellowship more than official membership rolls, and that a believer may move among congregations so long as real fellowship and accountability remain. That concern rightly guards against treating a membership list as a substitute for love. I hold, as one faithful option within historic Christianity, that ordinary discipleship includes identifiable membership under qualified elders. The apostolic letters were written to congregations, and the "one another" commands need a people who know your life, your gifts, and your sins.

If church-hopping has become your pattern, and you are not leaving because of abuse or a denial of the gospel, take this step before you visit another church: write down why you left the last one, pray that the Lord would search your motives (Psalm 139:23–24), and ask a mature pastor to help you discern whether you need a different congregation or a more patient heart. Then stay long enough, in a church that holds fast the gospel, to be known and to love people who are still being sanctified, just as you are. Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, and He is sanctifying her (Ephesians 5:25–27). His people learn that same patience with one another.

If you want to think this through in your own situation, what has usually prompted the move?

question: Dance in worship - what does the Bible say?
answer:
Dance in worship is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may disagree. Scripture celebrates dance as joyful praise in some settings, yet it never commands dance as a required element of the church’s gathered worship, so the difference turns on interpretive emphasis and on Christian liberty, not on whether someone belongs to Christ.

In the Old Testament, dance is a bodily expression of joy in God’s saving acts. After the Lord delivered Israel at the sea, Miriam and the women went out with tambourines and dancing (Exodus 15:20–21). When the ark came into Jerusalem, David danced before the Lord with all his might (2 Samuel 6:14). The Psalms call God’s people to praise His name with dancing (Psalm 149:3; Psalm 150:4), and the Lord is praised as the one who turns mourning into dancing (Psalm 30:11). At the same time, the Bible condemns dance offered to idols or tangled up with lust. Israel’s dancing before the golden calf was rebellion (Exodus 32:19), and the dance at Herod’s feast served sin and violence (Matthew 14:6–11). Holy joy is blessed. Self-display and idolatry are not.

In the New Testament, the church’s worship is described especially as the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (Acts 2:42), together with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs from the heart (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16). The Father seeks worshipers who worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:23–24). Everything in the assembly is to build others up and to be done properly and in order (1 Corinthians 14:26; 1 Corinthians 14:40). Dance is not named among those standing elements.

Two historic approaches follow, and neither is a test of orthodoxy.

Some Christians, including many in Pentecostal, charismatic, and global church cultures, take the Psalms and David’s example as a lasting warrant for dance in corporate praise. They argue that modest, orderly movement can be whole-person worship, akin to kneeling or lifting hands, so long as it glorifies God and does not distract the saints.

Other Christians, including many in Reformed and other Word-centered churches, hold to what is often called the regulative principle of worship: the elements of gathered worship are those God has instituted. They receive the Old Testament dances as real acts of praise in their own settings, without treating them as a pattern for the weekly assembly. For them, corporate worship centers on the Word read and preached, prayer, congregational singing, and the ordinances. Dance may fit cultural celebration or private joy, but not as a prescribed part of the liturgy.

Hold both your own practice and your neighbor’s conscience with care. Paul forbids us to despise or pass judgment on a brother in disputed matters, and he calls us to pursue what builds up the body (Romans 14:1–4; Romans 14:13–19). Whatever you do, do it for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). If dance in your setting pulls you toward display, sensuality, or disorder, refrain for holiness and for your neighbor’s good. If the lack of dance tempts you to scorn believers who rejoice with their bodies, repent of pride. The heart of worship is faith in the God who saves, not the size of the motion.

This week, read Exodus 15:1–21, 2 Samuel 6:12–23, and Psalm 150, then ask your elders how your congregation seeks both joyful praise and reverent order. Pray that your worship, in whatever posture your church practices, would rise from gratitude for Christ’s cross and resurrection and would serve the people beside you.

If you say whether you are thinking of the Lord’s Day assembly or of personal and cultural expressions of joy, I can speak more particularly to your situation.

question: What is secular humanism?
answer:
Secular humanism is a non-religious worldview that seeks meaning, morality, and human flourishing through reason, science, and human experience, without belief in God, revelation, or the supernatural.

Its modern form is often linked with the Humanist Manifestos of the twentieth century. It typically affirms naturalism, the claim that the natural world is all that exists, and treats people as responsible for ethics, justice, and progress without appeal to a Creator.

Many who hold this view sincerely care about dignity, learning, and compassion, and Christians should respect them as people made in God's image. Scripture teaches that this dignity is not self-made. God created humanity in His image, often called the imago Dei, so that worth, reason, and moral awareness are gifts from Him (Genesis 1:26-27). Those same Scriptures teach that people, though gifted, have turned from their Maker, suppressing the truth He has made plain and exchanging His glory for created things (Romans 1:18-23).

That is where secular humanism and the Christian faith part ways. Christians confess that God is holy and supreme, the source of all good, and that the Bible is His inspired Word, the final authority for faith and practice (2 Timothy 3:16-17). Human reason is a real gift, but it is not ultimate, and it cannot erase sin or reconcile us to God (Romans 3:23). The Gospel answers that need: Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died for sinners and rose bodily, and salvation is by grace through faith in Him, not by human moral achievement (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9).

If you are comparing these two ways of seeing the world, set aside time this week to read Genesis 1 and Romans 1 slowly, asking what each passage says about where human worth and the knowledge of right and wrong come from. If questions remain, bring them to a pastor who will open the Scriptures with you.

question: Does the Bible predict the destruction of Damascus?
answer:
Yes, the Bible prophesies the ruin of Damascus. Isaiah 17:1 announces, “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.” Related words of judgment also appear in Jeremiah 49:23-27 and Amos 1:3-5.

These oracles were spoken when Damascus was the capital of Aram, a kingdom that had often attacked Israel. In that ancient Near Eastern setting, such words declared the Lord’s verdict on a proud nation that harmed His people.

When and how fully this word is fulfilled is a non-essential matter of interpretation. Faithful Christians may disagree here because prophetic oracles can be read with different emphases on historical fulfillment and future events, and Scripture does not make one timeline a test of the faith. Hold your conclusion with liberty and charity (Romans 14:1-4).

One major view sees the prophecy fulfilled in history. In 732 BC the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III captured Damascus, slew its king, and carried the people away, ending the Aramean kingdom (2 Kings 16:9). On this reading, the “heap of ruins” describes that devastating overthrow and loss of power, even though the site was later rebuilt, as often happened with conquered cities.

Another major view notes that Damascus has remained inhabited and has never been left as a permanent uninhabited ruin, so it understands the fullest sense of Isaiah 17:1 as still future, possibly near the return of Christ. Those who hold this seek to take the language of total ruin in a straightforward way.

Neither reading should be treated as required for every Christian. What the text clearly teaches is the Lord’s sovereignty and His sure judgment on pride and violence.

That truth is meant to humble us, not mainly to feed speculation about headlines. The God who judges nations is the same God who, in mercy, gave His Son to bear judgment for sinners. Jesus Christ died on the cross for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, so that everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him alone is justified by grace through faith and delivered from final condemnation (Isaiah 53:5-6; Romans 3:23-26; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

This week, read Isaiah 17 slowly in context, then pray by name for the advance of the gospel in Damascus and Syria, asking the Lord to grant repentance and faith. If questions about prophecy weigh on you, study the passage with your local church elders.

Is a particular verse, or something in the news, what stirred this question?

question: What does it mean to watch and pray?
answer:
To watch and pray means to stay spiritually awake and to depend on God in prayer, so that you do not fall into temptation and so that you remain ready for Christ.

In Gethsemane, on the night before the cross, Jesus found His disciples sleeping and told them to watch and pray, lest they enter into temptation, because the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38). The call to watch means to stay alert, not spiritually drowsy. Prayer is how that alertness leans on God rather than on bare willpower. This belongs to progressive sanctification. The Spirit uses watchfulness and prayer as means of grace to keep believers from drifting into sin (Colossians 4:2; Ephesians 6:18).

Watchfulness also looks outward and forward. Scripture calls believers to be sober-minded because the adversary prowls about (1 Peter 5:8), and Jesus told His people to stay awake, since no one knows the day or hour of His return (Mark 13:33–37; Luke 21:36). Watching without prayer becomes anxious self-effort. Prayer without watching becomes careless. Together they are humble dependence joined to clear-eyed obedience.

A concrete way to practice this is to name one temptation that repeatedly finds you half-awake, whether anger, lust, worry, or spiritual neglect, and to meet it early with a short, specific prayer before the pressure rises. This week, set one fixed time each day, even ten minutes, to read a Gospel account of Gethsemane and then pray in your own words for alertness and strength, and ask one mature believer in your church to encourage you in it.

Christ Himself watched and prayed in that garden, then went willingly to the cross for weak disciples. Those who trust Him are not left to their own resolve. His Spirit keeps them as they stay awake and keep asking. If a particular temptation or a season of spiritual tiredness is on your mind, what does that look like for you right now?

question: How is eternity in Hell a fair punishment for sin?
answer:
It is understandable to feel that eternal hell seems unfair, especially if sin looks like limited mistakes in a short life, or if endless punishment appears hard to reconcile with a loving God.

The Bible teaches that eternity in hell is a just punishment because every sin is rebellion against the infinite holiness and glory of God, and His perfect justice measures guilt by the worth of the One offended. God is the standard of right, not our fallen sense of proportion: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25). David confessed the heart of the matter when he said, "Against You, You only, have I sinned" (Psalm 51:4). Sin is cosmic treason against the Creator who gives every breath (Acts 17:28), so its demerit is weighty beyond human calculation. Jesus spoke of "eternal punishment" with the same finality as "eternal life" (Matthew 25:46). Scripture describes the lost as suffering "eternal destruction, away from the presence of the Lord" (2 Thessalonians 1:9) and as tormented "day and night forever and ever" (Revelation 20:10). People store up wrath by suppressing the truth and preferring darkness (Romans 2:5; John 3:19), and they remain guilty because they do not turn to God.

God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). The deeper wonder is that He saves any at all. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), and the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). Yet Christ, truly God and truly man, bore that penalty in penal substitution on the cross, so that God might be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). He was buried and rose bodily on the third day.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and eternal life. This week, read John 3 and Romans 3 slowly, and if you can, bring your questions to a pastor who will open Scripture with you.

What part of God's justice or of endless judgment feels hardest to accept right now?

question: How is Satan god of this world (2 Corinthians 4:4)?
answer:
Satan is called the god of this world in 2 Corinthians 4:4 because he exercises a real but limited and temporary influence over this present fallen age, blinding the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

This title does not mean Satan is divine, equal to God, or outside God’s control. The one true God remains holy, sovereign, and supreme over all things (Psalm 24:1; Daniel 4:35). Satan is a created being who rebelled, and Scripture describes his role with terms such as the ruler of this world (John 12:31; John 14:30) and the prince of the power of the air, the spirit now working in those who disobey (Ephesians 2:2). The whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19), yet this is a usurped dominion that God permits only for a time within the present evil age (Galatians 1:4).

He blinds through deception, keeping people captive to the mindset and desires of this age so that the gospel stays veiled to those who are perishing (2 Corinthians 4:3–4; 2 Corinthians 11:14). His power is not final or absolute. Those who belong to Christ have been rescued from the domain of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son (Colossians 1:13). At the cross Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15), and the same God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” shines in hearts to give the light of the knowledge of His glory in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).

This calls for humble dependence: set aside time this week to pray by name for someone still in unbelief, asking God to open their eyes, and look for a simple opportunity to speak of Christ’s death and resurrection. If you sense this blindness in your own heart, repent and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died for sinners and rose again to deliver us from the power of darkness. What part of this verse or its hope feels most pressing to you right now?

question: Is faith intellectual assent?
answer:
No. The faith that saves is not mere intellectual assent. It is a Spirit-given trust that knows the gospel, agrees that it is true, and personally rests on Jesus Christ alone.

Scripture distinguishes bare agreement from saving faith. The demons believe that God is one and shudder, yet they remain lost (James 2:19). With the heart one believes and is justified (Romans 10:10). Historic Christian teaching therefore speaks of three elements in saving faith: notitia (knowledge of the truth), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (confident reliance upon Christ). Assent without fiducia does not justify. This faith is the open hand that receives Christ’s righteousness; it is not a work we offer to God (Romans 4:5; Ephesians 2:8-9).

We have all sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23).
