Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). His death was penal substitution: He bore the penalty we deserved so that God might justify the ungodly who trust Him (Romans 3:24-26). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by agreeing with facts or by any merit of our own.

If your confidence has rested only in correct ideas about Jesus, repent and trust in Him who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and new life. This week, read John 3:16-18 and Romans 3:21-26 slowly, and ask the Lord to show you whether you are resting on Christ Himself or only on truths about Him. If you can, speak with a pastor about what you find.

What led you to ask whether faith is only intellectual assent?

question: What does it mean to be saved by grace?
answer:
Being saved by grace means God freely forgives sinners and gives them eternal life as an undeserved gift, not as a wage earned by good works or religious effort. This is justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone.

God is holy, and our sin separates us from Him. Scripture says, "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23), and "the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 6:23). The Bible teaches, "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Grace is God's kindness toward people who have earned judgment, not a reward for those who have tried hard enough.

Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as our substitute to bear the penalty for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). His death is penal substitution, necessary and sufficient to reconcile sinners to God. We do not add our deeds to His finished work. We receive this salvation by repenting and trusting Him.

If you have been measuring your standing with God by how well you perform, lay that down and rest in what Christ has already done. Read Ephesians 2 slowly this week, and bring your questions to a pastor or mature believer who will open the Scriptures with you.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What has shaped the way you think about grace and your standing before God?

question: What is the kalam cosmological argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The Kalam cosmological argument is a philosophical case that the universe began to exist and therefore has a cause, which its defenders identify as a personal Creator.

It is usually set out in three steps. Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. Therefore, the universe has a cause. From there, defenders argue that this cause cannot itself be part of the universe. It must be timeless, spaceless, immaterial, and powerful enough to bring all space, time, matter, and energy into being. They also argue that the cause is personal, because only a personal agent with a will can choose to bring a beginning into being, rather than an impersonal set of conditions producing an effect from eternity.

The name comes from medieval Islamic theology. Christian philosophers, especially William Lane Craig, have restated it in modern form. Support for the second step is offered both philosophically, against a beginningless past, and scientifically, from evidence that the universe is expanding and is not past-eternal. Thoughtful people dispute those steps, and the argument does not settle every objection by itself.

Scripture does not depend on this syllogism. It teaches creatio ex nihilo, creation out of nothing, by the self-existent God. "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 1:1). "By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God's command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible" (Hebrews 11:3). The New Testament identifies the agent of that creation as the Son: "Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made" (John 1:3; see also Colossians 1:16).

The argument, at its best, points toward a personal Creator. It does not by itself reveal the Trinity, the incarnation, or the way of salvation. Those truths come from God's Word. Christians may use the Kalam argument as one humble reason for belief, while remembering that other faithful believers weigh philosophical arguments differently, and that our final authority is Scripture, not a syllogism (1 Peter 3:15).

If a friend asks why anything exists rather than nothing, you can walk through those three steps slowly, listen carefully to their objections, and then open Genesis 1:1 and John 1:1–3 with them, so the conversation moves from a first cause to the living God who has spoken.

question: Why is the virgin birth so important?
answer:
The virgin birth is important because it is how the eternal Son of God became truly human without sin, so that He could be the Savior sinners need.

God gave a sign long beforehand: a virgin would conceive and bear a son called Immanuel, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:22-23). Matthew and Luke record this as history, not as a symbol. Mary was a virgin. She conceived by the Holy Spirit, and the child born of her is holy, the Son of God (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-35).

Two truths meet in that miracle. Jesus is truly God and truly man. The church calls this the hypostatic union: one person, the eternal Son, taking a full human nature while remaining fully divine (John 1:1, 14; Galatians 4:4; Philippians 2:6-7). He did not become God. God the Son became man. He is also without sin. We are born in Adam’s fallen line, under sin and death (Romans 5:12). Jesus was not conceived that way. He was tempted as we are, yet without sin, and He knew no sin (Hebrews 4:15; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

That sinlessness is necessary for salvation. A Savior who shared our guilt could not bear our guilt. On the cross He stood in our place, what Scripture presents as penal substitution, died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 3:23-26). God justifies the ungodly by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9).

This week, read Matthew 1:18-25 and Luke 1:26-38 slowly, and thank the Father that He sent His Son to you rather than leaving you to save yourself. If you have never trusted Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who was born of the virgin, died for your sins, and rose again, for forgiveness and new life.

What about the virgin birth feels most precious, or most puzzling, to you?

question: How can I overcome disappointment with life?
answer:
Disappointment with life can weigh heavily on the heart, and I am truly sorry you are walking through this. Scripture does not hide the ache. It tells us that creation was subjected to frustration because of sin, and that we groan as we wait for full redemption (Romans 8:20-23). So often our hopes rest on things that cannot finally satisfy, because God has set eternity in the human heart (Ecclesiastes 3:11).

The answer is not a stronger plan or tougher resolve, but Jesus Christ. He is truly God and truly man. He lived without sin, died on the cross in penal substitution, bearing the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Everyone who trusts in Him is justified by grace through faith alone, not by works, and receives a living hope that does not disappoint (Romans 5:1-5; 1 Peter 1:3-4). In union with Christ, present sorrows are not wasted. God uses them to grow endurance and to fix our eyes on the glory ahead, which far outweighs them (Romans 5:3-5; 2 Corinthians 4:16-18). Jesus promised that in this world we will have tribulation, yet we can take courage because He has overcome the world (John 16:33).

When disappointment surges, pause and name the specific unmet longing to the Lord, then thank Him for one unchanging promise, such as His promise never to leave or forsake His people (Hebrews 13:5). This week, read Romans 8:18-39 slowly each morning and bring your disappointments to God in your own words, asking Him to renew your hope in Christ. Share the struggle with a trusted pastor or mature believer in a local church so you are not alone (Galatians 6:2).

If you have been carrying this in your own strength or looking for life in things that keep failing, turn from sin and self-reliance and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What part of life feels most disappointing to you right now?

question: What is the Gemara?
answer:
The Gemara is the later rabbinic commentary and debate that, together with the Mishnah, makes up the Talmud, the central written collection of Jewish oral tradition.

The Mishnah was compiled around AD 200 as a concise code of legal and religious teaching. The Gemara records centuries of discussion on that code, mainly in the academies of Babylonia (finished around the sixth century) and, in a shorter form, in the land of Israel. Those discussions cover law (halakhah), stories, ethics, and interpretation. In Judaism the Babylonian Talmud is usually treated as the more authoritative of the two.

Christians receive the Old Testament Scriptures as God’s word, and we honor the Jewish people through whom those Scriptures came (Romans 3:1–2; Romans 9:4–5). We do not, however, treat the Gemara as inspired or binding. Jesus rebuked traditions of the elders when they set aside God’s commandment (Mark 7:8–13). He came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets but to fulfill them (Matthew 5:17), and the apostolic writings bear witness that salvation is by grace through faith in him, not by observance of later rabbinic rulings (Galatians 2:16; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

A useful next step is to read a Gospel account of Jesus’ teaching on the Law, such as Matthew 5–7, and to weigh any later tradition by the plain sense of Scripture. If you are exploring this because of a question about Jesus, the Law, or how a person is made right with God, I would be glad to walk through that with you.

question: How can I stop being a people-pleaser?
answer:
The pull to please people is a heavy and common burden, often driven by the fear of man rather than a settled trust in God. You begin to lay it down by fearing the Lord more than people and by resting in the acceptance you already have in Christ.

People-pleasing is what Scripture calls the fear of man, and that fear is a snare (Proverbs 29:25). Paul pressed the issue plainly: if he were still trying to please people, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). Love of neighbor remains a real command (Matthew 22:39), yet that love is meant to flow from obedience to God, not from a craving for human applause (Colossians 3:23; Ephesians 6:6-7). Where the desire to keep others happy leads you to hide the truth, soften God’s commands, or say yes to what you know is unwise or wrong, name that as sin, confess it, and turn back to Christ, who is faithful to forgive (1 John 1:9).

This struggle often reaches down to justification. If you are in Christ, God has already declared you righteous by grace through faith. You are accepted in the Beloved because Jesus lived, died, and rose in your place, not because others think well of you (Romans 3:23-26; Romans 5:1; Ephesians 1:6). Their praise cannot secure you, and their disappointment cannot undo what Christ has finished. When approval becomes necessary for your peace, it has become an idol that only the cross can dethrone.

This week, take one concrete step. Choose a recurring moment where you usually agree out of fear. Pause, ask the Lord for courage to trust Him more than you fear their reaction, and give a truthful, kind answer even if it costs you someone’s favor. Then remind your heart that your standing with God did not shift. Share that step with a wise believer in your local church and ask them to pray for you as you learn a holy fear of the Lord (James 5:16; Proverbs 1:7).

If you do not yet know Christ, the deepest freedom starts with the gospel. We seek people’s approval because we sense our own lack, yet Jesus bore our sin on the cross and rose bodily so that everyone who repents and trusts Him is fully received by the Father. Turn from seeking your worth in others and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you.

What situation most often pulls you into saying yes when you know you should not?

question: What is the golden chain of salvation?
answer:
The golden chain of salvation is the unbreakable sequence of God’s saving acts in Romans 8:29-30, running from His eternal purpose to the believer’s final glory.

Those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified (Romans 8:29-30). This ordo salutis shows salvation as God’s work from first to last: He sets His love on His people, calls them effectually by the Spirit, justifies them by imputing Christ’s righteousness, and will certainly glorify them.

Christians have read “foreknew” in more than one way. A charitable historic view takes it as God foreseeing who would believe and predestining them on that basis, so that human response remains decisive. I understand foreknowledge as God’s prior covenantal love and choice, not conditioned on foreseen faith, because the entire chain displays His sovereign initiative and because faith itself is God’s gift (Ephesians 1:4-5; Ephesians 2:8-9). This reading also upholds the perseverance of the saints: everyone truly justified will be glorified, kept by God’s power.

That certainty lets you face today’s pressures without fearing that your hold on Christ might fail, since His hold on you cannot. This week, read Romans 8 slowly, thanking God for each action He performs in the chain and asking Him to conform you more fully to Christ.

All of this rests on the Gospel. We are sinners separated from a holy God and unable to save ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as our substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. If you have not yet turned from sin and trusted Him, repent and believe in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life.

Which link in this chain most strengthens your hope in Christ right now?

question: Should Mark 16:9-20 be in the Bible?
answer:
Faithful Christians disagree about whether Mark 16:9-20 formed part of the original Gospel of Mark, and this is a non-essential question of textual detail rather than a test of orthodoxy. Manuscripts differ, early Christian testimony is mixed, and the doctrines in view are already secure elsewhere, so believers may weigh the evidence without breaking fellowship.

One historic view holds that the verses belong in the Bible. They appear in the great majority of Greek manuscripts, were known to second-century writers such as Irenaeus, and supply resurrection appearances that round out Mark’s account. Translations in the received-text tradition therefore print the passage without brackets.

Another historic view holds that the verses were added later to complete an abrupt close. The earliest complete manuscripts end at Mark 16:8, and ancient scholars such as Eusebius reported that accurate copies of their day lacked the longer ending. Many modern translations therefore include the passage in brackets or with a footnote so readers can see the variation.

Neither conclusion is required of all Christians. We have liberty to examine the evidence while resting in what is unmistakable (Romans 14:5). Christ’s bodily resurrection, the call to believe the Gospel, and the mission to make disciples stand firm in the undisputed text of Mark and in passages such as Luke 24:1-12 and 1 Corinthians 15:3-8. God has preserved His Word so that the church may be thoroughly equipped (2 Timothy 3:16-17).

If the variant has unsettled you, read Mark 16 in a translation that notes the difference, meditate on the clear resurrection account in the preceding verses, and talk it over with your pastor. The risen Lord still speaks with full authority through the Scriptures we have received.

question: What is the difference between a sect and a cult?
answer:
In careful Christian usage, a sect is a breakaway religious group that still may confess the essentials of the faith, while a cult is a group whose teachings contradict those essentials, often while claiming biblical authority and centering trust on a human leader or added revelation.

The New Testament word sometimes rendered “sect” simply marked a party or school, including the Pharisees and even the early church as outsiders viewed it (Acts 24:5; Acts 28:22). The same family of language warns against destructive divisions and false teaching that twists the gospel (Galatians 5:20; 2 Peter 2:1). What decides the matter is not a modern label but fidelity to the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3).

Orthodox Christianity is bounded by non-negotiable truths: the Trinity, the hypostatic union (Jesus truly God and truly man), His virgin birth, His penal substitutionary death, His bodily resurrection, and justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone. A movement that denies these, treats extra-biblical words as equal to Scripture, or redirects worship and salvation away from Christ stands outside the Christian faith, whatever name it bears (1 John 4:1-3; Galatians 1:6-9).

If a particular group concerns you, set the popular labels aside and read its official statements on Jesus and salvation next to the Gospel of John and the letters of Paul, ideally with a mature pastor who will help you test everything by Scripture (Acts 17:11). Love the people, pray for their eyes to be opened, and hold fast to Christ, who alone is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6).

question: Is "name it claim it" teaching biblical?
answer:
No, the "name it and claim it" teaching is not biblical. It treats spoken faith as a force that obligates God to deliver health, wealth, or success on demand, but Scripture presents faith as trusting submission to the sovereign God, who answers prayer according to His wise will rather than our decrees.

Jesus Himself prayed in the garden, "Yet not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39). John writes that our confidence rests here: if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us (1 John 5:14). Verses such as Mark 11:22-24 are often pulled from their setting to support blank-check claims, yet the wider Bible rebukes asking with selfish motives (James 4:3) and shows that even great faith walks through unanswered requests. Paul pleaded three times for relief from his thorn, and the Lord replied that His grace is sufficient and His power is perfected in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). Hebrews 11 honors saints who trusted God amid suffering and, in some cases, did not receive the earthly deliverance they hoped for (Hebrews 11:39).

God is a generous Father who gives good gifts (Matthew 7:11) and supplies our needs according to His riches in Christ (Philippians 4:19), yet He also calls us to godliness with contentment rather than a love of money or guaranteed ease (1 Timothy 6:6-10). The deepest gift is not a formula that bends providence to our words, but Christ Himself, whose death and resurrection have already secured forgiveness and eternal life for all who trust Him.

This week, bring one concrete burden to God in prayer and deliberately add the words "Your will be done" (Matthew 6:10), then ask a mature believer in your church to pray with you as you test this teaching against the whole of Scripture.

question: What does the Bible say about cryonics or cryogenics?
answer:
The Bible does not mention cryonics or cryogenics. Cryogenics, the science of very low temperatures, can serve ordinary medical and research purposes without conflicting with Scripture. Cryonics, the freezing of a legally dead body in hope of later revival, is a modern proposal that must be judged by what Scripture teaches about death and resurrection.

God has appointed that people die once, and after that face judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The body returns to dust (Genesis 3:19; Ecclesiastes 12:7), and the believer’s spirit is at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). That intermediate state is not suspended animation. It is conscious fellowship with Christ while we wait for the resurrection of the body.

Christian hope is bodily resurrection, not reanimation. Christ will return, and God will raise His people with glorified bodies by the power that raised Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:20-23; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44; Philippians 3:20-21). This is God’s act of new creation, not a human repair of the old body. He does not need a preserved corpse in order to keep His promise (John 5:28-29).

Cryonics treats death mainly as a technical problem and the person mainly as tissue that might be restarted. Scripture calls death the wages of sin (Romans 6:23) and teaches that no one can ransom his own life (Psalm 49:7-9). Life beyond death is God’s gift in Christ, not an engineering outcome.

Because the Bible never names this technology, faithful Christians may disagree about the wisdom of the procedure itself, and that disagreement should not divide them (Romans 14:1-4). Some refuse cryonics as a confusing witness and a costly trust in an empty promise. Others would allow it only as a speculative medical step, provided no one trusts it for salvation or resurrection. What Scripture does not permit is shifting confidence from Christ to any human plan for defeating death.

We need a Savior because we have sinned against the holy God and cannot overcome death ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25-26). All who repent and trust in Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone and will share His resurrection life.

If fear of dying or grief is underneath your question, bring that fear to God in your own words. Thank Him for Christ’s victory, ask for a settled hope, and read 1 Corinthians 15 this week with a pastor or a mature believer. Let the church help you face death with resurrection hope rather than with a storage plan.

Turn from sin and from every substitute hope, and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and resurrection life.

What is weighing on you as you ask this?

question: How can I obtain favor from the Lord (Proverbs 8:35)?
answer:
Proverbs 8:35 teaches that whoever finds wisdom finds life and obtains favor from the LORD. This favor is the Lord’s gracious acceptance and delight, not a reward manufactured by human effort.

That wisdom begins with the fear of the LORD (Proverbs 9:10). Scripture further shows that Jesus Christ is the wisdom of God, the one in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (1 Corinthians 1:24; 1 Corinthians 1:30; Colossians 2:3). We do not possess this favor by nature. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and apart from Christ we remain under wrath (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:3). Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross in penal substitutionary atonement, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Through His finished work we are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8-9). Finding Him is how the favor of Proverbs 8:35 is truly obtained.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Read Proverbs 8 and John 1 slowly each day this week, asking God to show you Christ as wisdom, then talk with a pastor or mature believer about what you are seeing. How are you seeking the Lord’s favor in your life right now?

question: Why is solo Christo important?
answer:
Solo Christo means “Christ alone,” and it is important because the Bible teaches that Jesus Christ is the only Savior and the only Mediator through whom sinners are reconciled to a holy God.

God is holy, and we are not. All have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). No priest, saint, sacrament, or personal effort can close that distance. The eternal Son took on our nature, lived in perfect obedience, and died on the cross as a penal substitutionary sacrifice for sinners. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works (Romans 3:24–26; Ephesians 2:8–9).

That is why Scripture will not allow another go-between. There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Only someone who is truly God and truly man can represent both. Jesus said that no one comes to the Father except through Him (John 14:6), and the apostles preached that salvation is found in no other name (Acts 4:12). His priesthood does not need supplementing: by one offering He has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14).

This is both a boundary and a comfort. If you must add another mediator, Christ’s work is treated as incomplete, and your conscience never rests. Because He alone saves, you may draw near to God with confidence, not by proving yourself, but by trusting the Son who loved you and gave Himself for you (Hebrews 4:16; Galatians 2:20).

A simple next step: when you pray this week, come to the Father in Jesus’ name, and thank Him that you need no other priest. Read John 14:6 and Hebrews 7:23–25, and let those words answer the fear that you must add something to Christ.

If you have been trying to reach God another way, turn from that and trust Him. Repent of sin and believe in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and new life.

Where do you most feel the pull to add something beside Christ?

question: Does Genesis chapter 1 literally mean 24 hour days?
answer:
If by “literally” you mean the ordinary sense of the words, Genesis 1 reads as six normal days, each with evening and morning. If you mean that the chapter itself says “twenty-four hours” and settles every question of timing, it does not, and faithful Christians have differed here without denying the faith.

This is a non-essential. The Bible is explicit that God created all things, yet readers who submit to Scripture have disagreed about the length of these days because the Hebrew word yom, “day,” can mean daylight, a full day, or a period of time, and the context must decide. That kind of difference should not be made a test of whether someone belongs to Christ (Romans 14:1–5).

One major view takes the days as ordinary days. Six times the chapter marks a numbered day by evening and morning (Genesis 1:5, 8, 13, 19, 23, 31). The fourth commandment later ties Israel’s week of work and rest to that pattern: “For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested” (Exodus 20:11). On this reading, the light and darkness of the first three days are real, and on the fourth day the sun and moon are appointed to govern that day and night (Genesis 1:14–19). This follows the words in their most immediate sense, and many in the church have read them this way.

Another major view holds that the days need not be solar days of twenty-four hours. The day-age reading takes each day as a long period of God’s creative work. The framework reading sees a deliberate literary order, days of forming and days of filling, meant to display an ordered creation rather than to clock the hours. Both appeal to Genesis 2:4, where “day” covers the whole making of the heavens and the earth. A related reading, often called the analogical-day view, says these are real days in God’s work, like our days in pattern, given so that we would learn work and rest, without requiring an identical length. None of these readings should be heard as turning Genesis into a fable. God really spoke, and creation really came to be.

What must not be surrendered is the doctrine the chapter exists to give. This is creation by God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible (Genesis 1:1; Hebrews 11:3). He made man and woman in His image, and He saw all that He had made, and it was very good (Genesis 1:26–27; Genesis 1:31). Those truths are firmer, and more central to fellowship, than a debate about hours.

Weigh the evening-and-morning refrain and Exodus 20:11 carefully, because that is the most immediate sense of the text. Hold whatever conclusion you reach with a good conscience, and hold the brother who differs with charity. This week, read Genesis 1 aloud and mark every “And God said” and every “evening and morning.” Then ask your pastor, or another mature believer, what this chapter is most concerned to teach you about God, and let that lead you to worship rather than to a quarrel.

question: What is the power of the Holy Spirit?
answer:
The power of the Holy Spirit is the power of God Himself. The Spirit is not an impersonal force or a religious energy we manage. He is the third Person of the Trinity, fully divine, and His power is the sovereign strength of God at work in creation, in redemption, and in the lives of those who belong to Christ.

Scripture shows that power from the start. The Spirit of God was present in creation (Genesis 1:2). The power of the Most High overshadowed Mary in the incarnation of the Son (Luke 1:35). The resurrection of Jesus declared Him the Son of God with power through the Spirit of holiness (Romans 1:4), and the same Spirit who raised Christ now dwells in believers (Romans 8:11).

For the church, Jesus tied the Spirit’s power especially to witness: “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8). That power is not self-confidence. It is God strengthening His people where they are weak. Paul prays that believers would be strengthened with power through the Spirit in the inner being (Ephesians 3:16), and he speaks of overflowing with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit (Romans 15:13). The prophet’s word still stands: “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts” (Zechariah 4:6).

In the life of a Christian, that power is seen most clearly in what only God can do. By effectual calling and regeneration, the Spirit gives new birth and makes a sinner alive to God (John 3:5–8; Titus 3:5). He illumines the truth, convicts of sin, and glorifies Christ rather than drawing attention to Himself (John 16:8–14; 1 Corinthians 2:10–12). In sanctification, He enables believers to put sin to death and to bear the fruit of love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Romans 8:13; Galatians 5:16–23). He also gives courage for service that is marked by power, love, and self-control, not by fear (2 Timothy 1:7).

This power is received by faith in Christ, not manufactured by religious effort, though true faith is never idle (Galatians 3:2–3; Galatians 5:25). A practical step this week is to stop treating holiness or witness as something you must produce alone. Open a short passage such as Acts 1:8 or Galatians 5:16–25, ask the Father to strengthen you by His Spirit for one specific obedience, and then take that next step in dependence on Him.

If you mean a particular struggle, fear in speaking of Christ, weakness against a sin, or confusion about spiritual gifts, say which one, and we can look at it in Scripture together.

question: How is the word to be read and heard, that it may become effectual to salvation?
answer:
The Word becomes effectual to salvation as we attend to it with diligence, preparation, and prayer, receive it with faith and love, lay it up in our hearts, and practice it in our lives. The Holy Spirit alone makes the reading, and especially the preaching, of Scripture an effectual means of grace that convinces sinners and builds believers through faith unto salvation, yet He calls us to come to His Word as hungry hearers rather than careless ones.

Attend with diligence, as the Bereans did when they received the message with eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11). Prepare by putting away moral filth and humbly receiving the implanted word (James 1:21). Pray that God would open your eyes to see wonderful things in His law (Psalm 119:18). Receive it with faith, for the message did not benefit some because it was not united by faith with those who heard (Hebrews 4:2), and with love that treasures the Christ the Word reveals. Lay it up in your heart so you will not sin against Him (Psalm 119:11). Then practice it, for the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom and continues in it will be blessed in what he does, and we are to be doers of the word and not hearers only (James 1:22–25; Luke 11:28).

This week, before you open Scripture or sit under preaching, ask the Lord to make His Word living in you, then choose one clear truth to obey before the day ends. If you lack a church where the Word is faithfully preached, seek one so that hearing becomes a regular means of grace in your life.

question: What is millennialism?
answer:
Millennialism is the Christian teaching about the millennium, the thousand-year reign described in Revelation 20:1-6. It belongs to eschatology, the study of last things, and concerns how that reign relates to Christ’s return.

This is a non-essential matter. Faithful Christians may disagree here because Scripture is unmistakable that Jesus will return personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead (Acts 1:11; Revelation 20:11-15), while the precise nature and timing of the thousand years are less explicit. Such differences should not divide brothers and sisters (Romans 14:1-5).

Three historic views have long been held in the church:

- Premillennialism teaches that Christ returns before a future thousand-year reign on earth. Some expect a more literal, sequential kingdom after His coming; others look for that future reign without a detailed dispensational timeline.
- Amillennialism teaches that the thousand years symbolize the present age, in which the risen Christ reigns from heaven and Satan is restrained, until the final return and judgment.
- Postmillennialism teaches that the gospel will prosper over a long era, often called a millennium, and that Christ returns after that period of widespread faithfulness.

Whatever reading a believer holds, the shared hope is the same: the Lord who died and rose will come, evil will be judged, and God will make all things new (Revelation 21:1-5). A wise next step is to read Revelation 19-21 slowly in one sitting, then talk it through with your pastor, holding your conclusion with conviction and charity toward those who differ.

question: What does the Bible say about war?
answer:
The Bible treats war as a grievous fruit of human sin, not as a good in itself, while also teaching that God remains sovereign over nations and that civil rulers may use force to restrain evil.

In the Old Testament, some wars were unique acts of divine judgment under God’s direct command, especially the conquest of Canaan. Scripture frames those campaigns as judgment on persistent wickedness, not as a reward for Israel’s virtue or a template for later empires (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5). Israel was also given limits, including exemptions from service, offers of peace to distant cities, and a ban on needlessly destroying fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20:5–20). The same Scriptures look beyond the battlefield: the Lord “makes wars cease to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 46:9), and the prophets foresee nations beating “swords into plowshares” (Isaiah 2:4).

In the New Testament, Jesus blesses peacemakers and commands love of enemies in personal life (Matthew 5:9; Matthew 5:44). He told Peter to put the sword away when Peter tried to defend Him by force (Matthew 26:52), and He said His kingdom is not advanced the way earthly kingdoms are (John 18:36). When He said He came to bring a sword, He was speaking of division over allegiance to Him, not of a military policy (Matthew 10:34–36). At the same time, John the Baptist did not tell soldiers to desert, but to refuse extortion and be content with their wages (Luke 3:14). Paul says governing authorities are God’s servants and do not “carry the sword in vain” (Romans 13:4), while also commanding, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone,” and leaving vengeance to the Lord (Romans 12:18–19).

Faithful Christians have long disagreed here, and this disagreement does not decide whether someone belongs to Christ. Scripture is clear that murder, cruelty, and private revenge are sin, yet it does not hand the church a complete modern foreign policy, so believers weigh the same texts with different emphases.

One historic view is just war. On this reading, public force may be morally permissible only under strict limits: lawful authority, a just cause such as defense against grave evil, right intention, and restraint that refuses needless destruction. This view leans on the state’s God-given sword and on the difference between personal revenge and public justice (Genesis 9:6; Romans 13:1–4).

Another historic view is Christian pacifism. On this reading, followers of Jesus should not kill even in war, because the Sermon on the Mount and the way of the cross call the church to suffer evil rather than shed blood (Matthew 5:38–44). Mennonite and other Anabaptist churches have carried this witness with sincerity for centuries.

Neither view should be treated as the only path required of every Christian. In a matter of conscience such as military service, Romans 14 calls us not to despise a brother or sister who fears the Lord and is seeking to obey Him.

If this question is pressing on your own life, bring it to God in prayer, search these passages, and talk with your pastors before you act. Pray for rulers and for peace among nations (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Refuse private vengeance. And if news of war has left you angry or afraid, do not carry that alone. Ask a mature believer to pray with you, for “the prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail” (James 5:16).

Our final hope is not a flawless human army. It is Jesus, the Prince of Peace, whose cross reconciles sinners to God, and who will return to judge evil and make all things new (Isaiah 9:6; Colossians 1:20; Revelation 21:4).

Are you asking because of a hard passage, a conscience question about serving, or the weight of war in the news?

question: Are there errors in the Qur'an (Koran)?
answer:
Christians believe the Qur'an contains serious errors, especially where it contradicts the Bible’s testimony about Jesus Christ. The Bible presents Him as truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners, buried, and raised bodily from the dead. Those claims are not minor differences. They are the heart of the Gospel.

Many Muslims sincerely hold that the Qur'an is the flawless final word of God and that earlier Scriptures were corrupted. That conviction is understandable if one begins from the Qur'an’s own claims, and it is often held with real devotion. The Bible, however, presents itself as the inspired Word of God (2 Timothy 3:16). Jesus treated the Scriptures as enduring and unbroken (Matthew 5:17-18). The New Testament documents come from the apostolic circle, centuries before Islam, and they record what eyewitnesses proclaimed.

A central conflict is the cross. The Qur'an denies that Jesus was crucified. Scripture says He was. “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). The Gospels describe His death in plain historical detail (Mark 15:22-37; John 19:16-30). This matters because His death is penal substitution: the righteous one bearing the penalty of sinners so that God might be just and the justifier of those who trust Him (Romans 5:8-10; 2 Corinthians 5:21). Removing the cross removes the means of reconciliation.

Scripture also teaches that Jesus is the eternal Son, the Word who was with God and was God, and who became flesh (John 1:1, 14). In Him all the fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). Christians call this the hypostatic union: one person with two natures, truly divine and truly human. The Qur'an rejects that witness.

God is holy. Every person has sinned and falls short of His glory (Romans 3:23). The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). Jesus lived without sin, died on the cross in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He is Lord. Salvation is not by works. It is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9). He alone is the mediator (John 14:6; Acts 4:12).

If you are seeking what is true, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly and bring your questions to God in prayer. He receives those who seek Him.

What led you to ask about the Qur'an? I would be glad to hear and to keep pointing to what Scripture says about Jesus.

question: What is the spiritual significance to a déjà vu experience?
answer:
The Bible does not assign any specific spiritual significance to a déjà vu experience. That sudden sense that a new moment has already happened is never named in Scripture as a revelation, omen, or sign from God.

This is a non-essential matter, where faithful Christians may differ because Scripture gives principles for testing experiences rather than a detailed explanation of every sensation (Romans 14:5). One careful view treats déjà vu as an ordinary feature of memory and attention, not as special revelation, since God has spoken fully in His Son and the Scriptures are sufficient for faith and life (Hebrews 1:1–2; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). Another view, more common in experiential circles, may receive the moment as a prompt to pray or notice God’s providence, while still refusing to treat the feeling itself as a word from the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5:21).

I would not search for a hidden spiritual code in it. The Lord warns against omens (Deuteronomy 18:10–12) and against leaning on our own understanding (Proverbs 3:5–6), and the heart can deceive us (Jeremiah 17:9). Déjà vu also does not support past lives. People die once and afterward face judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Our hope is not a recycled existence but resurrection life through Christ.

If the experience leaves you uneasy, bring it to God in your own words, asking for wisdom, peace, and a deeper love for His Word, and mention it to a pastor or mature believer. A simple next step is to read Psalm 139:1–6 this week and thank the Lord that He knows your path even when a moment feels strangely familiar. I do not offer medical advice; if these episodes are frequent or come with other symptoms, please speak with a qualified physician.

question: What are the four beasts in Daniel chapter 7?
answer:
The four beasts in Daniel chapter 7 are four successive kingdoms, shown to Daniel in a night vision and explained in the chapter itself as four kings that arise from the earth (Daniel 7:3; Daniel 7:17). They come up out of the sea, a familiar picture of restless, threatening nations (Daniel 7:2–3).

Read with the statue in Daniel 2 and the ram and goat in Daniel 8, they are these kingdoms:

The first is like a lion with eagle’s wings. Its wings are plucked off, it is made to stand like a man, and a man’s heart is given to it (Daniel 7:4). This is Babylon, the proud and swift empire Daniel served, later humbled, as Nebuchadnezzar himself was.

The second is like a bear, raised up on one side, with three ribs in its mouth, and told to devour much flesh (Daniel 7:5). This is Medo-Persia, lopsided in power, with Persia dominant, and hungry to conquer.

The third is like a leopard with four wings and four heads, and dominion is given to it (Daniel 7:6). This is Greece. Alexander’s conquests were swift, and after his death the empire split into four, which Daniel 8 pictures as the four horns of the goat (Daniel 8:8; Daniel 8:21–22).

The fourth is different from the rest: dreadful, terrifying, and exceedingly strong, with great iron teeth, crushing and trampling what is left, and bearing ten horns (Daniel 7:7; Daniel 7:23). This is Rome, matching the iron kingdom that shatters the others in Nebuchadnezzar’s dream (Daniel 2:40).

A little horn then rises among the ten, speaking great things and wearing out the saints for a limited time (Daniel 7:8; Daniel 7:24–25). Faithful Christians have differed on that figure, because the text is more compressed there than in the sequence of kingdoms. Some see a persecuting power within the Roman world, others the final opponent of God’s people before Christ judges openly. That is a non-essential matter of interpretive emphasis, not a test of fellowship (Romans 14:1–5). What the chapter itself makes plain is that the court sits, the horn is destroyed, and the kingdom is given to the saints of the Most High (Daniel 7:26–27).

The vision does not end with the beasts. The Ancient of Days takes His seat, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14). Jesus applied that title and that coming to Himself (Mark 14:62). Human empires rise, crush, and fall under God’s hand. His messianic kingdom does not.

Daniel was deeply troubled by what he saw (Daniel 7:15; Daniel 7:28), so if these images feel heavy, you are in good company. This week, read Daniel 7 slowly and notice where your eyes rest, on the beasts or on the throne. When the news feels like another beast rising, bring that fear to the Lord in your own words, and ask Him to fix your hope on the kingdom that will not pass away.

question: What did Paul mean when he said, “I die daily” in 1 Corinthians 15:31?
answer:
Paul meant that he lived every day under the real threat of physical death because of his ministry for Christ. In 1 Corinthians 15 he is defending the bodily resurrection, and he asks why he would keep endangering his life if the dead are not raised: “I die every day! I affirm this, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:31). The surrounding verses make the sense plain. He speaks of endangering himself every hour and of fighting wild beasts at Ephesus (1 Corinthians 15:30, 32), language that points to mortal peril rather than a mere figure of speech about inner struggle.

The present-tense wording stresses an ongoing condition. Paul’s later catalog of beatings, shipwrecks, and constant danger shows he was not exaggerating (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). In the Greco-Roman setting, open loyalty to a crucified Lord often brought violence, so his daily dying was the ordinary cost of apostolic witness. That cost is rational only because Christ has been raised and those who belong to him will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:20–22). Scripture does call believers to die to sin and self in other places (Romans 6:11; Galatians 2:20; Luke 9:23), yet that is not the primary point here. The argument stands or falls with the historical, bodily resurrection.

This week, name one concrete fear (loss of comfort, reputation, or safety) that keeps you from obedient witness, and bring that specific fear to God in prayer, resting in the promise that labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

question: What does the Bible say about motivation?
answer:
The Bible teaches that God weighs not only what we do, but why we do it. Right motivation is a matter of the heart: love for God, love for neighbor, and a desire for His glory, rather than self-display or selfish gain.

The Lord looks at the heart. When Samuel was inclined to judge by outward appearance, God said that people look on the outside, but the Lord looks on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). Our ways can seem pure in our own eyes, yet the Lord weighs the motives (Proverbs 16:2). The heart is deceitful, and still the Lord searches it and tests it (Jeremiah 17:9–10). His Word discerns the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Hebrews 4:12).

Scripture also exposes motives that God rejects. Jesus warns against practicing righteousness in order to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1–6). Some prayers fail because they are driven by selfish desire (James 4:3). Paul refuses selfish ambition and people-pleasing, and calls believers to seek God’s approval and to count others as more significant than themselves (Galatians 1:10; Philippians 2:3–4). Even costly religious activity, if it lacks love, gains nothing (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

The positive aim is love and worship. The great commandments are to love God with all the heart and to love one’s neighbor as oneself (Matthew 22:37–39). Ordinary life, work, eating, and drinking included, is to be done to the glory of God and as service to the Lord, not merely to impress people (1 Corinthians 10:31; Colossians 3:23–24). The love of Christ is meant to control us, so that we no longer live for ourselves but for Him who died and rose again (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). We love because He first loved us (1 John 4:19).

This is not a call to manufacture pure motives by sheer effort. In regeneration God gives a new heart, and in sanctification the Spirit works in us both to will and to work for His good pleasure (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Philippians 2:13). Mixed motives remain a lifelong battle, which is why the godly ask God to search the heart (Psalm 139:23–24). Obedience still matters. Faith that never acts is dead (James 2:17). But God wants the act and the aim together.

Before your next significant choice this week, pause and ask two questions before the Lord: “Am I doing this to be seen, or to honor Christ?” and “Does this love my neighbor, or mainly serve me?” Then read Colossians 3:23–24, speak to God in your own words about what you find, and if the motive is tangled, tell a mature believer in your church so you are not left alone with a deceitful heart.

question: What does it mean to put off the old man (Ephesians 4:22)?
answer:
To put off the old man means to lay aside the person you were apart from Christ, the former way of life ruled by deceitful desires, and to live as the new self God creates in union with Jesus.

Paul is not describing an elderly man, and he is not speaking only to males. "Old man" is the older English rendering of the Greek *palaios anthropos*, the old self, or old humanity. In Ephesians 4:20–24, believers were taught in Jesus "to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires," to be renewed in the spirit of their minds, and to put on the new self, "created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:22–24). The picture is as plain as taking off a ruined garment. The old self is the whole pattern of life inherited in Adam, not a second person who keeps living inside the Christian as an equal rival.

Scripture holds two things together, and both belong to sanctification. The old self was crucified with Christ so that sin's dominion would be broken (Romans 6:6). That decisive break, often called definitive sanctification, comes by union with Christ in His death and resurrection. In daily life you are still called to refuse the old practices and put on the new, because the new self is also being renewed (Colossians 3:9–10). That ongoing work is progressive sanctification. What remains in the believer is not the old man as a rival self, but indwelling sin, which you must put to death by the Spirit (Romans 8:13). The old life is still "being corrupted by its deceitful desires," so returning to it is a return to a way of life that lies and decays.

The power for this is not self-reform. The new self is God's creation, in true righteousness and holiness, because Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. If you are in Him, you put off the old man by repentance and faith, not by pretending the command is already finished in your habits. If you have never trusted Him, no amount of moral effort can produce this new self. Turn from sin and trust Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, take Ephesians 4:25–32 as your map. Put off one concrete work of the old life, whether false speech, nursed anger, greed, or corrupting talk, and put on the opposite grace in its place. Read those verses slowly, ask the Lord to renew your mind, and tell a mature believer in your church what you are laying down so you do not fight alone.

What part of the old pattern feels hardest to lay down right now?

question: What is a freethinker?
answer:
A freethinker is someone who seeks to form beliefs by reason and evidence alone, setting aside religious authority, tradition, or divine revelation. The term took hold in the early 1700s among writers who urged people to examine Christian claims independently rather than submit to Scripture or the church.

God made us thinking creatures and invites us to use our minds. He says, “Come now, let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18, BSB), and “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10, BSB). At the same time, Scripture teaches that sin darkens human understanding, sometimes called the noetic effects of the fall, so that people can become “futile in their thinking” even while claiming to be wise (Romans 1:21–22, BSB; see also Ephesians 4:17–18). True freedom is not independence from the Creator but being set free by the truth of Christ. Jesus said, “If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32, BSB).

In practice that means taking every thought captive to obey Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5) and letting the inspired Word test what reason proposes. If you are weighing these questions, a steady next step is to read the Gospel of John with an open Bible, asking God to show you what real freedom is.

question: What is an overseer in the church?
answer:
An overseer in the church is a qualified man whom the Holy Spirit appoints to watch over, shepherd, and teach a local congregation. Scripture uses overseer, elder, and pastor for this one office, not for three separate ranks.

The word behind overseer means one who looks upon and cares for what has been entrusted to him. When Paul gathered the elders of Ephesus, he said, "Keep watch over yourselves and the entire flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which He purchased with His own blood" (Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28). Peter charges those same elders to shepherd God's flock, watching over them willingly and eagerly (1 Peter 5:1–2). Titus moves from appointing elders to the character of an overseer without changing the office (Titus 1:5–7), and Paul greets the overseers and deacons of one church (Philippians 1:1).

The work is a noble task, and the marks are plain. An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, hospitable, able to teach, not greedy, and a man who manages his own household well (1 Timothy 3:1–7). He must hold firmly to the trustworthy word, so that he can encourage believers and refute those who contradict sound doctrine (Titus 1:9). His authority is real, yet it is a shepherd's authority under Christ, the chief Shepherd, and he will give an account for souls (1 Peter 5:2–4; Hebrews 13:17).

Faithful Christians have not all arranged this office in the same way. Many in the episcopal tradition hold that the overseer, or bishop, is a distinct office above local presbyters, pointing to the early church's concern for visible unity and to the broader ministry of men such as Timothy and Titus. I hold, as one faithful reading within historic Christianity, that overseer and elder name the same local office, ordinarily shared by a plurality of qualified men who lead the congregation under Christ's word.

If God has given you such shepherds, pray for them and receive their biblical care with gratitude, for they watch over your soul. If you aspire to this work, bring that desire to your elders, and let 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 search your life, your home, and your doctrine.

question: Someone gave me a prophetic word/prophesied over me. What is the interpretation?
answer:
It is understandable to want a clear reading when someone has spoken a prophetic word over you, and that can stir both hope and uncertainty. I have not been given the words themselves, so I cannot interpret a message I have not heard.

Faithful Christians disagree about whether the New Testament gift of prophecy continues today. Continuationists argue, with real care for Scripture, that the Spirit may still give fallible words of encouragement, exhortation, and consolation for the building up of the church, as Paul describes in 1 Corinthians 14:3. I hold, as one faithful option within historic Christianity, that the foundational revelatory gift of prophecy ceased with the apostolic age (Ephesians 2:20), so a modern “prophetic word” is not new revelation and must never be set beside the Bible.

Whatever was spoken, the safe path is the same. Scripture tells us not to despise prophetic speech, yet also to test everything and hold fast only what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). A word from God will agree with the gospel of Christ, will not contradict the written Word, and will not draw you away from obedience to the Lord (Deuteronomy 13:1–4; 1 John 4:1). The Bereans were commended because they examined even apostolic preaching by the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). Warm, personal language can be sincere human encouragement without being divine revelation, and your identity and decisions should rest on Christ in Scripture, not on an untested impression.

Write the word down exactly, set it beside the Bible, and ask your pastor or elders to weigh it with you before you change any major course because of it. Pray and ask the Lord for wisdom, trusting the sufficiency of His Word (James 1:5; 2 Timothy 3:16–17). If you paste the exact words, I will help you test them in that light.

question: What is/isn’t a Christian married couple allowed to do, sexually?
answer:
A Christian husband and wife are free to enjoy sexual intimacy with one another as God’s good gift, and they are not free to involve anyone else or to use one another in ways that are coercive, harmful, or sinful.

God joins one man and one woman in marriage, and the two become one flesh (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). Within that covenant the marriage bed is honorable and undefiled (Hebrews 13:4). Husband and wife belong to one another. Each is to give the other the affection due in marriage, and neither is to deprive the other, except by mutual agreement for a time of prayer (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Scripture even invites delight: “May you rejoice in the wife of your youth… may her breasts satisfy you always; may you be captivated by her love forever” (Proverbs 5:18–19). The Song of Solomon celebrates that exclusive joy without embarrassment. Sex in marriage is not a grudging permission. It is part of covenant love.

What God forbids is also plain. Sexual union with anyone outside the marriage is adultery or sexual immorality (Exodus 20:14; 1 Corinthians 6:18; Hebrews 13:4). Pornography is not a marital aid. It trains lust toward other people, often participates in their exploitation, and violates the call to purity of heart (Matthew 5:27–28). Fantasizing about someone else, inviting a third person into the bed in person or on a screen, and any act one spouse experiences as violation are outside the freedom God gives. Coercion, manipulation, humiliation, and intentional harm contradict the command to love your spouse as your own body and to nourish and cherish one another (Ephesians 5:25–29). Love does not demand. Love does not degrade.

Scripture does not publish a list of positions or techniques. Where the Bible is silent, the governing questions are love, mutual consent, honor, and a clear conscience before God. “Everything is permissible for me, but not everything is beneficial. Everything is permissible for me, but I will not be mastered by anything” (1 Corinthians 6:12; see also 1 Corinthians 10:23). If both of you freely agree, if the act does not degrade either of you, if it does not injure the body, and if it can be received with thanksgiving, Christian couples have long understood a wide range of affectionate pleasure as belonging to the one-flesh union. Neither of you may press the other into what cannot be done from faith, “for whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). And neither of you may turn “conscience” into a permanent refusal of ordinary marital affection without honest, patient conversation. Freedom is for serving one another, not for selfishness.

A few pastoral boundaries are worth naming. Frequency and preference will differ. The aim is mutual care, not score-keeping. Pain, fear, or old wounds are not a failure of faith to be forced through. If intimacy is tangled with shame or conflict, talk with a mature pastor or a certified biblical counselor. If the body is hurting, see a medical professional. I cannot give medical advice. If either of you has sinned sexually, the way forward is repentance, not concealment or despair. The blood of Jesus cleanses those who confess (1 John 1:9), and His death and resurrection are enough for sexual sinners who turn to Him.

Set aside an unhurried conversation without accusation. Each of you name what helps you feel loved, safe, and desired, and what you cannot offer with a clear conscience. Then pray, asking the Lord to guard your fidelity and to make your marriage a place of joy and tenderness. If a particular practice is weighing on you, you are welcome to say more.

question: Why is God going to give us a white stone with a new name (Revelation 2:17)?
answer:
In Revelation 2:17 Jesus promises the one who overcomes hidden manna and a white stone inscribed with a new name that only the recipient knows. He gives it so His faithful people are vindicated, welcomed, and known by Him with an intimacy no one else shares.

The words come in the letter to believers in Pergamum, who were under pressure to compromise their loyalty to Christ (Revelation 2:12-17). The overcomer is not a special class who earns heaven by superior effort. It is the person who keeps trusting Jesus, for “everyone born of God overcomes the world” by faith (1 John 5:4-5).

In the Greco-Roman world a small white pebble (the word behind “stone”) could cast a vote of acquittal, or serve as a token admitting someone to a feast or public honor. Christians have long heard both notes in the promise, and both belong to the gospel. One is justification: God declares His people righteous because of Christ, not because their record is clean. The other is welcome: they are given a place in His joy and a share in His victory. You need not treat these as rival explanations. Together they say that guilt is answered and belonging is secure.

The new name continues a pattern God has used all through Scripture. He renamed Abram as Abraham and Simon as Peter, marking covenant love and a changed life (Genesis 17:5; John 1:42). Isaiah said the Lord Himself would bestow a new name on His people (Isaiah 62:2). That this name is known only to the one who receives it means the bond is not a performance for others. It is personal, as private as a name of delight between the Redeemer and the redeemed. John later speaks of names written on the overcomer that tie him to God and to the new Jerusalem (Revelation 3:12). The old names, failure, fear, or labels fixed by other people, do not get the last word.

Hidden manna belongs with the stone. God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness and kept a portion before Him. Jesus is the true bread from heaven who gives life to the world (John 6:31-35). The whole gift flows from His death and resurrection. Those who trust Him are justified, adopted into God’s family, and kept for the day when their identity fully matches what He has already declared.

If some failure still feels like your real name, let this promise steady you. This week, read Revelation 2:12-17 once each morning and bring one specific place of shame or weariness to the Lord in your own words. If you can, read it with a pastor or a mature friend in your church so you do not hold the hope alone.

question: What is the meaning of the strange fire in Leviticus 10:1?
answer:
In Leviticus 10:1, the strange fire was the unauthorized fire that Nadab and Abihu offered before the LORD, contrary to His command. The Hebrew phrase esh zarah describes fire that was foreign or alien to the worship God had appointed.

This took place immediately after the glory of the LORD appeared and fire from Him consumed the offerings on the altar, showing His acceptance of what He had commanded (Leviticus 9:23–24). Aaron’s sons then took their censers, put fire in them, added incense, and presented this strange fire, so fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them (Leviticus 10:1–2). They disregarded the holy instructions for drawing near, including the requirement to take burning coals from the altar before the LORD (Leviticus 16:12). Moses therefore told Aaron that God would be proved holy among those who approach Him and honored before all the people (Leviticus 10:3). The command that follows, forbidding priests to drink wine or strong drink when entering the tent of meeting (Leviticus 10:8–9), may indicate that clouded judgment played a part, yet the text itself centers on their acting apart from what God had commanded.

The passage displays the holiness of God and the danger of treating His worship as something we may invent. One concrete step is to read Hebrews 12:28–29 this week, ask the Lord to search any habit of prayer or gathered worship that rests more on preference than on His Word, and then talk it over with a pastor or mature believer in your church. The severity of this judgment also deepens gratitude for Jesus Christ, the sinless high priest who obeyed perfectly and opened the way into God’s presence by His own blood (Hebrews 9:11–12; Hebrews 10:19–22).

question: Is it possible to sell your soul to the devil?
answer:
No, you cannot sell your soul to the devil in the way stories describe. There is no biblical contract that transfers ownership of your soul to Satan and places you beyond God’s mercy.

Every soul belongs to God the Creator. Scripture says, “Behold, every soul belongs to Me” (Ezekiel 18:4). Satan is a created being who rebelled. He is a liar and a murderer, and he holds people in spiritual bondage through deception and sin (John 8:44; 2 Timothy 2:26; 1 John 5:19). He does not hold a title God must honor, and he cannot purchase what is not for sale.

Jesus warned that a person can forfeit his soul by gaining the world and rejecting God: “What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). That is not a signed bargain with the devil. It is the ruin of unbelief, when someone treasures created things more than the Creator.

It is possible to give yourself over to evil. Occult practices, sorcery, and seeking power from demonic sources are forbidden by God and are real spiritual danger (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Such choices can bring oppression and deeper slavery to sin. They do not, however, create an irreversible sale that Christ cannot break.

We are all sinners, separated from a holy God, and we cannot free ourselves by ritual, vow, or effort. The Son of God appeared to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). Christ died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily, and through that saving work He delivers people from the domain of darkness into His kingdom (Colossians 1:13–14). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by undoing a deal with Satan. His blood is the ransom (1 Peter 1:18–19).

If you fear you have pledged yourself to evil, or if you want to be right with God, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. No past vow or season of darkness is stronger than His mercy when a person truly repents and believes.

Read Colossians 1:13–14 and Acts 26:18, then speak honestly to God, confessing any desire to bargain with darkness and asking for mercy through Christ. If you have practiced occult things, renounce them, remove related objects, and talk with a faithful pastor who can walk with you.

What prompted you to ask this?

question: What does the Bible say about obedience?
answer:
The Bible teaches that obedience is glad, wholehearted submission to God's revealed will, and that for the Christian it is the fruit of saving faith, not the ground of justification.

God, as Creator and Lord, has the right to command His creatures, and He calls His people to fear Him, walk in His ways, and love Him with all the heart (Deuteronomy 10:12-13). In both Testaments, obedience is tied to hearing God's word and responding under His authority. Samuel rebuked Saul because religious activity cannot replace a surrendered heart: obedience is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22). Jesus said, "If you love Me, you will keep My commandments" (John 14:15). Love for Christ and obedience to Christ belong together (1 John 5:3).

The perfectly obedient one is Jesus Christ. He humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). Through His obedience, sinners are made righteous (Romans 5:19). That is the heart of the gospel. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by our works (Romans 3:28; Ephesians 2:8-9). Justification is God's once-for-all declaration that the believer is righteous in Christ, on the basis of His penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection. Yet those who are justified are also created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10). True faith is never barren. It produces obedience (James 2:17; 1 John 2:3-6).

This ongoing change is sanctification. God gives a new heart and puts His Spirit within His people so that they walk in His statutes (Ezekiel 36:26-27). Believers work out their salvation because God is at work in them both to will and to do His good pleasure (Philippians 2:12-13). Christian obedience is not grim legalism and not a way back into slavery. It is the grateful life of those who have been set free from sin's dominion and have become obedient from the heart (Romans 6:17-18).

No Christian obeys perfectly in this life. When you fail, do not hide behind partial compliance or religious activity. Confess the sin, rest again in Christ's finished obedience, and take the next concrete step of faithfulness. This week, name one clear command of Christ you have been resisting, bring that specific area before the Lord in honest prayer, and ask a mature believer in your local church to walk with you in it.

question: What does it mean that God is our refuge and strength and an ever-present help in trouble (Psalm 46:1)?
answer:
God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble, means that the Lord Himself is the safe shelter His people run to, the power that holds them up, and the help already near when distress comes (Psalm 46:1).

In the Hebrew, “refuge” (*machaseh*) is a shelter, and the words behind “ever-present help” say that in troubles He is found to be a help, exceedingly. Psalm 46 does not pretend the world is calm. Mountains slip and nations rage, yet God’s city is not moved, because God is in her midst (Psalm 46:2–5). The song returns to this confession: “The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress” (Psalm 46:7; Psalm 46:11). To be still and know that He is God is not escapism. It is quiet trust under His sovereign rule (Psalm 46:10).

This is God’s covenant nearness, His gracious immanence. He is present everywhere in power, yet here He draws personally near to protect and strengthen those who take shelter in Him (Deuteronomy 33:27; Nahum 1:7). The righteous, those who trust the Lord rather than their own strength, run to His name as to a strong tower and are safe (Proverbs 18:10). That presence comes to its fullness in Jesus Christ, Immanuel, God with us, who entered our trouble, died for our sins, and rose again, so that we may draw near to the throne of grace and receive mercy and help in time of need (Matthew 1:23; Hebrews 4:14–16).

When fear presses in, do not treat God as a last resort. Name the specific trouble before Him today, read Psalm 46 slowly, and ask Him for strength to trust rather than to panic. If the weight is heavy, bring it also to a mature believer or your pastor, for the prayer of a righteous person has great power (James 5:16).

What trouble is weighing on you, and how can I help you bring it to the Lord in the words of this psalm?

question: Should a Christian woman wear a bikini?
answer:
A Christian woman is called to modesty, yet whether a bikini is fitting is a non-essential matter of Christian liberty where faithful believers may disagree. Scripture gives principles of respectable dress and love for others rather than a detailed clothing code, and what appears provocative can vary by culture and setting.

One major view holds that a bikini is immodest in most settings because it leaves the body largely exposed in a way that conflicts with the call for women to adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control (1 Timothy 2:9-10). This approach stresses the duty not to become a stumbling block that stirs lust in others (Matthew 5:28; Romans 14:13).

Another major view maintains that modesty is chiefly a matter of the heart’s motive, so a woman may wear a bikini in limited private contexts under Christian liberty, provided her aim is not to allure and no one is led into sin (Romans 14:1-4; 1 Corinthians 10:31).

Both affirm that our bodies are meant to glorify God (1 Corinthians 6:19-20). The wiser path, when any doubt remains, is to choose greater covering so that attention rests on Christ rather than on the body, reflecting the gentle and quiet spirit that is precious in God’s sight (1 Peter 3:3-4).

Bring the question to the Lord in prayer while reading those passages, then seek concrete counsel from godly older women in your local church who know your setting.

question: Is Christian rap music appropriate?
answer:
Christian rap music is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture gives principles for music that honors God without commanding or forbidding particular genres. 

Some believers hold that Christian rap is appropriate when its lyrics faithfully teach Scripture, exalt Christ, and call hearers to repentance and faith, seeing cultural forms as lawful tools for communicating the gospel, as Paul adapted his approach to reach different people (1 Corinthians 9:19-23). Others urge caution or avoidance, concerned that the style’s cultural associations with pride, sensuality, or rebellion can shape affections in ways that resist the call to be transformed rather than conformed to this world (Romans 12:2; Philippians 4:8). 

In such disputable matters Christian liberty applies: welcome one another without quarreling, each being fully convinced in his own mind before the Lord, and refuse whatever does not proceed from faith (Romans 14:1-6; Romans 14:23). If a song troubles your conscience or stumbles a brother, love requires restraint (1 Corinthians 8:9-13; 1 Corinthians 10:31). 

This week, take one Christian rap track and test its words against Scripture, then ask your church elders whether it stirs holy love for Christ or dulls your zeal, praying for wisdom as you decide.

question: What is a "dark night of the soul"?
answer:
A "dark night of the soul" is a name for a severe season in which God feels absent, prayer feels empty, and former spiritual comforts give no light.

The phrase comes from the sixteenth-century Spanish Carmelite John of the Cross. In his poem and treatise by that title, he described God withdrawing felt consolations so the soul would stop living on spiritual sweetness and be drawn into a deeper, more trusting union with God. Many Christians since, including Protestants who do not adopt his full mystical scheme, have used the words more broadly for prolonged dryness, doubt, or the sense that heaven is silent.

Scripture does not require a mystical stage by that name, and it does not treat desolation as proof of advanced holiness. It does give voice to believers who walk without light. David cries, "How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?" (Psalm 13:1). Another psalm pictures tears as food day and night while the soul thirsts for God (Psalm 42:1-3). Isaiah counsels the one who fears the LORD and walks in darkness to trust in the name of the LORD (Isaiah 50:10). In such hours, faith is not warm feeling. It is taking God at his Word when sight fails (2 Corinthians 5:7).

That darkness is not all one thing. Sometimes it is the Father's refining work in sanctification. Sometimes it is grief, weariness, unconfessed sin, spiritual opposition, or a depression of body and mind. I do not provide medical or psychiatric advice. If the night includes thoughts of harming yourself, contact emergency services now and tell someone you trust. For a longer heaviness, seek your church elders and appropriate medical care together. Love does not romanticize despair.

The hope that holds is Christ himself. Jesus, truly God and truly man, entered a darkness that was not merely felt absence. On the cross he cried, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46), bore the curse our sins deserved (Galatians 3:13), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That penal substitution means the believer's night is never the night of the condemned. Justification is by grace through faith in Christ, not by the brightness of our emotions. God promises never to leave or forsake his people (Hebrews 13:5), and nothing in the dark can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God (Romans 8:38-39).

If you are in such a season, do not wait to feel spiritual before you seek the Lord. Stay near the means of grace. Read Psalm 13 or Psalm 42 slowly, and pray to the Father in your own words, even if the prayer is only an honest cry. Tell a mature believer, and keep gathering with Christ's people rather than withdrawing. The God who hides his face for a time has not forgotten his own.

Would you like help walking through one of those psalms, or thinking about whether this darkness seems spiritual, grievous, or also in need of a pastor and a doctor?

question: What does the Bible say about self-defense?
answer:
The Bible forbids murder and private revenge, and it also treats the protection of life from violent attack as something different from murder. This is not a belief that decides who belongs to Christ.
