The Lord will send His messenger to prepare the way, and the Lord whom they seek will suddenly come to His temple (Malachi 3:1). He will sit as a refiner and judge sorcerers, adulterers, false swearers, and those who oppress the hired worker, the widow, the fatherless, and the sojourner (Malachi 3:2–5).

**Return, and the charge of robbery.** “I the Lord do not change,” He says, and therefore Israel is not consumed (Malachi 3:6). That joins divine immutability to mercy, then calls them to return. Withholding tithes and offerings is named as robbery, and bringing the full tithe is set before that covenant people as a test of trust (Malachi 3:7–12). Christians differ, in liberty of conscience, on how the old-covenant tithe applies under the new covenant. The text still confronts stinginess toward God and calls for trusting, obedient generosity (2 Corinthians 9:6–8).

**A book of remembrance, and the day of the Lord.** Some say it is useless to serve God (Malachi 3:13–15). The Lord hears those who fear Him and records a book of remembrance (Malachi 3:16–18). A day is coming, burning like a furnace against the arrogant, yet for those who fear His name the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings (Malachi 4:1–3). The book ends by calling Israel to remember the law of Moses and by promising Elijah before the great and awesome day of the Lord, to turn the hearts of fathers to children (Malachi 4:4–6).

The New Testament reads that hope as history. The messenger, and the Elijah who prepares the day, is John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah (Malachi 3:1; Malachi 4:5–6; Matthew 11:10; Matthew 11:14; Mark 1:2; Luke 1:17). The Lord who comes to His temple is Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man. He lived in perfect obedience, bore the judgment sinners deserved through penal substitution on the cross, was buried, rose bodily on the third day, and reigns as Lord. Malachi’s sun of righteousness is not a better mood. It is a Person.

Malachi shows a holy God who will not treat polluted worship as harmless, and a people who cannot repair themselves by tighter rituals. Our sin separates us from Him. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Malachi in one sitting and mark every “How?” and “Where?” Then bring one area of half-hearted worship, a strained marriage, your giving, or a hard question about God’s justice before the Lord in your own prayer, remembering that He treasures those who fear His name (Malachi 3:16). If a broken relationship or a heavy doubt is weighing on you, speak with your pastor or a mature believer rather than carrying it alone.

Which section of Malachi would you like to walk through more slowly?

question: What are phylacteries?
answer:
Phylacteries are small leather boxes holding handwritten passages of Scripture, worn by Jewish men on the forehead and the arm during prayer. In Hebrew they are called tefillin.

They arise from the Lord’s command that Israel bind His words as a sign on the hand and as frontlets between the eyes, so that His word would govern both thought and action (Deuteronomy 6:6–8; Deuteronomy 11:18; Exodus 13:9; Exodus 13:16). By the Second Temple period this was practiced literally. Parchment copies of set texts, including the Shema, were placed in the boxes.

Jesus did not reject the Scriptures those boxes contained. He rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for broadening their phylacteries in order to be seen by others (Matthew 23:5). The sin was hypocrisy: outward religious display aimed at human praise, rather than a heart set on obeying God.

For the Christian, the abiding call is not a required leather case, but the word of God treasured inwardly and obeyed outwardly. Read one short passage before the day begins, and let it shape one concrete choice of your hands and one direction of your mind.

question: Who are true worshipers (John 4:23)?
answer:
True worshipers are those who worship the Father in spirit and in truth, the people the Father Himself is seeking (John 4:23–24).

Jesus said this to a Samaritan woman who was fixed on which mountain was the right place to worship. He announced that the hour had come when true worship would no longer be defined by a sacred site, whether Gerizim or Jerusalem, but by a renewed heart and by God’s own revelation (John 4:21–24). “In spirit” means worship that rises from the inner person, made alive by the Holy Spirit, not from mere outward ritual or inherited custom. “In truth” means worship that matches who God is and what He has spoken, centered on Jesus Christ, who is the truth (John 14:6). God is Spirit, so His worshipers must come in that way (John 4:24). Only those born of the Spirit can do this (John 3:5–8). Paul describes the same people as those who worship by the Spirit of God, glory in Christ Jesus, and put no confidence in the flesh (Philippians 3:3).

This is not a call to vague spirituality. It is a call to sincere, Scripture-shaped adoration offered through Christ, the one Mediator. External forms can be useful, but they cannot replace a heart cleansed by His blood and taught by His Word (Hebrews 10:19–22; Romans 12:1).

This week, before you pray or gather with God’s people, pause and ask the Lord to expose any pretense in you. Confess it, then fix your mind on Christ as the Scriptures reveal Him, so your worship is honest rather than habitual. True worship begins when a sinner turns from self-trust and rests in Jesus, who died for our sins and rose bodily on the third day. If you have not yet done so, repent and trust Him alone for forgiveness and new life, and the Spirit will teach you to worship the Father in truth.

What part of worshiping in spirit and in truth do you most want to understand or practice?

question: Book of Obadiah - Bible Survey
answer:
The book of Obadiah is the shortest book in the Old Testament, one prophetic oracle announcing the LORD’s judgment on Edom for pride and violence against Judah, and promising deliverance for God’s people and the coming of His kingdom.

Obadiah, whose name means “servant of the LORD,” received a vision concerning Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob’s brother (Genesis 25:19–34; Genesis 36:1–8). The book names no king and gives no exact date. Some place it in the ninth century BC, when Edom rebelled and raided Judah (2 Kings 8:20–22; 2 Chronicles 21:16–17). Others place it after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Edom rejoiced over Judah’s ruin (Psalm 137:7). Either setting fits the charge. The message does not depend on settling the date.

The oracle has two movements. First, God announces Edom’s fall (Obadiah 1:1–14). Edom trusted her mountain strongholds and said in her heart that no one could bring her down (Obadiah 1:3–4). The LORD answers that pride has deceived her, and that He Himself will bring her down. The indictment is personal as well as political. Edom stood aloof, gloated, looted, and cut off fugitives “on the day of your brother” (Obadiah 1:10–14). Violence against Jacob was treachery against a brother, and therefore against the God who had chosen Jacob in covenant mercy (Malachi 1:2–5).

Second, the vision widens to the Day of the LORD (Obadiah 1:15–21). What Edom did will be done to her, and the same standard reaches every nation: “As you have done, it will be done to you” (Obadiah 1:15). Yet judgment is not the last word for Zion. On Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy, and the house of Jacob will possess its inheritance (Obadiah 1:17). The book ends with the kingdom belonging to the LORD (Obadiah 1:21).

Obadiah therefore teaches divine justice and covenant faithfulness together. Pride is self-deception. Security built on height, wealth, or alliances cannot stand when God rises to judge. At the same time, the LORD does not abandon the people He has chosen. The promise that the kingdom is the LORD’s reaches beyond Edom’s historical collapse to the reign of Christ, the Son of David, who will judge the nations and gather His people (Matthew 25:31–32; Revelation 11:15).

A practical step: read all twenty-one verses in one sitting this week. Then ask the Lord to expose any quiet pleasure you take in a rival’s trouble, and to set your hope on the King whose kingdom cannot be shaken (Obadiah 1:3–4; Obadiah 1:12; Obadiah 1:21).

question: What does it mean to gain the whole world but lose your soul?
answer:
To gain the whole world but lose your soul means that every earthly prize, wealth, status, pleasure, and power, is an empty gain if a person forfeits eternal life with God and stands under His just judgment.

Jesus asked this while calling His disciples to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him (Mark 8:34–37; Matthew 16:24–26; Luke 9:23–25). In that setting, “the world” is the sum of temporal advantage, and “soul” (the Greek word psychē) is one’s true life before God, the self that will face judgment. No fortune can serve as a ransom for that life. The saying exposes the bankruptcy of securing what perishes while neglecting the only Savior.

This is not a call to despise God’s good gifts. It warns that those gifts become idols when they replace Christ. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), and the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord (Romans 6:23). Jesus, truly God and truly man, died on the cross in penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by gaining the world or by any work we do (Ephesians 2:8–9).

This week, name one pursuit, career, money, reputation, or comfort, that has been competing with Christ, and bring it to Him in honest prayer, asking Him to reorder your loves in light of Mark 8:34–37.

If you have been measuring life by what you can gain, hear the good news. Christ died and rose so that sinners might be forgiven and kept forever. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What is one area of your life where this question feels most pressing right now?

question: Why did God send the flood when He knew sin would continue after the flood?
answer:
It is understandable to wonder why God would send the flood when He already knew sin would continue, since the judgment can appear, from our limited view, not to have cured the human heart. The Bible teaches that God sent the flood because the wickedness of man was great on the earth, every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually, and the earth was filled with violence, so the holy and just God determined to blot out that generation (Genesis 6:5-7; Genesis 6:11-13).

He acted in mercy at the same time, for Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD and was preserved with his household as a preacher of righteousness (Genesis 6:8-9; 2 Peter 2:5). After the waters receded, God Himself declared that the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth, yet He covenanted never again to destroy all flesh in that manner (Genesis 8:21-22; Genesis 9:11-17). The flood therefore judged an overflowing corruption and restrained evil for a season. It did not remove original sin, which entered through Adam and remains in every person (Romans 5:12).

God’s complete knowledge of what would follow does not make the verdict unjust or pointless. He declares the end from the beginning and works all things according to the counsel of His will, even while the text shows Him grieving over the sin He condemned (Isaiah 46:10; Ephesians 1:11; Genesis 6:6). In wisdom the judgment upheld His holiness, displayed His wrath against evil, and guarded the line of promise leading to the Savior (Genesis 3:15).

The same history warns and invites. As the days of Noah were, so will be the coming of the Son of Man, and the present world is stored up for judgment (Matthew 24:37-39; 2 Peter 3:5-7). Yet Noah’s rescue through the ark pictures salvation by grace: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, so that sinners might be justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 1 Peter 3:18-21; Romans 3:23-26). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who bore the judgment we deserve, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Genesis 6-9 slowly and ask God to impress on you both the weight of sin and the greatness of His mercy, then talk over what you see with your pastor or a mature believer. What part of the flood account most stirs worship in you, or what further question does it raise?

question: Should a church tithe 10% of the offerings it receives?
answer:
Scripture does not require a church to give away 10 percent of the offerings it receives. This is a non-essential matter of stewardship on which faithful Christians may disagree, because the New Testament gives principles of generosity and accountable oversight rather than a fixed percentage for congregational spending.

The old covenant tithe supported the Levitical priesthood and temple service (Numbers 18:21-24). That order has been fulfilled in Jesus Christ, our great high priest, who offered one sacrifice for sins forever (Hebrews 7:23-28; Hebrews 10:11-14). Churches are therefore called to grace-shaped generosity, not to a renewed legal tithe.

Some churches freely set aside 10 percent, or another chosen share, of their receipts for missions and gospel partnerships beyond their own walls. They want outward mission to remain a real priority, and they draw encouragement from churches that supported Paul (Philippians 4:15-16) and from the call to aid workers for the truth (3 John 5-8).

Other churches do not practice a church tithe. They place the whole of the offerings under elder leadership and congregational accountability, honoring those who labor in the Word (1 Timothy 5:17-18; Galatians 6:6), caring for practical needs (Acts 6:1-3), and giving cheerfully to wider gospel work as God supplies (2 Corinthians 9:6-7).

In matters God has not commanded, each church should act in faith and refuse to bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5). A missions percentage can be a healthy voluntary habit. It should not be taught as a rule Scripture itself imposes. What the Lord requires is that every gift be handled as a sacred trust for Christ’s glory and the good of souls (1 Corinthians 4:2).

If this question is live in your congregation, ask your elders to explain how the budget serves the ministry of the Word, the care of the saints, and the spread of the gospel, and pray with them for faithful stewardship.

question: Easter Bible reading plan
answer:
A fruitful Easter reading plan walks with Jesus through his final week, so that his cross and bodily resurrection fill your mind and worship before the day itself arrives. These seven readings can begin on Palm Sunday or simply fill the week before Easter. Faithful churches sometimes order the midweek scenes a little differently, and that does not matter. What matters is attending to Christ.

**Day 1: The King comes lowly.** Read Matthew 21:1–11. Jesus enters Jerusalem as the promised King, yet he comes gentle and mounted on a donkey, to save rather than to grasp an earthly throne.

**Day 2: True worship.** Read Mark 11:15–19. Jesus drives out what has turned the temple into a marketplace, because God will not share his holiness with empty religious traffic.

**Day 3: Love that stoops.** Read John 13:1–17. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus washes his disciples’ feet. The love that kneels here is the same love that will soon be nailed to a cross.

**Day 4: Surrender in the garden.** Read Matthew 26:36–46. In Gethsemane, Jesus prays in agony and yields to the Father’s will. Redemption will not come by escape, but by obedience unto death.

**Day 5: The cross.** Read John 19:16–30. Jesus is crucified, and he cries, “It is finished,” before giving up his spirit. This is penal substitution: the Righteous One bears the judgment sinners deserve. The New Testament reads his death as the fulfillment of the suffering Servant, who was pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 5:8; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

**Day 6: Dead and buried.** Read Matthew 27:57–66. Joseph lays Jesus in a tomb, and the tomb is sealed. The burial matters. Jesus truly died, and the promise seemed, for a day, to lie in silence.

**Day 7: He is risen.** Read Matthew 28:1–10; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8; Romans 4:25. The tomb is empty, and the risen Christ appears to his own. His bodily resurrection is not a symbol. It is the historical victory over sin and death, and it is bound up with our justification: he was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

Here is a simple way to use the plan. Set one steady time each day, read the passage slowly, write one sentence about what it shows you of Christ, and then pray to God in your own words, confessing sin, thanking him for the cross, and asking for a living hope. If you can, ask a mature believer in your church to pray with you through the week, for “the prayer of a righteous man has great power as it is working” (James 5:16). Let these readings also prepare you to gather with God’s people for Good Friday and Easter, if your church meets.

We need this Savior because we are sinners, separated from the holy God and unable to rescue ourselves. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. If you have never trusted him, or if your love has grown cold, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What do you most want these readings to do in you this Easter?

question: What is ignosticism? What is an ignostic?
answer:
Ignosticism, sometimes called theological noncognitivism, is the view that the question of God’s existence cannot be meaningfully asked or answered until the word “God” is given a coherent definition. An ignostic is a person who holds that talk of God lacks clear content and therefore suspends judgment rather than affirming or denying that God exists.

The Bible teaches that God is knowable because He has revealed Himself. This is the doctrine of revelation: through general revelation in the created order and special revelation in Scripture, God discloses His eternal power, divine nature, and personal character, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20; Hebrews 1:1-2). Exodus 34:6-7 shows God proclaiming His own name and attributes, giving the term real content rather than leaving it empty.

A concrete way to weigh the claim is to place that biblical self-description beside the objection and ask whether it supplies the definition an ignostic says is missing.

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath?
answer:
Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath means that He possesses divine authority over the Sabbath as the eternal Son who gave the commandment and who fulfills its promise of rest in Himself.

When Pharisees accused His disciples of unlawful work for picking grain, Jesus answered that the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath, and then declared, "The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath" (Matthew 12:8; Mark 2:27-28; Luke 6:5). The Sabbath belongs to the Lord God who instituted it (Exodus 20:8-11). By claiming this title, drawn from the dominion given to one like a son of man in Daniel 7:13-14, Jesus identifies Himself as equal with the Father. That claim belongs to the hypostatic union: He is truly God and truly man in one person, and therefore Lord over every covenant sign He Himself ordained.

The Sabbath was a gift of rest and a sign pointing forward to something greater (Exodus 31:13). Jesus is that greater reality. He invites the weary, "Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). Hebrews 4:9-10 shows that a Sabbath rest remains for God's people, and those who enter it rest from their own works just as God rested from His. Our sin leaves us restless and unable to earn God's favor by any law-keeping, including Sabbath rules. Jesus, the Lord of the Sabbath, lived without sin, died on the cross in penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and the true rest your soul needs. This week, read Mark 2:23-28 slowly and bring to God in prayer one place where you are still striving in your own strength instead of resting in His finished work.

How has the idea of rest in Christ met you, or challenged you, in ordinary days?

question: What does it mean that Jesus Christ conquered death?
answer:
Jesus Christ conquered death by His sacrificial death on the cross and His bodily resurrection on the third day, breaking death’s dominion so that all who trust in Him share His victory over the grave.

In the first-century world, death was an unbreakable tyrant that held people in lifelong fear. Yet because Jesus is truly God and truly man, He entered death and overcame it. Hebrews 2:14-15 teaches that through death He destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and delivered those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery. Romans 6:9 declares that Christ, having been raised from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over Him. His resurrection is the firstfruits guaranteeing the future resurrection of His people (1 Corinthians 15:20-23).

This victory meets our real condition. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), and the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). On the cross Christ bore that penalty in our place by penal substitution, and the empty tomb confirms the payment was accepted. Death is swallowed up in victory, and God gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:54-57). He holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18) and is the resurrection and the life for everyone who believes (John 11:25-26). Those justified by grace through faith alone therefore need not face death as final defeat.

If you have not yet repented of your sin and trusted in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, I invite you to do so for forgiveness and eternal life. He alone is the mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5; John 14:6).

A concrete step is to read John 11 and 1 Corinthians 15 this week, asking God to make the reality of Christ’s triumph clear to your own heart.

How does the truth that Jesus conquered death meet any fear or hope you are carrying?

question: What are the books of the Bible? What does it mean that the Bible is composed of different books?
answer:
The Bible consists of 66 books, 39 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New Testament, which together are the inspired Word of God. That it is composed of different books means it is a canon, a recognized collection of writings from many human authors, centuries, and literary forms, yet one Holy Scripture with God as its ultimate Author.

**Old Testament (39 books)**

- Law: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy
- History: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther
- Poetry and wisdom: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Solomon
- Major Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Ezekiel, Daniel
- Minor Prophets: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi

**New Testament (27 books)**

- Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John
- History: Acts
- Letters of Paul: Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon
- General letters: Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude
- Apocalypse: Revelation

The English word "Bible" comes from the Greek *biblia*, which simply means "books." These books were written over many centuries by roughly forty human authors, in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek. They include law, history, poetry, prophecy, gospel, letter, and apocalypse. In the ancient Hebrew arrangement, some writings now counted separately, such as Samuel, Kings, and the twelve Minor Prophets, were grouped together, but the content matches the 39 Old Testament books above. The New Testament books were received by the early church as apostolic Scripture.

Different books do not mean competing opinions. Scripture teaches that all Scripture is God-breathed, and that men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Timothy 3:16-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21). The theological term for this is inspiration. God so superintended the writers that their words are His Word, trustworthy in all they affirm. He revealed Himself progressively across history, and that revelation reaches its center in Jesus Christ, to whom the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings bear witness (Luke 24:27; Luke 24:44; Hebrews 1:1-2). So we read each book in its own setting and genre, and we also read every book as part of one story of redemption.

Some churches, including Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches, include additional writings often called the Apocrypha or Deuterocanon. Historic Protestant churches do not receive those books as Scripture, though they can sometimes illuminate the history between the Testaments. The 66 books listed here are the Bible.

If you are beginning, do not try to hold all 66 at once. This week, read one book straight through as a book. The Gospel of John, or a short letter such as Philippians, is a wise start. Ask what the author is saying, how the parts fit, and how the book bears witness to Christ. Then speak to the Lord about what you have read, and if you can, ask a mature believer in your local church to read that same book with you.

question: What is the creation mandate / cultural mandate?
answer:
The creation mandate, also called the cultural mandate, is God's command to humanity to be fruitful and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and rule over the other creatures as those made in His image (Genesis 1:26-28).

This calling flows from the imago Dei and shows that family, work, and developing the earth's potential belong to God's good design from the beginning (Genesis 2:15). Sin corrupted how we carry it out, turning dominion toward exploitation and work toward frustration (Genesis 3:17-19), yet the mandate itself was not canceled. Jesus Christ, the exact image of God and the last Adam, fulfills what Adam failed and redeems a people who now honor God in ordinary callings (Colossians 1:15; 1 Corinthians 15:45; Colossians 3:23-24).

Faithful Christians agree on this biblical foundation, though they differ on how it shapes the church's mission today, largely because Scripture gives less explicit detail on the precise relationship between cultural work and gospel proclamation. One historic view stresses broad cultural transformation under Christ's lordship; another holds that the church's commissioned task is making disciples, while cultural engagement remains a matter of Christian vocation and liberty under God's common grace (Matthew 28:18-20; Romans 14:4-6). This week, take one ordinary responsibility in your work or home and consciously offer it to God as stewardship, asking Him to shape it according to His design rather than mere self-interest.

question: What does it mean that friendship with the world is enmity with God (James 4:4)?
answer:
Friendship with the world is enmity with God because it means giving your heart’s loyalty to the world in its rebellion against God, so that you stand in hostility toward Him rather than in faithful allegiance.

In James 4:4, friendship with the world is hostility toward God, and whoever chooses to be a friend of the world becomes an enemy of God. James is not forbidding ordinary kindness to neighbors, nor is he despising the good creation God made. Here “the world” is the present age as it organizes itself against God, with its cravings, pride, and rival loves (1 John 2:15-17). “Friendship” is an affectionate alliance, not a passing contact. He calls them adulteresses because, like unfaithful Israel in the prophets, they were courting another lover while professing loyalty to God (Jeremiah 3:20). That spiritual adultery is divided worship. You cannot hold two supreme allegiances. “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24).

The verses around it show what this friendship looks like in ordinary life. Quarrels, coveting, and prayers aimed at spending what we receive on our pleasures all flow from desires at war within us (James 4:1-3). Worldliness is not only scandalous public sin. It is also a quiet agreement with the world’s measure of success, comfort, and approval, so that those things steer the heart more than the will of God (Romans 12:2). Christians remain in the world to love people and bear witness, yet we are not of the world (John 17:15-18). The line James draws is allegiance, not isolation.

He does not leave the warning without grace. “But He gives us more grace,” and “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). The way back is not proud self-repair. It is submitting to God, resisting the devil, and drawing near to the God who draws near to the humble (James 4:7-8). Cleanse your hands, purify your heart from double-mindedness, and humble yourself before the Lord (James 4:8-10). This week, ask Him to expose one specific desire where the world’s friendship has been pulling you, confess that to Him in prayer, and bring it to a mature believer or elder who can walk with you in repentance. While we were enemies, God reconciled us through the death of His Son (Romans 5:10), and He still gives grace to those who come low before Him.

Is there a particular desire, relationship, or pressure where this verse is weighing on you?

question: Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart?
answer:
God hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that He might display His power, cause His name to be proclaimed in all the earth, and bring Israel out of slavery under His righteous judgment.

The Lord states this purpose plainly. In Exodus 9:16 He tells Pharaoh that He raised him up “for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth,” a word Paul quotes in Romans 9:17 to show that God has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills (Romans 9:18). Again and again Scripture records that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart (Exodus 4:21; Exodus 7:3; Exodus 9:12; Exodus 10:1; Exodus 10:20; Exodus 10:27; Exodus 14:4; Exodus 14:8; Exodus 14:17) so the signs would multiply and Egypt would know that He is the LORD (Exodus 7:5; Exodus 10:1-2).

Pharaoh also hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:15; Exodus 8:32; Exodus 9:34). He was no innocent man forced into evil. He was a proud, idolatrous king who oppressed God’s people and refused the clear command to let them go. Divine sovereignty and human responsibility stand together. This is judicial hardening: the holy God confirmed a rebel in the stubborn path he had chosen, so that both His justice against sin and His mercy toward Israel would be seen (Romans 1:24-28; Romans 9:18). God is never the author of sin (James 1:13), yet He sovereignly works all things according to the counsel of His will, even the sinful acts of rulers, for His glory and the good of His people (Ephesians 1:11; Genesis 50:20; Acts 4:27-28).

Paul faces the objection that this seems unfair and answers that the Potter has authority over the clay (Romans 9:19-21). The Judge of all the earth does right (Genesis 18:25). This should humble us. Apart from grace every heart is hard toward God (Jeremiah 17:9; Ephesians 2:1-3). If He has opened your heart, it is mercy alone (Romans 9:15-16).

Set aside time this week to read Exodus 9 and Romans 9:14-24 slowly, asking the Lord for reverence before His holiness and gratitude for His mercy, and bring any remaining questions to your pastor. If you sense your own heart resisting Him, do not harden it further. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died on the cross for sinners and rose bodily from the dead, so that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness and life. How does this account of Pharaoh affect the way you see God’s justice and mercy?

question: How should we treat our enemies according to Proverbs 25:21–22?
answer:
According to Proverbs 25:21–22, we should treat our enemies with practical kindness, giving them food when they are hungry and water when they are thirsty.

The passage says, "If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you" (Proverbs 25:21-22). The image of heaping burning coals has been discussed in different ways, yet Paul quotes these words to show that such mercy overcomes evil with good instead of returning injury for injury (Romans 12:20-21). Jesus teaches the same pattern: "But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (Matthew 5:44).

This is grace, unmerited kindness, extended even to those who oppose us. We can offer it because we first received it: while we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son (Romans 5:10). This week, name one person who has acted against you, pray for their good, and look for one concrete way to meet a real need they have, trusting the Lord both for the outcome and for His reward.

question: What does the Bible say about indecision / being indecisive?
answer:
The Bible treats harmful indecision as a divided heart, while it honors careful wisdom that ends in obedient action. James says the person who asks God for wisdom but keeps doubting is “like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind,” and calls him “a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways” (James 1:6–8). Double-mindedness means a soul pulled two ways at once, unwilling to rest its trust in God.

Where God has already spoken, Scripture calls for a clear choice. Elijah asked Israel, “How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow Him” (1 Kings 18:21). Joshua told the people to “choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve” (Joshua 24:15). Jesus said, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). In those places, wavering is not humility. It is a refusal to give the Lord an undivided allegiance.

Not every hard choice is that kind of sin. God commends counsel: plans fail without advisers, but they are established with many counselors (Proverbs 15:22). He also warns against delay that never acts. The one who keeps watching the wind never sows, and the one who keeps studying the clouds never reaps (Ecclesiastes 11:4). Waiting on the Lord in faith is obedience when He has said to wait (Psalm 27:14). Freezing when it is time to act is something else. On matters God has left free, Paul says each believer “should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). Faithful Christians may weigh such choices differently, and Christian liberty means we do not bind consciences where Scripture is silent.

The way through indecision is trust in God’s providence, not a demand for perfect foresight. “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and lean not on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make your paths straight” (Proverbs 3:5–6). “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us” (Deuteronomy 29:29). Obey what is clear. Where Scripture does not decide the matter, pray, seek counsel from mature believers in your church, choose what best honors Christ and loves your neighbor, and then act, saying, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15; Colossians 3:17).

If the real issue is fear of getting it wrong, do not keep rehearsing the options. Ask God for wisdom with a single heart (James 1:5–6), and bring the anxiety to Him in prayer with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6–7). This week, write the decision in one sentence, mark what Scripture already settles, speak with one godly counselor, set a reasonable time to decide, and then walk forward. God instructs and watches over those who look to Him (Psalm 32:8). He is more committed to guiding His children than we are to controlling every outcome.

Is the choice before you a matter of clear obedience, or a freedom where Scripture leaves room for wise judgment?

question: What does it mean that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4)?
answer:
Revelation 21:4 means that in the new heaven and new earth, God himself will personally and finally end every sorrow of his people. He will not merely hush their crying. He will remove every reason for tears.

John hears this in the vision of the consummation, when God dwells with his people and makes all things new (Revelation 21:3–5). The promise echoes Isaiah 25:8, where the Lord swallows up death forever and wipes tears from every face, and it repeats what John has already heard of the Lamb’s flock in Revelation 7:17. The Greek word behind “wipe away” (exaleiphō) can mean to blot out or erase completely, the same kind of word used when the record of our debt is blotted out at the cross (Colossians 2:14). The comfort is total, not partial.

“Every tear” is matched by what follows: no more death, mourning, crying, or pain, “for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4). This is new creation and glorification, the reversal of the curse that entered through sin. It is a real future, given in the vivid language of apocalyptic vision, not a slogan that empties present grief. Tears now are not a failure of faith. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35), and Scripture says God keeps account of his people’s tears (Psalm 56:8). The promise does not shame weeping in this age. It assures us that weeping will not have the last word.

That future belongs to those who are Christ’s, whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life (Revelation 21:27). Death remains the last enemy until he destroys it (1 Corinthians 15:26), and that victory rests on his death for sinners and his bodily resurrection. If grief is heavy, bring it to the Lord in prayer today, and read Revelation 21:1–5 slowly, asking him to steady your hope in what he has promised. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and this coming life with God.

What sorrow, if any, makes this promise feel especially near or especially hard to believe right now?

question: What is the meaning of “there but for the grace of God go I”?
answer:
The phrase “there but for the grace of God go I” means that, apart from God’s undeserved kindness, you would be in the same place as the person you are looking at, whether in sin, shame, suffering, or judgment. It is a confession of humility, not a claim that you are better by nature.

The words are not a Bible verse. They are traditionally linked to John Bradford, a sixteenth-century English Reformer, who, seeing prisoners led to execution, is said to have remarked, “But for the grace of God, there goes John Bradford.” The details of that story are traditional, but the posture it teaches is thoroughly biblical.

Grace is God’s unmerited favor, favor you do not earn and cannot treat as your own achievement. Paul asks, “For who makes you so superior? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). He also warns, “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12). And salvation itself leaves no ground for boasting: “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Jesus pictured this heart in the tax collector who “would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner’” (Luke 18:13). The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other men. This saying belongs with the tax collector.

When you see someone publicly fallen or badly broken, let the words check your pride and stir your compassion. Thank God for the mercy that has held you, pray for that person, and ask Him to keep your own heart soft and watchful.

question: How can we walk in God’s ways (Psalm 128:1)?
answer:
We walk in God’s ways by fearing the LORD and ordering our lives by His Word, through faith in Christ and the power of the Holy Spirit (Psalm 128:1).

Psalm 128:1 ties blessing to two things that belong together: reverent fear of the LORD and a life that follows His paths. In Israel’s covenant life, to fear the LORD and walk in His ways meant loyal obedience to what He had revealed, not a private feeling (Deuteronomy 10:12). That same call meets us in Christ. Jesus said, “If you love Me, you will keep My commandments” (John 14:15). Walking with God is progressive sanctification, the Spirit forming us into Christ’s likeness, not a way to earn God’s favor.

We cannot produce this walk by trying harder. Sin has bent our steps away from God (Romans 3:23). Christ lived the obedience we failed to live, died on the cross for our wandering, and rose bodily so that sinners might be forgiven and made new (Romans 6:4). We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, and those He justifies He also sanctifies. We are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for the good works He prepared for us (Ephesians 2:8–10). If you have never turned from sin to trust Him, that is the first step onto His path. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

For those who already belong to Him, the walk is sustained by the means of grace. Know His ways in Scripture, for His word is a lamp to our feet (Psalm 119:105). Walk by the Spirit, and you will not carry out the desires of the flesh (Galatians 5:16). When you stray, confess it quickly and receive His cleansing (1 John 1:9). Stay near a local church, where the Word, prayer, and the care of God’s people keep your feet from wandering alone. God Himself works in you both to will and to do what pleases Him (Philippians 2:13).

This week, set aside a quiet time each morning. Read a short passage, perhaps a section of Psalm 119 or the Gospel of John, and ask the Lord to show you one concrete step of obedience for that day. Then take that step in dependence on Him, and tell a mature believer in your church so they can encourage you. Pray directly to God about a heart that fears Him, any path you have left, and strength from His Spirit to return.

What part of life feels hardest to bring under His ways right now?

question: What does the Bible say about the ice age?
answer:
The Bible does not mention an ice age. It records that God created the heavens and the earth in six days (Genesis 1:1–31), brought a global flood in the days of Noah (Genesis 6:13–8:19), and promised that cold and heat, summer and winter, would continue as long as the earth endures (Genesis 8:22).

How believers connect those accounts with geological signs of past glaciation is a non-essential matter. Faithful Christians may disagree because Scripture gives limited detail on post-flood climate and because interpreters differ on how special revelation relates to observations of the natural world. In such questions we are to welcome one another without quarreling over opinions (Romans 14:1).

One major view, often called young-earth creationism, understands a single ice age as a relatively brief period after the Flood. Proponents argue that warm oceans and volcanic effects left by the Flood produced heavy snowfall and advancing ice for some centuries before conditions stabilized, and they sometimes link the poetic description of ice and frozen depths in Job 38:29–30 to God’s providence over that world.

A second major view, held by many old-earth creationists, accepts multiple ice ages across long ages. These Christians commonly read the days of Genesis as extended periods or as a literary framework, while still affirming that God truly created all things and that the Flood was a real divine judgment. They do not treat an ice age as a contradiction of Scripture because they see the Bible’s aim as revealing God and His saving purposes rather than supplying a complete geological chronology.

A reading that keeps the creation days as ordinary days and the Flood as global often pairs naturally with a single post-Flood ice age, and many find that this best honors the plain sense of the text while still reckoning with evidence of glaciation. Others reach different conclusions in good conscience. This difference should not divide fellowship where the gospel is held in common.

Whatever view one takes, the Lord is the one who gives snow like wool and then sends His word to melt it (Psalm 147:16–18). A helpful next step is to read Genesis 1–11 slowly this week, noting exactly what the text claims about creation and the Flood, and then talk with your pastor so that wonder at God’s works strengthens unity rather than argument.

question: What is the significance of the city of Nineveh in the Bible?
answer:
Nineveh was the great capital of the Assyrian Empire and, in Scripture, a clear picture of both God’s judgment on violent wickedness and His mercy toward those who repent.

In the ancient Near East, Assyria was feared for cruelty and imperial power, and Nineveh stood at the center of that empire. The Bible first names the city in the table of nations (Genesis 10:11-12). God later sent Jonah to proclaim coming judgment, and when the king and people humbled themselves in repentance, God relented from the disaster He had threatened (Jonah 3:4-10). Jonah’s story therefore displays divine mercy even toward a Gentile city that Israel despised, and it rebukes a narrow spirit that resents God’s compassion.

The prophets also announced Nineveh’s fall. Nahum declared that the Lord would not leave the guilty unpunished and that the city’s bloodshed and oppression would meet justice (Nahum 1:1-3; Nahum 3:1-7). Zephaniah likewise foretold its desolation (Zephaniah 2:13-15). Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, and those oracles were fulfilled.

Jesus treated Nineveh’s repentance as a real historical warning. He said the men of Nineveh would rise at the judgment with His generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and now One greater than Jonah had come (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32). Their response highlights both the hope of mercy for those who turn and the seriousness of rejecting Christ.

When you read Jonah or Nahum, let Nineveh remind you that no person or people is beyond God’s mercy if they truly repent, and that lasting hardness of heart will not escape His justice. A simple next step is to read Jonah 3-4 this week and ask the Lord to give you Jonah’s message without Jonah’s resentment.

question: What is Epicureanism? What did Epicurus teach?
answer:
Epicureanism is the philosophy taught by Epicurus (341–270 BC), who founded a school in Athens called the Garden. He taught that the wise life aims at lasting calm: pleasure understood as freedom from pain and fear, not wild indulgence.

Epicurus was a materialist. He held that the world is made of atoms moving in void, so events are not governed by divine providence. He did not deny that gods exist, but he taught that they live in undisturbed blessedness and do not involve themselves in human affairs. Because of that, he said people should neither fear the gods nor look to them for help.

On ethics, pleasure (*hēdonē*) is the highest good, but Epicurus meant something quieter than the later caricature of “eat, drink, and be merry.” He prized simple food, friendship, and freedom from anxiety (*ataraxia*) and bodily pain (*aponia*). Intense desires, he argued, often create more disturbance than they remove. A short summary later called the fourfold remedy said: do not fear the gods, do not fear death, what is good is easy to obtain, and what is terrible is easy to endure.

On death, Epicurus taught that death is nothing to us. When we exist, death is not present; when death is present, we no longer exist. There is no judgment and no life beyond the grave to dread. Politics and public ambition were generally to be avoided, because they disturb the soul. Friendship, by contrast, was one of the greatest goods.

The New Testament meets this outlook in Athens. “Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also began to engage him in discussion,” because Paul was preaching Jesus and the resurrection (Acts 17:18). Paul’s answer does not treat Epicurus as a fool to mock, but it does reject his core claims. The God who made the world is not distant or uninvolved. He gives life and breath to all, calls everyone to repent, and has set a day to judge the world in righteousness through the man He raised from the dead (Acts 17:24–31). If the dead are not raised, Paul says, then “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” would follow; but Christ has been raised, so death is not the end (1 Corinthians 15:20, 32).

Christians can receive good things in creation with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4), and Scripture does not despise friendship, rest, or ordinary joys. The difference is the center. Epicurus made undisturbed pleasure the chief good and treated God as unconcerned with us. Scripture teaches that the living God is holy and near, that we are accountable to Him, and that true peace is reconciliation with Him through Christ’s death and bodily resurrection, not the absence of a future judgment (Hebrews 9:27; Romans 5:1).

If it would help, I can compare Epicurus point by point with Paul’s sermon in Acts 17.

question: Book of Philippians - Bible Survey
answer:
Philippians is a letter from the apostle Paul to the church in Philippi, written from prison, calling believers to joy, unity, and a life shaped by Christ.

Paul names himself as the sender, with Timothy beside him, and addresses “all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons” (Philippians 1:1). He is in chains, yet the gospel is advancing among the palace guard, and he sends greetings from those of Caesar’s household (Philippians 1:12-13; Philippians 4:22). That setting fits his Roman imprisonment, commonly dated about AD 60-62. Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, the first city in Europe where Paul planted a church. There the Lord opened Lydia’s heart, freed a slave girl, and saved a jailer and his household (Acts 16:11-40). Because Philippi prized Roman citizenship, Paul’s words about a better citizenship land with special force (Philippians 3:20).

He writes for several connected reasons. The Philippians had sent a gift by Epaphroditus, and Paul thanks them for their partnership in the gospel (Philippians 1:3-5; Philippians 4:10-20). Epaphroditus had fallen gravely ill, and Paul sends him home with honor so the church will not be distressed (Philippians 2:25-30). Along the way Paul urges unity, warns against confidence in the flesh, and shows how to rejoice when circumstances are hard.

A simple outline runs like this:

- Greeting, thanksgiving, and prayer (Philippians 1:1-11)
- The gospel advancing through Paul’s imprisonment (Philippians 1:12-26)
- A call to stand firm and live worthy of the gospel (Philippians 1:27-30)
- Christ’s humility as the pattern for unity (Philippians 2:1-18)
- Commendation of Timothy and Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:19-30)
- Righteousness through faith, and pressing on toward the goal (Philippians 3:1-21)
- Rejoicing, prayer, right thinking, contentment, and final thanks (Philippians 4:1-23)

Joy is the letter’s refrain. Forms of “joy” and “rejoice” sound again and again, not because prison was pleasant, but because Christ is enough. “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Paul can even rejoice when some preach Christ from poor motives, because Christ is still proclaimed (Philippians 1:15-18). The same Christ who began a good work in His people will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

The theological center is the person and work of Jesus. Paul says that Christ, existing in the form of God, did not cling to His rights, but emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:6-8). Theologians call this self-humbling the kenosis, from the Greek word for “emptied.” He did not cease to be God. He remained truly God while truly becoming man, which the church has summarized as the hypostatic union, and He laid aside the display of His glory for the path of humble obedience. God then highly exalted Him, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Philippians 2:9-11). Paul is applying to Jesus the words the LORD speaks in Isaiah 45:23. That is a clear confession of Christ’s deity.

Paul also refuses every righteousness of his own. He counts his religious credentials as loss so that he may be found in Christ, not with a righteousness from the law, but with the righteousness from God that comes through faith (Philippians 3:7-9). That is justification: a right standing given by grace, received by faith, not earned. He then presses on to know Christ and the power of His resurrection (Philippians 3:10-14). “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” is not a call to earn acceptance. It is sanctification, the lived obedience of people in whom God Himself is already at work (Philippians 2:12-13). Paul also looks to Christ’s return, when the Savior will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body (Philippians 3:20-21).

Near the end, Paul teaches contentment. “I can do all things through Him who gives me strength” is not a promise that every ambition will succeed. In context, it is Christ’s strength for plenty and for need, for hunger and for abundance (Philippians 4:11-13). And the peace of God guards hearts that bring their requests to Him with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6-7). His God will supply every need according to His riches in glory in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:19).

Set aside about fifteen minutes this week and read the whole letter in one sitting. Then bring one real anxiety to God in your own words, thanking Him for specific mercies, as Philippians 4:6-7 directs, and ask a mature believer in your church to pray with you.

question: In what ways was Moses like Jesus?
answer:
Moses was like Jesus as a prophet, deliverer, and mediator whom God raised up, serving as a type that points forward to Christ’s greater work.

God promised a prophet like Moses whom Israel must heed (Deuteronomy 18:15-18). The apostles identified Jesus as that prophet (Acts 3:22-23; Acts 7:37). Moses delivered Israel from slavery in Egypt by God’s power (Exodus 3:7-10; Exodus 14:21-31), foreshadowing how Jesus frees people from slavery to sin (John 8:34-36). As mediator, Moses received God’s words and interceded for the people after they sinned (Exodus 19:3-8; Exodus 32:11-14), while Jesus is the one mediator who gave Himself as a ransom (1 Timothy 2:5-6).

Scripture both compares and distinguishes them: Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house, but Christ is faithful as the Son over the house and is worthy of greater honor (Hebrews 3:2-6). These connections train us to see Christ throughout Scripture (Luke 24:27). When the law given through Moses shows your need, remember that grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory (Romans 3:23), yet Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone for forgiveness and new life. Which of these likenesses most helps you treasure Jesus?

question: What is Socinianism?
answer:
Socinianism is a sixteenth- and seventeenth-century movement, named for Faustus Socinus, that denied the Trinity and taught that Jesus is not God incarnate but a uniquely endowed man.

It took shape among the Polish Brethren and was set out in the Racovian Catechism (1605). Socinians rejected original sin and penal substitution. They treated the cross mainly as a moral example and understood salvation as imitation of Christ’s obedience rather than justification by grace through faith in a divine Substitute. They appealed to Scripture, yet let human reason set aside whatever seemed unreasonable, including Christ’s eternal deity. Even when they spoke of honoring Jesus, they denied that He is God by nature. Later Unitarianism drew heavily on these ideas.

That teaching stands outside the Christian faith. Scripture reveals one God in three persons, and a Savior who is truly God and truly man, the hypostatic union. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and “in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (Colossians 2:9; see also Matthew 28:19; John 20:28). We are sinners who cannot save ourselves (Romans 3:23). Christ did not merely model goodness. He bore our sins, died in our place, was buried, and rose bodily, so that God justifies the ungodly who trust Him (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:24–26; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4).

If a teacher says Jesus is only a great man, or that the cross is only an example, test that claim by Scripture and stay near a church that confesses the apostolic Gospel. Forgiveness rests on who Christ is and what He has done. If you have trusted a lesser Christ, turn from that error and trust the Lord who is God, crucified and risen for you.

If you are weighing this against what the Bible says about Jesus, which part would you like to look at more closely?

question: Can an unmarried man be a deacon or elder?
answer:
An unmarried man can be a deacon or an elder. 
Some Christians maintain that marriage is required, since the texts state that an overseer or deacon must be the husband of one wife and must manage his household well, treating family leadership as the proving ground for caring for God’s church (1 Timothy 3:2, 4-5; 1 Timothy 3:12; Titus 1:6). 
I hold, as one faithful option within historic Christianity, that singleness does not disqualify a man. The phrase calls for a “one-woman” pattern of sexual fidelity and purity rather than mandating marriage itself, so a single man meets it by a blameless life of self-control. In the first-century setting of widespread immorality, this standard ensured leaders were examples of holiness, and Paul himself shows that undivided singleness can serve the Lord well (1 Corinthians 7:32-35). 
The broader qualifications in 1 Timothy 3:1-13 and Titus 1:5-9 focus on being above reproach: temperate, sensible, hospitable, gentle, not greedy, and, for an elder, able to teach sound doctrine. Household management applies to the life a man actually has; a single man displays order in his conduct, work, and relationships. If you are weighing service or your church’s practice, read these passages carefully, pray for discernment, and discuss them with your elders, who examine candidates before God.

question: Is it better, spiritually, to be poor than to be rich?
answer:
No, it is not spiritually better to be poor than to be rich. Scripture does not treat material poverty as a higher form of holiness, nor wealth as automatically unspiritual. God weighs the heart, and both conditions bring real temptations that can either drive us to Him or draw us away.

Jesus blesses the poor in spirit, those who know their spiritual need before God, in Matthew 5:3. He also warns that it is hard for a rich person to enter the kingdom because riches so easily become a false trust, yet with God this is possible, in Matthew 19:23-26. The love of money, not money itself, is a root of all kinds of evil, while godliness with contentment is great gain, in 1 Timothy 6:6-10. Agur prayed for neither poverty nor riches, lest he steal or forget the Lord, in Proverbs 30:7-9. Paul learned contentment in both plenty and want, in Philippians 4:11-13.

Poverty can tempt us toward anxiety, envy, or dishonest gain. Wealth can tempt us toward pride, self-reliance, and neglect of others. Those who are rich are told not to be arrogant or to hope in uncertain riches, but to be generous and rich in good works, in 1 Timothy 6:17-19. God often chooses the poor of this world to be rich in faith, in James 2:5, yet it is faith He honors, not an empty purse. Some believers have freely embraced simpler lives, even voluntary poverty, out of love for Christ and for the sake of ministry, and that can be honorable. It is not required of every Christian, and it does not by itself make anyone more spiritual.

Our justification, right standing with God, comes by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, who died for our sins and rose again. Bank accounts add nothing to that gift and take nothing from it, in Romans 5:1; Ephesians 2:8-9. Whether you have been given little or much, the call is to seek first His kingdom, in Matthew 6:33, and to steward what you have as one who will give an account.

This week, read 1 Timothy 6:6-19 and Proverbs 30:7-9 slowly. Ask the Lord to show you any discontent or misplaced trust, then take one concrete step of obedience, such as a gift, a wise adjustment in how you handle money, or a conversation with a pastor or mature believer in your church.

question: Will the sun really be turned to darkness and the moon to blood (Joel 2:31)?
answer:
Joel 2:31 is a true word from God: before the great and awesome Day of the LORD, "The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood." You may wonder whether that is only ancient picture-language, or whether Peter already treated it as fulfilled at Pentecost when no such sky was seen. Scripture presents a real coming day of God, not a disposable myth. Faithful Christians differ on the manner of the sign, and that difference is not essential to the faith.

In context, Joel ties these wonders to the outpouring of the Spirit and to this promise: "everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved" (Joel 2:32). On Pentecost, Peter said this prophecy was what God was bringing to pass, and he quoted the lines about the sun and the moon (Acts 2:16-21). The prophecy belongs to the gospel age and to the Day of the LORD.

How the sun and moon are affected is a place where Christians may disagree in charity. Prophetic texts often speak with bold cosmic imagery, and the Bible is more explicit about the certainty of that Day than about the exact physics of every sign.

One historic reading takes this as apocalyptic language for God's real intervention, the kind of wording Isaiah uses when judgment falls and the sun and moon withhold their light (Isaiah 13:10). On that view, Joel's words meet their meaning in the mighty works of Pentecost, and for some also in later historical judgments, without requiring the moon to become literal blood.

Another historic reading holds that Pentecost began "the last days," while the full signs still await Christ's return. Jesus spoke of the sun being darkened and the moon not giving its light (Matthew 24:29), and John saw the sun turned black and the moon like blood (Revelation 6:12). On that view, what Joel foresaw will be visible in creation when the Day of the LORD arrives in fullness.

A wise way to hold the texts together is the already and not yet of biblical eschatology. The Spirit has already been poured out (Acts 2:17). The Day of the LORD is still ahead, when Jesus Christ returns personally and bodily to judge the living and the dead. The signs may include real disturbances in creation, described in the strong pictures prophets use when God shakes heaven and earth. I offer that as one faithful reading, not as the only orthodox one. What I will not soften is this: the Day is great and awesome, and it is not symbolic of nothing.

Do not let the sky crowd out the center. Joel's signs are a warning and a summons. Peter did not stop at wonders. He preached Jesus, crucified and risen, as both Lord and Christ, and he called hearers to repent and call on His name for the forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:36-38). The Lord who will judge is the Savior who died for sinners and rose on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by decoding signs.

This week, read Joel 2:28-32 beside Acts 2, and ask the Lord for a heart that trusts Him rather than only watching the heavens. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What is weighing on you most in this verse, the fear of judgment, or the question of how literally to take the sky?

question: How can I overcome spiritual apathy?
answer:
Spiritual apathy, that heavy indifference toward God, Scripture, and prayer, is a real burden, and you are not alone in carrying it. The Lord is not distant from His people in dry seasons, and He knows how to renew what feels cold.

Scripture treats this condition with both warning and hope. Jesus rebukes lukewarmness and calls His people to repent and be zealous, precisely because He loves them and disciplines those He receives (Revelation 3:15-19). The psalmist also shows a way forward by speaking truth to his own soul and choosing to hope in God (Psalm 42:5, 11). Overcoming apathy is not about forcing feelings through bare willpower. It belongs to progressive sanctification, in which the Holy Spirit uses the means of grace to rekindle love for Christ.

Look again at Jesus Himself. He is the author and perfecter of faith, and fixing your eyes on Him strengthens weary hearts (Hebrews 12:1-2). Read slowly through one Gospel and notice how He draws near to the tired and the dull. When you feel nothing, let His recorded compassion confront your coldness rather than staring only at your lack of emotion.

Pray with simple honesty. Confess the dryness and ask God to restore to you the joy of His salvation (Psalm 51:12). He already knows you fully (Psalm 139:1-4). Short prayers of dependence please Him more than polished words you do not mean. Do not withdraw from other believers. God designed regular fellowship to stir one another toward love and good works, and isolation usually deepens the fog (Hebrews 10:24-25).

Keep returning to the Gospel that gives life. Christ died for the ungodly, and His resurrection secures a living hope (Romans 5:6-8; 1 Peter 1:3). Zeal grows as you behold His finished work. Abide in Him, for apart from Him you can do nothing, yet joined to Him fruit comes in time (John 15:4-5). If specific sin is feeding the coldness, bring it into the light and receive His cleansing (1 John 1:9).

Here is one concrete step for this week: each morning read Psalm 63 slowly, then spend five quiet minutes telling God exactly where you feel dry and asking Him to satisfy your soul with His steadfast love. After a few days, share this struggle with a pastor, elder, or mature friend in your church and ask them to pray with you and follow up. If the dryness is joined to lasting despair that disrupts sleep, work, or the will to live, please also speak with a qualified medical professional, since I cannot offer medical advice, while still seeking care from your church leaders.

He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). His faithfulness does not rise and fall with your feelings.

What part of walking with Christ feels most distant or heavy for you right now?

question: How can I experience healing and recovery after an abortion?
answer:
The weight of seeking healing after an abortion is real, and bringing that ache into the light is a brave place to start. Scripture is clear that God forms each person in the womb and that the intentional ending of that life is sin against Him and against the child He made (Psalm 139:13–16; Exodus 20:13). Naming that does not add a heavier sentence than you already feel. It shows why only the Gospel can reach the guilt, grief, and shame that so often follow.

All of us have sinned and stand separated from a holy God (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived a perfect life, died on the cross as our substitute bearing the penalty our sins deserve, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4; Romans 5:8). His atoning death is sufficient even for this sin. Those who repent and trust Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone, not by works or by trying to make up for the past (Romans 3:24–26; Ephesians 2:8–9). There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). If you will turn from sin and rest in Christ alone, He receives you and cleanses you completely (1 John 1:9; John 6:37).

Healing is not found by minimizing what happened, by isolating in shame, or by attempting to pay God back. It comes as you confess this sin honestly to Him, receive His promised forgiveness as real, and walk in the new life the Spirit gives. Grief for the child may linger, and you may bring that sorrow to the Lord who is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18; Psalm 51). He does not ask you to pretend the loss was small. He asks you to come and be restored.

A concrete next step is this: set aside thirty quiet minutes today or tomorrow, read Psalm 51 and then 1 John 1:5–2:2 slowly, and speak to God in your own words about what you have done and your need for His mercy through Christ. This week, tell a pastor or a mature believer in a Bible-teaching church so you are not carrying this alone (Galatians 6:1–2). If the sorrow feels overwhelming, seek a certified biblical counselor who will keep pointing you to the cross rather than to self-atonement. I am not a substitute for that pastoral care, and I do not offer medical or psychiatric advice.

If you have never trusted Jesus, or if you are unsure you belong to Him, do not wait. Repent and believe the good news: Jesus died and rose for sinners, and He will forgive and make you new. How heavy does this feel for you right now, and is there a local church where you could take that next step with someone who will walk with you?

question: What does God mean when He says, “Seek me and live” (Amos 5:4)?
answer:
God means that Israel must turn from false worship and pursue Him personally, because only He gives life instead of the judgment their sin deserves.

In Amos 5 the LORD speaks to the northern kingdom while they still practiced outward religion. They traveled to Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba, places long associated with worship, yet those sites had become substitutes for God and partners with injustice. So He says, “Seek Me and live” (Amos 5:4), and immediately forbids them to seek those places (Amos 5:5). The word translated “seek” means to inquire of God and resort to Him, not merely to visit a shrine. “Live” means to be spared the death their covenant-breaking deserved and to receive the life that comes from His presence. It is like a sick man pacing the halls of a hospital while refusing the physician. The shrines were familiar halls. The LORD alone gives life.

He makes the call concrete in the same chapter. Seeking Him includes seeking good and not evil, hating evil, loving good, and maintaining justice (Amos 5:14-15). This is repentance, a turning of the heart that shows itself in righteousness. It is not a vague feeling, and it is not a way to earn standing with God.

That call reaches its fullness in Jesus Christ. “Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near” (Isaiah 55:6). The wicked must forsake their way and return to the LORD, who freely pardons (Isaiah 55:7). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived in perfect obedience, died on the cross as our penal substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He is the life God offers. He is the way, the truth, and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him (John 14:6). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by religious effort.

This week, read Amos 5:4-15 in one sitting and ask the Lord to show you one place where you have sought a habit, a place, or your own performance instead of Him. Confess that specifically, and rest again in Christ’s finished work. If you have never truly sought Him, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What part of this call feels most pressing for you right now?

question: If aborted babies go to heaven, why is abortion wrong?
answer:
Abortion is wrong because it deliberately takes the life of an innocent human being made in the image of God, and that is murder, even if God in mercy receives that child.

Scripture does not treat the child in the womb as a mere cluster of tissue or a potential person. David says, "For You formed my inmost being; You knit me together in my mother's womb... Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book" (Psalm 139:13-16). In Luke, the unborn John is called a baby, and he leaps in Elizabeth's womb, and the same word is later used for the newborn Jesus (Luke 1:41-44; Luke 2:12). From conception, this is a human neighbor bearing God's image (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 9:6). To end that life is to shed innocent blood, which the Lord hates (Proverbs 6:16-17), and it breaks the command, "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13).

I understand the force of the question. If the child is safe with God, some wonder whether the act is less grave, or even a mercy in a hard case. That hope about the child does not license the killing. Many Christians, myself included, entrust infants who die to the Judge of all the earth, who will do right (Genesis 18:25). David found comfort that he would go to his dead child (2 Samuel 12:23). If God saves such a little one, it is not because the child was sinless, for we are brought forth in iniquity (Psalm 51:5), but by grace through Christ, who saves elect infants who cannot yet hear the Word. Scripture does not hand us a public list of every soul, so we speak with reverent hope, not with a permit to kill.

The logic still fails. If a grown Christian dies and enters glory, murdering that Christian remains a great sin. The victim's salvation does not wash the killer's hands. Paul condemns the idea that we should do evil so that good may come (Romans 3:8), and he rejects the thought that we should sin so grace may increase (Romans 6:1-2). God alone numbers our days (Psalm 139:16). We may not send someone into eternity early any more than we may steal because God can restore, or lie because God can overrule the lie. Abortion also wounds mothers and fathers, hardens a people against the weakest neighbor, and rejects the Giver of life. Real compassion protects the small and helps the frightened (Proverbs 31:8-9). It does not solve fear or shame by ending a child's life.

If this question is only a puzzle, hold the line clearly: never counsel, pay for, or take part in an abortion. Seek instead to protect the child and care for the mother with truth and practical help. If it is heavier than a puzzle, and you or someone you love has been part of an abortion, do not hide from the sin, and do not despair of mercy. We all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). God justifies the ungodly by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Romans 3:24-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Bring this honestly to the Lord in your own words, and take it to a pastor in a faithful local church who can open the Scriptures with you. What is stirring this question for you?

question: Should communion be open or closed?
answer:
The question of whether communion should be open or closed is a non-essential matter where faithful Christians may disagree, because Scripture stresses worthy participation and the church's responsibility for purity without laying down an exhaustive policy for every guest at the table.

Those who hold open communion welcome all who make a credible profession of faith in Christ and are not under church discipline, arguing that the Supper is the Lord's Table and that we should receive fellow believers as Christ has received us (1 Corinthians 11:28; Romans 15:7). Those who hold closed or close communion restrict participation to baptized church members in good standing, whether of the local body or of like-minded congregations, so that the church can faithfully apply discipline and keep the ordinances in their New Testament order (Acts 2:41-42; 1 Corinthians 5:11-13).

This calls for Christian liberty and mutual charity rather than division, since Romans 14:3-4, 10 warns us not to judge or despise one another in matters of conscience. Speak with your pastors about how they practice fencing the table, examine your own heart before the Lord as you come to remember His death for sinners, and let love for the brethren guard the unity of the Spirit.

question: What is the Remnant Fellowship?
answer:
Remnant Fellowship is a religious group based in Brentwood, Tennessee, founded in 1999 by Gwen Shamblin, later Gwen Shamblin Lara. It grew out of her Weigh Down Workshop, a widely used program that tied weight loss to prayer, self-denial, and obedience.

In 2000 she publicly rejected the Trinity, teaching that God is not one God in three persons. That denial places Remnant Fellowship outside historic orthodox Christianity. Scripture presents the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as distinct persons, each fully God, yet one God (Matthew 28:19; John 1:1; John 20:28; 2 Corinthians 13:14). Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, and sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in His death and bodily resurrection, not by works, dieting, or religious performance (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9).

The name echoes a biblical idea, the faithful remnant God preserves (Romans 11:5), but the group's teaching does not match that faith. Many people were first drawn in by a real longing for discipline and a serious walk with God. Former members and Christian observers have also raised serious concerns about authoritarian control and pressure to cut off family members who dissented. Gwen Shamblin Lara died in a plane crash in 2021, and the movement has continued since then.

If you are weighing their message, test it by Scripture, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11). A wise next step is to read John 1 and Ephesians 2 with a pastor who confesses the Trinity and justification by faith, and to ask whether a church exalts Christ's finished work or human performance.

question: Who wrote the book of 2 John? Who was the author of 2 John?
answer:
The book of 2 John was written by the Apostle John, the same John who wrote the Gospel of John, 1 John, 3 John, and Revelation.

He does not sign his personal name. He opens as “the elder” (2 John 1:1), writing as an aged apostle and shepherd. The letter’s stress on truth, love, and warning against those who deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (2 John 1:7) matches 1 John so closely that the church from the earliest centuries received 2 John as his.

question: What is false guilt, and how can I avoid it?
answer:
