Guilt can press hard on the conscience, yet not every accusing feeling is from God. False guilt is condemnation that does not come from the Holy Spirit’s conviction of real sin against Scripture. It may be the voice of the accuser, the weight of human rules beyond God’s Word, or a heart that will not rest in Christ’s finished work even after genuine repentance.

Scripture distinguishes godly sorrow, which brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, from worldly sorrow that brings death (2 Corinthians 7:10). When we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). God is greater than our hearts and knows all things (1 John 3:19-20). The accuser of the brothers charges God’s people day and night, but his charges do not overturn the verdict secured by Christ (Revelation 12:10).

You avoid false guilt by testing every accusation against the Bible, not against raw feelings or other people’s expectations. If the matter is truly sin, name it, turn from it, and believe the promise of forgiveness rather than replaying the failure. Your justification rests on Christ’s penal substitution, not on the perfection of your performance. Sanctification is real and progressive by the Spirit, yet it never becomes the ground of your acceptance with God. If the matter is not sin, refuse the condemnation and walk in the liberty Christ purchased.

This week, when guilt rises, pause and ask the Lord two questions in your own words: “Is this something Your Word calls sin?” and “Have I already brought this to Christ in repentance and faith?” Then read Romans 8:1 and 1 John 1:9 slowly, and thank God that the blood of Jesus cleanses you. If the weight stays heavy or confusing, bring it to a trusted pastor or elder who can help you apply Scripture with care. I do not offer medical or psychiatric advice. If guilt is tangled with anxiety that disrupts ordinary life, seek wise help from your church and, as needed, a qualified professional, while keeping Christ and His Word at the center.

What particular accusation or situation has been stirring this guilt for you?

question: Are baptism and communion means of grace?
answer:
Yes, baptism and communion are means of grace in the understanding of most historic Christian traditions.  
Those who disagree, holding a memorial view, argue charitably that these ordinances are acts of obedient remembrance whose benefit comes only from the gospel truths they illustrate, protecting believers from trusting rituals instead of Christ alone (Luke 22:19).  
My position, one faithful option within historic Christianity, is that they truly are means of grace: God has appointed believer’s baptism and the Lord’s Supper as signs and seals that the Holy Spirit uses to strengthen faith, assure us of Christ’s promises, and nourish our souls through spiritual communion with Him. This rests on passages such as Romans 6:3-4, where baptism signifies our union with Christ in His death and resurrection, and 1 Corinthians 10:16, where the cup is a participation in the blood of Christ. Unlike views that locate saving power in the elements themselves, this affirms that grace flows from Christ by the Spirit to those who receive the ordinances in living faith, consistent with justification by faith alone. Other orthodox Christians, including those who baptize infants or affirm a stronger presence in the Supper, share the conviction that these rites are far more than empty symbols when joined to the Word.  
This week, as you prepare for communion, spend time in prayer thanking God for the cross and asking Him to make the bread and cup a fresh means of grace to your heart, then talk with a pastor or elder if you want help understanding your church’s practice.

question: What is the spirit of the law?
answer:
The spirit of the law is the purpose God intends in His commands: love for God and neighbor, and holiness that begins in the heart, not bare outward compliance with rules.

Scripture sets the letter of the law, an external written code that condemns when it is only performed on the surface, over against the Spirit who gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6; Romans 7:6). The prophets already promised this new-covenant work, God writing His law on the heart and putting His Spirit within His people (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27). Jesus did not set the law aside. He fulfilled it and showed that its true demand reaches the inner person: anger is the root of murder, and lust is the root of adultery, so righteousness must go deeper than the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 5:17; Matthew 5:20–28). He taught that love for God and love for neighbor uphold the Law and the Prophets, and Paul says love is the fulfillment of the law (Matthew 22:37–40; Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14).

The spirit of the law is not permission to ignore what God has spoken. Legalism keeps the appearance of obedience while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23). Treating love as a reason to discard clear commands is the opposite error. The biblical way is this: Christ fulfilled the law’s righteous requirement in the place of sinners, and by the Spirit that requirement is lived out in those who trust Him (Romans 8:3–4). That is justification received by grace through faith, and sanctification pursued by the same grace, not a ladder we climb to earn God’s favor.

This week, take one command you tend to keep mostly on the outside, perhaps your speech, your eyes, or your money. Read Matthew 5:21–48 slowly, ask the Lord to show you the motive under the habit, and bring that specific place to Him in prayer. If you have a pastor or a mature believer nearby, let them encourage you in it.

question: Should pastors be paid a salary?
answer:
Yes, Scripture teaches that pastors who labor in preaching and teaching should be financially supported by the church, and a salary is a fitting way to provide that support. Elders who lead well are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching, for the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages” (1 Timothy 5:17-18). The Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the one who receives instruction in the word must share in all good things with his instructor (Galatians 6:6).

This provision frees shepherds to devote themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word (Acts 6:4). Some believers, wary of a professional clergy, prefer that every pastor remain unpaid and self-supporting, and that concern for pure motives is worth hearing. Yet Paul himself defended the right to support as the Lord’s command and only set it aside voluntarily in certain places so as not to hinder the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:15-18; Acts 18:3). A church may therefore honor a bi-vocational pastor when love or limited means requires it, while still treating generous support as the normal biblical duty.

If you belong to a local congregation, ask your elders to review whether the pastor’s compensation lets him serve without constant financial anxiety, adjusting salary, housing, or other provision as the church is able. Faithful Christians may differ on the exact amount or form of that support, and Christian liberty covers those practical details (Romans 14:1-4), yet the call to honor those who feed the flock remains clear.

question: What does it mean that man shall not live by bread alone (Deuteronomy 8:3)?
answer:
"Man shall not live by bread alone" means that physical food cannot be the whole of human life. God made us to live by every word that comes from His mouth.

In Deuteronomy 8, Moses reminds Israel of the wilderness. The Lord humbled them, let them hunger, and then gave them manna they had never known, "so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deuteronomy 8:3). Bread is a real gift, and hunger is a real need. The lesson was God's providence. Life rests on what He speaks and supplies, not on a storehouse they could control. The phrase points to everything that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD, both the word that brought manna each morning and the word that directed their steps. Forgetting that, especially when life grew easy, was the danger Moses names next (Deuteronomy 8:11-17).

Jesus takes up the same sentence when He is hungry and Satan tells Him to turn stones into bread (Matthew 4:4; Luke 4:4). He will not secure even a good gift by leaving the Father's will. He answers from Scripture and trusts the written word. Bodily hunger is lawful to feel. Grasping life apart from God's word is not. In that test Christ stands as the faithful Son, where Israel so often failed.

This is not a call to neglect ordinary food, work, or care for the body. It is a warning against the lie that bread, money, or success can be your life. A full cupboard can still leave a soul starving. Scripture is a means of grace, daily food for faith. This week, read Deuteronomy 8 and Matthew 4, and name one place where you are tempted to live by bread alone. Pray about that directly to the Lord, and if the worry is heavy, ask a pastor or a mature believer to pray with you (James 5:16).

The deepest fulfillment is in Christ, the Word who became flesh (John 1:14). He calls Himself the bread of life, so that whoever comes to Him will not hunger (John 6:35). Manna kept Israel alive for a journey. Jesus gives Himself for the life of the world, crucified and risen, so that those who trust Him receive life that lasts (John 6:51).

question: What does the Bible say about parenting?
answer:
The Bible presents parenting as a sacred stewardship: children are a gift from the Lord, and parents are called to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

Children are not accidents or accessories. "Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is His reward" (Psalm 127:3). That gift carries a holy charge. Parents are to keep God's words on their own hearts and teach them diligently to their children in the ordinary rhythms of home and daily life (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Parenting, then, is discipleship, not a weekend addition to an otherwise secular household. Mothers and fathers share this work (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 6:20).

The New Testament presses this especially on fathers. "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). In the Greco-Roman world a father often ruled by raw authority. Paul redirects that authority toward nurture, so children are not discouraged (Colossians 3:21). The aim is formative training and loving admonition, aimed at the heart, not mere outward compliance.

Children, for their part, are called to obey their parents in the Lord and to honor father and mother (Ephesians 6:1-3; Colossians 3:20). Honor does not mean obeying a command to sin. If a parent requires what God forbids, God must be obeyed. In the ordinary path, though, Scripture calls for respectful obedience.

Discipline belongs to love, not to anger. "Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently" (Proverbs 13:24). The rod in Proverbs is corrective training under a parent's care. It is never cruelty, rage, shame, or harm. God Himself disciplines those He loves, and that discipline, painful for a moment, is meant to yield a harvest of righteousness and peace (Hebrews 12:6-11). Faithful Christians may differ on particular methods, and Christian liberty applies there (Romans 14:1-4). Abdication and harshness do not.

"Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6) is proverbial wisdom, a general pattern, not a guarantee that godly parenting always produces a godly adult. Parents plant and water. God gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). You cannot regenerate your child's heart. You can teach the truth, model repentance, pray steadfastly, and point them to Jesus, who welcomed children and refused to have them hindered (Matthew 19:13-14).

The pattern for all of this is the fatherhood of God. He is holy and tender, just and merciful. Christian parents will fail. When you do, confess it to the Lord and, where fitting, to your children. That humility tells the truth about the Gospel more clearly than a polished performance. Christ died for sinners and rose again, and parents and children alike are justified by grace alone through faith in Him, not by family success.

This week, read Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and Ephesians 6:1-4 with your household, or with a trusted believer if you parent alone, and choose one daily moment, a meal or bedtime, to read a short passage and pray to God in your own words.

If you tell me the ages of your children and what feels heaviest right now, I can help you apply this more specifically.

question: Who was Jeremiah in the Bible?
answer:
Jeremiah was a prophet of the LORD in Judah during the final decades before Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 586 BC. God called him to warn the nation of judgment for breaking the covenant and to hold out hope of restoration.

He was the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin (Jeremiah 1:1). Before Jeremiah was born, the LORD knew him, set him apart, and appointed him a prophet to the nations (Jeremiah 1:5). He spoke through the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah as Babylon closed in. His message was plain and costly: turn from idols and injustice, or the city and the temple would fall. The people rejected him. Officials beat him, put him in stocks, and later lowered him into a cistern (Jeremiah 20:1-2; Jeremiah 38:6). He is often called the weeping prophet because he grieved over the ruin of the people he loved (Jeremiah 9:1). The book of Lamentations, long linked with him in the church, gives voice to that same sorrow after the city fell.

Judgment was not God's last word. Through Jeremiah the LORD promised a new covenant, in which He would forgive iniquity and write His law on the hearts of His people (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Even during the siege, Jeremiah bought a field as a sign that the land would be possessed again (Jeremiah 32:6-15). The New Testament teaches that this new covenant promise is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, whose blood establishes it (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:6-13). Jeremiah's tears and his hope belong together: God judges sin truly, and God saves truly.

If you want to know him better, read Jeremiah 1 and Jeremiah 31 this week, and ask the Lord to give you steadfastness to trust His word when obedience is costly.

question: Why did Jesus allow the demons to enter the herd of pigs?
answer:
Jesus permitted the demons to enter the herd of pigs in order to display His sovereign authority over them and to set a tormented man free. Some readers question this moment, wondering why the Lord would allow the animals to perish or bring loss to their owners. The Gospel accounts present it as a real act of deliverance under Christ's lordship, not as indifference.

In Mark 5:1-20 (see also Matthew 8:28-34; Luke 8:26-39), Jesus met a man possessed by a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes. The spirits knew Him as the Son of the Most High God and begged not to be sent into the abyss (Luke 8:31). They asked instead to enter a nearby herd of pigs. Jesus granted the request. The demons left the man, entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the bank into the sea and drowned (Mark 5:13).

That permission was itself a display of authority. Unclean spirits could do nothing apart from His word. The destruction of the pigs made the exorcism plain to everyone: those who came found the man sitting clothed and in his right mind (Mark 5:15). Many in the region, however, prized the lost herd more than the restored person and begged Jesus to leave (Mark 5:17). He sent the man home to tell what the Lord had done for him (Mark 5:19).

The scene shows Jesus destroying the works of the devil (1 John 3:8) and bringing freedom to the captive (Luke 4:18). A human being matters more to Him than livestock. This week, read Mark 5:1-20 slowly, then speak directly to God about Christ's power over every evil force and about any fear or question the passage raises in you. You might also talk through the chapter with a mature believer in your church.

question: What are the Analects of Confucius?
answer:
The Analects of Confucius are a collection of short sayings, conversations, and anecdotes traditionally attributed to the Chinese teacher Confucius (Kongzi, about 551–479 BC) and his disciples. They are the foundational text of Confucian moral and political thought.

The work, known in Chinese as the Lunyu (“selected sayings”), was not written by Confucius as a single book. It was gathered by followers over time, and scholars debate exactly when it reached its present form. Its chapters address learning, filial piety, ritual propriety, humane conduct (often called ren), and government by personal virtue rather than by force alone. For many centuries the Analects shaped education, family life, and public ethics across China and much of East Asia, and they remain one of the Four Books of the later Confucian tradition.

Christians can read them with respect as a serious ancient reflection on character and social order. Scripture, though, teaches that wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 1:7) and that the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3). Moral instruction can restrain and guide, yet it cannot reconcile a sinner to a holy God. That gift comes by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again.

question: Can faith change God's plan?
answer:
Faith cannot change God's eternal plan, because the Lord is immutable and works all things according to the counsel of His will.

You may feel the pull of this question if you have prayed earnestly and wondered whether stronger faith could move God to rewrite what He has already purposed, or whether a fixed plan makes asking pointless. That tension is real in the biblical story, where God both declares His purpose unchangeable and responds to the cries of His people.

Scripture is clear that God's plan stands. He declares the end from the beginning, and His purpose will stand (Isaiah 46:10). He works all things according to the counsel of His will (Ephesians 1:11). God is not a man that He should lie or change His mind (Numbers 23:19), and He says, "I the LORD do not change" (Malachi 3:6). What He has purposed in His sovereignty cannot be revised by any creature.

At the same time, God has ordained faith and prayer as the means by which He carries out that unchanging plan. When Hezekiah prayed, the Lord added years to his life (2 Kings 20:5-6). When Nineveh believed God's word and turned from evil, He relented from the disaster He had announced (Jonah 3:5-10). These are not cases of faith overriding a decree. They show God fulfilling what He always intended, using the very prayers and repentance He stirred in His people. Your faith does not twist His arm or alter His decree. It is the instrument through which His providence accomplishes what He has purposed from eternity. Jesus teaches us to ask in faith, and the apostle John adds that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us (Matthew 21:22; 1 John 5:14-15). The prayer of a righteous person is powerful and effective because God has chosen to work through it, not because it rewrites His counsel (James 5:16).

This week, bring one specific burden to the Lord each morning, praying through Philippians 4:6-7 and resting that your request is already held inside His good and unchanging purposes. Ask one mature believer to join you in that prayer. If a particular situation is weighing on you, I would be glad to point you toward Scriptures that speak to it.

question: What is Pneumatology?
answer:
Pneumatology is the study of the Holy Spirit, both who He is and what He does. The word comes from the Greek pneuma (spirit) and logos (word or study).

Scripture reveals the Holy Spirit as truly God, the third person of the Trinity, not an impersonal force. He speaks, teaches, and can be grieved (Matthew 28:19; Acts 5:3-4; Ephesians 4:30). He applies Christ's saving work: He convicts of sin, grants regeneration, indwells every believer, seals them for the day of redemption, and carries on their sanctification (John 16:8; John 3:5-8; Romans 8:9; Ephesians 1:13-14; Galatians 5:22-23).

When you open the Bible this week, do not treat understanding as a merely human task. Ask the Spirit to illumine the Word and to form Christ's character in your ordinary obedience (1 Corinthians 2:12-13; John 16:13).

question: What does the Bible say about children's church?
answer:
The Bible does not describe a program called children's church, and it neither commands nor forbids separating children from the main gathering for part of corporate worship. What it does insist on is that children belong among the people of God and must be taught His Word, with parents bearing the first responsibility.

This is a tertiary matter of church practice, not an essential of the faith. Faithful Christians disagree because Scripture gives governing principles rather than a fixed plan for every age group. In such things we owe one another Christian liberty and charity (Romans 14:1-4).

One long-standing approach keeps children in the main assembly for the whole service. Those who do this point to gatherings where men, women, and children together heard the law read and explained (Deuteronomy 31:12-13; Joshua 8:35; Nehemiah 8:1-3). They want children to see the church worship, to learn reverence by being present, and to hear the same Word their parents hear.

Another widespread approach offers age-suited teaching for part of the service, often called children's church or a children's class. Those who do this note that Scripture cares about understanding, not mere attendance. In Nehemiah's day the Levites helped the people grasp the meaning of the Word (Nehemiah 8:7-8), and the Lord Jesus welcomed little children while also speaking in ways hearers could receive (Matthew 19:13-15; Mark 4:33). The aim is to proclaim Christ clearly to young minds and to help parents worship without constant distraction, without removing children from the church's care.

Neither pattern is the only faithful option. Children are part of the covenant community, and they need the gospel, not mere activity or moral lessons: that Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that they must trust Him (Psalm 78:4-7). The Lord Jesus did not treat children as a nuisance, but as those to whom the kingdom belongs (Matthew 19:14).

Whatever your church practices, do not hand off discipleship. Fathers, and mothers with them, are to bring children up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4; Deuteronomy 6:6-7). This week, ask your pastor or an elder how your congregation includes children, then at home retell one truth from the service or lesson in simple words, and pray with your children that the Lord would give them faith in Christ. Look for a church where the Word is honored, children are loved rather than sidelined or merely entertained, and parents are equipped. Unity in the gospel matters more than sameness in the children's ministry schedule.

question: Why is the humanity of Jesus important?
answer:
Jesus’ full humanity is essential because only as a true man could He represent sinners, obey where we failed, and die as our substitute. In the hypostatic union, the eternal Son took on a complete human nature without ceasing to be God, so that one person, truly God and truly man, could reconcile us to the Father.

The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). He had to be made like His brothers in every respect so that He might become a merciful and faithful high priest and make propitiation for the sins of the people (Hebrews 2:17). As the man Christ Jesus, He is the one mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). Because He shared our humanity, He sympathizes with our weaknesses, tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). His real body also means His death was a real sacrifice and His resurrection a real victory over death (1 Corinthians 15:21).

We are sinners who fall short of God’s glory and stand separated from Him (Romans 3:23). Christ, fully God and fully man, lived without sin, died on the cross for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Hebrews 4:14-16 slowly and bring one specific weakness to Him in prayer, knowing He understands it from the inside and intercedes for you. What part of Jesus’ humanity feels most needed in your life right now?

question: What is the new birth?
answer:
The new birth is the Holy Spirit’s sovereign work of regeneration, by which He imparts new spiritual life to a sinner dead in trespasses and sins, so that the person is enabled to repent and trust in Christ.

Jesus told Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or born from above (John 3:3). The word used there stresses a birth that comes from God rather than from human decision, lineage, or effort (John 1:12-13). It is as free and mysterious as the wind (John 3:8), a divine act, not a moral self-improvement we produce.

This new birth is necessary because we are born in sin, separated from the holy God, and unable to save ourselves (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:1-3). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross as our penal substitute, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, securing forgiveness for all who trust Him (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). By regeneration the Spirit applies that salvation, granting a new heart and the gift of faith (Ezekiel 36:26-27; Titus 3:5; Ephesians 2:8-9). Those born of God turn from sin and bear the fruit of love for Christ (1 John 3:9).

If you feel any conviction or hunger for God, do not try to manufacture new life by better behavior. Look to Jesus crucified and risen, and ask God Himself for the new heart He promises. Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and eternal life.

What stands out to you, or what questions does this raise about your own need before God?

question: What does the Bible say about education?
answer:
The Bible teaches that true education is the formation of a whole person in wisdom, and that wisdom begins with the reverent fear of the Lord, not with information alone.

"The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge" (Proverbs 1:7), and "the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding" (Proverbs 9:10). In Proverbs, this fear is reverent awe that submits to God, and the knowledge in view is understanding that leads to a godly life. Education is never morally neutral. It shapes what a person loves, trusts, and obeys. If anyone lacks wisdom, God invites that person to ask Him for it (James 1:5).

Scripture places the primary duty of teaching children on parents. God's words are to be on the heart and taught diligently in ordinary life, when sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down, and rising up (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). Paul says, "Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). Those words point to ongoing training and corrective teaching, not a single lesson. The aim is that the next generation would know God and not forget His works (Psalm 78:4–7).

The Bible also honors learning, skill, and growth. Moses was educated in the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22). Daniel was trained in Babylon and still remained faithful to God (Daniel 1:8–20). God filled Bezalel with skill for craftsmanship (Exodus 31:1–5). Even the Lord Jesus, truly God and truly man, "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man" (Luke 2:52). Study has limits, though. Much learning can weary the flesh, and the end of the matter is to fear God and keep His commandments (Ecclesiastes 12:12–13). Knowledge without love only puffs up (1 Corinthians 8:1).

All of this learning is to be brought under Christ. In Him "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Colossians 2:3), and He "has become for us wisdom from God" (1 Corinthians 1:30). Human wisdom that stands against God is folly, for "the foolishness of God is wiser than man's wisdom" (1 Corinthians 1:25). Believers are called to love God with the mind (Matthew 22:37), to be transformed by the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2), and to take every thought captive to obey Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5). That renewing is part of sanctification, the Spirit's ongoing work of making God's people more like Christ. Scripture is the standard for this growth, "God-breathed and useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness" (2 Timothy 3:16).

The church shares in this teaching. Jesus commanded His people to make disciples, "teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you" (Matthew 28:20). The word of Christ is to dwell among believers richly as they teach and admonish one another (Colossians 3:16), and church leaders are to teach what accords with sound doctrine (Titus 2:1).

How a family arranges formal schooling is a non-essential, a matter of Christian liberty rather than a test of faithfulness, because Scripture does not prescribe one institution for every time and place (Romans 14:1–5). Faithful Christians have educated at home, in Christian schools, and in public schools while teaching the faith carefully at home and in the church. What Scripture requires is not a single model, but that parents not hand over the formation of their children's hearts and minds, and that every believer keep growing in the knowledge of God.

This week, read Proverbs 1–4 slowly and write down one truth to obey in your studies, work, or home. If you have children or influence younger believers, choose one regular moment, a meal or bedtime, to speak God's Word with them (Deuteronomy 6:7). Pray to the Lord yourself. Ask Him for wisdom, for humility so that knowledge does not make you proud, and for grace to love Him with your mind.

question: What is the Edenic covenant?
answer:
The Edenic covenant is the covenant of works God made with Adam in the garden, promising life for perfect obedience and death for disobedience.  
Some historic Christians, especially in dispensational traditions, hold that Eden was a dispensation of innocence and a divine test rather than a formal covenant, since Genesis never uses the word covenant for this arrangement and later categories should not be pressed onto the text.  
I affirm it as a true covenant of works, one faithful reading within historic Christianity, because Hosea 6:7 speaks of Adam transgressing the covenant, and Paul presents Adam as federal head whose one trespass brought condemnation while Christ’s obedience brings justification (Romans 5:18-19; 1 Corinthians 15:21-22).  

In the garden the Lord God generously gave every tree for food, yet He commanded Adam not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, warning that disobedience would bring certain death (Genesis 2:16-17). Adam stood as our representative; his failure imputed sin and death to all who descend from him (Romans 5:12). This leaves every person unable to earn life by personal obedience.  

Jesus Christ, the last Adam, fulfilled what the first Adam broke. He obeyed perfectly, bore the curse, and rose bodily, so that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by works (Romans 5:19; Galatians 3:13). This week, read Genesis 2–3 beside Romans 5:12-21, and thank God that your standing rests on Christ’s finished obedience rather than your own.

question: What is Wahhabism? What is Wahhabi Islam?
answer:
Wahhabism is an eighteenth-century reform movement within Sunni Islam founded by Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and Wahhabi Islam is the strict form of belief and practice that developed from his teaching. It urges a return to what its followers regard as the pure monotheism and worship of the earliest Muslim community, treating many later customs as forbidden innovations.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab taught that practices such as seeking intercession at saints’ tombs or certain Sufi rites constituted shirk (associating partners with God) and therefore contradicted tawhid, the absolute oneness of God. His movement formed a lasting alliance with the family of Muhammad ibn Saud, and that partnership deeply shaped the religious life of the Saudi states. Wahhabi influence remains strongest in Saudi Arabia, where it has guided religious institutions and education, and it has also spread through teaching and funding networks abroad. Many who hold these views prefer to be called Salafis, pointing to the salaf (the early pious generations), and they often view “Wahhabi” as a name given by critics. This stream is one part of the wider Sunni tradition, not the faith or practice of most Muslims.

Christians can respect the earnest desire to honor God alone and to reject idolatry, a concern Scripture itself commands (Exodus 20:3-5; Isaiah 42:8). At the same time, the Bible reveals the one true God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and it teaches that sinners are brought to Him only through Jesus Christ. Jesus, truly God and truly man, offered Himself in penal substitutionary atonement, died on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (John 14:6; Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). No other mediator can reconcile us to God (1 Timothy 2:5).

If you are learning about this tradition because of Muslim friends or neighbors, pray for genuine love and clear understanding, then listen carefully to what they themselves believe rather than relying only on a label. Keep reading the Gospels so that you can speak both truthfully and gently about the Savior when the opportunity arises.

question: What is the Watchtower Bible and Tract Society?
answer:
The Watchtower Bible and Tract Society is the publishing corporation and legal organization that produces literature for Jehovah's Witnesses and carries out much of their organized work. It began in the 1880s under Charles Taze Russell and remains under the direction of the Jehovah's Witnesses' Governing Body.

Jehovah's Witnesses honor the Bible and speak of Jesus, yet their official teachings deny core doctrines that Scripture presents as essential. They reject the Trinity, holding that Jesus is a created being rather than truly God, and that the Holy Spirit is an impersonal force rather than a divine person. The Bible reveals Jesus as truly God and truly man. John 1:1 states, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God," and the risen Christ received the confession "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). They also tie a person's hope to loyal service within their organization, whereas Scripture teaches justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, on the ground of His atoning death and bodily resurrection (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 3:23-26).

These are not minor differences of emphasis. A message that redefines Christ's identity and the way of salvation stands outside historic Christian orthodoxy (Galatians 1:6-9). Many who follow Watchtower teachings are sincere, and they deserve patient respect. The faithful step is to examine those teachings directly against Scripture, as the Bereans did (Acts 17:11), especially by reading the Gospels and asking who Jesus Himself claims to be. If a particular teaching or personal situation is on your mind, I am glad to look at it with you from the Bible.

question: What sort of interfaith ministries are appropriate?
answer:
Appropriate interfaith ministries are cooperative works of mercy and justice, such as disaster relief, feeding the hungry, or housing the homeless, that never require Christians to compromise the Gospel or join the worship of other gods.

Scripture calls us to love our neighbors as ourselves, and the parable of the Good Samaritan shows that this love reaches across religious lines (Luke 10:25-37; Matthew 22:37-39). We are also told to do good to all people (Galatians 6:10). At the same time, we must not enter partnerships that would silence or reshape the message of Christ (2 Corinthians 6:14-18). Paul reasoned with people of other beliefs in synagogues and in Athens, yet he always directed them to the risen Jesus and never treated their worship as valid (Acts 17:16-34). There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12; John 14:6). Any ministry that presents all religions as equally saving paths, or that joins in prayer and worship as though our God and other deities are the same, denies justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone and is not appropriate.

A church can, for example, join neighbors of other faiths to serve meals after a flood, offer practical help, and remain free to pray in Jesus' name and explain the hope of His cross and resurrection when asked. This respects every person as made in God's image while keeping Christ's exclusive mediation clear. Bring any specific opportunity to your elders, and read Acts 17 with 2 Corinthians 6 as you pray for wisdom to love your neighbors without losing the Gospel's distinctiveness.

What situation are you considering?

question: What is presuppositional apologetics?
answer:
Presuppositional apologetics is a method of defending the Christian faith that begins with the triune God and the authority of Scripture as the necessary foundation for knowledge, rather than trying to reach God from a neutral starting point.

Every person already reasons from basic commitments, called presuppositions. Because of the noetic effects of sin, the darkening of the mind by rebellion, unbelievers suppress the truth about God and try to make sense of the world by autonomous reason (Romans 1:18-21). Presuppositionalists argue that logic, moral duty, and the reliability of nature are intelligible only if the God of Scripture is real. That claim is often called the transcendental argument: the Christian worldview is the precondition of rational thought. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Proverbs 1:7), and believers are called to take every thought captive to obey Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5). Cornelius Van Til shaped this approach in the twentieth century, and it has been especially common among Reformed Christians.

This method is not required for faithful Christianity. Classical and evidential apologists offer arguments from cause, design, history, and the resurrection of Jesus, appealing to standards of reason they believe can be shared, so that they may give a gentle answer for the hope within them (1 Peter 3:15). Their desire to set evidence before the conscience is a real strength. Presuppositionalists answer that those standards themselves depend on the God under discussion, so neutrality is a fiction. Christians may disagree here in charity, since the disagreement concerns method, not the Gospel.

In conversation, you might patiently ask a skeptic what makes logic binding or injustice truly wrong if there is no holy God, and then point them to Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3).

question: What does the Bible say about chanting? Should a Christian chant?
answer:
The Bible does not command chanting, and it does not treat any repeated sound or formula as a way to draw near to God. It calls believers to pray, sing, and meditate on His Word with understanding, and it warns against empty repetition.

Jesus said, “And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard” (Matthew 6:7). The warning is not against ever repeating a true prayer. It is against mindless or manipulative speech, as if God could be moved by volume or technique. Scripture itself uses holy repetition. Psalm 136 returns again and again to the refrain that the Lord’s loving devotion endures forever, and the creatures before God’s throne cry, “Holy, holy, holy” (Revelation 4:8). The church is told to sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with thankfulness in the heart (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16). Paul insists that prayer and song engage the mind as well as the spirit (1 Corinthians 14:15). God is to be worshiped in spirit and in truth (John 4:24).

Biblical meditation is also different from a mantra. In the Old Testament, to meditate on God’s Word includes quietly turning it over, even murmuring it, so that it fills the heart and directs obedience (Joshua 1:8; Psalm 1:2). The aim is a mind stocked with God’s truth, not a mind emptied in search of an inner state.

Whether a Christian should chant is a matter of worship style, not an essential of the faith. Scripture gives the content and aim of worship more clearly than it fixes one musical form, so believers have long differed here in Christian liberty (Romans 14:1–6). Some churches, especially in older liturgical traditions, have chanted psalms and prayers slowly so the words can be heard, remembered, and offered with reverence. Others, including many Baptist and Reformed congregations, prefer clear spoken prayer and congregational singing in which every line is readily understood. Neither approach is required of every Christian. Both can honor Christ when the words are biblical, the mind is engaged, and the goal is God’s glory rather than a spiritual sensation.

What a Christian must not do is chant in ways borrowed from other religions. Repeating sacred syllables, names of other gods, or techniques meant to empty the self and unite with an impersonal force is not a neutral aid to prayer. It conflicts with love for the Lord with all the mind, and with the refusal to share in the worship of other powers (Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Matthew 22:37; 1 Corinthians 10:20–21). Nearness to God is not produced by a method. It is given through Christ, received by faith, and sustained by the means of grace: the Word, prayer, and the fellowship of the church.

If you mean slowly speaking or singing a psalm or a short promise of Scripture so your scattered thoughts rest on truth, that can be a wise help. Test any practice by this: does it make Christ’s person and promises clearer, or does it bypass the mind and the gospel? This week, take one short passage, such as Psalm 23, and speak it slowly in your own prayer, asking the Lord to press its meaning into your desires. If you are unsure whether a particular form honors Him, bring it to your pastor or elders rather than treating the technique as your guide.

What do you mean by chanting: singing Scripture in worship, or a repeated phrase meant to quiet the mind?

question: Who is Jesus — Day 4 — Jesus the Prophet
answer:
Jesus is the Prophet God promised, the One we are commanded to hear and the final revelation of the Father.

Moses told Israel, “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). The apostle Peter later applied those words to Jesus (Acts 3:22–23). At the Transfiguration the Father’s voice settled the matter: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to Him!” (Matthew 17:5). In His prophetic office Jesus does not merely pass along a message from someone else. He is the Word who was with God and was God, and the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us, full of grace and truth (John 1:1; John 1:14). God spoke in many ways through earlier prophets, but in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). Jesus taught with divine authority, exposed the heart, announced the kingdom, and foretold His own death and resurrection.

We need more than a true teacher. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and left to ourselves we do not listen to Him (Romans 3:23). Jesus came not only to speak but to save. He died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. God justifies the ungodly by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Set aside a few quiet minutes today to read John 14:1–6 slowly, and ask the Lord to give you ears to hear His Son and a heart to follow Him.

Which word of Jesus do you most need to listen to right now?

question: Will there be a second chance for salvation after death?
answer:
Scripture teaches that there is no second chance for salvation after death. People are appointed to die once, and after that comes judgment (Hebrews 9:27).

The account of the rich man and Lazarus shows a great chasm fixed after death, so that no one crosses from torment to comfort, and those still living are directed to the witness of Scripture they already have rather than to any later opportunity (Luke 16:19-31). Paul writes that now is the favorable time and now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2). Death seals a person’s standing before God; it does not open a new period of probation.

This is weighty because God is holy and just, and every person has sinned and falls short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from Him and brings death as its wage (Romans 6:23). In love God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man. Jesus lived without sin, died on the cross in penal substitution to bear the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He is exalted as Lord. Those who trust Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Those who do not believe remain under condemnation (John 3:18; John 3:36).

If you have not yet turned to Him, do not delay. Repent of your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and eternal life. A practical next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly this week, asking God to make Christ clear to you, and to talk with a pastor or mature believer about what you read. You can pray directly to God, confessing your need and asking Him for faith to believe.

What has prompted you to ask about salvation after death?

question: What is biblical homemaking?
answer:
Biblical homemaking is the wise, Godward stewardship of a household: ordering daily life, caring for the people under your roof, and making the home a place where Christ is honored.

Scripture treats the home as a real sphere of worship and discipleship, not a lesser stage of life. In the New Testament household instructions, written into a Greco-Roman world that already had strict domestic expectations, the apostles dignify this work and reshape it by the gospel. Older women are to train younger women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled and pure, and to be managers of their households, kind and subject to their own husbands, so that the word of God is not discredited (Titus 2:3-5). Younger widows are counseled to marry, have children, and manage their households (1 Timothy 5:14). The wisdom portrait in Proverbs 31:10-31 shows a woman who fears the Lord, works with skill and strength, provides for her family, and speaks with wisdom. Her labor is not idle, and it is not confined to a tiny list of chores. It is the management of a whole household for the good of others.

That calling sits inside a complementary design. The husband is to love his wife as Christ loved the church, to lead without harshness, and to provide for his own (Ephesians 5:25-33; Colossians 3:19; 1 Timothy 5:8). The wife’s management of the home is a noble vocation, not a punishment, and her submission is to her own husband, not to men in general (Ephesians 5:22-24; Colossians 3:18). Parents together are to bring children up in the training and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). Hospitality, order, shared meals, prayer, and patient teaching all belong to this work (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9).

Christians differ on how strictly these texts fix a modern schedule. A charitable alternative holds that the household instructions mainly reflect first-century custom, so homemaking is simply shared labor with no lasting priority for the wife. I read Genesis 2, Titus 2, and Ephesians 5 as teaching a lasting pattern: the husband bears primary responsibility to lead and provide, and the wife is especially entrusted with nurturing and managing the home. That does not forbid all work beyond the house, since Proverbs 31 itself includes enterprise that serves the family, and it does not excuse a husband from sharing daily labor in love. The non-negotiable center is a home ordered by God’s Word, not a particular income arrangement.

None of us does this perfectly. A well-kept house cannot justify us before God. We are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, who died for sinners and rose again, and from that mercy we learn to love the people He has given us (Ephesians 2:8-9; Titus 3:4-7). If you want to grow here, choose one small rhythm this week: read a short passage of Scripture aloud in your home and thank God by name for the people you are called to serve. Are you asking for your own household, or to understand what these passages require?

question: How should Christians view statues of Jesus?
answer:
Christians should not worship statues of Jesus or treat them as divine, for Scripture commands exclusive worship of God and condemns idolatry (Exodus 20:4-5; Isaiah 42:8).

Whether such statues may be made or kept as artistic reminders is a non-essential matter on which faithful Christians disagree, because of differing interpretations of how the second commandment applies in light of the incarnation.

Catholic and Orthodox believers hold that images of Christ can honor His true humanity and aid meditation on His saving work, provided the statue itself receives no worship.

Many Protestant believers, particularly in Reformed churches, hold that religious statues of Jesus exceed biblical warrant and can draw the heart toward a crafted likeness instead of the living Lord who must be worshiped in spirit and truth (Deuteronomy 4:15-18; John 4:24).

In this area of conscience, practice Christian liberty with charity, neither despising nor judging those who differ, while remaining fully convinced before God (Romans 14:1-6, 22-23).

If the question touches your own home or church, read Exodus 20 this week and ask the Lord to guard your worship, then talk it through with your pastor or elders.

question: I am in the process of getting a divorce. Can I start dating, or do I have to wait until the divorce is final?
answer:
The process of getting a divorce is heavy, and the loneliness that comes with it is real. You should not start dating until the divorce is final. Until then you are still married, and giving your heart to someone else would be unfaithfulness to the covenant you made before God.

Marriage is a one-flesh covenant, not a feeling that ends when the paperwork starts (Genesis 2:24; Malachi 2:14-16). Jesus said that divorcing a spouse and marrying another is adultery, except for sexual immorality (Matthew 5:31-32; Matthew 19:3-9). He also taught that adultery begins when the heart desires someone who is not your spouse (Matthew 5:27-28). Paul told believers who separate to remain unmarried or else be reconciled, not to take up with a new partner (1 Corinthians 7:10-11). Dating now, even if you call it casual, asks another person to share a bond that is not free. If a romantic attachment has already begun, the right step is to end it and bring it into the light, not to keep it quiet until the decree is signed.

Waiting is also wise for the people around you. A new relationship in the middle of a divorce often inflames conflict, hurts children, and complicates legal matters. I cannot give legal advice, so lean on your attorney for the court process, but Scripture has already spoken to the moral question.

Once the divorce is final, do not assume you are immediately free to date. Christians agree that marriage is meant for life, and sincere believers have differed on the narrow question of remarriage. One historic view holds that only death frees a person to marry again, so the call after separation is reconciliation or a chaste single life (Romans 7:2-3; 1 Corinthians 7:10-11). The view I hold, as one faithful reading within historic Christianity, is that sexual immorality, and willful desertion that the church cannot remedy, can break the bond so that the innocent party may remarry in the Lord (Matthew 19:9; 1 Corinthians 7:15). That question belongs to patient counsel after the first marriage has actually ended, not to a new romance while you are still married.

Here is a practical step for this week. Sit down with your pastor or elders, tell them what has happened and whether reconciliation has truly been pursued, and ask them to help you walk in repentance and purity. Do not pursue a romantic relationship while this marriage still stands. Pray honestly about your loneliness, asking God for a clean heart, patience, and wisdom, and let mature believers in your church carry this with you (Psalm 51:10; James 5:16; Hebrews 10:24-25).

If you carry guilt, there is real hope. We have all sinned and fallen short of God's glory, and Christ died in the place of sinners and rose bodily on the third day (Romans 3:23-25; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). God justifies those who trust in Jesus, not those who have kept a spotless record. Turn from any path that treats your marriage covenant lightly, and trust in Christ alone, who loved the church and gave Himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25).

If you are in physical danger, seek safety right away through the proper authorities and your church. Getting safe is not the same as starting a new relationship.

Would you like help thinking through that conversation with your elders, or through what Scripture says about the grounds of divorce in a situation like yours?

question: What is the importance of the empty tomb?
answer:
The empty tomb matters because it is the historical witness that Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead, and that His death truly dealt with sin.

On the first day of the week, the women, and then Peter and John, found the tomb vacant and the grave clothes left behind. An angel said, “He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay” (Matthew 28:6; see also Luke 24:1–12; John 20:1–9). Scripture presents this as a real event in history, not a symbol. The tomb was empty because the crucified Lord had been raised in the same body that had been buried.

That emptiness is the public sign of the Gospel’s center. Paul writes that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). If Christ has not been raised, faith is futile and we are still in our sins (1 Corinthians 15:17). But He has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The empty tomb therefore confirms penal substitution and justification: He “was delivered over to death for our sins and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25). It also declares Him to be the Son of God in power (Romans 1:4) and gives believers a living hope (1 Peter 1:3).

Because the tomb is empty, death does not have the last word. Those united to Christ by faith share His resurrection life now and will be raised with Him (Romans 6:4–5; 1 Corinthians 15:51–57). A holy God judges sin, and we cannot remove our guilt by effort or religion. Jesus, truly God and truly man, died as the substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Matthew 28, Luke 24, and 1 Corinthians 15 slowly, and ask the Lord to let the empty tomb steady you when fear or guilt presses in. What part of the resurrection accounts would you like to look at more closely?

question: What is traducianism?
answer:
Traducianism is the view that a child’s soul is transmitted from the parents, so that body and soul are propagated together, rather than each soul being created immediately by God.

This belongs to the doctrine of humanity, and it is a non-essential matter. Faithful Christians have disagreed about it because Scripture teaches that God gives life and forms each person, yet it does not explicitly describe the precise way every soul originates. Charity, not division, should mark the difference (Romans 14:1).

One historic view is traducianism. It holds that the soul, like the body, is derived from the parents. Some early teachers, especially Tertullian, defended this, and later writers have sometimes preferred it because it seems to fit the way a sinful nature passes to us through our union with Adam (Romans 5:12–19).

The other major view is creationism. It teaches that God creates each soul directly and unites it to the body He is forming. Many Christians, including a strong stream in the Reformed tradition, have held this, pointing to God breathing life into Adam (Genesis 2:7) and to God as the Father of spirits (Hebrews 12:9). The notion that souls existed before their bodies has been rejected by historic orthodoxy.

Both views can affirm what Scripture makes plain: every person is a body-soul unity made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27), and the Lord knits each life together in the womb (Psalm 139:13–16). The debate concerns the mode of origin, not human dignity or our need for redemption. I find creationism more natural to the Bible’s stress on God’s direct care for each soul, while I respect traducianism as a serious effort to honor our solidarity in Adam. Neither view is required for faithful Christianity.

Receive your own life as God’s gift, and treat every neighbor as an image-bearer whose soul matters eternally. If you want a simple next step, read Genesis 2:7 and Psalm 139:13–16 this week, and thank the Lord for the life He gives and the salvation He offers in Christ.

question: I am a Buddhist, why should I consider becoming a Christian?
answer:
I appreciate your honesty in asking this, and I respect the seriousness of your Buddhist path in seeking an end to suffering and a life marked by wisdom and compassion. You may feel that Christianity’s claim of one exclusive Savior is narrow beside a tradition centered on personal insight and ethical effort, or that trusting a historical death and resurrection seems less direct than meditation and the disciplined path toward liberation. Those concerns are understandable.

The Bible teaches that the one true God is holy and personal, the Maker of all things, and that every person has sinned by turning from Him, bringing real guilt and separation that self-effort cannot remove (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). Christians believe Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, who entered history, lived without sin, died on the cross as a penal substitutionary sacrifice bearing the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day (John 1:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). That finished work secures justification by grace alone through faith alone, not by our attainments (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 4:5). He alone is the mediator, as He said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). The hope offered is forgiven relationship with God and resurrection life, not another cycle of striving.

I invite you to turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A concrete step is to read the Gospel of John over the coming weeks, paying attention to who Jesus claims to be and what He offers those who believe. What aspect of your Buddhist practice has been most meaningful, or which part of this Christian claim feels hardest to consider?

question: How should a Christian view the intellect?
answer:
A Christian should view the intellect as a good gift from God, part of bearing His image, meant to be redeemed from sin’s distortion and used in wholehearted love and obedience to Him.

God created humanity in His image, which includes the capacity to reason, know, and discern truth (Genesis 1:26–27). Jesus Himself commands us to love the Lord our God with all our mind (Matthew 22:37). The apostle Paul calls believers to be transformed by the renewing of the mind and to take every thought captive to obey Christ (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 10:5). Wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, not with unaided human cleverness (Proverbs 9:10).

Sin has real noetic effects: it darkens understanding and exchanges the truth of God for a lie (Romans 1:21–22; Ephesians 4:17–18). The intellect is therefore neither despised nor treated as autonomous. It is a faculty to be sanctified under the authority of Scripture, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, so that we think God’s thoughts after Him rather than exalting our own (1 Corinthians 2:10–16). Faith seeks understanding; it does not surrender to unbelief or to pride.

This week, set aside a few quiet minutes each day to read Romans 12:1–2 slowly and ask the Lord to renew one specific area of your thinking, then act on what He shows you in obedient love.

question: What does the Bible say about being zealous / having zeal?
answer:
The Bible treats zeal as intense devotion, and it can be either holy or harmful depending on its object. Holy zeal is a burning concern for God’s glory, His truth, and the good of others. Misplaced zeal is heat without light.

In Scripture, the same family of words can mean zeal or jealousy. The Hebrew *qin’ah* and the Greek *zēlos* describe a strong, exclusive devotion. That is why the Lord is called a jealous God: He will not share His glory or His covenant people with idols (Exodus 34:14; Isaiah 42:8). His own zeal secures what He has promised. Of the Messiah’s kingdom, Isaiah says that the zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish it (Isaiah 9:7).

Jesus lived this zeal. When He cleansed the temple, His disciples remembered, “Zeal for Your house will consume Me” (John 2:17; Psalm 69:9). He was not protecting His reputation. He was honoring His Father and guarding true worship.

Believers are called to the same earnestness, as a fruit of grace rather than a payment for it. Paul urges Christians not to let their zeal grow cold, but to keep spiritual fervor in serving the Lord (Romans 12:11). Christ gave Himself to redeem and purify a people “zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14). The risen Lord tells a lukewarm church to be zealous and repent (Revelation 3:19). Godly sorrow over sin produces this kind of earnest care (2 Corinthians 7:10–11), and it is always good to be zealous for a good purpose (Galatians 4:18).

Scripture also warns that fervor can be badly aimed. Israel had a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge, and so missed the righteousness that comes by faith in Christ (Romans 10:2–4). Before Paul knew Jesus, his zeal made him a persecutor of the church (Philippians 3:6; Galatians 1:13–14). James says bitter jealousy and selfish ambition are earthly and destructive (James 3:14–16). Jehu even boasted of his zeal for the LORD, yet he did not walk carefully in God’s ways (2 Kings 10:16; 2 Kings 10:31). Intensity is not the same as faithfulness.

So biblical zeal is not mere emotion, and it is not a way to earn justification. In progressive sanctification, the Spirit both warms a cold heart and restrains a harsh one. True zeal is shaped by truth, joined to love, and aimed at God’s glory (Romans 10:2; 1 Corinthians 10:31; 1 Corinthians 16:14). Even a faithful servant can grow weary in that zeal. Elijah said he had been very zealous for the LORD, and God met him not in the wind, earthquake, or fire, but with a gentle word and a renewed calling (1 Kings 19:10; 1 Kings 19:11–13).

This week, ask the Lord to show you one place where love has grown lukewarm, and one place where fervor may be running ahead of Scripture. Then take one concrete step of obedience, whether renewed prayer, a humble conversation, or faithful service in your local church, and let love govern the heat.

Where do you sense your own zeal needs either to be kindled or to be submitted more fully to God’s Word?

question: What is the grace of God?
answer:
The grace of God is His free, unmerited favor toward sinners who deserve judgment, not reward. It is kindness given, not wages earned.

Scripture sets this against human merit. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:23-24). We were dead in trespasses, and God made us alive together with Christ: by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast (Ephesians 2:1-9). That saving grace is not a vague kindness. It comes to us in Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Titus 2:11). Justification is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

Grace also trains those who belong to Christ to renounce ungodliness and to live in grateful obedience, not as a way to earn favor already freely given (Titus 2:11-14). This week, set aside a quiet time to read Ephesians 2:1-10 slowly, and speak to God directly about one place where you are tempted to trust your own effort instead of His gift.

If you have never trusted Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. What about God’s grace feels most real to you right now, or most difficult to receive?

question: How young can you be to ask Jesus to be your Savior? Can a 3 or 4 year old truly believe?
answer:
Yes, a three or four year old can truly believe in Jesus as Savior. Scripture sets no minimum age, and Jesus welcomed little children, saying the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these (Matthew 19:14; Mark 10:14).

Faith is not a high intellectual achievement. It is trusting the Lord Jesus, and that trust is the gift of the Holy Spirit who gives new birth (John 3:3-8). Every person, including a small child, is a sinner who falls short of God’s glory and needs a Savior (Romans 3:23; Psalm 51:5). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross as the substitute who bore the penalty for sin, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by how much they can explain or by any work they perform (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 10:9-13).

A young child can grasp these truths in a simple way: that they do wrong, that Jesus loves them and died for them, and that they may ask Him to forgive them and be their Lord. Timothy knew the holy Scriptures from childhood, and those Scriptures are able to make one wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus (2 Timothy 3:15). True belief is more than repeating a parent’s words or feeling a moment of emotion. Over time it shows itself in love for Jesus, a growing desire to obey, and dependence on Him. Parents and churches should watch for that fruit with patience rather than pressure a quick profession.

If you are guiding a little one, keep the Gospel plain and steady. Read a short Bible story each day, explain simply that Jesus took the punishment we deserve and is alive, and pray that the Lord would open the child’s heart. Seek the wisdom of your local church elders as you discern what is genuine. Do not doubt that God can save the young, and do not treat a recited prayer as a formula that saves by itself.

If you have never turned from your sin and trusted Jesus, who died and rose for you, repent and believe in Him today for forgiveness and new life. He receives all who come to Him in faith, whether young or old.

How are you hoping to share these truths with the child you have in mind?

question: Is it wrong for a Christian husband and wife to attend separate churches?
answer:
Attending separate churches is not always sinful for a Christian husband and wife, since Scripture gives no explicit command that spouses must belong to the same local congregation. It is ordinarily unwise, however, because it can work against the unity God intends for marriage.

Marriage is a one-flesh union in which husband and wife are called to walk together in life and faith (Genesis 2:24; Ephesians 5:31). The husband bears loving spiritual headship and the wife offers respectful partnership, and worshiping side by side in a healthy local church normally strengthens that calling rather than straining it (Ephesians 5:22-33; Hebrews 10:24-25).

Some believers hold that separate attendance contradicts this unity and the New Testament pattern of households sharing one faith-expression, and therefore should be avoided except in rare cases such as clear heresy or brief necessity. Others appeal to Christian liberty in disputable matters and believe spouses may attend different churches when secondary convictions differ, provided they pursue peace, continue gathering with believers, and refuse to let the difference divide their home (Romans 14:1-13; Romans 14:19).

The wiser path in most situations is for a husband and wife to worship and serve together in the same church. Separate attendance can quietly erode oneness, complicate the shared discipleship of any children, and make loving leadership harder to practice. Where convictions differ, pray, speak honestly, and seek a congregation both can join with a clear conscience, the husband taking gentle initiative in that search.

If this describes your marriage, set aside time this week to read Ephesians 5 together, name your concerns without accusation, and ask the Lord for wisdom and unity. You may also seek counsel from a trusted pastor or a mature couple who knows you both.

question: What is the Druze religion?
answer:
The Druze religion is a distinct, closed monotheistic faith that arose in the early 11th century in Fatimid Egypt and is practiced today mainly by hereditary communities in Syria, Lebanon, Israel, and Jordan. Adherents, who often call themselves Muwahhidun, affirm one God, teach the transmigration of souls, and reserve their core scriptures (the Epistles of Wisdom) and fuller teachings for an initiated minority, while living by an ethic of truthfulness and loyalty within their people.

Christians believe the Bible is God’s inspired and final Word, revealing one God who exists eternally as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and declaring that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. He died for sinners and rose bodily from the dead, so that forgiveness and eternal life are given by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by secret knowledge or repeated earthly lives (John 1:1; John 1:14; John 14:6; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9). We are called to honor every person and to share this hope with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). If you want to explore what Scripture says about God or the way of salvation, I am glad to walk through it with you.

question: What is an invocation prayer?
answer:
An invocation prayer is a prayer that calls upon God, usually at the opening of worship, asking Him to draw near, bless His people, and help them as they come before Him.

In Scripture, the people of God are marked by calling on His name. Paul addresses the church as those who "call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:2), and the psalmist says the Lord is near to all who call upon Him in truth (Psalm 145:18). Christian invocation is not a charm or a formula that forces God to act. It is humble petition offered through the mediation of Christ, our great High Priest, who gives us access to the throne of grace (Hebrews 4:14–16; John 14:13–14). Many churches also name the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, acknowledging the one God we worship.

The exact wording is a matter of Christian liberty. Some congregations use a set form, and others pray freely. What matters is that the prayer is offered in faith, in Jesus' name, and for God's glory rather than as empty ceremony (Matthew 6:7–9).

A simple next step is this: the next time you begin family worship, a small group, or your own quiet time, address the Father, confess your need, ask the Spirit to help you hear His Word, and close in the name of Jesus.

question: What is the spiritual gift of prophecy?
answer: The spiritual gift of prophecy is the Holy Spirit’s enablement to proclaim a revelation from God for the edification, encouragement, and comfort of the church (1 Corinthians 12:10; 1 Corinthians 14:3). Continuationists offer a charitable argument that this gift continues in a subordinate form that must be carefully tested, since the apostles told believers both to desire prophecy and not to treat it with contempt (1 Corinthians 14:1; 1 Thessalonians 5:20). As one faithful option within historic Christianity, I hold to cessationism, convinced that prophecy as new revelation ceased once the apostolic foundation was laid and the canon was complete, so that nothing now rivals the full sufficiency of Scripture (Ephesians 2:20; 2 Timothy 3:16-17). This week, set aside time to read 1 Corinthians 14 slowly, asking the Lord to increase your confidence in the preached Word as the church’s sure and sufficient guide.

question: What does the Bible say about purification?
answer:
The Bible presents purification as God’s work of making people clean so they may draw near to Him, first through ceremonial rites that foreshadowed a greater cleansing, and finally through the blood of Jesus Christ.

Under the old covenant, God gave Israel laws for ritual purification after contact with death, disease, or bodily impurity. These involved washing, waiting, and sacrifice so a person could rejoin the community and worship (Leviticus 11–15; Numbers 19). The rites taught that the Lord is holy and that impurity separates people from Him (Leviticus 11:44–45). Animal blood and water could restore outward cleanness for a time, yet they could not perfect the conscience or remove sin (Hebrews 9:9–10; Hebrews 10:1–4). They were shadows pointing forward.

Jesus Christ fulfilled what those shadows promised. By His once-for-all sacrifice He made purification for sins (Hebrews 1:3). His blood cleanses from all sin, and when we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:7; 1 John 1:9). This cleansing rests on penal substitution: Christ bore the penalty our sins deserved so that sinners might be justified, declared righteous before God, and set apart as His own people (Romans 3:25–26; Titus 2:14; Hebrews 9:14). Hearts are sprinkled clean and we may draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Hebrews 10:22).

Those who belong to Christ also pursue ongoing purification. We cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit out of reverence for God, relying on the Holy Spirit and the washing of water by the Word (2 Corinthians 7:1; Ephesians 5:25–26; John 17:17). This is progressive sanctification, the fruit of already being accepted in Christ, not a ladder we climb to earn His favor. Everyone who hopes in Him purifies himself as He is pure (1 John 3:3).

If guilt or a sense of uncleanness weighs on you, the way forward is not self-cleansing by effort or ritual but honest confession and fresh trust in the cross. This week, read 1 John 1:5–10 slowly and bring specific sins to the Lord in prayer, asking Him to cleanse you according to His promise. If you have never trusted Christ, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Is there a particular burden or passage you would like to bring into the light of this truth?

question: Does the Bible say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times?
answer:
No, the Bible does not say that an increase in technology is a sign of the end times.

The verse most often connected with this idea is Daniel 12:4, which states that at the time of the end many will roam to and fro and knowledge will increase. Details of biblical eschatology form a non-essential area where faithful Christians may disagree, because prophetic texts use symbolic imagery and do not map every future development in explicit terms. Charity and liberty should mark our differences here, as Romans 14:1-5 calls us not to pass judgment on one another over disputable matters.

Some Christians read Daniel 12:4 as describing the surge in travel and information that modern technology has produced, and they view that surge as one marker that Christ’s return is near. Other Christians take the same verse as promising that people will search out the meaning of Daniel’s long-sealed prophecies, so that knowledge of God’s plan grows as the end approaches, without a necessary reference to human inventions.

Jesus named wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, and the gospel preached to all nations as coming events, yet He called them the beginning of birth pains and declared that no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:6-14; Matthew 24:36). Paul pictured the last days mainly in terms of moral confusion and false teaching (2 Timothy 3:1-5). A steady path is to remain spiritually awake rather than matching each new device to a prophecy. This week, read Matthew 24 slowly and ask the Lord to help you live ready for His return by trusting Him and serving faithfully in your local church.

Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. The way to be prepared is to repent and trust in Him who died for our sins and rose bodily from the grave. If you want to talk about what that trust looks like in daily life, I am glad to listen.

question: What does the Bible say about caring for our old parents?
answer:
The Bible commands believers to honor and care for their parents, including in old age, as a matter of loving obedience to God.

God’s law says, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12), and the New Testament repeats this command with a promise of blessing (Ephesians 6:1–3). Honor is more than polite words. It includes practical provision and respect when parents grow weak. Scripture specifically warns, “Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old” (Proverbs 23:22). Jesus rebuked religious people who used pious excuses to withhold support from their parents, calling that a rejection of God’s commandment (Mark 7:9–13).

The apostle Paul is equally plain. Children and grandchildren ought to show godliness first at home by caring for their own family, “for this is pleasing in the sight of God” (1 Timothy 5:4). He adds that anyone who fails to provide for relatives, and especially for members of his household, “has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). Even in His suffering, Jesus entrusted His mother to the care of a disciple (John 19:26–27), showing that this duty remains holy.

This care belongs to progressive sanctification: the Spirit forms us to love as Christ loved, putting another’s real needs ahead of our convenience.
