In practice that may look like regular visits, patient listening, help with daily tasks or decisions, financial support according to your ability, or coordinating with siblings so the burden is shared.

A wise next step is to have an honest conversation this week with your parents, or with your brothers and sisters if your parents cannot speak for themselves, and ask what help they actually need. Then bring that situation to your local church elders or a mature believer for prayer and counsel, so you do not carry it alone. Ask God for patience, wisdom, and a tender heart, trusting that the same Lord who gives the command also supplies grace for it (Philippians 4:19; Hebrews 4:16).

Is there a particular need or difficulty with your parents that you would like help thinking through in light of Scripture?

question: Does salvation affect more than just the afterlife?
answer:
Yes, salvation affects both this present life and the life to come. It is God’s rescue of sinners from the guilt of sin, the enslaving power of sin, and finally the very presence of sin, beginning the moment a person trusts Christ and reaching its fullness at His return.

Through faith, God justifies the believer, declaring them righteous on the basis of Christ’s penal substitutionary death and perfect obedience, so that they have peace with God now rather than waiting only for a future verdict (Romans 5:1; Romans 3:21-26). He adopts them as His children and regenerates them by the Holy Spirit, making them a new creation in union with Christ (Galatians 4:4-7; 2 Corinthians 5:17; John 3:3-8). This gift is by grace alone through faith alone, not by any works a person can offer (Ephesians 2:8-9).

That new standing shows itself in progressive sanctification. The Spirit steadily conforms believers to Christ’s image, giving them power to turn from sin, love others, endure trials with hope, and serve in the church through the Word, prayer, and fellowship (Romans 6:11-14; Philippians 1:6; Romans 8:1; Hebrews 10:24-25). A Christian can therefore know forgiveness today, walk in new obedience, and find purpose that is not postponed until death.

The same salvation will be completed when Christ returns. He will raise His people bodily and dwell with them forever in a renewed creation where death, mourning, and sin are gone (1 Corinthians 15:20-23; Revelation 21:3-4; Romans 8:18-23). What begins in justification and continues in sanctification ends in glorification.

Everyone needs this rescue, because all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, standing separated from Him (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary. He lived without sin, died on the cross bearing the penalty sinners deserve, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; John 1:14). He alone is the mediator between God and people (1 Timothy 2:5; John 14:6).

If you have never trusted Him, repent of your sin and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ alone for the forgiveness of sins and the gift of eternal life that starts now (Acts 16:31; John 3:16). One concrete step is to read Romans 5–8 this week, asking God to show you how justification, present change, and future hope belong together, and to speak with a pastor at a Bible-teaching church about what you read.

What part of life with God, whether present peace or future hope, feels most unclear or most needed to you right now?

question: What is the difference between Judaism and Islam?
answer:
Judaism and Islam both confess one God and honor Abraham, yet they differ in their sacred texts, their account of later revelation, and above all their judgment concerning Jesus Christ.

Judaism receives the Tanakh (the Hebrew Scriptures) as God’s Word and still awaits a Messiah who will restore Israel, grounding its life in the covenants given to Abraham, Moses, and David and in ongoing faithfulness to the Torah. Islam, which arose in the seventh century, receives the Quran as the final revelation through Muhammad and regards earlier prophets as true messengers whose writings were later corrupted. Muslims honor Jesus (Isa) as a virgin-born prophet who worked miracles, but they deny that He is the eternal Son of God, that He was truly crucified, and that He rose from the dead.

These are not small disagreements. Scripture presents Jesus as the Christ, truly God and truly man in one person (the hypostatic union), who bore the penalty of sin in the place of sinners and was raised bodily on the third day (John 1:1; John 1:14; Isaiah 53:5-6; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That confession of penal substitution and of justification by grace alone through faith alone stands at the center of the Gospel. Traditional Judaism looks for another deliverer; Islam teaches that the cross did not accomplish what the apostles proclaimed. The Bible declares that all have sinned and that righteousness before the holy God comes only through faith in Christ’s atoning death and resurrection, not by Torah observance or by works of submission (Romans 3:23-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). Jesus said, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me” (John 14:6; see also Acts 4:12).

Christians are called to love their Jewish and Muslim neighbors and to speak this good news with gentleness. If you are weighing these matters, read the Gospel of John alongside Isaiah 53 and ask the living God to show you whether Jesus is the promised Messiah who died and rose for sinners. Turn from sin and trust in Him alone for forgiveness and new life.

question: What does it mean to trust in the person and work of Jesus Christ?
answer:
To trust in the person and work of Jesus Christ means to rely entirely on who He is and what He has accomplished to save sinners, rather than on your own goodness, religious effort, or moral record. It is the faith by which God justifies the ungodly, freely counting Christ’s righteousness as yours.

The person of Christ is the eternal Son, truly God and truly man in one person (the hypostatic union). He took on human nature by the Holy Spirit and was born of the Virgin Mary, lived without sin, and is Lord over all (John 1:1; John 1:14; Philippians 2:6-11; Colossians 2:9). The work of Christ is His perfect obedience, His sacrificial death on the cross as our substitute (penal substitution), His burial, and His bodily resurrection on the third day, by which He conquered sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 3:23-26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Isaiah 53:5-6). On the cross He bore the wrath our sins deserve, and in the resurrection God vindicated Him and secured forgiveness and new life for all who are united to Him.

Biblical trust is more than nodding at facts. It includes knowing the truth about Christ, agreeing that it is true, and personally resting on Him alone for forgiveness and eternal life. Scripture calls this being justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 4:5; Romans 10:9-13; John 3:16; Acts 16:31). You stop presenting your own record to God and receive Christ as Savior and Lord, so that His death counts for your guilt and His righteousness counts for your acceptance.

A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John and Romans 3-5 this week, asking God to open your eyes to Christ, and to speak with a pastor or mature believer in a Bible-teaching local church who can walk with you. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What is stirring in you as you consider resting on Christ rather than on yourself?

question: Who was Plato? How did Platonism / Platonic thought influence society in Bible times?
answer:
Plato (about 428–348 BC) was a Greek philosopher, a student of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, who founded the Academy in Athens. He is best known for the theory of Forms, teaching that eternal perfect realities stand behind the changing physical world, and for his view that the soul is immortal and distinct from the body.

Platonism shaped parts of society in Bible times chiefly after Alexander the Great, when Greek language and ideas spread across the eastern Mediterranean. By the first century, when the New Testament was written, educated circles in cities such as Athens and Alexandria knew Middle Platonic themes: a higher invisible realm more real than the visible world, and the soul’s superiority to the body. Most Jews in the land of Israel stayed centered on the Law, the Temple, and the hope of God’s kingdom. In the diaspora, however, some thinkers such as Philo of Alexandria used Platonic categories to read Moses allegorically. The apostles did not adopt that method. They announced God’s historical acts, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

Paul reasoned in Athens with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, and the broader Greek climate, including Platonic strains, was in the air (Acts 17:18). Many of those hearers could imagine the soul surviving death, yet they mocked when he preached the resurrection of the dead (Acts 17:32). Scripture teaches a different hope. God made the material world good (Genesis 1:31), and believers will be raised bodily, sharing the glory of Christ’s resurrection rather than escaping the body as a prison (1 Corinthians 15:42-49). That is why Paul warns the church not to be taken captive by philosophy built on human tradition instead of on Christ (Colossians 2:8). Biblical anthropology therefore rejects Platonic dualism and confesses the bodily resurrection as part of God’s renewal of all things.

A practical next step is to read Acts 17:16-34 and 1 Corinthians 15 this week, asking God for discernment to test every cultural idea by His Word. Which part of this background, Plato’s own teaching or the apostles’ response, would you like to look at more closely?

question: Is a virtual/online communion service biblical?
answer:
Virtual or online communion does not follow the biblical pattern for the Lord’s Supper, which Scripture presents as an ordinance of the physically gathered church.

The strongest charitable argument on the other side is that, when providence truly prevents assembly, believers may still take bread and cup in their homes while joined by livestream, exercising faith in Christ’s spiritual presence and obeying the charge to remember His death until He comes.

I hold that the Supper’s biblical shape calls for the embodied gathering of the local church under its elders, because the New Testament ties right observance to coming together as one body and portrays that unity through shared bread and cup; regular online communion therefore falls short of that pattern. This is one faithful reading within historic Christianity, not the only orthodox conclusion, since some churches have allowed narrow emergency exceptions while still agreeing the Supper is a church ordinance rather than a private devotion.

Paul’s correction assumes a physical assembly: “when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. … when you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat,” and he tells them to “wait for one another” (1 Corinthians 11:17, 20, 33). The shared loaf itself preaches union: “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf” (1 Corinthians 10:17). That corporate, embodied sign is what the ordinance is given to display, alongside self-examination and discerning the body (1 Corinthians 11:28-29). Christ’s spiritual presence is truly enjoyed in the Supper when it is rightly observed, yet that presence does not detach the meal from the gathered church.

In ordinary times, keep the Table for when the church can meet in person. If illness, distance, or crisis keeps you away, speak with your elders about how the congregation cares for the absent, rather than treating a livestream as a full substitute, and use the waiting to examine your heart before the Lord.

question: Why do some churches thrive while others die?
answer:
Some churches thrive because they stay anchored to Jesus Christ and the gospel, while others fade when they drift from Him into compromise, coldness, or self-reliance.

The Lord Jesus promised to build His church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). That promise secures the Church across the ages. Local congregations, however, can lose their witness. Jesus warned the believers in Ephesus that if they did not repent and return to their first love, He would remove their lampstand (Revelation 2:4-5). In Scripture, a church’s life is measured by faithfulness to Christ more than by size or reputation.

Healthy churches devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer, and they see the Lord at work among them (Acts 2:42; Acts 2:47). They grow as God gives the increase, for the planter and the waterer are nothing apart from Him (1 Corinthians 3:6-7). They speak the truth in love and build one another up under Christ’s headship (Ephesians 4:15-16). At the heart of that health is clear gospel proclamation: sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, who died for our sins and rose bodily on the third day.

Congregations decline when they tolerate false teaching or immorality (Revelation 2:14-16; Revelation 2:20), grow lukewarm and proud of their resources (Revelation 3:15-17), or fracture through rivalry and immaturity (1 Corinthians 1:10-13; 1 Corinthians 3:3). Neglect of gathering for mutual encouragement also weakens a church (Hebrews 10:24-25). Sometimes a faithful church remains small or even closes its doors because of persecution, population shifts, or other hardships, yet Christ still counts it rich, as He did the suffering church in Smyrna (Revelation 2:9-10). We should be slow to assume that every closed building signals spiritual failure, and quick to examine our own hearts.

A practical step is to read Revelation 2 and Revelation 3 slowly this week, asking the Lord to search your congregation and your own love for Him. Then pray each day that your church would treasure Christ, repent where needed, and hold fast to the gospel. If you are able, encourage your elders by asking how you can support the ministry of the Word and prayer in concrete ways.

question: How much authority should a pastor have over a church?
answer: Pastors should have real but servant-hearted authority to teach, shepherd, and oversee the local church under Christ, shared among elders and always bounded by Scripture. Some faithful Christians in strongly congregational traditions argue that a pastor should hold mainly a teaching role while the membership keeps nearly all ruling authority, because this best guards against abuse and honors the priesthood of all believers. I hold to elder-led congregationalism as one sound historic approach within the church: a plurality of pastors exercises genuine leadership in doctrine, direction, and discipline, while the congregation affirms key decisions such as membership and discipline, since the New Testament both calls believers to submit to their leaders and involves the whole assembly in weighty judgments (Hebrews 13:17; 1 Timothy 5:17; Matthew 18:15-17; 1 Peter 5:1-3). In practice, this means your pastor should be free to preach the whole counsel of God without a vote on every text, while you and your fellow members stay responsible to test that teaching by Scripture, support godly oversight, and act together if an elder must be corrected.

question: What is Luciferianism?
answer:
Luciferianism is a religious and philosophical outlook that honors Lucifer as a figure of enlightenment, knowledge, and self-rule, rather than as the enemy of God.

The name comes from the Latin word lucifer, “light-bearer.” In Isaiah 14:12 the Berean Standard Bible translates the Hebrew as “morning star, son of the dawn.” The immediate subject there is the proud king of Babylon, who said, “I will make myself like the Most High,” and was brought down (Isaiah 14:13–15). Christian readers have long recognized in that pride the same rebellion Scripture attributes to Satan, whom Jesus said He saw fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18).

People who call themselves Luciferians do not all agree. Some venerate Lucifer as a real spiritual being. Others treat the name as a symbol of the person who rejects God’s authority in the name of freedom. What they share is a reversal of the biblical story: pride is renamed liberation, and the holy God is treated as a tyrant to outgrow. That is idolatry. It gives a creature the honor that belongs to God alone. Scripture also warns that the offer of light can itself be a lie: “Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14).

The true light is not a fallen creature but the Lord Jesus Christ. He said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). Real freedom is not becoming your own god. It is being forgiven by the One who died for sinners and rose bodily on the third day.

If this question comes from curiosity, or from a pull toward that path, read Isaiah 14 and John 8 slowly, and bring your questions to God in prayer and to a pastor in a Bible-teaching church. The hunger for light and freedom is not foolish. It is simply aimed at the wrong source until it rests in Christ. Turn from self-exaltation and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and true life.

Would you like to look more closely at what Scripture says about Satan, or at why Jesus claims to be the light?

question: What is the satisfaction or commercial theory of the atonement?
answer:
The satisfaction theory of the atonement, also called the commercial theory because it uses the language of debt and payment, teaches that Christ’s death satisfied God’s offended honor and justice by paying the infinite debt human sin had incurred. Anselm of Canterbury set this view forward in the Middle Ages, arguing that only the God-man could offer a satisfaction finite sinners could never provide.

This account rightly sees the cross as meeting a real demand of God’s holiness rather than merely moving human feelings. Scripture presents the fuller truth of penal substitutionary atonement: Christ bore the penalty due to sinners so that God remains just while justifying everyone who trusts in Jesus (Romans 3:25-26; Isaiah 53:5-6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

Because that satisfaction is already complete, you do not have to balance your own moral ledger to be accepted. Rest in Christ’s finished work this week, and let gratitude for His payment shape both your prayers and your obedience.

question: Who are the Shakers?
answer:
The Shakers were members of the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing, a religious movement that began in England in the eighteenth century and later formed communal villages in America under Ann Lee.

They were called Shakers because their worship included trembling, singing, and dancing. They practiced celibacy, shared property, lived simply, refused military service, and gave men and women equal roles in community life. Their furniture and crafts became well known. Because they forbade marriage and childbearing, the movement depended on new converts. It reached a few thousand members in the nineteenth century and has nearly disappeared, with only a very small remnant in recent years.

Their central claim set them outside the Christian faith. They taught that Christ's second appearing had come in Ann Lee, as a female manifestation of Christ. Scripture teaches one incarnation: the eternal Son became flesh, truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary (John 1:14; Luke 1:34–35). That union of divine and human natures in the one person of Jesus is what Christians call the hypostatic union. He will return personally and bodily, just as the apostles saw Him ascend (Acts 1:11). No later leader completes or repeats that appearing.

They also required celibacy of every member. Scripture honors marriage (Hebrews 13:4) and warns against teachings that forbid it (1 Timothy 4:1–3). Singleness is a gift for some, not a law for all (1 Corinthians 7:7–9). Entrance into a celibate community does not justify anyone before God. People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Their love of simplicity can still prompt a useful question: have comforts and possessions quietly taken hold of the heart? The remedy is not a new founder, but the Lord Jesus, who died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily, and who alone is the way to the Father (John 14:6).

question: What is the favor of God, and how can I get it?
answer:
The favor of God is His unmerited grace and kind approval, freely given to sinners who trust in Jesus Christ. It is not earned by human effort or religious performance.

It is understandable to hope that a moral life or religious duties might win God's smile, yet the Bible teaches that every person has sinned and falls short of God's glory, so that apart from Christ we stand under His righteous wrath instead of His favor (Romans 3:23; Ephesians 2:3). In love, God sent His Son, Jesus Christ, who is truly God and truly man. Conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the virgin Mary, He lived a sinless life, died on the cross bearing the penalty of sin in the place of sinners through penal substitution, was buried, and rose bodily from the dead on the third day (Luke 1:35; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8).

Those who repent and believe are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, receiving God's favor, forgiveness, and peace with Him as a gift, not a wage (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 5:1). This is the heart of the gospel.

I invite you to turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of your sins and the gift of God's everlasting favor. As a next step, read the Gospel of John this week, especially chapters 1 and 3, and speak honestly to God about your sin and your need for a Savior, asking Him to open your eyes to trust Christ. Find a church that treasures the Bible so you can hear the Word and walk with other believers.

What fears or questions arise in your heart when you think about receiving God's favor through Jesus alone?

question: What does it mean that Jesus is the Savior?
answer:
Jesus is the Savior because He alone rescues sinners from guilt, the power of sin, and the righteous judgment of a holy God. He does not merely point the way. He accomplishes a deliverance we could never achieve for ourselves.

The angel told Joseph to name the child Jesus, "because He will save His people from their sins" (Matthew 1:21). His name means "the Lord saves." In the Greco-Roman world, "savior" was a title given to gods and rulers who claimed to rescue people from danger. Scripture reserves true salvation for God, and then confesses that Jesus is that Savior: "Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12; Titus 2:13).

We need a Savior because God is holy and we are not. "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). Sin is rebellion against the God who made us, and "the wages of sin is death" (Romans 6:23). Good intentions, moral effort, and religious activity cannot remove our guilt or reconcile us to Him.

Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, and He lived the perfect life we have failed to live. On the cross He died in our place. That is penal substitution: the sinless One bore the penalty our sins deserved, "so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God" (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily from the dead, defeating sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). God has exalted Him as Lord.

Those who trust Him are justified, which means God declares them righteous by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Romans 3:24-26; Ephesians 2:8-9). He also begins to free them from sin's power now, and He will one day free them from its presence forever.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A simple next step is to read John 3 and Romans 5 this week, and to speak honestly to God about your sin and your need of Him.

What question is still on your heart as you hear this?

question: What is baby dedication? Is child / baby dedication biblical?
answer:
Baby dedication is a public act in which parents present their child to the Lord before the church, give thanks, and vow to raise that child in the training and instruction of the Lord. It is not baptism, not a church ordinance, and it does not save the child or make the child a member of the new covenant.

The ceremony itself is not commanded in Scripture the way baptism and the Lord's Supper are. The heart of it is biblical. Hannah vowed Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:27-28). Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple according to God's word (Luke 2:22-24). Parents are told to teach God's words diligently to their children and to bring them up in the Lord's discipline and instruction (Deuteronomy 6:6-7; Ephesians 6:4). The Lord Jesus received little children and blessed them (Mark 10:13-16). Those texts give a godly pattern of stewardship and prayer. They do not turn dedication into a sacrament, and they do not copy the Mosaic rites into the church.

Faithful Christians differ here because they differ on baptism, a secondary matter that shapes church practice without deciding who belongs to Christ.

Those who baptize infants argue, with real weight, that the children of believers belong to the covenant community, that baptism replaces circumcision as the covenant sign, and that household baptisms show the sign rightly given to such children, so dedication without baptism leaves them unmarked (Colossians 2:11-12; Acts 16:15).

I hold believer's baptism, credo baptism, as one faithful reading within historic Christianity: the New Testament joins baptism to repentance and faith, so baptism waits for a credible confession of Christ (Acts 2:38; Acts 8:36-38). Dedication is then a fitting way for parents, and often the congregation with them, to own their calling in public without confusing a ceremony with regeneration or justification. The child is a living trust from God. The parents are the ones making the promise.

Dedication does not justify anyone before God. Parent and child alike need forgiveness through Christ's death and resurrection, received by faith, not by a family rite or a church service (Romans 3:23-26; Ephesians 2:8-9).

If you are preparing for this, sit with your pastor or elders, read Deuteronomy 6:4-9 and Ephesians 6:4 together, and name a few concrete ways you will pray, teach, and keep your child under the Word in a local church. Bring that need to the Lord in your own words, and ask a mature believer to pray with you (James 5:16).

Are you weighing a dedication in your own church, or comparing it with infant baptism?

question: Will God continue to forgive you if you commit the same sin over and over again?
answer:
The weight of repeating the same sin can make you fear that God's forgiveness has run out. God continues to forgive those who are in Christ and who keep turning back to Him in genuine repentance, because forgiveness rests on Jesus' finished sacrifice, not on an unbroken record of success.

If you belong to Christ by faith, your justification is secure: God declares you righteous by grace alone through faith alone, on the basis of Christ's life, death, and resurrection, so there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Ongoing confession belongs to the normal Christian life. If we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9). That justice was satisfied at the cross in Christ's penal substitutionary atonement, which is why His mercy does not expire when the sin is familiar (Psalm 103:8-12).

Repentance, though, is more than words offered while you plan to return to the sin. True faith produces progressive sanctification. No one born of God makes a practice of sinning without grief or resistance; the new heart keeps coming home (1 John 3:9; Proverbs 24:16). Treating forgiveness as a license to keep sinning denies the grace that trains us to renounce ungodliness (Romans 6:1-2; Titus 2:11-12). A settled pattern of sin without turning is a merciful warning to examine whether you have truly trusted Christ.

This week, confess that specific sin to God without excuses, thank Him that Jesus bore its penalty and rose again, and ask one mature believer in your church to pray with you and walk with you in accountability. Read slowly through Romans 6-8, asking the Spirit to put that sin to death in you (Romans 8:13).

We have all sinned and need a Savior. Jesus Christ died on the cross for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for full forgiveness and new life.

What does turning back to Him look like for you in this particular struggle right now?

question: Can monotheism be proven?
answer:
Monotheism cannot be proven by a mathematical demonstration or a laboratory test that removes every possibility of dissent, yet the one true God has given sufficient evidence of His existence and uniqueness that unbelief is without excuse.

You may wonder whether the sheer number of religious claims, or the fact that God does not submit to scientific instruments, leaves monotheism unprovable and therefore optional. Those hesitations are common and understandable. Christians believe, however, that God has made Himself known both in the created world and in Scripture, so that the issue is not a total lack of evidence but a response of the heart.

What may be known about God is plain, because He has shown it. Since the creation of the world His invisible attributes, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived in the things that have been made, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:19-20). The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1). This general revelation displays a single, coherent order rather than the rival wills of many ultimate gods. One uncaused Cause, one Designer, and one Moral Lawgiver accounts for the unity, contingency, and moral structure of the world more coherently than polytheism or sheer chance. In the ancient Near East, surrounded by the worship of many gods, Israel’s confession stood out sharply: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Lord Himself declares, “I am the LORD, and there is no other; besides me there is no God” (Isaiah 45:5). The New Testament maintains this same monotheism while revealing that the one God eternally exists as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 8:4-6; Matthew 28:19). That is the doctrine of the Trinity: one divine essence, three distinct persons, not three gods.

Such witness can answer objections and remove excuses, yet it does not mechanically produce faith. People suppress the truth in unrighteousness (Romans 1:18), and saving knowledge of God comes by grace through the Word (Romans 10:17; Ephesians 2:8-9). The one God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). He sent His Son, Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, who died on the cross as a penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). There is one God and one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works or by a vague belief that some deity exists.

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. A concrete next step is to read Romans 1 and John 1 slowly this week, asking God to give you understanding, and to speak with a pastor at a church that teaches the Bible.

What stands out to you most as you weigh this evidence, or what questions do you still have about Jesus?

question: What is impartation?
answer:
Impartation is the practice, common in charismatic and Pentecostal churches, of one believer conferring spiritual gifts, anointing, or special empowerment on another, usually through prayer and the laying on of hands.

Scripture records Paul longing to impart a spiritual gift to strengthen the Romans (Romans 1:11) and Timothy receiving a gift through prophecy and the laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6). Faithful Christians differ on whether miraculous gifts and this kind of impartation continue after the apostles. Continuationists hold that the Spirit still distributes gifts as He wills for the common good and that laying on of hands remains a biblical means of imparting them (1 Corinthians 12:11; Hebrews 6:2). I hold the cessationist view as one faithful option within historic Christianity, because those extraordinary signs and the apostolic impartation of them authenticated the foundational gospel message and ceased with the apostles and the completion of Scripture (2 Corinthians 12:12; Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 2:3-4).

Seek the Spirit’s ongoing grace through regular time in the Word, prayer, and faithful service under the shepherding of a local church, rather than through special impartation gatherings.

question: What is Atenism? Did either Judaism or Christianity borrow from Atenism?
answer:
Atenism was the short-lived religious reform of Pharaoh Akhenaten in fourteenth-century BC Egypt, in which he promoted exclusive worship of the sun disk Aten, suppressed the traditional gods, and relocated his capital to Akhetaten. It collapsed after his death and was not a lasting faith.

Neither Judaism nor Christianity borrowed its core faith from Atenism. The Bible teaches that the one true God revealed Himself by special revelation to the patriarchs and then to Moses, calling His people to worship Him alone as the holy Creator and covenant Lord, centuries before Akhenaten by the chronology of 1 Kings 6:1 (Genesis 12:1-3; Exodus 3:13-15; Deuteronomy 6:4). Some writers have proposed dependence, citing parallels between Akhenaten’s Hymn to the Aten and Psalm 104 or speculating about Moses, yet Scripture portrays the Lord executing judgment on the gods of Egypt rather than adopting their worship (Exodus 12:12). Aten remained a created solar power tied to the pharaoh, while the God of Israel is the personal, eternal, morally holy Lord who saves by grace.

Christianity continues this same revealed faith, fulfilled in Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, not in any Egyptian solar reform. When such theories surface, test them by the plain testimony of Scripture and ask the Lord to confirm His Word to you as you read Exodus 3 and Hebrews 1:1-2.

question: What happens to babies and young children when they die? Where do I find the age of accountability in the Bible?
answer:
The Bible never names an “age of accountability,” and you will not find that phrase, or any specific age, anywhere in Scripture. What it does give is a real hope for babies and very young children who die, joined to a clear refusal to rest that hope on innocence or on a number we invented.

Infants are not saved because they are innocent. David confessed, “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me” (Psalm 51:5). That is original sin. Death reaches even those who never sinned in the same way Adam did, because sin and death entered the human race through him (Romans 5:12–14). If a little one is received into heaven, it is only by the grace of Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, whose penal substitutionary death and bodily resurrection reconcile sinners to God.

Scripture does mark a difference between those who know good and evil and those who do not, without ever turning that difference into a cutoff age. Moses spoke of children who did not yet know good from evil (Deuteronomy 1:39). Isaiah spoke of a time before a boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good (Isaiah 7:15–16). God described many in Nineveh as unable to tell their right hand from their left (Jonah 4:11). Jesus took up actual little children and said, “Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matthew 19:14). These passages do not publish an age. They do show that God does not treat the morally unaware as He treats those who knowingly reject the light they have (John 9:41; Romans 1:18–20).

The most personal window is a father’s grief. After his infant son died, David said, “I will go to him, but he will not return to me” (2 Samuel 12:23). He was not describing a shared emptiness in the grave. He expected to go to the child. That is not a full system of doctrine, but Scripture records it for our comfort.

Faithful Christians have not all spoken with the same certainty here, and this difference does not decide whether someone belongs to Christ. Some, careful not to say more than is written, hold that elect infants who die are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and how He pleases, while leaving the extent of that mercy to God’s secret counsel. The strongest form of that caution is simply this: salvation is by grace in Christ, not by a rule we inferred, and the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25).

My own conviction, shared by many pastors in the Reformed tradition, is that babies and young children who die before they can understand and answer the gospel are saved by God’s sovereign mercy in Christ. Not by an age, not by a ritual that works by itself, and not by innocence, but by the same Savior who alone saves. I hold that because of God’s justice and tender mercy, David’s hope, Christ’s welcome of children, and the way Scripture ties personal guilt to light received. I will not pretend the Bible names a birthday on which accountability begins.

For you and me, the case is different. We do know good and evil. We have sinned against a holy God, and no age now shields us. Jesus lived without sin, died on the cross in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, not by works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

Do not wait for an imaginary age before you teach a child the gospel. A child who can grasp sin, the cross, and the call to trust Christ should be lovingly called to believe. Uncertainty about infants is no reason to postpone the good news with children who can hear it.

If this question is pressing because of a real loss, do not carry it alone. Bring your sorrow straight to the Lord, letting 2 Samuel 12 and Psalm 23 give shape to what you say to Him, and sit with a pastor or elder who can open the Scriptures with you in person.

Are you asking because you are walking through the death of a child, or because you want help explaining this to someone else?

question: What is the Church of Spiritualism?
answer:
The Church of Spiritualism belongs to the Spiritualist movement, a religion that teaches the living can communicate with the spirits of the dead, usually through mediums, and that souls continue and progress after death.

Spiritualist congregations took organized form in the nineteenth century, especially in the United States and Britain. Their services often include prayer, claimed messages from the departed, and spiritual healing. Many use the word “church” and speak of God, yet their center is mediumship, not the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

Scripture forbids this. In the ancient world around Israel, people commonly sought the dead for guidance, and the Lord set His people apart from that practice. He commanded that no one among them consult a medium or spiritist, or inquire of the dead, and He called such things detestable (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Leviticus 19:31). Isaiah asks why a people would consult the dead on behalf of the living instead of inquiring of their God (Isaiah 8:19). King Saul’s visit to the medium at Endor was not a permitted exception. It belonged to the unfaithfulness for which he was judged (1 Samuel 28:7–19; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14).

The Bible teaches that people die once and afterward face judgment (Hebrews 9:27). Those who die in Christ are with the Lord, which is far better (2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23). Jesus taught that a great chasm stands between the dead and the living, not a channel a medium can open (Luke 16:26). Messages that claim to come from departed loved ones are not a safe comfort. Scripture warns that deceiving spirits can present themselves as something they are not (2 Corinthians 11:14; 1 Timothy 4:1).

If grief has drawn you toward a voice from the other side, that ache is real, and God is not indifferent to sorrow. But the dead cannot mediate for us. There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). We are sinners, separated from a holy God. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. He alone is the way to the Father (John 14:6). Forgiveness and eternal life are given by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by contact with spirits or by moral progress after death.

Turn from seeking the dead, repent of sin, and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you. If this has touched your life, stop any involvement with mediums or séances, read Deuteronomy 18 and John 11, and bring both your grief and your questions to the Lord in prayer and to a pastor who submits to Scripture.

Are you asking because you have attended a Spiritualist church, or because you want to understand how this differs from the Christian hope?

question: What is Chrislam?
answer:
Chrislam is a term for religious syncretism that blends Christian and Islamic beliefs and practices, most often linked to certain groups in Nigeria that mix prayers, teachings, and rituals from both.

This blending lies outside the Christian faith because it denies truths Scripture presents as essential. The Bible reveals one God eternally existing as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man in the hypostatic union, died as a penal substitutionary sacrifice for sinners and rose bodily from the dead, so that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone. Islam denies the Trinity, the incarnation and deity of Christ, His crucifixion, and salvation apart from works. These claims cannot be joined without replacing the Gospel with a different message.

Jesus taught that He alone is the way to the Father (John 14:6). Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father (1 John 2:23). A different gospel is to be rejected even if an angel preached it (Galatians 1:8-9). Love for Muslim neighbors therefore means genuine kindness and respect joined to a clear witness that salvation is found in Christ alone (Acts 4:12; 1 Peter 3:15). A practical step is to read the Gospel of John carefully, marking the claims Jesus makes about Himself, so any conversation stays anchored in His words rather than in compromise.

question: Why should I forgive?
answer:
Forgiveness can feel impossible when someone has truly wounded you, and Scripture never treats that pain as small. You should forgive because the Lord commands it, and because He has already forgiven you an infinitely greater debt in Christ.

Jesus taught His disciples to pray, "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). He then said that if we forgive others their trespasses, our heavenly Father will also forgive us, and if we do not, neither will He forgive ours (Matthew 6:14-15). That is not a way to earn salvation by effort. It is the mark of a heart that has received mercy. In the parable of the unforgiving servant, a man forgiven an enormous debt refused to release a fellow servant from a small one, and the king called that refusal wicked (Matthew 18:21-35). We forgive because we have been forgiven.

This rests on the Gospel. God is holy, and all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). Our sin separates us from Him. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross in our place, bearing the penalty our sins deserved, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Those who repent and trust Him are justified by grace alone through faith alone, not by works. "Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you" (Ephesians 4:32). Forgiveness is how a justified sinner begins to resemble the Savior.

Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good, pretending the hurt never happened, or immediately trusting someone who remains unsafe. It means releasing your claim to personal vengeance and leaving justice with God, who says, "Vengeance is Mine; I will repay" (Romans 12:19). Where there is repentance, reconciliation may follow (Luke 17:3-4). Where there is ongoing harm, seek protection, wise counsel, and, when needed, proper authorities. Bitterness only corrodes the one who holds it (Hebrews 12:15).

A concrete next step: set aside time today to name the person and the wound before the Lord. Ask Him to show you the depth of His forgiveness toward you, and ask for grace to release that person from your demand to repay you. If the wound is deep, walk this with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can pray with you and help you discern wisdom from mere self-protection.

If you have never trusted Christ, the forgiveness you need first is His. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What is making forgiveness especially hard for you right now?

question: Who is Jesus — Day 2 — Jesus the Miracle Worker
answer:
Jesus is the Miracle Worker, the incarnate Son of God whose signs and wonders displayed divine authority, fulfilled messianic hope, and revealed the Father’s compassion.

In the Gospels He healed the sick, cast out demons, calmed storms, multiplied bread, and raised the dead. These were purposeful signs, not spectacles. John records that they were written so you may believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name (John 20:30-31). When the wind and waves obeyed Him, the disciples asked in awe who this could be (Mark 4:41). By the Spirit He drove out demons and declared that the kingdom of God had come upon them (Matthew 12:28). His works confirmed His words and showed that the promised reign of God had arrived in His person.

These acts also display the hypostatic union: Jesus is truly God, with authority over creation, disease, and death, and truly man, moved with compassion for the harassed and helpless (Matthew 9:36; Mark 1:41). He never used power to avoid suffering or to entertain crowds. Every temporary healing pointed beyond itself to a deeper need.

All of us have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and our iniquities have separated us from Him (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). The Miracle Worker did not remain only a healer of bodies. He went to the cross, bore the penalty of sin as our substitute, died, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, conquering sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That resurrection is the supreme sign that He is Lord and that forgiveness and new life are offered freely.

Turn from your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life. His power that stilled storms and raised the dead is the same power that saves and keeps all who belong to Him.

For a concrete next step, read one miracle account slowly this week, such as the man born blind in John 9 or Lazarus in John 11. Notice both what Jesus does and the heart behind it. Then bring one personal need or fear to Him directly in prayer, asking for faith to trust His wisdom even when the answer is not immediate relief.

Which miracle of Jesus most draws your attention right now, and why?

question: Who are the Mormons and what do they believe?
answer:
The people commonly called Mormons are members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, a religious movement founded by Joseph Smith in 1830. They teach that the early church fell into total apostasy and that God restored true authority and new scriptures through Smith, above all the Book of Mormon, which they receive alongside the Bible (accepted only “as far as it is translated correctly”), the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price.

They believe the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are three separate beings united in purpose, not one God. In their teaching God the Father has a body of flesh and bones, was once a man who progressed to godhood, and faithful people may likewise become gods through Christ’s atonement plus lifelong obedience, baptism, and temple ordinances that secure the highest glory, called exaltation. Jesus is honored as Savior, yet understood as the spirit offspring of heavenly parents rather than the eternal God who took on human nature.

These claims cannot be reconciled with the Bible or with the faith historic Christianity has confessed from the beginning. Scripture declares, “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4), and reveals the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as one God in three persons (Matthew 28:19; 2 Corinthians 13:14). “God is not a man, that He should lie” (Numbers 23:19). Jesus Christ is the eternal Word who “was with God” and “was God” (John 1:1-3), truly God and truly man, not a being who became divine. Sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, “not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 4:5). Paul warned that a different gospel, even if brought by an angel, is to be rejected (Galatians 1:8-9).

Many Latter-day Saints are sincere, morally earnest neighbors who genuinely believe they are following Jesus, and that desire for God is understandable. Sincerity, however, does not alter who God is or how He saves. All have sinned and fall short of God’s glory (Romans 3:23). Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). There is salvation in no other name (Acts 4:12; John 14:6).

Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, the eternal Son who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. If you would like, I can walk with you through how the Gospel of John presents Jesus, or how to speak with Latter-day Saint friends in both clarity and gentleness.

question: Is it allowable for a Christian to eat halal food?
answer:
Yes, it is allowable for a Christian to eat halal food. This is a non-essential matter of Christian liberty and diet, where faithful believers may disagree because Scripture supplies principles about foods, conscience, and love rather than a direct ruling on meat prepared with Islamic rites.

One major view holds that such food may be received freely. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), Peter was shown not to call common what God has cleansed (Acts 10:15), and everything created by God is good when received with thanksgiving, sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4-5). Believers may eat what is sold in the market without raising questions of conscience, for the earth is the Lord’s (1 Corinthians 10:25-26).

Another historic approach is that some Christians abstain. They regard the invocation of Allah at slaughter as akin to food identified with other gods, and so they refrain when that association is made plain, for the sake of conscience and to avoid any sense of sharing in worship not offered to the Triune God (1 Corinthians 10:20; 1 Corinthians 10:28).

Neither practice is required of every Christian. Romans 14 teaches us not to judge one another over food, but to act from faith, pursue peace, and build one another up (Romans 14:13-23). Whether you eat or abstain, do it to the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Bring the question to your pastor or elders for help applying these passages in your setting, whether at the store, in travel, or at a shared table, and ask the Lord for a conscience shaped by His Word and by love for your neighbor.

question: What does the Bible say about the role of youth pastor / minister?
answer:
The Bible does not establish a distinct office called youth pastor or youth minister. It provides elders (also called overseers and pastors) to shepherd the whole church and deacons to serve practical needs, while calling every believer to help others grow in Christ.

Elders must pay careful attention to the entire flock, because the Holy Spirit has made them overseers to care for the church of God (Acts 20:28). That flock includes young people, whom the Lord Jesus welcomed and blessed (Mark 10:13-16). Peter exhorts elders to shepherd God’s people willingly, eagerly, and as examples (1 Peter 5:1-3). Their work is to equip the saints for ministry so that the body of Christ is built up (Ephesians 4:11-12).

Scripture also stresses care for the next generation. Parents, and especially fathers, hold the primary duty to raise children in the training and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4; Deuteronomy 6:6-7). Alongside that, older believers are to teach what accords with sound doctrine and to train younger men and women in godly living (Titus 2:1-8). The whole church instructs and admonishes one another through the Word (Colossians 3:16). Youth itself is no barrier to faithful service. Paul told Timothy, “Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in purity” (1 Timothy 4:12).

A modern youth pastor or minister usually concentrates teaching, counseling, and discipleship on teenagers or young adults. How a church organizes that work is a matter of Christian liberty rather than a required office, since Scripture does not prescribe the title or structure. Some congregations appoint a dedicated youth pastor under the elders. Others disciple youth through the regular preaching, family ministry, and shared life of the church without a separate staff role. Both can be faithful when they stay under elder oversight, remain centered on Scripture, and refuse to isolate young people from the rest of the body.

Because “pastor” names the shepherding office, anyone who regularly teaches and exercises spiritual oversight in that role should meet the biblical qualifications for an elder: above reproach, self-controlled, able to teach sound doctrine, not a new convert, and managing his household well (1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9). Those passages, read with 1 Timothy 2:11-12, indicate that this office belongs to qualified men. Godly women serve indispensably by teaching other women and children and by many other ministries of the church (Titus 2:3-5).

Whatever form the ministry takes, its aim is to point young people to Jesus Christ, the chief Shepherd, who laid down his life for the sheep and rose again (John 10:11; 1 Peter 5:4). That means proclaiming his penal substitutionary atonement, calling them to trust him, and helping them grow in sanctification within the whole congregation rather than in a separate subculture.

If you lead or support youth ministry, set aside time this week to read 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 2:6-8 beside your current practices. Note where the work reflects sound teaching, godly example, and care for the whole church, then bring any needed adjustments to your elders with humility and prayer.

question: Why do Jehovah's Witnesses refuse blood transfusions?
answer:
Jehovah’s Witnesses refuse blood transfusions because they believe God forbids taking blood into the body, and they treat a transfusion as the same kind of act as eating blood.

They appeal especially to Genesis 9:4, Leviticus 17:10–14, and Acts 15:28–29. Those texts forbid consuming blood because life is in the blood: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11). Their organization teaches that this ban covers whole blood and its main components, while some smaller fractions are left to personal conscience. Accepting a prohibited transfusion has also brought congregational discipline, so the refusal is reinforced by real social cost, not only by private Bible reading.

Historic Christianity does not read those passages as a medical rule. In their ancient setting they address diet, sacrifice, and the sanctity of life, and in Acts 15 they also protect early-church unity by asking Gentile believers to avoid practices that would deeply offend Jewish consciences. They are not instructions about a procedure unknown in that world. The same Lord who honored the life in the blood also taught that mercy and saving life outweigh ceremonial restriction. He asked, “which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?” (Luke 6:9; see also Mark 2:27). Using donated blood to preserve a neighbor’s life honors that sanctity of life. It does not profane it.

This policy is a distinctive of the Jehovah’s Witness organization, not a teaching of the orthodox Christian faith. That body also denies essentials such as the Trinity and the full deity of Christ, so its claim to bind the conscience should be tested by Scripture itself, not by organizational decree.

I am not a physician, and this is not medical advice. If a transfusion decision is urgent, seek emergency medical care at once, and involve pastors who submit to the whole Bible. A useful next step is to read Leviticus 17:10–14 and Acts 15:1–29 in context, noting what is commanded, eating blood, and what is not addressed, modern medicine. If you want, we can walk through those passages together.

question: Does God pursue us?
answer:
Yes, God pursues us, actively seeking sinners who by nature do not seek Him.  
Many faithful Christians in Arminian traditions argue that God pursues every person with enabling grace through the Gospel, so His call is universal and our free response remains decisive.  
From a Reformed perspective, which I hold as one faithful reading within historic Christianity, God pursues His people with sovereign effectual calling, renewing their wills so they come willingly to Christ, since no one can come unless the Father draws him (John 6:44) and all the Father gives will come (John 6:37).  

This pursuit is the story of Scripture. After the fall the Lord called to Adam (Genesis 3:9). Jesus, the Good Shepherd, came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10; Luke 15:4-7). We require such pursuit because sin leaves us dead, unwilling, and unable, with no one righteous or seeking God (Romans 3:10-11; Ephesians 2:1).  

Yet God, holy and loving, sent His Son. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, died on the cross in penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He justifies the ungodly by grace alone through faith alone in Him alone, not by works (Romans 3:23-24; Ephesians 2:8-9).  

If you sense this pursuit, repent of your sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life. Read Luke 15 today and speak honestly to God about your heart, then share what you find with a pastor or mature believer at a local church.  

What has stirred this question for you?

question: Is God imaginary?
answer:
No, God is not imaginary. The Bible teaches that He is the eternal, living Creator who exists in Himself, whether or not anyone believes in Him.

You may wonder if God is only a comforting idea people invent, or if suffering and the limits of science mean He cannot be real. Those questions are understandable. Yet Christians believe God has made Himself known. The created world displays His power and divine nature, so that people are without excuse (Psalm 19:1; Romans 1:20). This witness is often called general revelation. God has also spoken in Scripture and, supremely, in His Son. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, said that anyone who has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9).

God’s existence does not rest on human imagination. The term aseity names this truth: God exists from Himself, uncreated and independent, as He revealed when He declared, “I AM” (Exodus 3:14).

Scripture is also clear that we are not neutral. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and that sin separates us from Him (Romans 3:23). God showed His love in this, that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). Jesus bore the penalty our sins deserved in what Christians call penal substitution, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). His resurrection is a real event in history, not a story we tell to feel better. Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works and not by persuading ourselves that God exists (Ephesians 2:8-9).

A practical step is to read John 1–3 this week and speak to God directly about your doubts, even if you are unsure He hears. If you are willing, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What has led you to ask whether God is imaginary?

question: What is a mandala in Hinduism?
answer:
A mandala in Hinduism is a sacred diagram, usually circular and symmetrical, used to represent the cosmos, a deity, or consecrated space, and to focus ritual or meditation.

The Sanskrit word *mandala* means “circle,” and can also mean a district or an assembly. In Hindu practice, especially in temple design and in tantric ritual, a mandala maps a sacred order: the center is the most holy point, and the surrounding geometry marks ordered realms around it. Priests and devotees may draw, visualize, or walk these patterns in worship, initiation, or meditation. A well-known architectural form is the *Vastu Purusha Mandala*, a ritual grid used in planning temples and sometimes homes. A mandala is related to, but not identical with, a *yantra*, which is usually a more linear geometric diagram linked to a particular deity.

The same word is also used in an older Indian political sense, the “circle of kings,” describing neighboring states arranged around a central ruler. That is a different use from the ritual diagram.

Christians do not use mandalas as a means of worship or spiritual formation. Where a mandala directs honor, visualization, or devotion to other gods, Scripture calls that idolatry and reserves worship for the one true God alone (Exodus 20:3–5; Isaiah 42:8). Art and geometry are not themselves sinful, but they must not become objects or channels of devotion. Believers are called to worship the Father through Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit, by the Word and prayer, not by sacred diagrams (John 4:23–24; John 14:6).

question: Who is the angel Moroni?
answer:
Moroni is not an angel named in the Bible. He is a figure in the teaching of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, presented as a resurrected ancient prophet who appeared to Joseph Smith and pointed him to golden plates later published as the Book of Mormon.

In that tradition, Moroni is the son of Mormon and the last writer of those plates, and a statue often identified as Moroni stands on many Latter-day Saint temples. Many people meet his name through missionaries or that temple figure, and the story can feel compelling if someone longs for a restored ancient record or further revelation beyond the Bible. Latter-day Saints sincerely profess faith in Jesus and honor the Bible, yet they also receive the Book of Mormon and later revelations as scripture.

Christians who receive the Bible as the inspired, inerrant, and sufficient Word of God do not receive Moroni as a messenger from heaven. The Bible teaches that God has spoken finally in His Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). The apostles warned that even an angel from heaven must be rejected if he preaches a gospel contrary to the one already delivered (Galatians 1:6-9). That gospel is justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:1-4; Romans 3:23-26). Scripture also warns that Satan can disguise himself as an angel of light, so every spirit and message must be tested by the Word already given (2 Corinthians 11:14; 1 John 4:1; Jude 1:3).

This is not a minor difference among Christians. Historic Christianity confesses one God in three persons, Christ’s finished saving work, and Scripture alone as the final written authority. Adding another revelation that changes the account of God or of salvation is a different message, not the faith once for all delivered to the saints.

If you are weighing this, read the Gospel of John and Galatians slowly, asking what they say about who Jesus is and how a sinner is made right with God. Pray directly to God for light through His Word, and sit with a pastor who will open the Scriptures with you. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life (John 14:6; Acts 4:12).

What led you to ask about Moroni?

question: Is God a moral monster?
answer:
Many people ask this after reading Old Testament accounts of the flood, the conquest of Canaan, or other severe judgments, or after hearing critics call the God of the Bible cruel and bloodthirsty. Those passages can sound shocking if they are read only through modern moral feelings, and that discomfort deserves a serious answer.

The Bible teaches that God is not a moral monster. He is holy, good, just, patient, and merciful, and He is the standard of what is right rather than a defendant in our court. Abraham appealed to this when he asked whether the Judge of all the earth would not do what is right (Genesis 18:25). Christians believe our moral instincts, real as they feel, are not the final measure, because every person has sinned and falls short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23).

God's wrath is His settled opposition to evil, not petty rage. He revealed Himself as compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in love and faithfulness, while also refusing to leave the guilty unpunished (Exodus 34:6-7). Judgment on the Canaanites came after centuries of patience, in response to entrenched wickedness that included child sacrifice (Genesis 15:16). It was not ethnic hatred. When Israel later practiced the same evils, God judged His own people by invasion and exile. Those hard texts display justice, often long delayed, not a deity who delights in cruelty.

The clearest revelation of God's character is Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man. He taught that anyone who has seen Him has seen the Father (John 14:9). In His life He showed compassion to the outcast and truth to the proud. At the cross, justice and mercy met in penal substitution: Christ, who knew no sin, bore the penalty sinners deserve, so that God could be both just and the One who justifies those who have faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25-26; 2 Corinthians 5:21). He died, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. That is not the work of a moral monster. It is the costly love of a holy God.

If God's justice weighs on you, do not walk away from Him. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life (John 3:16; Romans 10:9).

This week, read the Gospel of John and bring one specific hard passage to God in honest prayer, asking Him to show you the Father as Jesus reveals Him. A pastor in a local church can also walk through the text with you.

What passage or accusation against God feels most pressing to you?

question: What are the main arguments against limited atonement?
answer:
The main arguments against limited atonement are that Scripture speaks of Christ dying for all and for the world, that a sincere gospel offer to every person seems to require that he died for all who are invited, and that some texts appear to include even people who perish among those he bought.

The best argument for particular redemption, the main opposing view, is that the cross does not merely make salvation possible but actually accomplishes it, so that everyone for whom Christ died will certainly be saved.

I hold particular redemption as one faithful option within historic Christianity, not as the only orthodox position, because the New Testament presents the cross as effective penal substitution for a definite people, his sheep and his church, rather than a merely potential atonement (John 10:11; John 10:15; Ephesians 5:25; Matthew 1:21). Brothers and sisters who affirm unlimited atonement offer a serious reading of passages such as 1 John 2:2 and 1 Timothy 2:5–6, understanding Christ’s death as sufficient for every sinner and sincerely offered to all, while efficient only for those who believe, and many godly Christians have held that view. This is a secondary matter that should not break fellowship. This week, read John 10 and 1 John 2 side by side and ask a trusted pastor or elder to walk through them with you, letting the finished work of Christ be your comfort rather than the debate itself.

question: Christmas Story — Day 5 — Did Jesus, the Messiah, come to save the Jews only?
answer:
No. Jesus, the Messiah, was born King of the Jews, and He came to save people from every nation who turn to Him in faith.

The Christmas story already says so. Angels announce a Savior, Christ the Lord, born in the city of David (Luke 2:10–11). When Simeon holds the child, he praises God for a salvation “prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel” (Luke 2:30–32). Magi from the east, outsiders to Israel, bow and worship Him (Matthew 2:1–2; Matthew 2:11). The infant in the manger is Israel’s promised Messiah and the world’s only Savior (John 14:6; Acts 4:12).

In His earthly ministry Jesus went first to Israel. He said, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). That describes the order of His mission, not a locked door. In that same chapter He honors the faith of a Canaanite woman and heals her daughter (Matthew 15:21–28). Samaritans who heard Him confessed, “this man truly is the Savior of the world” (John 4:42). Paul explains the pattern: Christ became a servant to the Jewish people to confirm the promises to the patriarchs, “so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy” (Romans 15:8–9). The blessing pledged to Abraham was always meant to reach all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:3; Galatians 3:8).

The Gospel is not a Jewish treasure that Gentiles may only admire, nor a Gentile faith that leaves Israel behind. It is “the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). God has not rejected His people (Romans 11:1). Jew and Gentile alike have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and both are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:22–24). That justification is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, not by ancestry or effort (Ephesians 2:8–9). On the cross, by penal substitution, Jesus bore the penalty our sins deserved. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily, so that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16; 1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The risen Lord then sent His people to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:18–20).

This week, read Luke 2:25–32 and Romans 3:22–24 slowly. Then speak to the Lord about one person near you whose background differs from yours, and ask Him for courage to tell them that this crucified and risen Savior came for them too.

If you have wondered whether His mercy reaches you, it does. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What part of this promise feels most surprising, or most needed, for you right now?

question: How does prayer work?
answer:
Prayer works as real communion with the living God, not as a formula that forces His hand. Through Jesus Christ, the Father welcomes His people to speak with Him, and He hears and answers according to His holy wisdom.

Jesus taught His disciples to pray, "Our Father in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). That nearness is a gift of grace, not a wage earned by eloquent words. Scripture says there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Christ lived without sin, died in the place of sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. On that ground, those who trust Him may approach the throne of grace with confidence (Hebrews 4:16). This is mediation: we come to the Father through the Son.

The Holy Spirit helps us in this. When we do not know how to pray, the Spirit Himself intercedes for us (Romans 8:26), and Christ also lives to intercede for His people (Hebrews 7:25). Prayer is dependence, not a performance.

To ask "in Jesus' name" (John 14:13) means to come on the merit of Christ and in line with His will, not to treat His name as a password. If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us (1 John 5:14). God already knows our needs before we speak (Matthew 6:8). Prayer does not inform Him. It is worship, confession, thanksgiving, and petition, and it is one of the means by which He carries out His good purposes. He may answer yes, no, or wait. A refusal can be fatherly mercy, as when Paul pleaded for his thorn to be removed and was given sufficient grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Selfish motives can also keep us from receiving what we ask (James 4:3).

Two things often hinder prayer: pride, and cherishing sin. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), and the psalmist knew that treasuring iniquity in the heart would mean the Lord would not listen (Psalm 66:18). Confession is simply coming back into the light.

This week, set aside a few quiet minutes each morning and let the Lord's Prayer shape your own words (Matthew 6:9–13). Praise God for who He is, name a specific sin and turn from it, thank Him for one concrete mercy, and ask for what you and others truly need, willing for His will to be done. Speak to Him yourself. He invites you to come directly, and His peace guards the hearts of those who bring their requests to Him (Philippians 4:6–7).

If you do not yet know Christ, the open door into this communion is to repent and trust in Jesus alone, who died and rose for you.

What is one burden you would like to bring before Him?

question: Where was God on September 11th?
answer:
That question usually comes from a real wound. On September 11th, 2001, wicked men murdered thousands of people made in God's image, and the grief and anger of that morning have not simply faded. If you are asking because it still feels unbearable, or because it made you doubt whether God is good, you are not the first to cry out that way. Job, Habakkuk, and the psalmists did too.

You may be thinking that a loving and powerful God would have stopped those planes, so He was either absent, weak, or uncaring. Some conclude He is not there at all, or that religion itself is the problem because the attackers claimed God's name. Those objections are serious. Scripture does not ask you to pretend the evil was small.

The Bible teaches that God was not somewhere else that morning. No one can flee from His presence (Psalm 139:7-10). He is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), and He is a refuge and strength, an ever-present help in trouble (Psalm 46:1). He was with the dying, with those who ran into the fire to save strangers, and with families who waited in vain. Presence is not approval. God is holy. He tempts no one, and He is not the author of sin (James 1:13). The men who did this committed murder, and they bear guilt before Him. His wrath against sin is real, and He will judge the living and the dead in righteousness (Acts 17:31).

Jesus also warned us not to treat every disaster as proof that the victims were worse sinners than everyone else. When people told Him about a massacre, and about a tower that fell and killed people, He said those who died were not more guilty than the rest. Then He said that unless you repent, you will all likewise perish (Luke 13:1-5). So that day does not license us to sneer at the dead. It exposes how dark human sin is, and it calls every one of us to repentance.

God is also sovereign. He was not surprised or overthrown. People freely choose evil and will answer for it, and nothing slips outside the Lord's knowledge and purpose. He can work good through what He never calls good (Genesis 50:20; Romans 8:28). That is not a line to toss at a widow. It is a promise that evil does not get the throne.

If you want to see where God stands when the innocent suffer, look at Jesus Christ. He is truly God and truly man. He entered our world, wept at a grave (John 11:35), and was Himself killed by unjust men. On the cross He bore the penalty sinners deserve. That is penal substitution: the innocent stood in the place of the guilty, so forgiveness could be offered without God ignoring evil. He was buried, and on the third day He rose bodily. For those who belong to Him, not even death can separate them from His love (Romans 8:38-39). One day He will wipe away every tear, and death will be no more (Revelation 21:4).

We are all sinners, separated from a holy God, and outrage at other people's crimes does not erase our own need of a Savior. Christ died for sinners and rose again. Salvation is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Him alone, not by our works. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

If this question is personal, take it to God in your own words. Read Psalm 13 or Psalm 46 slowly, and tell Him the grief or anger you actually feel. If you can, talk with a pastor who will sit with you in it rather than rush past it.

What is weighing on you most as you ask this, the people who were lost, a struggle to trust God, or something else?

question: Is Jesus Calling a good book? Are there any doctrinal problems with Jesus Calling?
answer:
Jesus Calling is not a sound devotional, and I would not commend it. Its central problem is that it puts Sarah Young’s own impressions into the mouth of Jesus, which undermines the sufficiency of Scripture.

In the introduction, Young describes longing for something more personal than the Bible and then writing what she believed Jesus was saying to her, in the first person, as if Christ Himself authored each entry. That is a serious category mistake. “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16-17). God has spoken finally in His Son, and the apostolic Scriptures are the Spirit-inspired witness to Him (Hebrews 1:1-2; John 20:31). We are not waiting for a second canon of fresh sentences from Jesus.

A believer may know the Spirit’s comfort, warning, or help while praying and reading. That is not the same as publishing a book in which every page functions as, “Jesus said this.” Impressions must be tested by the Word. They are never the Word (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1).
