What did die was the human nature of the Son. In the hypostatic union, Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. He was crucified, buried, and raised bodily on the third day. He is "the Living One," who was dead and is alive forever (Revelation 1:18). His death does not mean God failed. His resurrection means death has been defeated (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

If "God is dead" names a feeling that heaven is silent, that ache is real, but it does not change who God is. We are the ones who have turned away. Sin separates us from the holy God, and we cannot close that gap by our own effort. Christ died in our place and rose so sinners might be forgiven and brought to the living God. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What prompted the question for you, a philosopher's claim, a season of silence, or something else?

question: Why does God allow evil?
answer:
This question is heavy, and it is right to ask it. You may wonder how a God who is both all-powerful and perfectly good could permit cruelty, loss, and pain, or you may feel that any explanation sounds thin beside real suffering.

The Bible teaches that God is holy, good, and sovereign, and that He is not the author of evil. He cannot be tempted by evil, and He tempts no one (James 1:13). Evil entered human history when Adam and Eve rebelled against God's good command, and sin, death, and corruption spread to all people through that fall (Genesis 3:1-19; Romans 5:12). Sin is not a small defect. It is rebellion that separates us from a holy God and fills the world with real harm.

God permits evil without approving it, and He remains Lord over it. Joseph could tell the brothers who sold him that they meant evil, yet God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). Peter preached that Jesus was delivered up by God's set plan, and that lawless men were still guilty for crucifying Him (Acts 2:23). For those who love God and are called according to His purpose, He works all things together for good (Romans 8:28). He has not given us every reason (Deuteronomy 29:29). Job suffered terribly and never received a full explanation, yet he met a God worthy of trust.

Some Christians explain evil mainly as the misuse of human freedom, wanting to protect real love and real responsibility. That concern matters. Scripture's stronger emphasis is that God sovereignly governs all things, including the existence of evil, while remaining perfectly holy and never the author of sin, and that He permits evil so His justice and His mercy toward sinners might be displayed (Romans 9:22-23).

The clearest answer God has given is not a formula but His Son. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, entered this broken world, lived without sin, and died on the cross as a substitute, bearing the penalty our sins deserve. That is penal substitution. He was buried, and He rose bodily on the third day, defeating sin and death (Romans 5:8; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4). He will return to judge the living and the dead, and He will make all things new, wiping away every tear (Revelation 21:1-4).

We are sinners who cannot save ourselves. If this question has left you angry, grieving, or unsure whether God can be trusted, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read Romans 8 slowly, and bring both the question and any personal pain to a pastor or mature believer in a local church. When you pray, speak honestly to God about what troubles you, and ask Him for wisdom, comfort, and a trusting heart, letting Psalm 23 and Hebrews 4:14-16 guide what you say.

What is pressing on you most as you ask this, a particular sorrow, or the question of whether God is still good?

question: Why does God allow the innocent to suffer?
answer:
This question usually comes from a real wound, and the sight of pain that looks undeserved can make God's goodness feel hard to trust. Many people conclude that a loving and powerful God would never permit the innocent to suffer, so He must be unkind, weak, or absent. That reaction is understandable when grief is sharp.

Scripture takes the cry seriously, and it also corrects the assumptions underneath it. God is holy, good, and sovereign. No human being stands innocent before Him, for all have sinned and fall short of His glory (Romans 3:23). That does not mean every sorrow is a direct punishment for some hidden personal sin. When the disciples assumed a man's blindness came from his sin or his parents' sin, Jesus refused that explanation and said the works of God would be displayed in him (John 9:1–3). When people pointed to sudden deaths, He warned them not to treat the victims as worse sinners than everyone else, and He called all to repentance (Luke 13:1–5).

Suffering is not part of God's original good creation. It entered through the fall, when humanity rebelled against God, and we now live in a world marked by that rebellion (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12). Creation itself groans under the curse (Romans 8:20–22). People are harmed by their own sin, by the sins of others, by sickness, and by a world that no longer works as it was made to work. God is never the author of evil, and wickedness remains truly wicked. Yet He remains Lord over what He permits. Joseph could tell the brothers who sold him that they intended evil, while God intended good (Genesis 50:20). Even the crucifixion was carried out by sinful men, and still it unfolded according to God's set purpose (Acts 2:23).

We are not always given the specific reason for a particular sorrow. Job was upright, and he still suffered. God did not hand him a full explanation of the contest behind his pain. He gave Job Himself. The secret things belong to the Lord (Deuteronomy 29:29). Faith rests on God's character when the details are withheld.

The clearest answer is not a formula but a Person. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. He alone lived without sin, and He, the truly innocent one, suffered willingly. On the cross He bore the penalty sinners deserve. That is penal substitution, the righteous given for the unrighteous (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 3:18). He was buried, and He rose bodily on the third day. Death did not have the last word. He can sympathize with weakness, and those who draw near to Him find mercy and help in time of need (Hebrews 4:15–16). For those who belong to Him, present suffering is not worth comparing with the glory to come, and God works all things for the good of conforming them to Christ, not for a painless life (Romans 8:18, 28–29). A day is coming when He will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, and pain will be no more (Revelation 21:4). Until then, His people are called to weep with those who weep, not to cover wounds with thin answers (Romans 12:15).

If a particular sorrow is pressing on you, bring it to God in honest prayer this week. Pray through Psalm 13 or Romans 8, telling Him what you cannot understand and asking Him to steady your trust in Christ. Then sit with a pastor or a mature believer who will not rush you. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working (James 5:16).

You and I need a Savior. Christ died for sinners and rose again. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What is behind this question for you right now, a particular loss, or a longer wrestle with whether God is good?

question: Why won't God heal amputees?
answer:
This question is honest and heavy. Watching permanent loss, and hearing prayers for a new limb go unanswered, can make a person ask whether God is good, whether He hears, or whether He is real at all. Two objections often sit underneath it: first, that a loving and all-powerful God who healed in the Bible ought to restore amputated limbs today, especially because such a miracle could not be explained away; second, that the lack of clear cases means either God does not answer prayer or He does not exist.

The Bible teaches that God is fully able to restore what is missing. Nothing is too difficult for Him (Jeremiah 32:17). Jesus Himself restored a withered hand in an instant, showing both compassion and divine authority (Matthew 12:9-13). Yet Scripture never promises that every sickness or disability will be removed in this present life. Some healings displayed the arrival of God's kingdom and confirmed the message of Christ and the apostles (John 20:30-31; Hebrews 2:3-4). Even in those days, faithful people remained unhealed. Paul begged the Lord three times to remove his thorn in the flesh, and received this answer instead: "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:8-9). Trophimus was left sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).

Limb loss, like every other form of bodily decay, belongs to a creation that has been subjected to frustration because of human sin (Romans 8:20-22; Romans 5:12). Christians believe the deepest problem is not the missing limb but our separation from a holy God. Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, entered that brokenness. He lived without sin, died on the cross in penal substitution for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, defeating sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; 1 Peter 2:24). All who repent and trust in Him alone are forgiven, justified by grace through faith, and promised a future in which their bodies will be raised imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). In the new creation God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death, mourning, crying, or pain (Revelation 21:4). Until that day, His love is not measured by whether a limb grows back, but by the cross, where He gave His Son for us (Romans 5:8).

If this question has left you angry, sad, or unsure, I invite you to turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and the living hope of a body and a world made new.

A concrete step you can take is to read John 9 and 2 Corinthians 12 this week, bringing your questions directly to God in prayer, and to talk them over with a pastor or a mature Christian friend who will listen without rushing you.

What has brought this particular question to your mind?

question: Is Jesus real?
answer:
Yes, Jesus is real. He is the eternal Son of God who became truly human, lived in history, died on the cross, and rose bodily from the dead.

You may wonder whether the accounts of Jesus are later legends rather than reliable history, or how a first-century teacher can still be known and trusted today. Those are fair questions to ask honestly.

The Bible presents Jesus as a real person whose life, death, and resurrection were witnessed and carefully recorded. Luke investigated eyewitness reports so that readers might know the certainty of these things (Luke 1:1-4). John writes so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in his name (John 20:30-31). Paul states that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many, including more than five hundred people at once (1 Corinthians 15:3-8).

Christians believe Jesus is truly God and truly man, one person in two natures (the hypostatic union). He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary (Matthew 1:18-25; Luke 1:26-35). God is holy, and every person has sinned and is separated from him (Romans 3:23; Isaiah 59:2). Jesus lived a sinless life and gave himself as a penal substitutionary sacrifice, bearing the judgment sinners deserve so that we might be reconciled to God (Romans 5:8; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). He was buried and rose again, showing his victory over sin and death, and he is exalted as Lord (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Philippians 2:9-11).

Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A clear next step is to read the Gospel of John this week, asking God to show you who Jesus truly is, and to speak with a pastor at a Bible-teaching local church who can walk with you.

What has led you to ask whether Jesus is real?

question: Did Jesus really exist? Is there any historical evidence of Jesus Christ?
answer:
Yes, Jesus of Nazareth really existed. The historical evidence for his life, public ministry, and crucifixion under Pontius Pilate is strong and comes from both Christian and non-Christian sources in the first and early second centuries.

You may have heard that Jesus is only a later legend, or that nothing outside the Bible supports him, or that the Gospels were written too late to be useful. Those are common and understandable concerns. They do not hold up under the actual sources.

Roman and Jewish writers who had no interest in promoting Christianity still refer to him. The Roman historian Tacitus, writing about AD 116, notes that Christus was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius. The Jewish historian Josephus, near the end of the first century, refers to Jesus and also to James, “the brother of Jesus who was called Christ.” Pliny the Younger, a Roman governor around AD 112, describes Christians worshiping Christ as God. Later hostile Jewish tradition likewise assumes Jesus was a real teacher who was put to death. These are not friendly witnesses inventing a founder.

The New Testament writings are early and specific. Paul, writing in the 50s AD, passes on a tradition he had received about Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection appearances, and he personally knew eyewitnesses such as Peter and James the Lord’s brother (1 Corinthians 15:3-8; Galatians 1:18-19). Luke states that he carefully investigated everything from those who were eyewitnesses from the beginning so that the reader might know the certainty of what was taught (Luke 1:1-4). The Gospels were composed within living memory of the events. Historians across a wide range of beliefs, including many who reject Christian faith, generally agree that Jesus was a Jewish teacher baptized by John and crucified under Pilate. What divides people is not whether he lived, but who he is.

The Bible presents this same Jesus as truly God and truly man. The eternal Son took on human nature through miraculous conception by the Holy Spirit and was born of the Virgin Mary (the incarnation). He lived without sin, died on the cross as a substitute bearing the penalty sinners deserve (penal substitution), was buried, and rose bodily on the third day, demonstrating victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 1:4). He is the only mediator between God and people (John 14:6; 1 Timothy 2:5).

All have sinned and fall short of the glory of the holy God, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 3:23; Romans 6:23). No good works can remove that guilt. God, rich in mercy, gave his Son so that whoever believes in him would not perish but have eternal life (John 3:16). People are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9).

If you recognize your need, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly this week, noting what Jesus says about himself, and to speak honestly to God about your questions rather than keeping them at a distance.

What part of the historical evidence, or of Jesus’ own claims, would you like to examine more closely?

question: What is the Skeptics' Annotated Bible?
answer:
The Skeptics' Annotated Bible is a website and book by Steve Wells that reprints the King James Version with critical notes meant to flag supposed contradictions, absurdities, injustices, cruelty, and moral failures in Scripture. Its aim is to argue that the Bible is not a trustworthy or divinely given book. It is popular polemic, not a careful academic commentary, though it does include a smaller set of notes marking passages the author regards as good.

Christians confess something very different. Scripture presents itself as God-breathed, useful for teaching, conviction, correction, and training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16-17), and its human authors "spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit" (2 Peter 1:21). That claim is what the church has called inspiration, and with it historic Christianity has held the Bible's inerrancy: in all that it affirms, Scripture tells the truth.

Many of the notes isolate a verse, attach a sharp heading, and treat tension between passages as proof of error. Often the difficulty shrinks once you ask about genre, who is speaking, the historical setting, and how the rest of Scripture, especially the New Testament, reads the passage. Some texts are genuinely hard. Violence in Judges, severe laws, and psalms that call for judgment deserve patient study, not a slogan. Difficulty is not the same thing as falsehood. Jesus himself treated Scripture as the word of God that "cannot be broken" (John 10:35; Matthew 5:17-18).

If you are reading it, do not let a marginal heading do your thinking for you. Read the whole passage in a clear translation such as the Berean Standard Bible, and bring stubborn questions to a pastor or a mature believer who will open the text with you. If one note is weighing on you, tell me the reference and we can look at it in context.

question: Is the Bible a fairy tale?
answer:
Many wonder if the Bible is a fairy tale because it speaks of miracles, a virgin birth, and resurrection from the dead, events that can seem impossible, or because it comes from an ancient world very different from our own. Some also notice surface similarities to other old stories.

The Bible is not a fairy tale. Christians believe it is the inspired and inerrant Word of God, the true record of God's words and acts in real history. The Bible teaches that all Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16). Prophecy never had its origin in the human will, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21).

Luke investigated everything carefully from the beginning so that readers might know the certainty of what they had been taught (Luke 1:3-4). Paul treats Christ's death, burial, and resurrection as historical events of first importance, and he says that if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, 17). These claims are not presented as imaginative tales. They call for repentance and faith because they reveal what God has actually done.

At the heart of Scripture is this good news: all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), yet while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8). Jesus, truly God and truly man, bore the penalty for sin on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day. Whoever believes in Him has eternal life (John 3:16). Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9).

I invite you to turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A practical next step is to read the Gospel of John over the coming days, asking God to help you weigh whether these things are true, then talk through what you find with a pastor or a mature Christian friend.

What questions or concerns about the Bible are weighing on you right now?

question: Is the Bible mind control?
answer:
Many people raise this concern because religious authority has sometimes been abused to silence questions, or because the Bible’s claims about sin, judgment, and exclusive truth can feel coercive rather than freeing. Others simply assume that any text calling for allegiance over personal autonomy must be a form of psychological manipulation.

The Bible is not mind control. Christians believe it is God’s inspired and inerrant Word, special revelation given so that people may know the truth about God and be set free, not dominated (John 8:31-32). It calls us to love God with all our mind and to examine its claims carefully, as the Bereans did when they searched the Scriptures daily to test what they heard (Matthew 22:37; Acts 17:11).

Real mind control depends on deception, isolation, and overriding a person’s will. Scripture does the opposite. It tells us plainly that we are sinners separated from a holy God, that Jesus Christ (truly God and truly man) died on the cross as our substitute and rose bodily from the dead, and that forgiveness comes by grace alone through faith alone in Him, not by surrendering our minds to human controllers (Ephesians 2:8-9; Romans 10:9-10). The change it describes is the renewing of the mind by the Holy Spirit, a willing response to God’s mercy (Romans 12:2).

If painful experiences with controlling religious people lie behind your question, that grief is real, and it does not match the gentle yoke Jesus offers (Matthew 11:28-30). A concrete next step is to read the Gospel of John slowly, watching how Jesus engages skeptics, and to bring your hardest questions to the text itself, ideally with a pastor who welcomes honest inquiry.

If you see your own need for forgiveness, turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for the free gift of new life. What has led you to ask whether the Bible is mind control? I would like to understand your concern more clearly.

question: Does the Bible contain errors, contradictions, or discrepancies?
answer:
No, the Bible does not contain errors, contradictions, or discrepancies. It is the inspired, inerrant, and infallible Word of God, fully trustworthy in all that it affirms.

Scripture itself declares this. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 teaches that all Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness. Proverbs 30:5 states that every word of God is flawless, Jesus affirmed that Scripture cannot be broken (John 10:35), and Psalm 119:160 says the sum of God’s word is truth.

Many readers meet details that seem difficult to reconcile at first, such as varying emphases among the Gospel accounts or differing numbers in parallel Old Testament narratives. These arise from ancient compositional practices that highlight purpose and perspective alongside fact, or from minor copying differences in later manuscripts that leave the original message intact. Patient attention to literary context, historical setting, and the unity of the whole canon shows harmony rather than genuine contradiction. This is the doctrine of inerrancy: when all the facts are known, the Bible in its original writings never affirms what is false.

If a particular passage still weighs on you, ask God directly for wisdom as James 1:5 invites, and bring the question to a pastor or elder in a church that receives Scripture as God’s perfect Word. Careful reading in that setting often turns apparent difficulty into deeper confidence in the Lord’s sure revelation.

question: What is Christian apologetics?
answer:
Christian apologetics is the reasoned defense of the Christian faith, a clear and humble answer for the hope believers have in Christ. The word comes from the Greek apologia, meaning a defense or reasoned response, and it names the work of showing that the Gospel is true, coherent, and worthy of trust.

Scripture commands this posture. Peter says believers must always be prepared to give a defense to anyone who asks, and to do so with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Jude urges the church to contend earnestly for the faith once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 1:3). In Acts, Paul reasons from the Scriptures and speaks with philosophers in Athens, not to win a contest, but to proclaim the risen Christ (Acts 17:2-3; Acts 17:22-31).

Apologetics is not a substitute for saving faith. Justification is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by the cleverness of an argument. A sound defense removes obstacles, answers honest questions, and clears the way for the good news of Christ's death and resurrection to be heard.

This week, choose one question you often hear, such as why Christians trust the Bible or why the resurrection matters, and practice answering it in plain words with a friend or in your church. Then ask the Lord for wisdom and a gentle heart the next time someone raises that question with you.

question: Does the Bible call Christians to defend the faith / argue for the faith?
answer:
Yes. Scripture calls every believer to be ready to defend the faith and to contend for it, not as a specialist hobby but as part of ordinary Christian faithfulness.

The classic text is 1 Peter 3:15: “Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect.” The word translated “defense” is the Greek *apologia*, the root of what Christians have long called apologetics: a reasoned account of why the gospel is true, given when someone asks. Jude presses the same duty more urgently: “contend earnestly for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 1:3). Paul describes his own imprisonment as being “for the defense of the gospel” (Philippians 1:16), and he expects elders to be able both to encourage with sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it (Titus 1:9). In the marketplace and synagogue he “reasoned” from the Scriptures (Acts 17:2, 17). So the Bible does not treat a thoughtful defense of the faith as optional or unspiritual.

At the same time, Scripture draws a clear line between godly defense and sinful quarreling. The Lord’s servant “must not be quarrelsome but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not resentful,” gently instructing opponents in the hope that God will grant them repentance (2 Timothy 2:24–25). We are told to demolish arguments that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5), yet the manner is humility, patience, and respect, never sarcasm, pride, or a love of winning. Truth and love stay together.

A practical next step is simple: this week, write out in a few plain sentences the reason for the hope you have in Christ (his death for sinners and his bodily resurrection), then practice saying it gently to one trusted believer so you are more ready when an unbeliever asks. Pray that God would give you both clarity and a quiet spirit when the moment comes.

question: What are the cosmological arguments for the existence of God?
answer:
Cosmological arguments reason from the existence or beginning of the universe to God as its ultimate cause or necessary ground.  
The best-known forms are the Kalam argument, the argument from contingency, and Thomas Aquinas’s ways from motion and causation.  

The Kalam argument holds that whatever begins to exist has a cause, that the universe began to exist, and therefore that the universe has a cause. That cause must be uncaused, immaterial, and powerful enough to bring space, time, and matter into being, and personal enough to will a finite creation rather than an eternal one.  

The argument from contingency notes that contingent things (realities that might not have existed) require an explanation beyond themselves. Because the universe as a whole is contingent, it depends on a necessary being who exists by His own nature, what theologians call aseity. Aquinas’s First and Second Ways make a similar point from change and efficient causation: chains of movers and causes cannot regress forever, so there must be an Unmoved Mover and a First Cause.  

These lines of thought cohere with Scripture’s witness that God is the eternal Creator who made all things and upholds them (Genesis 1:1; John 1:3; Colossians 1:16-17; Hebrews 1:3). Romans 1:20 teaches that God’s eternal power and divine nature are clearly perceived in what He has made, so that people are without excuse. They do not by themselves deliver the full Christian confession, yet they have helped many see that trust in the Creator is a reasonable response to the world we inhabit.  

If these reasons are stirring questions for you, set aside time this week to read Psalm 19:1-4 and Romans 1:18-25, then bring what you find to a local pastor who can walk with you through both the arguments and the Scriptures.

question: What is the purpose of the church?
answer:
The church exists to glorify God by worshiping Him, building believers up in Christ, and proclaiming the gospel to the world.

God does not save people and then leave them as isolated individuals. He gathers them as the church, the people Christ purchased with His blood and joined to Himself as His body (Ephesians 1:22–23; Acts 20:28). Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her, so that she might be holy (Ephesians 5:25–27). Her purpose is not invented by us. It is given by the Lord who is her head.

That purpose shows itself in three ways.

The church exists to worship God. The Father seeks those who worship Him in spirit and truth (John 4:23–24). From the beginning, believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer (Acts 2:42). Gathered worship is not a performance for our enjoyment. It is the glad offering of ourselves to the God who saved us (Romans 12:1).

The church exists to build up the saints. Christ gives pastors and teachers to equip His people for ministry, until we grow up into maturity in Him (Ephesians 4:11–16). Believers are to stir one another to love and good works, and not neglect meeting together (Hebrews 10:24–25). Through the means of grace, the Word, prayer, fellowship, baptism, and the Lord's Supper, the Spirit carries on progressive sanctification in ordinary church life. A church is faithful to this calling where Christ is preached, the ordinances are observed as He appointed them, and the saints are known and shepherded.

The church exists to bear witness. The risen Christ commands His people to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey all He commanded (Matthew 28:18–20). The church is a people called to proclaim the excellencies of Him who called us out of darkness into His marvelous light (1 Peter 2:9). Even the heavenly powers are meant to see the manifold wisdom of God through the church (Ephesians 3:10).

None of this stands apart from the gospel. The church is the company of sinners justified by grace through faith in Christ, who died for our sins and rose bodily on the third day. Her worship, her love, and her mission all flow from that finished work.

If you belong to Christ, take one concrete step this week. Gather with a local church where the Scriptures are opened and Christ is honored. Pray that God would make that congregation faithful in worship, love, and witness, and ask Him to show you one person to encourage and one person who needs to hear of Jesus.

If you tell me whether you are looking for a church or wanting to serve more faithfully in one, I can speak more directly to your situation.

question: What is the Moral argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The moral argument for the existence of God is the claim that objective moral values and duties are real, and that they are grounded in God's holy character rather than in human opinion.

It is often set out in three steps. First, if God does not exist, then nothing is truly right or wrong in a binding sense. Preferences, customs, and survival instincts may remain, but they cannot create real moral obligation. Second, some things are truly right or wrong. Justice, faithfulness, and kindness are good, and cruelty, treachery, and murder are evil, even when a culture celebrates them. Third, therefore God exists as the source of that moral order.

Scripture gives the deeper reason this holds. God made man and woman in His image, so we are moral creatures by nature (Genesis 1:26-27). Those who never received the law of Moses still show the work of the law written on their hearts, with conscience bearing witness (Romans 2:14-15). Goodness is not a standard floating above God, and it is not whatever He might arbitrarily declare apart from who He is. It reflects His own holy and righteous character (Leviticus 19:2; Psalm 145:17).

Accounts that appeal only to evolution or social agreement can describe how moral feelings arise. They do not explain why an act would remain truly evil even if every person approved of it. The "ought" we cannot escape points beyond us.

That same moral knowledge also exposes our need. We have all fallen short of God's glory. The gospel answers that need: Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose bodily on the third day, and all who repent and trust in Him alone are justified by grace through faith, not by moral effort (Romans 3:23-26; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Ephesians 2:8-9). A practical next step is this. The next time your conscience accuses you, do not silence it or excuse the wrong as mere preference. Confess it to God in prayer, and set your hope on Christ, who bore the penalty your guilt deserves.

Which part would you like to explore further, the reason objective right and wrong cannot be reduced to preference, or how this moral need meets the cross of Christ?

question: What is Ecclesiology?
answer:
Ecclesiology is the branch of Christian theology that studies the church: what it is, why Christ established it, and how He orders its life and mission. The name comes from the Greek word ekklēsia, the term the New Testament uses for the assembly of God’s people.

Scripture presents the church as the body of Christ, with Jesus as its head (Ephesians 1:22–23; Colossians 1:18), and as the household of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth (1 Timothy 3:15). It is the people Christ purchased with His own blood (Acts 20:28), not a mere human association. Jesus promised that He would build His church and that the gates of Hades would not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).

Ecclesiology therefore asks who belongs to the church, how the gospel is displayed in baptism and the Lord’s Supper, how Christ governs His people through His Word and appointed shepherds, and how the church carries out the mission to make disciples. Historic Christianity has recognized a true church where the Word is purely preached, the ordinances are rightly observed, and loving discipline is practiced.

Because Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), do not treat gathering with God’s people as optional. Join a local congregation, sit under the preaching of Scripture, and walk with the saints in worship, fellowship, and service (Acts 2:42; Hebrews 10:24–25).

question: What is the Teleological argument for the existence of God?
answer:
The teleological argument holds that the order, purpose, and apparent design in nature are best explained by an intelligent Designer, God. Its name comes from the Greek word *telos*, meaning end, purpose, or goal.

In classical form, Thomas Aquinas argued that things without intelligence regularly act toward ends, as an arrow is aimed at a target, and that such directedness implies an intelligence that orders them. William Paley later compared the world to a watch found on open ground: parts fitted to a purpose imply a maker, not bare chance. Later forms point to the fine-tuning of physical laws and the coordinated complexity of living things.

Christians receive this as natural theology, fitting general revelation. Scripture teaches that creation displays God’s glory and leaves people without excuse: “The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands” (Psalm 19:1), and Paul says God’s eternal power and divine nature are clearly perceived through what has been made (Romans 1:20). The argument can make a powerful, wise Creator reasonable. It does not by itself name the Trinity, the cross, or the risen Christ. Those come through Scripture’s special revelation.

Critics answer that chance, physical necessity, or natural selection can mimic design. Those replies deserve a fair hearing, and not every scientific detail is settled. Even so, means ordered toward ends still raise the question of why the world is intelligible and life-permitting at all. Secondary causes, where they operate, do not erase the need for the God who establishes and sustains them.

This week, read Psalm 19 and Romans 1:18–23 slowly, then notice one concrete feature of creation, a cell, an eye, or the night sky, and thank God for it rather than stopping at curiosity. If questions remain, study them with a pastor or a mature believer in your local church.

question: What is the difference between the universal and local church?
answer:
The universal church is the whole company of true believers in Jesus Christ across every age and place, and the local church is a particular congregation of professing believers gathered in one location under His Word.

Scripture speaks of the church in both ways. Jesus said, “I will build My church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18), speaking of the one people He is gathering. Paul calls that church Christ’s body and bride, the people He loved and gave Himself for (Ephesians 1:22–23; Ephesians 5:25–27). At the same time, the New Testament addresses real congregations such as “the church of God in Corinth” (1 Corinthians 1:2), directs the appointment of elders in every church (Acts 14:23), and places discipline in the hands of the local assembly (Matthew 18:15–17). The letters in Revelation 2–3 likewise speak to distinct churches in distinct cities.

Christians have long described the universal church as invisible in the sense that only the Lord knows with certainty who is truly united to Christ by faith, and the local church as visible because it is a recognizable gathering. That language does not invent two churches. It names one body of Christ that becomes concrete wherever believers assemble to hear Scripture, share baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and watch over one another.

Historic Christians have not all drawn the lines in the same place. A charitable account of the Roman Catholic view is that visible unity under a continuing apostolic office best guards the church from division and error. The New Testament, however, presents Christ alone as Head of the church (Colossians 1:18) and shows many local churches, each accountable to Him and to Scripture, while all true believers are one body by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). Faithful Protestants, including the Reformed Baptist tradition, therefore receive both realities: the universal church is the spiritual communion of all the elect, and Christ has given the work of worship, care, and discipline to particular churches.

This is not a merely technical distinction. Love for the universal church is shown by commitment to a local one. If you belong to Christ, look for a congregation that preaches the gospel, baptizes believers, shares the Lord’s Supper, and is led by qualified elders, and give yourself to those people in worship and accountability. This week, pray for wisdom about where the Lord would have you serve, and take one clear step toward that commitment, whether by attending, speaking with an elder, or renewing your care for the believers already beside you.

question: Why should I believe in God?
answer:
You may be asking this because the evidence feels thin, or because a good God seems hard to square with the suffering and evil in the world. Those are honest concerns, and they deserve a straight answer rather than a shrug.

Christians believe God has not left Himself without witness. The created world points beyond itself to a powerful and wise Creator, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:20; Psalm 19:1-2). The shared sense that cruelty is truly wrong, not merely inconvenient, points to a holy Lawgiver rather than to blind chance (Romans 2:14-15). Most decisively, God has spoken in Scripture and acted in history through Jesus Christ.

That matters for you personally because God is holy and we are not. All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). Sin separates us from Him, and the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, lived without sin, died on the cross in our place, was buried, and rose bodily on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3-4). That is penal substitution: He bore the judgment sinners deserve so the guilty could be reconciled to God. Salvation is not earned by effort or sincerity. It is justification by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8-9; John 14:6). Anyone who draws near to God must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who seek Him (Hebrews 11:6).

The reason to believe is not that faith will make life easy, but that God is real, He has revealed Himself, and He offers forgiveness and new life in His Son. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

A wise next step is to read the Gospel of John over the next several days and to speak honestly to God about what you read. What is the main thing that makes belief in God hard for you right now?

question: How is the church the Body of Christ?
answer:
The church is the Body of Christ because every believer is united to Jesus by faith and joined to every other believer by the Holy Spirit, so that together they form one living organism under His headship.

Scripture does not treat this as a loose comparison. Christ is “head over everything for the church, which is His body” (Ephesians 1:22-23), and He is “the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18). The same Spirit who unites us to Christ also baptizes us into one body, so that “we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (1 Corinthians 12:13; Romans 12:5). This is the doctrine of union with Christ: what is true of the Head is shared, by grace, with the members.

The image holds unity and diversity together. A physical body has many parts with different functions, yet one life; if one member suffers, the whole suffers, and if one is honored, the whole rejoices (1 Corinthians 12:12-27). Christ nourishes and cherishes this body, and it grows only as each part works properly in love (Ephesians 4:15-16; Ephesians 5:29-30). The body exists because Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her (Ephesians 5:25), so the church’s life flows from His atoning death and bodily resurrection, not from human effort or organizational skill.

In practice, this means a Christian cannot thrive in isolation. Your local church is where this body becomes visible through the Word, the ordinances, and mutual service. Ask a pastor or elder this week how your particular gifts can strengthen others, and commit to gathering regularly so that you both receive and give the life Christ supplies.

question: What are some undeniable examples of divine intervention?
answer:
The Scriptures record many direct acts of divine intervention as real historical events, chief among them God’s parting of the Red Sea to deliver Israel and, supremely, His raising of Jesus Christ bodily from the dead.

People often object that miracles cannot be undeniable because they seem to break natural laws, or because the reports come from committed believers rather than detached observers. Those concerns are understandable in a culture that treats the universe as a closed system. Yet the Bible presents these interventions as public acts of the sovereign Creator, who is free to act within the world He made. In Exodus 14:21-28 the Lord drives the sea back so Israel crosses on dry ground, then returns the waters upon the pursuing army, displaying His power to save. Centuries later God intervenes decisively by raising Jesus on the third day. Paul records that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised, and appeared to Cephas, to the Twelve, and to more than five hundred brothers at once, most still living when he wrote (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). This bodily resurrection confirms that Jesus is truly God and truly man, and that His death was a penal substitution sufficient to reconcile sinners to God.

A concrete next step is to read Exodus 14 alongside the final chapters of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John this week, noting the specific details each writer includes, and to ask God directly for wisdom to see His hand clearly. What particular claim or experience has prompted you to look for examples like these?

question: What is the institutional church?
answer:
The institutional church is the visible, organized expression of Christ’s people in local congregations, with recognized leaders, membership, the ordinances, and gathered practices of worship and discipline.

It is distinguished from the invisible or universal church, the full company of all who truly belong to Christ by faith, whom God alone knows completely (2 Timothy 2:19). Scripture holds both together: the Lord builds His church as His redeemed people (Matthew 16:18), and the apostles plant particular assemblies, appointing elders to shepherd them in doctrine and life (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5; 1 Timothy 3:1-13). The Greek word ekklesia simply means an assembly called together, and the New Testament applies it both to the whole people of God and to these ordered local gatherings.

Some Christians stress a more informal, “organic” fellowship because they fear that structures can grow rigid, worldly, or abusive. That concern is understandable where churches have drifted from Scripture. At the same time, the apostolic pattern includes recognizable order so the body is built up in truth and love, everything done decently and in order (Ephesians 4:11-16; 1 Corinthians 14:40; Hebrews 10:24-25). Historic Protestant convictions, including the Reformed Baptist understanding of elder-led congregational churches, treat these local institutions as Christ’s gift and a means of grace, not a rival to the Spirit’s work.

A concrete step is to commit yourself to a local church that preaches the gospel clearly, baptizes believers, shares the Lord’s Supper, and practices loving accountability, so you can both give and receive encouragement in Christ.

question: Is Christianity true?
answer:
Yes, Christianity is true. It is the revelation of the one holy God in the historical person and work of Jesus Christ, not a mere philosophy or cultural story.

You may wonder how claims from long ago can be trusted today, or how one faith can be exclusively true when so many voices compete. Those questions are understandable, and many have wrestled with them honestly. The Bible teaches that every person has sinned and falls short of God’s glory, standing guilty and separated from Him (Romans 3:23). Jesus Christ, truly God and truly man, entered our world, lived a sinless life, and died on the cross as the penal substitute for sinners. He was buried and rose bodily on the third day, securing victory over sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). That resurrection, attested by eyewitnesses who then faced persecution rather than recant, anchors the claim in history. If Christ is risen, His words stand, and the Christian faith is true.

Salvation is by grace alone through faith alone in Christ alone, not by moral effort or religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–9). Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

What question or objection feels most weighty to you as you consider this?

question: What is ministry?
answer:
Ministry is Christian service: the work of loving God by serving His people and making Christ known, so that the church is built up and God is glorified.

In the New Testament, the word often translated “ministry” is diakonia, which simply means service. This calling belongs to every believer as part of the priesthood of all believers. 1 Peter 2:9 describes God’s people as “a royal priesthood,” and 1 Peter 4:10 urges each one to use whatever gift he has received to serve others as a faithful steward of God’s grace. At the same time, Christ gives pastors and teachers “to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ.” Ephesians 4:11–12. The heart of that service is the ministry of reconciliation: God making His appeal through His people that sinners be reconciled to Him through Christ, who died and rose again. 2 Corinthians 5:18–20.

A concrete next step is to ask your pastor or an elder this week where your gifts can strengthen your local church, whether in prayer, hospitality, teaching, mercy, or another ordinary act of service.

question: What is classical apologetics?
answer:
Classical apologetics is a method of defending the Christian faith that first uses reason and evidence to show that God exists, and then shows that this God has revealed Himself in Jesus Christ.

It usually moves in two steps. First comes natural theology: arguments from cause, design, morality, and the contingency of the world, drawn from general revelation. Second come the historical evidences of special revelation, especially the reliability of the apostolic witness and the bodily resurrection of Jesus. Voices in this stream include Thomas Aquinas and, more recently, men such as R.C. Sproul. It does not treat reason as a savior. It holds that creation can show that God is, while only the gospel shows how sinners are reconciled to Him.

Scripture gives room for both steps. Paul says God’s eternal power and divine nature are clearly perceived in what He has made, so that people are without excuse (Romans 1:20). In Athens he reasoned from the Creator to the risen Christ and the coming judgment (Acts 17:24–31). Peter tells believers to be ready to give a defense for their hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15).

Faithful Christians do not all share one method. Some begin with the authority of Scripture and argue that only the Christian worldview makes sense of reason and morality. That difference is about approach, not about the gospel. What they share is that Christ died for sinners, was buried, and rose bodily, and that sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone in Him.

A simple way to practice this is to answer a friend’s “Why do you believe?” with one clear pointer from creation to a Creator, then open the Gospel of John together and let them meet the risen Lord in the text.

question: Why does God allow birth defects?
answer:
This question often comes from real hurt, and if birth defects have touched your life or someone you love, that sorrow is worth naming before any explanation. Two objections are especially common: that a truly good and powerful God would never permit this, and that it is unjust when it falls on children who have done nothing wrong. Both feelings recognize something important. This is not the world as it ought to be.

Scripture teaches that God created all things very good (Genesis 1:31), yet human sin brought death, corruption, and futility into the whole creation (Genesis 3:17-19; Romans 5:12; Romans 8:20-22). Birth defects belong to that brokenness. They are not God's original design, and they are not usually a direct punishment for one person's particular sin. When the disciples assumed a man born blind must be paying for guilt, Jesus answered, "Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him" (John 9:3). God is not the author of evil (James 1:13). He remains sovereign and good, and He can weave even grievous things into His wise purposes for those who love Him (Romans 8:28), though many specific reasons stay hidden this side of eternity (Deuteronomy 29:29).

Every person, including those with profound disabilities, bears the image of God and has unshakable dignity (Genesis 1:27; Psalm 139:13-16). The church is called to honor and include them as full members of the body, not as problems to be managed (1 Corinthians 12:22-26).

The deepest hope is not a formula but Jesus Christ. He entered this suffering world, lived without sin, and died on the cross in our place, bearing the penalty our sins deserved. That is penal substitution. He was buried, rose bodily, and will make all things new, when there will be no more pain, defect, or tears (Revelation 21:4; 1 Corinthians 15:42-57). We are all sinners who need that Savior. Turn from sin and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and new life.

This week, read John 9 and Romans 8 slowly, and share this burden with a pastor or mature believer in a local church who can walk with you in prayer and care (Galatians 6:2). Speak to God directly about the fear or anger this raises. He already knows it.

Is there a particular situation behind your question that you would like to talk through in light of Scripture?

question: Why doesn't God heal everyone?
answer:
God does not heal everyone in this life, even though He is able, because He sovereignly accomplishes wise purposes we do not always see, and because complete healing belongs to the resurrection age still ahead. This question usually rises from a heavy heart, when prayers have been offered and the sickness remains.

Many wonder whether unanswered requests mean God is distant, unloving, or that faith was simply too weak. Scripture does not teach that. God heals when He wills. Jesus restored many as signs that the kingdom had drawn near (Matthew 8:16-17; John 9:1-3), and believers are told to pray for the sick (James 5:14-16). Yet the same Scriptures show He does not heal all. Paul carried a persistent thorn and heard the Lord say, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20) and counseled Timothy to use ordinary care for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). Healing is a mercy, not a debt God owes our faith.

We still live in a world groaning under the curse that followed sin (Romans 8:20-23). Sickness belongs to that brokenness. The God who is holy, sovereign, and good works even through affliction for the good of those who love Him and for His own glory (Romans 8:28). His ways are higher than ours (Isaiah 55:8-9), and He does not always disclose the particular reason (Deuteronomy 29:29). Sometimes weakness displays that His grace is enough. Sometimes trial refines faith (1 Peter 1:6-7). None of this cancels His compassion.

The surest window into His heart is Jesus Christ. He entered our suffering, bore our sins in His substitutionary death on the cross, was buried, and rose bodily, conquering sin and death (1 Corinthians 15:3-4; Romans 5:8). Present healing, when given, is a foretaste. The promise of no more pain, tears, or death awaits those who are His, when He makes all things new (Revelation 21:4; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44).

Bring your grief and your request honestly to the Lord. Ask for healing according to His will, and ask for strength to trust Him if the answer is wait or no. If you belong to a local church, ask the elders to pray with you (James 5:14), and rest in promises such as Psalm 23 and 2 Corinthians 12:9-10. If you have never trusted Christ, or if this pain has shaken you, turn from sin and self-reliance and trust in Jesus Christ alone, who died and rose for you, for forgiveness and eternal life.

What situation has made this question especially heavy for you right now?

question: What does it mean that the Bible is self-authenticating?
answer:
The Bible is self-authenticating because it bears witness to its own divine origin, so that its authority as the Word of God does not finally depend on the approval of any church, council, or scholar.

This is the self-attesting character of Scripture, made personal and persuasive by the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit. The Scriptures display a heavenly subject, a living power to search the heart, and a unified witness to God’s glory and man’s salvation, and the Spirit enables believers to recognize that voice as God’s own (Psalm 19:7-11; Hebrews 4:12; 2 Timothy 3:16-17). The Thessalonians received the apostolic message not as the word of men but as what it truly is, the word of God at work in those who believe (1 Thessalonians 2:13), and Jesus taught that His sheep hear His voice and follow Him (John 10:27).

In practice, this means you may open the Bible as the final rule for faith and life, testing every teaching, tradition, and personal impression by what God has spoken there, and asking the Spirit to confirm and apply His Word to your conscience.
